speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my view, many schemes in the Budget are a continuation of the strategic agenda laid out in previous years or jigsaw pieces of a longer term plan fleshed out elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: COVID-19, however, has accelerated some plans and thrown a spanner in the works of others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, digitalisation has found new impetus while the Changi Air Hub plans have been put on hold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Following Minister Lawrence Wong's comments at the recent Singapore Perspectives conference, I was looking forward to indications in the Budget of a reset of the Government's agenda in the areas Minister Wong highlighted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of particular interest to me was Minister Wong's mention of a reset in our social compact to tackle inequality to keep society fluid and mobile.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His discussion of a permanent shift towards stronger social safety nets, a commitment towards a greener Singapore, and a reset to strengthen solidarity in our people also made for a refreshing vision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the Budget did not sound like a reboot of ideas and the direction of yesteryear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To some extent, this is understandable as the country remains in the throes of a pandemic, along with talk of a K-shape recovery.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With many uncertainties on the horizon, an instinct to stay the course and to adopt a nimble posture is not unexpected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on three main areas that address specific aspects of Deputy Prime Minister Heng's Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, on emerging stronger with skilled workers and innovative businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng said in his speech that a balance has to be struck with the focus on the complementarity of local and foreign manpower, alongside the stepping up of industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The CTP funds the salary and training for both foreign and local trainers and local trainees by between 30% and 90%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the scheme was launched in 2017, about five years ago, MOM positioned it as a scheme that would strengthen the Singaporean Core of workers and enhance how local and foreign workers would complement rather than compete with each other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Considering that there are quite a few sectors in which there is a real need for talent transfer to Singaporeans, such as IT where a common complaint from employers is the lack of Singaporean talent, I would have expected to see many more Singaporean workers improving their prospects through the CTP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, with the establishment of industry clusters through the Industry Transformation Roadmaps, identifying improved jobs and skills prospects across 23 sectors as a key ITM deliverable, one would have imagined more CTP applications, with more than a fair share qualifying for the highest tiers of the grant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The example that the Minister highlighted in his Budget speech of a technical officer at SP Services learning new skills in network support for the rollout of advanced electricity meters, suggests there is significant downstream reach of the CTP, regardless of industry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What skillsets have been transferred to Singaporean workers by sector, and which industry clusters is the Government earmarking for greater talent transfer through the CTP?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also seek greater clarity on the Minister's commitment of $24 billion to enable firms and workers to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister detail what this multi-year allocation entails?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, in view of the headline numbers, how does the Government plan to release information and account for the tangible and intangible outcomes of the money spent on these multi-year initiatives?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After the seventh weekly report, the reports stopped becoming weekly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead, periodic reports were released, focusing on the available opportunities in each sector on a monthly basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public sector opportunities are significantly funded by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As such, the job situation reports need to be buttressed with significantly more detail.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, while the reports state the number of successful placements and chart the salary range for major job roles in specific sectors, there is little detail on the salary levels and the age ranges of those who have been successfully placed, particularly those in long-term jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Shortly before COVID-19 struck, the tripartite partners acknowledged the importance of strengthening support for older workers through a range of measures, including progressively raising the CPF contribution of older workers in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public should be given greater insight into the effectiveness of multibillion-dollar initiatives that aim to improve job opportunities and outcomes for all our workers, but especially our mature workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is in light of the fact that a significant number of workers will also enter their 50s by 2030.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The effectiveness of Government measures should be readily determinable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without such scrutiny, a perception may crystallise of large sums of money being deployed to address an issue for which effectiveness is hard to establish.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This follows on from my call in September for more and not less information from the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I encourage Singaporeans to look out for the reports of the Estimates Committee, a standing parliamentary Select Committee, one of whose roles is to examine the Government's Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government were to consider a more aggressive reset in this regard, the establishment of an independent parliamentary Budget Office may well be another complementary addition towards the judicious use and accountability of taxpayer dollars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it would be in step with Deputy Prime Minister Heng's call for fiscal prudence and add an important element of public accountability and transparency in light of the massive drawdown of reserves to fight COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I spoke of what a living wage ought to be for those who man our critical infrastructure and keep the country's heart beating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like many Singaporeans, a high point for me in Deputy Prime Minister Heng's Budget was the announcement of a hike in the salaries of our nurses and healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A crisis usually leaves lasting lessons about those you can count on and who are always there in one's most challenging times.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would urge the Government to look at reviewing the wages of other front-liners and, particularly, essential workers like our waste disposal workers, transport workers and many others who proved indispensable in this COVID-19 fight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second part of my speech covers the Minister's comments on strengthening the nation's social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Government schemes, ranging from SIRS to various COVID-19 grants, have certainly helped stave off hardship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are, nonetheless, serious concerns about the state of these families and households today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Beyond Social Services is a community organisation which reaches out to 64 rental blocks where more than 10,000 individuals live.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This represents a fairly large and determinative sample of Singapore’s rental housing population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The organisation released a report earlier this month and some findings read starkly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have to clarify that these numbers do not take into account the not insignificant COVID-19 financial assistance pumped in by the Government over the course of the last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That said, according to Deputy Prime Minister Heng in his comments to CNA over the weekend, the inequality situation measured by the Gini coefficient has actually improved over the past year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It, therefore, appears that there is divergence in what the absolute data on inequality reveals and what the lived experience is on the ground in our rental flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government will look into this more deeply, to assess how COVID-19 has affected our low-income households and their employment prospects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This cannot be objectionable and, indeed, given the revenue and scale of operations of some of these heartland shops, incentives to purchase the goods and services they offer would indeed be helpful for shop owners and proprietors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This use of CDC vouchers follows the intervention of the former Workers' Party Member of Parliament for Hougang, Mr Png Eng Huat, who, in his Unity Budget speech last year, queried whether the Grocery vouchers announced in the Unity Budget ought to have been allowed for use in neighbourhood mom-and-pop shops as well, rather than the bigger supermarket chains only.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a follow-up, may I ask the Minister to clarify the current scheme?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister’s statement does not say whether the CDC vouchers can also be used at Giant, Sheng Siong, Prime or NTUC FairPrice, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that the current scheme be focused solely on heartland shops and hawkers, of which there is a broad range, such as local provision shops, Chinese sinsehs or traditional Chinese medicine providers, fruit sellers, barbers, hairdressers and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a risk that if this is not done, the bulk of the vouchers would be spent at supermarkets, like NTUC FairPrice, and bypass the heartland shops.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the major supermarket chains are involved, the scheme could effectively mirror a cash top-up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My final query is with regard to the implementing agency of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The CDCs have come into the spotlight after the last General Elections because many Singaporeans are of the view that the salaries of Mayors are outrageous, principally because they are not perceived to commensurate with a Mayor's roles and functions today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other Singaporeans of the view that the CDCs' functions can be carried out by other existing entities or by Ministries and Statutory Boards, including other organisations under the People's Association, particularly since the social footprint of each CDC is uneven and can differ greatly compared to another.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, others simply do not know what the CDCs do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Effectively, the need for full-time Mayors continues to be widely questioned and it would appear that there is scope for a serious review of the necessity of having full-time Mayors today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the CDC voucher specifically, it is widely known that the representatives of Merchants Associations are commonly represented on the Citizens' Consultative Committees, and there is one for each ward or constituency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would follow that these local bodies like CCCs are even more closely connected to the ground than the five CDCs, rendering the CDCs' role in the voucher scheme potentially superfluous.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the third and final area of my speech, Sir, I refer to where the Minister spoke of building a sustainable home for all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The science and environment correspondent of The Straits Times, in an article of 11 February 2021, observed that upon closer inspection, the Government's Singapore Green Plan 2030 was, and I quote, "more or less a compilation of existing sustainability initiatives" unquote, even as she acknowledged there were some new targets worth watching.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government's move towards a future where electric vehicles replace internal combustion vehicles is arguably one central plank of the Green Plan, nudging Singaporeans to select more environmentally friendly vehicles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there is much frustration and unhappiness on the ground with respect to the timing of the hike in petrol prices to support this goal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The main reason for this is that the infrastructure and registration regime for a greater adoption of EVs has not even been rolled out in great numbers, but yet, the petrol duty hike was implemented immediately on Budget Day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even the road tax rebate is slated only to kick in six months later.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, many Singaporeans are asking why do petrol duties go up immediately all at one go?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Did the Deputy Prime Minister consider a phased and gradual increase of the petrol duties in step with the availability of EVs as a realistic consumer choice and a rise in their numbers on the roads in the years to come?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, given the economic environment and uncertainty, there is a real prospect of a simultaneous cost of living pain-point, with the Government committed to raise the GST well before the General Elections, and in my estimation at least, over a window that traverses 2022 to 2023, after the petrol duty subsidies ends.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For middle class Singaporeans or the "sandwiched class" who do not qualify for the full extent of GST subsidies in particular, and for whom EVs may not be a compelling option in the short term, the next few years may well precipitate added cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are expected to offset the petrol duty hike of up to a year for taxis and motorcycles, and around seven to eight months for cars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, I urge the Government to review this Budget announcement and implement a more thoughtfully phased in increase of the petrol duty in proportion to the actual growth of EV usage on the roads.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The rebates proposed can be given out in a similarly phased manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a move will be fairer for road users, as compared to the Minister's current plan, which is also implicitly contingent on a large number of EV charging points becoming available in 12 months' time when the subsidies end.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In comparison, the Government's roadmap for 60,000 EV points has 2030 as its end date.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With regard to the rise in petrol duty, I have two additional questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, is the Government prepared to proactively look into the prospects of profiteering by unscrupulous businesses that seem to ride on this increase in petrol duties?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, there remain many uncertainties about the pace and unevenness of an economic recovery across sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a hub economy, until the aviation sector reopens in a significant way and the movement of people across our borders returns to some semblance of normalcy, a sense that the Singapore growth engine is not able to fire on all cylinders is likely to persist given our reliance on the global economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the opportunity for a reset in some aspects is clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With a tighter fiscal environment in the years ahead, as stressed by the Deputy Prime Minister Heng over many speeches, closer scrutiny of expenditure should not be seen one dimensionally as political one-upmanship, but as an administrative necessity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned last year that he addressed the House nine times over five Budgets and two Ministerial Statements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Well, we certainly needed that many doses of reassurances, support and interventions last year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Otherwise, the fall-out and impact from the pandemic would have been even more devastating for our businesses and for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have put to good use the war chest and firepower that we have built up over the decades, and by any measures, we have achieved the intended outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Interim assessment by MOF and MAS determined that the relief measures from the five Budgets have helped avert a deeper economic recession.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Households were also supported with various packages such as CSP, SIRS, CSG and TRF.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These measures help mitigate the inequality during this difficult year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans felt safe and our fatality rate from COVID-19 is still among the lowest in the world at 29.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many schemes are still on-going and their effects are still working through the system and economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But I can say that the strong and decisive interventions by the Government have made a significant difference in saving lives and livelihoods during this "crisis of a generation".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Into 2021, the battle against the onslaught of COVID-19 continues on both the healthcare and non-healthcare fronts; and continues to require considerable amounts of financial resources to safeguard Singaporeans, families and businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the key highlights for Budget 2021 are the $11 billion COVID-19 Resilience Package and the $900 million Household Support Package, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are necessary measures to tackle the on-going crisis and to strengthen social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Overall, Budget 2021 remains highly expansionary with total expenditures projected to grow by 8.8% from FY2020, which is a high-spending year, and 35% above pre-COVID-19 FY2019 spending level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the big-ticket items continue to be the COVID-19 related costs such as vaccination which amounts to $1 billion; testing, clinical management and tracing, which is likely to cost another $3.1 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Compared to the broad-based approach in last year's Budget, in this year's Budget we heard a lot more words like "targeted" and "differentiated".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And with many businesses resuming either most or all of their activities, it is timely and prudent to start tapering down the assistances so as to manage down the overall costs of the support packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the overall expenditure remains very high and notably higher than the revenue projected for the year; and hence, we would still have to count on our past reserves to fund the gap, albeit a much smaller amount this time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the Deputy Prime Minister said, we must never stop thinking of the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is indeed the hallmark of our nation's success and what makes us an exceptional nation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have ambitious plans to continually expand and strengthen our overall infrastructure and to build a sustainable home for all; under the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In charting our next future trajectory, we not only talk about the "whats" but the "hows" as well, including critically, how we can fund those investments at a time where our fiscal space is at the most constrained period.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister announced the Government's decision to issue infrastructural bonds, the SINGA Bonds, to fund lumpy capital expenditure items such as rail lines and infrastructures to protect against rising sea levels and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If these items are funded under the Annual Budget cycles, which is on a cash flow basis, it will put significant strains on our other Budget to other allocations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As these long-term infrastructures benefit current and future generations of Singaporeans, it is more equitable to distribute these fiscal responsibilities across generations, by way of a longer term financing structure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I support to partly fund these massive outlays through long-term borrowings via the SINGA Bonds; and especially during this current low interest rates environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The $90 billion borrowing cap is a necessary safeguard in addition to the scrutiny from the President's office and Parliament.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, having a wider variety of high-quality assets like SINGA and green bonds also helps develop our capital markets and facilitate better liquidity management among our financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even as we tackle the immediate challenges, we must not lose sight of our medium to longer term economic imperatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: COVID-19, while it has caused havoc to the global economy and our lives, has also triggered structural shifts on many fronts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Coupled with the accelerated technological changes and geopolitical shifts, the current forces at play actually open up interesting opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister highlighted a few areas, such as the how we can plug ourselves into the critical parts of the reconfigured global supply chain network – an interesting area to be in – rapid digitalisations where we can build new frontiers in digital connectivity or making available of capital tools to co-fund transformation and help our companies transform and grow, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore needs to quickly adapt to the changed world and to be in the position to seize these opportunities and to build new competitive edges, and to do it among the early phrases of these new structural shifts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the Deputy Prime Minister has elaborated, we need to decisively build three enablers: firstly, a vibrant business eco-system; secondly, make available a wide range of capital sources; and, thirdly, to develop our own future-ready human capital and talents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I will speak further on these enablers during the COS debate for MOF, MTI and MOM.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But just to state, these are exciting developments that will give our economy that pivotal lift and we should be among the early movers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But for now, for this speech, I would focus on the funding for these $24 billion investments to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister indicated in his speech that he expects the economy to recover, and the revenue projected will be able to support these expenditures for the investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, he also caveats that this is subject to the global health situation and economic outlook.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And to use the Deputy Prime Minister’s words, there is still a "wide cone of uncertainty".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is also the potential downside risk to our revenues with regard to the on-going discussion to revise international tax rules under the Base Erosion Profit Shifting or BEPS 2.0 project.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding, the Deputy Prime Minister said that even if the economic and fiscal conditions turn out to be worse than expected, we must still press on to invest in these areas and to ride on the opportunities presented by these structural changes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I agree with the Deputy Prime Minister that we must move now.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Delaying or deferring these investments until our finances are back in good shape is an option but that will mean passing on the opportunities to provide an early boost to our capabilities and to stay ahead of the curve, while other economies are still grappling and coping with the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The question then is should we draw on past reserves to support these additional spending?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned in his speech that he has briefed the President on the potential draw in the next few years, if we are unable to generate sufficient revenue to pay for these investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have already drawn on our reserves in the last two Financial Years in a row and we should only consider this as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Reserves are our emergency backstop and we need to hold or grow the base amount to ensure a growing, if not a steady, NIRC.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Each time when we draw on our past reserves, it also means divesting a part of our financial investments and, hence, we will lose out on the returns from these investments over the long term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a prudent safeguard, we should also still set strict caps on such borrowings and it should be still subjected to the approval and the consent of the President and to Parliament's scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that no finance minister likes to talk about tax increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Well, similarly, Members of Parliament would not like to debate such issues as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We all like to talk about how much we can spend, where we can spend.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have debated intensely the justifications during the last three Annual Budget Statement debates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I agreed with the Government’s fiscal principle that recurrent expenditure should be funded by recurrent revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And, in particular, in the healthcare spending, we must ensure that it is adequately and sustainably funded to give Singaporeans the peace of mind that their long-term healthcare needs will be well taken care of and with certainty.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Last year, I asked the Deputy Prime Minister as to who pays the biggest share of the GST based on past collections.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: He shared that foreigners residing in Singapore, tourists and the top 20% of resident households account for 60% of the net GST borne by all households and individuals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We do want to collect more taxes from the top 20% households and the foreigners.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The unique critical feature of our GST system is that it comes stapled with a series of permanent GST offsets to mitigate the impact to our low- and middle income households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, the top income groups and foreigners contribute the main bulk of the GST while the low- to middle income group pay no or lower GST on a net basis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The majority of households will receive offsets to cover at least five years’ worth of increases, while the lower income Singaporeans will receive even much more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, those living in 1- to 3-room HDB flats will receive offsets worth about 10 years of increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   What I am most concerned about in this Budget is whether the GST hike would affect the cost of living of the lower and middle income Singaporeans and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the past few years, Government spending has indeed been growing rapidly especially in the area of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On one hand, we need to constantly plan and provide more healthcare amenities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, we need to ensure that there are sufficient, sustainable and diversified tax revenue to cope with these rising cost.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to balance this expenditure and income, so that Singaporeans, especially older Singaporeans, will have a greater peace of mind and a sense of reassurance in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is what a responsible Government should do, and we do not want the Government to cut spending on healthcare and social welfare because of fiscal imbalances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Personally, I still hope that the Government will continue to build more clinics, hospitals and nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I also hope that the Government will give Singaporeans more subsidies in healthcare, housing, education and transport, all of which require financial resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: All these expenses and subsidies need to have financial resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, most households will receive rebates to offset the impact of a GST hike over the next five years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Lower income households will receive more rebates to offset the additional GST cost over the next 10 years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This Budget also sets in place the framework to fund our long-term infrastructure with long-term borrowings to avoid situations of extremely large outlays in each Budget year and to achieve better inter-generation equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a shift from our past approaches where we tend to cash fund all our expenditure with current budget allocations or using accumulated surpluses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to move with times in the way we manage our Government finances, just like how we have evolved the NIRC framework about a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it is important to remain steadfast to the values of prudence and discipline, and to ensure that we operate on a balanced budget basis and also to jealously safeguard our reserves so as to continue growing it for our future generations; just like how the past generations have saved it for us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is always a good position to be there, to be in a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, let us keep thinking long term, continue to build new frontiers of growth opportunities, continue to strengthen our position of strength and to emerge stronger together from this crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The impact of COVID-19 on our economy might well have resulted in a deep and enduring recession, had it not been for the series of fiscal and monetary policy moves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Besides intervention in public health management, the wide-ranging support from the Job Support Scheme (JSS), the loan moratorium to rental waivers helped sustain jobs and businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Going forward, support will be targeted and loan repayments will need to resume.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we taper down the support schemes that have kept many businesses afloat, we should be prepared for the increased risk of business closures and lay-offs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For this Budget, I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat that switching our focus to transformation and growth will give us the best chance to secure the best opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have to prepare ourselves for a post-COVID-19 world that is completely and forever changed, and secure a prominent role for ourselves in it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To sustain relief in the immediate term, Singapore will draw on the reserves for the second year running.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government has not borrowed since the 80s for infrastructure development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Using debt to fund large, long-term infrastructure will go some way to reduce the pressure of raising revenue and not crowd out important long-term infrastructure investment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the prevailing low interest rates coupled with Singapore’s AAA credit rating, the cost of borrowing should not place undue burden on future generations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is good debt and there is bad debt.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must guard against going down the slippery slope of other countries where the burden of debt repayment becomes a major component of the country's finances.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It would not be sustainable to depend on borrowings to fund our recurrent spending needs, such as healthcare and education.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is in this spirit that we would not borrow money to pay for daily consumption.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Would this limit be adjusted as GDP grows?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How vulnerable would we be if interest rates move up?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What is the expected repayment burden on future generations?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The trend of getting the wealthy to contribute more is gaining traction globally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In fact, the wealthy themselves are stepping forward to give back in significant ways, with philanthropy featuring as a key agenda in their wealth planning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Argentina imposed a one-time levy on millionaires in December.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Several other countries, including the UK, has brought wealth tax into the spotlight with an independent Wealth Tax Commission issuing their final report.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Proposals to make wealth levies easier to administer, for example, include targeting a smaller group of extremely wealthy people, relying on advances in financial transparency and technology.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From the various reports, a one-off wealth tax may seem economically efficient, structured as a one-off exceptional response to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: UK had introduced one-off "windfall taxes", including the 1997 windfall tax on privatised utilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The construct of pandemic Excess Profit Tax, to extract higher revenues from businesses that are able to exploit the effects of the pandemic, has also surfaced.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered major shifts in the global economic landscape.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore needs to urgently bolster its attractiveness as a regional and global hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I welcome the slew of capital tools to co-fund transformation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The growing awareness of climate change is spurring businesses and countries the world over to embrace sustainability as an urgent agenda.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Singapore Green Plan 2030 is therefore well-timed to galvanise a national movement, not only to achieve sustainable development, but also to build "exportable" capabilities such as sustainable urban solutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our Green agenda holds much promise for our future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The issuance of green bonds will provide a substantial capital base for sustainable developments, not only in Singapore but also throughout the region.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore is well-positioned to serve as a living lab and testbed for emerging green technologies as well as a hub to foster collaboration and co-creation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critical that in our drive for sustainability, we fully leverage this opportunity to groom a new generation of green local firms, support them to build their green capabilities and position them to capture emerging opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I expect that this will continue to sustain green shoots of recovery in the labour market and create opportunities for this year's cohort of graduates entering the workforce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, whilst unemployment is kept at bay, we must be vigilant against underemployment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The mismatch of skillsets, which occur when workers take any available jobs just to stay employed, will cause their deep and hard-earned skills to "atrophy" over time, along with their motivation and commitment to their work.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This issue is particularly pertinent amongst older PMETs whose careers are being disrupted, resulting in a reservoir of unused skills and experience.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must develop new models to support mid-career professionals transition to new careers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These should include some form of financial support that enables them to take time off to study and build new expertise, so that they can meet the financial commitments they incur at their particular stage of life.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has also provided employers an opportunity to relook at their reliance on foreign labour.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many employers have told me about their frustrations with foreign workers' demands for pay increases and their changing work attitudes resulting from a scarcity of workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Together with costs resulting from workers' Stay-Home Notices and safe management measures, employers' foreign labour costs have escalated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By contrast, I have seen many businesses thrive by cultivating a strong local team who are committed to the long-term success of their employers' business, often by focusing on the right compensation and nurturing a healthy work culture.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think Sheng Siong must have received many job applications since announcing their bonus.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, there is no better time to build a strong Singaporean Core for long-term sustainability.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: COVID-19 has shown the world yet again what Singapore is capable of.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In a fragmented world where trust is sorely lacking, Singapore has much to offer as a "safe, trustworthy node", as Deputy Prime Minister said.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The strategic value of our reserves has never been clearer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The world is on fire with COVID-19, with protectionism, with disruption to supply chains, trade networks, businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Climate change threatens all of us and is changing how companies and entire economies operate and compete.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Climate change is also accelerating the onset of new pandemics that will threaten the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And all these is a serious and grave challenge for small countries like Singapore, small, open economies which need to connect to the world to survive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, even as we improve on existing capabilities, getting better at what we already know how to do, we need to go further.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to move boldly, to do things which we have not done before, learning how to do things which we could not do before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Tony Blair, former UK Prime Minister, last month published an article on pandemic response in a COVID-19 world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One quote stood out: "The question which should be asked of policymakers in government is not what is possible, but what is necessary." "Not what is possible, but what is necessary."  Our existing work is important.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Builds our capabilities, maintains what we already know is possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But beyond our report card, we must ask ourselves: "In a world on fire, on a burning platform, what is necessary for Singapore to continue to survive and thrive tomorrow?" Sir, let me outline three areas.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are more but I will speak on three topics today – vaccine development, R&D and commercialisation, and public sector recruitment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen what happens amidst this pandemic, when countries are burning with fear, when the world and countries grow desperate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen what happens with PPE nationalism, where protective equipment is hoarded.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the early days of COVID, there were some countries that blocked the exports of PPE, even if the purchase contracts had already been signed, even if the bill had already been paid.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, we see vaccine nationalism – certain countries placing export controls on vaccines for COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, imagine when "Disease X" hits the world, it will be worse than COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: To survive such a future, Singapore has to go beyond asking what is possible today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to ask ourselves and search ourselves to ask what is necessary for a more dangerous tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can, of course, continue collaborating with other centres of excellence around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we should have the development and manufacturing capability onshore, in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even before "Disease X", there is the chance that COVID-19 will mutate into new strains which no current vaccines can protect against.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, there are very real reasons to build this capability, in Singapore, onshore, today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know what is possible, we know what is in the report card.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we can and must do even better, to meet the challenge of what is necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember an overseas meeting with the Chief Scientist of the national innovation authority from a small country with a reputation for innovating against the odds and punching above its weight.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What this Chief Scientist from another country told me – he left a deep impression – he said that his national innovation agency wants to fund projects which the market would not normally fund.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That the most interesting projects are not the ones where the outcome is guaranteed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That the potential breakthroughs are where half the experts say it cannot be done, while half the experts think it can.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must also be unafraid to try new things, to break new paths, blaze new trails.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the USA, there is an agency called DARPA.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It brings together experts from industry and academia to work on urgent challenging problems facing the real world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Although the US military was the original customer for DARPA, its innovations have created and shaped many multi-billion dollar industries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Innovations such as today's Internet, carbon composites used in advanced manufacturing, the GPS navigation system that our smartphones use to operate, telepresence surgery which allows robotic surgery to take place.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even Siri, the iPhone personal assistant, is a spin-off from a DARPA artificial intelligence project.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the UK, there is a research foundation called the Wellcome Trust.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They have funded a new R&D agency called Wellcome Leap – a DARPA model for human health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of their mission statements for projects are inspiring.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, "What if we could develop a universal cancer vaccine to stimulate an immune response at the earliest sign of abnormal cells?"; "What if we could grow fully functional replacement human organs in a lab" – to help people with kidney failure, on dialysis?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But if a reputable research organisation like the Wellcome Trust is imagining this, aspiring to this, making the leap – it tells us something.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Martin Wolf, Chief Economics Commentator at the Financial Times, recently wrote an op-ed, "Why once successful countries like the UK get left behind".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He sees a need for greater government support for innovation in the advanced economies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are lessons for us to avoid being left behind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mariana Mazzucato, an economist, who has advised the European Commission, talks of mission-oriented research, bold missions which mobilise the public sector, private sector and academia.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, again, "Not just what is possible, but what is necessary." Not just the report card on what we have achieved today, but what is necessary for Singapore tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My third point on public sector talent recruitment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: During the past year, I met a number of Clementi residents who had returned from overseas jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I had coffee in one of our Clementi coffee shops with a Clementi resident who used to manage a multi-billion-dollar cash portfolio for a MNC regional office.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: His regional role was relocated because of COVID-19 and he was not keen to uproot his very young family to relocate, especially in a pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He told me about how he was looking at jobs in the public sector, now that he was based back in Singapore for the foreseeable.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And a breadth of experience from all over the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are highly qualified Singaporeans who because of COVID-19, are no longer keen to continue overseas.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have young family, some have ageing parents back in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All the more so amidst a burning platform for Singapore and other small open economies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is the report card of our people, our agencies, our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must also ask ourselves beyond what is possible today what is necessary for tomorrow?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What do we need to do that we cannot yet do?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Socially, we had to learn how to live with the pandemic by changing the ways we interact and socialise.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At workplaces, companies had to pivot their operations and rejig their business models overnight.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the COVID-19 pandemic still raging on in many parts of the world, it is fair to say that we are far from being out of the woods.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recovery is likely to be uneven, with some sectors of the economy perhaps taking longer to recover than others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus glad to learn that the Government has made further commitments to ensure that the hardest hit sectors in our economy will continue to receive the support that they need.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, with a relatively weakened financial position, Government support will have to be more calibrated and targeted and Budget expenditures be geared towards helping Singapore thrive in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we continue to preserve the immediate livelihood of our workers, we need to keep an eye on the gaps that have also appeared and undertake systematic steps to close them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many years after SARS, we were reminded once again during the COVID-19 pandemic about the tremendous sacrifices that our healthcare workers make on their jobs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, as a nation, we owe our healthcare workers, especially our nurses and allied healthcare workers, a deep, deep debt of gratitude.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from enhancing their pay scale, I hope that the Government will also continue to enhance the career prospects for nurses and healthcare professionals, especially those who desire progression.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under MOH’s classification, nurses are classified as "enrolled nurses" and "registered nurses".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Registered nurses are required to attain a tertiary qualification and can specialise in different practice areas.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have a clear career pathway that enables them to eventually become, perhaps, even nurse managers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from salary and career progression, I urge the Government to also consider enhancing the work environment and conditions for nurses as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has traditionally depended heavily on foreign nurses, as we all know, to supplement our pool of local nurses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And it is not for want for trying.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe we have been trying consistently to attract more Singaporeans and PRs into the nursing profession.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe the reasons as to why Singaporeans are generally unwilling to enter the profession, perhaps, go beyond just wages alone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We could consider implementing mandatory leave and even possibly paid holidays as additional benefits for local nurses so that they can take a break from being on the frontline and recharge from time to time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As part of a longer term plan, I would also like to urge the Government to develop a mid-career conversion programme for those who wish to enter the nursing profession.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans were employed as temporary-swabbers or as allied healthcare professionals during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans who, perhaps, have not worked in the healthcare sector or experience what our healthcare professionals and nurses go through now find themselves on the frontline, as it were, and have the experience that would be so critical to enabling them to succeed in this profession.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I hope the Government can consider more options for these mid-career professionals to enter into the nursing and healthcare profession, perhaps, under a train-and-place model or other similar scheme that would enable us to recruit these people into the healthcare sector on a full-time basis.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a topic that will be spoken about in the House and I have received much feedback from my interactions with many Singaporeans on the ground with regard to this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am speaking, of course, about those who need their vehicles to ferry young children, elderly or disabled family members around; and those who need their vehicles for work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As part of the Budget, I do note the Government has acknowledged that taxi and private hire car drivers who have been hit hard by the drop in ridership will continue to receive various forms of financial assistance support till the COVID-19 pandemic eases somewhat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it is part of the measures I spoke about earlier, of the Government targeting specific groups in the industry who needed more support.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At a broader level, the hike in petrol duties could also be accompanied by a series of price increases downstream – that is something that I am also quite concerned about, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, logistics companies could pass on cost increases to retailers and retailers could similarly pass the increase on to consumers; consumers who make online purchases could end up paying more for their delivery if these costs were passed on; school bus drivers might raise their fees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I guess there are many many other examples that could see companies and organisations raising their prices and fees, citing the rise in petrol prices as justification.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I noted that the Government has also mentioned the measures to help households as a whole, manage increased costs of living and to deal with some of the financial challenges that they could face, not just in 2021 but in the future as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are not sure what 2021 will bring, but I am confident that if we stay together, as one people, one Singapore, then we will be able to deal with whatever challenges come our way.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My previous clarifications notwithstanding, I conclude my speech in firm support of the Budget.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The new element added is that of great uncertainty about the length of the adverse economic-health shock that is hitting the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The emphasis in my last sentence is on the words "uncertainty about the length".

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's recession in 1985 was deep and sharp, but its recovery was rapid.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of the shock from the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, the recovery was also rapid.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Budgets could therefore be strongly expansionary in the short term to save jobs and businesses, and thus, fulfil the stabilisation function of the Government.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Once out of the recession, subsequent Budgets could focus on structural transformation of the economy, gearing the economy to expand is productive capacity to create good jobs with good pay for its residents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This fulfils the allocation function of the Government.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, in our current environment – even though the big storm that ravaged our economy and the rest of the world started more than a year ago – there is much uncertainty about when normal economic conditions will return.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The 2% growth rate is the rate at which advanced economies have been able to grow over the 20th century.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: At that rate, you double your standard of living every 35 years.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If the slum is prolonged and becomes a multi-year affair, how does the Government balance between using its fiscal resources to fulfil its stabilisation function on one hand, and allocation function on the other hand?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, in crafting the Budget, we should make optimal use of the best information we currently have.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There are some aspects of the nature of the slum caused by COVID-19 that are now reasonably well understood: a negative supply shock in a contact-intensive and travel-related sector – let us call it the affected sector – produces a negative demand shock which affects the whole economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Massive loss of jobs in the affected sector will be socially costly for several reasons.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As workers, especially low-wage workers, typically phase credit constraints so that they are unable to borrow against future incomes, they and their family members would face severe economic hardship.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With a loss of income, there is also a contraction of demand for all goods, not just goods produced by the affected sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Job retrenchments in the affected sector will also imply that there is a loss of firm-specific capital that workers would have built up over time during their employment with their current employers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: I think Budget 2021 recognises the uneven nature of the COVID-19 shock, quite different from other shocks that tend to be aggregate in nature, affecting many sectors in the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, my second point about what we can recognise as we try to establish good fiscal principles with the dilemma of this shock that I mentioned.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the occurrence of prolonged slums, such as the Great Depression in the 1930s.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the US, it began in 1929, recovery began only in 1933, but it took much of the 1930s for the slum to end.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, the study of today's advanced economies over the whole of 20th century suggest that economies do return to their trend growth path.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Despite a prolonged slump like the Great Depression, nearly a decade in length, the economy resumed to grow at roughly 2% per annum over the 20th century.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is so as to allow a process of creative destruction to enable entrepreneurs with good ideas to launch new businesses, even as other firms exit.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It has been observed by many that onslaught of COVID-19 has led to a rapid adoption of digital technology and more generally of digital transformation that can position Singapore well as it seeks to raise the firm's productivity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Building a common digital platform with other countries will enable start-ups as well as SMEs to sell overseas and enlarge their market.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As new business processes as well as new products and services are created to cater to a COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 world, there will be demand for workers with new skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: I am gratified that Budget 2021 keeps a focus on facilitating structural transformation, even as it meets the short-term needs I mentioned, to enable the economy to return to a strong trend path that will deliver good jobs with good pay over the longer term.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, and my final point, given the uncertainty surrounding the length of the COVID-19 slump, there is a question of fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Would a government that is required to maintain budget balance over its term of government have the required fiscal resources to achieve its stabilisation function in a prolonged slump?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: How do we prevent workers and their dependents, from suffering a sharp drop in consumption when fiscal stimulus is removed because the recession drags on for several years.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is not an easy problem, we have never quite had to encounter this problem, because past recessions were deep and sharp but recovery was rapid, possibly not this one.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, this provides sufficient resources to meet emergency needs arising either from health or economic considerations.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, in general, how do we think about this problem?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Faced with the prospect of being laid off, workers might increase their savings to insure against a drop in consumption, that is self insurance.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To be very clear, this is not something to implement in the midst of the pandemic, but it is an option to be studied when this storm is past.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, having such an insurance scheme enables workers and their dependants to have access to cash to finance consumption when breadwinners lose their jobs for an extended period.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Whether or not to have a national unemployment insurance scheme is not an easy question to answer because it involves trading off the benefits of providing liquidity on one hand and you have to match that against the cost of higher unemployment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It poses a challenge to find a balance between the Government's stabilisation and allocation functions.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the near term, fiscal resources should still be directed to keep businesses afloat and save jobs in the affected sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With attention given in this Budget to short-term needs, but also investing and steepening the trend growth path, while being open to policy ideas, I support this Budget.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many business owners and leaders I have spoken to have shared that, while they are grateful that things are stabilising and improving, and their businesses are somewhat stabilised, what we now need is to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For many individuals, their jobs have been affected in one way or another.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some, while they are employed, many are under-employed and they can and want to do more.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech today, I will focus on three topics: positioning for transformation and change – building resilience and deep capability in the Singapore Core to seize opportunities; number two, something that no one wants to talk about, is rising GST and to fund increased spending; and third, ensuring that no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated the need and momentum for transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to position for transformation and change and the window of opportunity to do so is now.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Relevant grants and support programmes are available from previous Budgets to build skills and support transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The extensions of these programmes announced in Budget 2021 builds on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These programmes help both mid-career workers and fresh graduate get into the industry or stay in the industry as well as prepare them for jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But beyond these grants and Government support, what we now need is an eco-system to drive and step up the momentum to build capability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to identify capabilities required to build the depth of expertise and knowledge for long-term resilience and competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These capabilities include technical, functional and leadership skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This was most likely attributed to the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as we open the economy, we need to pay attention to the conversions to full employment for these attachments and traineeships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Traineeships and attachments provide the platforms for learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Workers need to not only get the opportunity to learn but they need to also get deeper long-term commitment to develop and to build the required expertise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are seeing new employment trends as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: People are moving and changing jobs more frequently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employment models are also evolving with an increasing trend of companies hiring contract workers or freelancers, rather than full-time employees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With this pace of change and business transformation, the development of skills and capability is even more important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With increasing challenges in the workforce, retention and a growing proportion of non-permanent employees in the workforce, it will be increasingly more difficult for employers to develop build skills in their own workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while individuals must continue to own their own development, the scale will not be the same.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, with these trends and the pace of change, how can we continue to transform and build deep skills in the Singapore Core?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have witnessed supply chain disruptions with COVID-19 and the need to rethink our supply chains to strengthen and build resilience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this same analogy, if I could say, applies to that of capability building in our workforce and the Singapore Core.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not realistic for us to be fully self-sufficient and I am not advocating for it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do, however, feel strongly on the need for us to invest in the Singapore Core by identifying and investing in building deep skills in the areas that matter.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enable Singaporeans not only to take on jobs in the emerging growth sectors but more importantly, innovate, lead and thrive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is beyond the current and important work that our education system and our efforts on continual training is doing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If I can be so bold to say this, is that we need to invest in building deep skills and this is a big effort in itself and may require us to consider if there should be a body to synthesise, coordinate and drive this effort.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This requires deliberate effort across the eco-system of companies, workers and the industry sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But data from IMDA does shown that representation of women in this sector is still not as high.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, with the strong trend in digitalisation and the competition for talent, employers must leverage the talent pool of women in STEM or risk missing out on tapping on almost half of the talent pool.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The inaugural Singapore Women in Tech list of Singapore 100 Women in Tech last year, I think is a very good initiative to encourage women to join the workforce to take on tech careers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While Deputy Prime Minister Heng did say that GST will not be increased this year and he did confirm that GST will need to be increased between 2022 and 2025, and this is to finance increased recurrent expenditure especially in the area of healthcare.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng also said that the Government will continue to absorb the GST on publicly subsidised healthcare and education.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And will it be sufficient to fund the increase in healthcare spending?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If not, then is the Government considering other forms of tax to fund increasing healthcare spending?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And if so, I do hope that it would be calibrated and that we would not be implementing similar caps as we saw in Budget 2016 on total tax relief because at that time, I had feedback from many working mothers claiming the Working Mother's Child Relief, who were impacted and had to pay higher taxes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know, if you need to spend more, something has to give, you have to pay it somehow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But it is affecting a big group of middle income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now, let me touch on the point of leaving no one behind.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has and made more evident potential gaps.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digitalisation and the need for and increasing reliance on digital, while not intentional, does increase the risk of alienating some segments of the population and increasing the divide.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He said he had a simple task to do.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He had to get PMD inspected before he would be slapped to the penalty.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He came to see me and he said, "I received an SMS saying I had to go and do an inspection." And he tried to call, could not get through, went down to get his inspection done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He could not get his inspection done because he did not make an appointment and he could only made an appointment online.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, he came to me and said, "Jessica, can you tell me what is an 'e-letter'?" He showed me an SMS and said, "What is an 'e-letter'?" And it really dawned on me that things we take for granted, things that we do daily and we think it is something that is a matter of fact in the digital world – I mean, he is the phone, he is using a smartphone but he did not know what an "e-letter" was.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And then, I said, "Let me try and show you", because he said all the information is inside in this "e-letter".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I realised he is not connected to data.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And then, he did not have his SingPass!

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, basically, what happened was, we set it up and he is now being supported by a Digital Ambassador.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The point I want to make here is that you can see from the story that while my resident was not tech savvy, the gap was not caused by a resistance to getting help, a resistance to use the digital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Rather, it shows that there are many moving parts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it is not just about technology but the changes and how we do things, things that we take for granted and leads to a vicious cycle.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, what this shows, it takes a whole system's approach and change management to bring people along.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must all participate to ensure that while the progress and support are available, each of us need to make sure that we bring everyone along.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has also accelerated the pace of disruptions and impacted jobs and employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: All segments of society have not been spared and the impact on jobs has not been seen only on the lower income or the low-wage workers, but also on the middle and the PMETs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there are support packages in last year's five Budgets to help workers and families, for example, the COVID-19 Support Grant, the Self- Employed Person Income Relief Scheme, GST Vouchers, many in the middle income were not eligible given the criterion of annual value of the homes they live in.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do agree on the need for eligibility criteria for support schemes as funds are finite.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, some of these criteria may be too broad and may miss those that should be supported or result in a delay in the support reaching them, as the exceptions are being reviewed and approved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pace of disruptions or shocks like COVID-19, while individuals may have assets like their home, they do need short-term support to help them tide over.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In some cases, the affected individuals do not own the properties they live in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Last week, after Deputy Prime Minister Heng's Budget 2021 announcement, SBF organised a closed-door dialogue with some trade associations and chambers or TACs and myself.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Participants all expressed gratitude for the strong leadership by the Singapore Government and acknowledged that Budget 2021 is balanced with realism and sensitivity to the on-going crisis, while at the same time, is forward-looking and projects a hopeful and exciting future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Ang, would you like to remove your mask?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I hope I could still have been heard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Participants all expressed gratitude for the strong leadership by the Singapore Government and acknowledged that Budget 2021 is balanced with realism and sensitivity to the on-going crisis, while at the same time is forward looking and projects a hopeful and exciting future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Many understand the prudence in the gradual opening up of travel but have expressed concerns that the continued restrain on the opening up of global borders will have its impact on recovery.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: It is hoped that the Government will continue to calibrate its risk management approach, to gradually ease the COVID-19 restrictions, both on the domestic front as well as allowing for business travel and tourism bubbles without Stay-Home Notice.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: That aside, the Government shifting investments and support in Budget 2021 toward enabling companies to accelerate digitalisation, seize new opportunities of growth in tech, in green and in the region, while continuing to uplift the skills of our workers, is applauded.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The Enterprise Financing Scheme will add the capital boost needed to help our companies spur ahead.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
