text: And, we believe that expert help from CTO-as-a-Service and Digital Leaders will help their digitalisation transformation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Businesses are also excited about the Singapore Green Plan 2030 which serves to give the Whole of Singapore a visionary goalpost to shoot for.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: A key challenge for many of them, however, is availability of manpower.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: They cannot find enough Singapore workers to take up the roles, especially when it comes to expertise and in-demand skills they need to recover and grow.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, what will determine success for Singapore to emerge stronger, is going to be how we execute and the speed of execution.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: COVID-19 has given the impetus for many of our companies to "pivot" to new business models, for example, e-commerce, to accelerate technology adoption and digitalisation, and to look for new revenue-generating activities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The time for companies and industries to push on with their transformation efforts, taking advantage of Government support and industry collaboration, is now.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: COVID-19 hit a global reset and I think it is an opportunity for us – workers, industry and Government – to review, rethink and re-imagine the way we execute.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For today's speech, I would like to start the dialogue on three issues: skills for transformation; fair practice in the workplace; and organisations to re-think their stewardship responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In product development, for example, there is no substitute for experience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Experienced developers are able to start contributing quicker to the company's product development, and be ahead for advancement to take on higher level roles in project leadership and IT solution architecture.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: If our Singapore graduates do not start with those jobs, they cannot possibly take on those higher value jobs especially in tech.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Perhaps the SGUnited Traineeship top-ups can help make the difference, and over time, we will have more Singaporean Core experienced developers who can move on to higher value jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Singapore has the aspiration to build more digital product companies and we need to have a deeper "Skills for Transformation" strategy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We need all hands on deck – companies, Government and workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Point two, I urge the business community to continue to work with education institutions to ensure a ready pipeline of labour with the right skill sets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I believe there is opportunity for more collaboration within and across sectors to uplift the labour eco-system, as having a larger pool of skilled labour would benefit businesses in the long run.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Nett, we are calling for companies to train more than what they need, or more than the number of skills that they need, and make it available to the rest of the industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And as for in-demand skills like tech and digital, there are more jobs than there are Singaporeans with the skills and experience, and desire to take on those jobs at the salaries that companies currently are paying.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For example, the construction and IT industries face challenges with hiring local talents with the right skill sets, while the nightlife, hospitality and F&B sectors struggle to fill critical "rank-and-file" roles with local employees.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Foreign talents with the skills we need do complement our Singaporean talents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I believe that our Singapore workers are confident, determined and ready to work hard, and our companies should invest in them and give them the opportunities from when they graduate through their life-long professional learning journey.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The Government is trying to help with the programmes and policies but in the meantime, some companies with contracts need the workers to fulfil their commitments, while other companies need to be sure that they can get the workers if they bid for the work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The business community hopes that the Government could fine-tune manpower policies to strike a better balance with regard to hiring of local and foreign talent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Perhaps the Government can consider a differentiated intervention for different businesses and industries and skills, to support them to recover, and for them to recover, they need the manpower.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: My personal opinion having worked in the tech industry for more than 37 years, and having been a resident foreign talent myself – I lived three years in Tokyo and eight years in Beijing – we are in a global war for talent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We should attract the best foreign brains and talents to come to Singapore, and they add value by way of skills, experience, expertise and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The foreign skills also complement us in numbers where we do not have enough.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We must remember that we are not competing for jobs amongst ourselves.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Every day, we are coming out for jobs, competing for jobs, not just when the jobs are here in Singapore but globally.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Over the years, many Singaporean workers believe that they have not been given the fair chance for jobs that are created here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I think that is a good first step.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I believe it is time for a renewed dialogue amongst stakeholders – Singapore workers, businesses and the Government – to re-think the social compact and in so doing, create positive momentum for win-win-win.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I was an IBMer for 33 years, and am very blessed to be a reasonably successful product of Singapore’s MNC or FDI strategy along with the likes of Mr Koh Boon Hwee who started with HP, Mr Russell Tham with Applied Materials, Mr Lee Kok Choy with Micron, Ms Teo Lay Lim with Accenture, our Deputy Speaker Jessica Tan with IBM and then Microsoft, DBS’ Ms Tan Su Shan with Citi and Morgan, and scores more.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I hope my friends do not mind me calling them out.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We were all trained and developed by foreign bosses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In those days, our foreign bosses were probably evaluated – and their promotions depended on it – based on how many Singaporean leaders they have developed, not only for Singapore but for the region and for the world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Skills transfer and knowledge transfer as well as leadership development are some of the key values in successful partnerships between MNCs and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: My next point: organisations to re-think their stewardship responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: During COVID-19, Singapore Business Federation Foundation together with seven TACs launched the Industry-Led Compassion Fund.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I was so heartened to see the response by the businesses, who probably themselves are not having an easy time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: They came together to set up the fund to support the employees in their own industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: This is very heartwarming to see – companies coming forward to help themselves and the employees who are affected in their own industries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: During these trying times, there are also vulnerable groups trying to enter and re-enter our workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The best way we can help them is actually the dignity of work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Of course, we hope that the Civil Service can also join in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Talking about the vulnerable groups, those who are affected by COVID-19, now we take it at a little bit more macro level.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Many around the world are waking up to the massive issue of growing inequality, and business leaders and civil society and even governments are calling for a re-thinking and re-framing of capitalism.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: How society can be better off for all and not just for a few?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: What corporate values need to be renewed and what are those that need to be reset?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: How can our companies reframe their purpose so as – to quote Konosuke Matshushita – "to improve human life through enterprise management?" What government policies are needed to drive behaviour and to support businesses in this effort?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I believe that when business leaders come together and galvanise other business leaders, we can effect change for the vulnerable groups which include the marginalised or disadvantaged SMEs, amongst us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We need on-going dialogue amongst stakeholders to listen to each other, to better understand the issues and find the solutions together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And I am so blessed that our Singapore Dream is already a work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In closing, I challenge us with this quote by St Francis of Assisi: “Start by doing what is necessary, then do what is possible and suddenly you are doing the impossible”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that the theme for the Budget is "Emerging Stronger Together" and I believe all in this House share the Deputy Prime Minister's hope that we will, indeed, find a way to emerge from this crisis with greater strength and unity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are three areas in the Budget Statement that I would like to speak on today.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to learning more details on the level of increment which our healthcare workers can look forward to from the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our nurses have devoted their time and energy, as well as faced numerous risks, to keep our healthcare system going.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is past due that their remuneration is relooked.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Even though 2020 had been a challenging year economically, Singapore is still on par with the countries in this survey in terms of GDP per capita.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It seems odd that the remuneration for essential healthcare workers would continue to be lower than those of their counterparts elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Inadequate remuneration could lead to other problems down the road as well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A shortage of nurses is not a new problem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the last decade alone, MOH has acknowledged this a few times as an issue to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Further, Singapore is not the only country facing a shortage of nurses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In April 2020, the World Health Organization estimated that the world faced a shortage of six million nurses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have been able to attract nurses from other countries to come and work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They make up for the shortage of local nurses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, if remuneration levels are not considered adequate, you face the potential of our nurses being drawn to foreign shores.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will make it even harder for us to handle the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As such, I would like to propose that we consider either pegging the salaries of our nurses to a weighted basket of salaries from the countries of a similar economic status as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another possibility is for us to use the salary scales of our uniformed services as a benchmark.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our nurses also put their lives on the line at work each day.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is no one who could disagree that we must take urgent action in order to address climate change and I appreciate that the Government intends to help all those affected by the increased duties by offering rebates which are expected to defray the increased cost for a year.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I have to question why the increased rates had to take immediate effect.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such an approach creates a shock amongst vehicle users, especially for those whose livelihood depends on internal combustion engine vehicles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They have seen reduced demand and have struggled to make up for the loss of income.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While the situation has improved, private hire drivers are a long way from stability.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With practically no tourism and fewer people heading to their offices on a daily basis likely to be the prevailing scenario for the foreseeable future, the outlook for drivers is bleak.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A TODAY news article from December 2020 captured the struggles of not only the private hire drivers, but also taxi drivers, many of whom have seen severe drops in their income even with relief measures, such as the Self-employed Income Relief Scheme (SIRS), the COVID-19 Driver Relief Fund (CDRF) and the vehicle rental rebates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The drivers interviewed for the news article related their efforts to stay afloat by taking on extra jobs, and some are considering leaving the industry entirely.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, not all drivers will be able to upskill and/or reskill themselves for other industries in the near to medium term because they are locked in contracts which were signed before COVID-19 became a global pandemic.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge the efforts by MOT and LTA to mitigate the suffering of our drivers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The new requirement for private hire drivers to be 30 years old and above and having Singapore citizenship, similar to the standards required for taxi drivers, should be described as a market correction that was timely.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The announcement of higher payouts for drivers in the point-to-point transport sector to cushion the end of SIRS is also welcome news.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the increased petrol duties could mean that the money that was meant to bring relief for our drivers would end up being redirected towards Government coffers instead.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While it is important to set behavioural norms away from a reliance on fossil fuels, this is not an excuse to inflict unnecessary trauma on an already besieged group.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: By the time the rebates reach the pockets of the drivers, some of them may have resorted to drastic measures already, to keep themselves and their families economically afloat.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am also concerned that the increased petrol duties will lead to increases in the price of other goods, especially the daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is inevitable that companies will pass the burden to consumers, at least in part.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Will the rebates be sufficient to help families, especially the lower income earners, to cope with the increased costs of living?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In January 2021, the Straits Times reported that while electricity, petrol and outpatient services were cheaper in 2020, the price of food, as well as public transport fares, went up.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that the Government has provided significant amounts of relief for lower income groups and will be setting aside more to continue assisting them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the increased petrol duties may have an indirect negative impact if, as a result, the price of consumer goods, especially essential goods, increase as a result of higher fuel and transport costs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The third and final point I would like to raise is an extension of the second, and is related to the issues of sustainability and the environment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government has signalled that it will be making bold steps towards more sustainable and environmentally friendly practices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It was not too long ago that this House adopted a Motion declaring that the climate situation presents an emergency which needs to be addressed, and many of my colleagues have spoken on what can be done.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The tone of the Budget Statement is also a welcome one.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, it has to be more than just the tone that shifts.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have seen this with land reclamation, construction of highways, MRT lines and stations and other infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The latest incident whereby a patch of forest was mistakenly cleared was a tragic example of how we can get this wrong.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government has recently launched Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As mentioned by Minister Heng in his Budget speech, "This is an ambitious long-term plan that builds on on-going efforts to secure a green, liveable and sustainable home for generations of Singaporeans to come".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Planning for future and continuity is critical and of paramount importance, and, as the saying goes, "If you fail to plan, you are planning to fail".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, Sir, at this juncture, I believe it is worthwhile for us to pause and consider the lessons which we can learn from the erroneous clearing of Kranji Forest which happened recently, before we move any further on our 2030 Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We also should ponder if we should be working towards a more harmonious relationship with our natural environment in Singapore instead of imposing our own artificial solutions for sustainability.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is a saying in Malay “Bagai enau di dalam belukar, melepaskan pucuk masing-masing”, a reference to a kind of plant that grows in the underbrush.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Its meaning is a reference to a situation whereby narrow interests are prioritised over the greater good.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For too long, we have prioritised urban development over the environment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Green Plan is a major step in rebalancing our priorities.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   The announcement by the Deputy Prime Minister, who is also the Minister for Finance, on the salary increase for nurses and healthcare sector workers is most welcome.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Since the COVID-19 pandemic began, we have seen various efforts by every segment of society displaying strong support and expressing gratitude for our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Among the efforts undertaken include F&B businessmen providing free food and beverages, thank-you notes by students using home-made cards as well as simultaneous applause and cheers from Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, financial support and rewards are equally important especially in the current situation where the cost of living is increasing.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the announcement of salary increases for nurses and health sector workers is most welcome.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The question now is, how much is the amount of increase that has been decided?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As stated by Minister Heng, this announcement will be made by the Minister for Health at the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because the quality and standard of our health systems and expertise are equivalent to these countries.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's level of economic development is also similar to those countries.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, the benefits given to our health sector workers should commensurate with their counterparts in these countries.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to comment on Minister Heng's speech on the Government’s plan to balance the number of local and foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: By allowing the tudung to be worn as part of the nurses' uniform, perhaps more Muslim women can fulfil their wish to work as nurses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to more sharing from the respective Ministries on the issues mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is indeed a very uncertain time and it is very difficult for the Minister to forecast with any certainty what are the possible scenarios as vaccination gains momentum in Singapore and globally.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Viruses constantly change through mutation, and new variants will occur from time to time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, you have the UK variant, you have the South African variant, we also have the Brazil variant.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am not sure tomorrow, what will be the next variants.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We also have to assess whether the current vaccination – are they effective against protecting us against the new variant?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While we can postulate some of the possible scenarios and outcome, things are still very fluid and very unpredictable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The four issues are: first, the distribution of the CDC Vouchers; second, incentives for Singaporeans who opt in for COVID-19 vaccination; third, the issuance of the Green Bonds; and fourth, the Electric Vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I shall start off with the CDC Vouchers distribution.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will definitely boost our local consumption as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The idea is good except that this distribution is by per household.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And as we know, per household means that number of people within the household differs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This project will benefit those with small households rather than those with larger households because more people under one roof for larger households have to share the $100.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is it being considered when the concept of per household was being mooted?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why not adopt previous distribution method of all Singaporeans above aged 21 years and above?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: You can distribute about $50 per person and the total amount amount would still be about the same.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second, incentives for Singaporeans who opt in for COVID-19 vaccination.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The faster we get vaccinated, the faster we can get ourselves protected and lower the risks of local cluster outbreaks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know many are fearful of unknown future side effects of this new vaccine.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I have faith in the science behind this development.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: All the data and facts have been carefully considered by MOH and our vaccine expert committee before approval for public use.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In order to encourage more to opt in for the vaccination, I would like to suggest the Government consider giving some incentives to all Singaporeans who opt in for the vaccination.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This can be in terms of additional CDC Vouchers or even CPF MediSave top-ups.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is one problem which we know is pressing and it is more predictable than the second-guessing of virus mutation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If Minister can share his thoughts on this The last topic is on electric cars.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is well and good to push our plans on Electric Vehicles (EVs), but we have to recognise it takes a lot to win over Singaporeans to move in this direction.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, how many charging points do we have, I mean, in the public, as well as how many EV to each charging points now do we have?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Two things stand in the way of mass adoption of EVs now are vehicle economics and charging infrastructure availability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is not unique to Singapore but global as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Let us say 80% of our car owners switch over to EVs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, how many charging stations do we need to attract car owners to switch to EVs?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That means giving drivers ease of mind to know that they do not need to desperately hunt for a charging point when their batteries run low.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Plus, they do not need to go into long queues to wait for their turns.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans want to get things done fast and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The question is how many public charging stations do we need to have to cater for 800,000 EVs?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the UK, according to a recent report by Auto Express, a weekly motoring magazine, there is less than one charging point for each six Electric Vehicles sold in the country in 2017.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Another motoring publication, Autocar, said in total, the British version of low-speed electric vehicles, also known as quadricycles, electric motorcycles, and plug-in commercial delivery vans, every public charging point caters to 8.9 plug-in vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is "close to the European Union’s preferred maximum ratio of 10 vehicles per public charging point," it said.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The total number of motor vehicle population as of July 2019 is 340 million.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: China is the country with the most EV charging points in the world – with 1.2 million in 2019.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is still 283 EVs to one charging point.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And it is looking to add another 600,000 more charging points like a petrol station.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Despite this aggressive building of charging stations, as of November 2019, 324,000 EVs in China do not have a charging facility alongside the space where the vehicle is normally parked.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, there is still a lot of room for EVs to grow and for charging stations to be built.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Finding space for charging stations is just one hurdle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The stations have to provide fast and normal charging so that the turnaround can be faster.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In land scarce Singapore, we now have to struggle to give space for charging stations all over the island, including HDB car parks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Residents would now be fighting for charging points and Members of Parliament will have a new wave of complaints.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Battery manufacturers are still working out on producing better batteries with longer driving range, with longer lifespan and support faster charging.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is over and above producing them at competitive prices.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: After the batteries have outlived their lifespan, we also have to take a look at how do we dispose of these batteries?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are also many other issues to be addressed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Around the world, EVs are still sort of an advanced stage of work-in-progress, in my view.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are our engineers, technicians and mechanics sufficiently equipped to handle EVs?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are many independent motor workshops would have to upgrade their skillsets to maintain and repair EVs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Overall, how cost effective will it be to use an EV versus an internal combustion engine vehicle?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The amount of energy that we have to produce additional to power 800,000 vehicles on a daily basis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Do we have enough power supply to do that as well?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And what is the cost to the whole country?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why are motorists penalised or coerced to move to EVs when we have not got enough infrastructures in place?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And the cost of EV is still high.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With ERP resuming and the raising of petrol price, would it not cause inflation to rise?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The cost of higher petrol cost will impact all sectors of economy from retail to manufacturing, to transport for office workers and students, as well as goods and services.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While we want to support our lower and middle income households, no one would be spared from inflation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will help ease the cash flow for our residents.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, now, for internal combustion engine COEs, I can understand.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As the car gets older, it becomes less efficient, it becomes more pollutive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We definitely want to conserve as much resources as possible.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One last ground feedback is regarding the Government taking the lead to convert all public vehicles to EVs, including the Police, LTA, NParks, SCDF.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And there should also be incentive to get the commercial vehicles to be converted to EVs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although he did not a degree, he had the opportunity to work for a national carrier in the early glory days.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How tough it was for my amazing parents to put up a brave front for my brother and I to pick up something new.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fast forward to today, and families across Singapore find themselves in a similar circumstance due to COVID-19 and I find myself in the position of having a voice in this House, which was unimaginable to the teenage me 18 years ago.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand deeply the worries that come with an uncertain view of one's future, the opportunity costs that come with dreams deferred.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this in mind and in heart, my speech today is in hopes for continued commitment to an inclusive, sustainable and equitable Singapore for all in Budget 2021.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An earlier version of our pledge that was suggested by former Deputy Prime Minister S Rajaratnam in a letter dated February 1966 said, "We, as citizens of Singapore, pledge ourselves to forget differences of race, language or religion and become one united people; to build a democratic society where justice and equality will prevail, where we will seek happiness and progress by helping one another." The nuance of that last sentence is beautiful.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this pandemic, we have indeed seen Singaporeans seeking happiness in progress by helping one another – from keeping food on the table to keeping each other safe from the virus.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amidst the pandemic, we have yet again shown that this young nation can stay united in pursuit of common goals despite our differences, emerging stronger.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is stimulus to spur the growth of green industries and liquidity for local businesses to sprout and adapt to the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is for this reason that I ask we ensure that the potential for abuse remains low as we administer these funds so that the funds fulfil the intended purpose.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In his speech, the Deputy Prime Minister spoke about the purpose of economic transformation, being to grow opportunities for our people to realise their full potential and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With stiffer competition from global talents as well as long-term wage support being untenable, I would like to touch on employment opportunities for two groups in particular.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that the future for our youths is less certain, less stable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many are also required to support elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But there have been efforts to give our youths options and I recognise that.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a push towards entrepreneurship to initiatives in Institutes of Higher Learning's accelerator programmes supported by corporates or even grants like the Youth Action Challenge, a programme I know from my days at the National Youth Council.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And we also have the SGUnited Traineeship Programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these policies provide opportunities, I am also wary of the potential consequences that our fresh graduates may face in the medium or longer run.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Grants do not translate to salaries and some may turn to temporary gig jobs to make ends meet and get stuck where they do not want to be.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the training allowance does help our graduates gain employment in the short run, I hope we also consider how employment might look like for them after six months.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, under-employment issues and access to subsequent employment opportunities or wage growth after trainee allowances for these young entrants to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can the Government lead by example and how will our institutions, such as a Singapore Prison Service, be able to offer timely training opportunities in relevant industries?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do inmates have the opportunity to develop other job-ready skills, so that re-integration and ability to provide for their family upon release is a smoother transition?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond incentives, it is also about society, reducing stigma against this group of workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents in my Meet-the-People sessions have shared how tough it can be to get a job except in, perhaps, certain industries, such as logistics or F&B.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How are we going to ensure that they will be able to access the jobs that are currently being created?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our Green Plan can incorporate some of the recommendations of the Blue Plan.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our blue spaces are precious and generally multi-used for the volume of activities that it accommodates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We see more and more people appreciating our blue spaces, our oceans, through rising number of visitors in our Southern Islands, for example.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I hope for a stronger commitment so that our blue spaces are not left out of Green Plan conversations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, our Park Connector Network connects green spaces around Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to consider the protection of blue connectors in our marine systems, which connect open seas, seagrass meadows, reefs, intertidal habitats and are impacted by debris pollution and coastal development.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope there will be resources for better management of marine species, for example, which will lead to healthier oceans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The community groups, such as Friends of the Marine Park is ready in to contribute to these efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aside from continued improvement to our public transport system, policies that encourage EV adoption is a way forward in giving our citizens the ability to participate in the reduction of their carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: EVs are a discontinuous innovation which requires significant behavioural change from customers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do believe the financial incentives announced are welcome and will create visible change in the landscape of vehicles that we see on our roads in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, in fact, EV sales have picked up in January.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we are a far cry away from crossing the chasm.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The economics and infrastructure considerations of installing charging stations are complex, from how our AC power grids affect considerations for charging stations to policies that help keep charging affordable for consumers and profitable for partners interested in installing these stations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government keeps the public informed on the mechanisms it intends to deploy on these and other factors so as to allay consumer concerns.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And beyond land transportation, I hope more can be done to encourage cleaner energy and electric marine vehicles and boats in our waters The ability for all Singaporeans to share in the progress of the nation is a cornerstone in ensuring our collective success.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a younger male woman, I am conscious that in the Fourteenth Parliament, we have the fifth, sixth and seventh Malay women Members of Parliament in this House since the beginning of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, Malay women occupy spaces in advocacy, education, law, the arts, environmental issues, research and many more, and we will continue to progress with continued access to the opportunities to do so.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I never thought I would have the opportunity to study law or become a lawyer and for some of the young women I have befriended and worked with during their time in prison and after release, I know that many of them do not dare to plan for a future or have the social capital to apply to someone, somewhere in hopes of getting a job.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One girl had shared that she was awarded a bursary assistance to do a course and joined the Armed Forces – her childhood ambition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But due to bad company, being locked out of home by her family, she relapsed and offended again before she could even try to pick up the pieces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He was asked if Singapore believes in the notion of a safety net for those who fall between the cracks of a successful economy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, in response, Senior Minister Tharman spoke about the notion of a trampoline which we are familiar with.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An economy that helps people bounce back is hard to argue against and I think that most people would agree with the visual narrative of people being able to bounce back higher with effort from the difficulties that we face.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Particularly during a time like this when families who have never had to ask for help before, now find themselves in that position.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I ask this House to visualise the diversity of people we see in Singapore in our house visits, in our Meet-the-People sessions and in our daily activities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do some people have others around them that care enough to help teach them the best way to jump on the trampoline while others may not?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who are unable to jump as high, is it possible that some of their trampolines need fixing?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And is it possible that some of them do not have the physical or mental faculties to jump on a trampoline?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think for most of us, we would say yes to the above.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, how are we going to provide for access to opportunities for the different levels of people on the trampoline?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the quality of life for those who, through no fault of their own, can no longer jump on?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: May this Budget and the ones in years to come help us find ourselves in a caring, compassionate and confidence society, long into the future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is likely that our route back to growth will be slow and gradual as we are dependent on how the world recovers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, our continued resilience and resolve are central outcomes in this year's Budget and this has to include being even more targeted so that Singapore and Singaporeans emerge stronger amidst COVID-19 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have an opportunity to supplement our current classification of companies beyond just by vertical industry sectors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since last year, as someone in business, I have personally seen: (a) the emergence of many new companies that are not only created by young technopreneurs but by a much wider profile; (b) the restructuring of many incumbent companies as they focus on their cost structures; and (c) the repositioning of traditional businesses to go beyond their current industry sector in search of new revenue opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Added to this, many traditional businesses are family owned and how these businesses evolve and pivot across different generations of leadership determine their contribution to our economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such family inter-generation leadership changes require better understanding.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A good example of a Singapore company that has evolved horizontally, not founded by a techonopreneur and repositioned from a traditional family business, is PBA Group.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: PBA was founded in 1987 by Mr Tony Yap as a hardware shop trading in ball-bearings, bolts, nuts and belts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of sticking to the less risky business model of trading, Mr Tony Yap and his son Mr Derrick Yap pivoted PBA to a precision robotics manufacturer.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: PBA now provides businesses with precision and general robotics across verticals to allow them to scale up their operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They developed and manufactured precision robotics for the semiconductor, electric vehicle battery, mobile devices, fibre optics sectors; collaborative robots for industries like construction, medical, the logistics sector such as SingPost's smart letterbox; automonous mobile robots to transport goods autonomously to replace forklifts for warehouses, and most recently, the COVID-19 disinfection robot, a first for Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Derrick also shared that a robotic arm cooking his favourite local food "bak chor mee" may also be on the cards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: PBA used to stand for "precision, bearings and accessories".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fast forward today, PBA now stands for "platform for bots and automation".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: PBA's evolution as a business exemplifies how a traditional business pivots across verticals as part of its business life stage and cycle, and the heartwarming story of how a family business transcends across generations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, as PBA sets itself up as a platform for bots and automation across verticals, it finds it challenging to navigate different rules, regulations, Statutory Boards, departments that are currently structured on industry verticals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At each of this phase, entrepreneurs face a different set of challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the start-up phase, I believe we will see greater entrepreneurial efforts over the next two to three years and we may want to provide targeted help here, especially for those who can see this as another option to the traditional employment route.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the early growth phase, entrepreneurs and their firms' capability needs will face the challenge of time and resources.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, targeted help to get them to adopt training will have to go beyond financial support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the scaling up or pivoting phases, both short-term financing and even financial restructuring could be essential for the company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being even more contextual is important for our efforts to be relevant.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Different companies in the same sector, at different growth stage or at different part of the value chain, face different challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The extent to which a sub-sector can automate differs too.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to understand the nuances and be precise in our support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, a hawker stall and a restaurant in the food services sector may grow differently, grappling with different issues.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The consumers of hawker centres are more price sensitive and any increase in food prices will cause disappointment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, hawkerpreneurs are less likely to increase the price of food, even as manpower costs or other operating costs increase.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With targeted support and measures, all our businesses – small, medium, and large – will be able to restart, pivot and grow, resulting in job security and more good job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do believe that both WSG and ESG can provide a lot of expertise in this area.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, training in the form of consultative training can take into account what the entrepreneur or the business owner needs to be exposed to and upskilled at the particular stage of the company's growth, to the workers skillset that is required, so that training can be more targeted and translate to a company's top line and bottom line growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is crucial that as we beef up workers' training, we need to also beef up training for business owners so that management can be more insightful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This dovetails the investments in consultancy and training, and maximises on the return on investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even our manpower policy can be further calibrated by business growth stage and sub-sector classifications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will enable a more targeted approach to optimise our lean manpower resource base.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On a global level, investors, clients and end consumers are increasingly adopting the environment, social and government-recommended measurements to decide on which business to support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we can further seize opportunities in the social impact space in addition to green economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to create benchmarks and standards for our business to rally around this green beacon.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will share more about how the Government can play a role in establishing standards and a benchmark for our businesses to create the best eco-system for such a leap forward in my MTI cuts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Putting together precise, bespoke and updated policies will strengthen our Singapore business for a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In my conversations recently with some astute overseas investors, who are also keen observers of Singapore, I have received many positive feedback.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They felt that Singapore has continued to demonstrate the ability to identify challenges ahead of time and more importantly, has clear and concrete action plans to address them.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, our plans for rising sea levels and raising our local food supply.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They were also impressed with the way we handled the COVID-19 situation; not just in tackling the public health crisis, including mobilising the support and unity of our people, but also with the proactive and pragmatic approach taken to mitigate supply chain and economic disruptions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Against the backdrop of the pandemic, polarising geopolitical competition and the social unrests in some cities in the region, Singapore stands out even more.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Our long-standing socio-political order, our commitment to a plural and multi-ethnic society, our strong legal system and our highly liveable city, are a few of the things that make us stand out.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The question is, going forward, how will Singapore balance economic growth against challenges of domestic issues.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: New sectors of growth will require talents with skills which the people from sectors in decline may not possess.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, our local talent pool may not even be sufficient in numbers or expertise to meet the growth demand of some of the sectors, such as technology.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Our economy and labour market will undergo massive re-ordering.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The division between the haves and have-nots will increase.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, standing still is not an option.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I hope as a society, we will not opt to level down and forego growth for fear of the challenges that it brings.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we will be pragmatic as we have always been, by seizing the growth opportunities, while working hard on addressing empathetically, the social and human challenges that will arise.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Such as, how to reskill our workers and also how to better share the benefits of growth equitably.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I believe in a balanced and pragmatic approach for sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Balancing the three pillars is key to success.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Continued economic success gives us more means to fulfill the needs of the other pillars.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, with our ageing population, the associated health care costs will increase.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To provide more support for the less advantaged families and individuals, we will also need more resources.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, growing our economy sustainably will enable us to do more good.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We should seek balanced and constructive ways to move ahead and not get stuck in binaries which polarises.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans and observers of Singapore take reference from what we say in public as indicators for the direction the country is heading.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As we push for our personal subject of passion, we should strive to minimise any form of polarisation.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To be constructive, we need to recognise the trade-offs the other side has to make.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, we have to make hard choices, but if we focus our energy on finding common grounds, we might end up with synergistic and creative solutions that make us collectively better off.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Besides balancing the three key pillars of sustainability, in Singapore, whatever we do, we are always making a trade-off between the short term and the long term.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If we believe in SG100 or SG150, then our land use policies, for instance, cannot safeguard the needs just for the next 10 to 20 years.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We have to think the next 50 or 100 years.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Precisely because we cannot predict the future, we should be careful not to circumscribe the flexibility or options for the many generations of Singaporeans down the road.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Because the planners in the 1960s and 1970s had the foresight to do so and safeguard future development options, we now enjoy the luxury of the choices we can make.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Dealing with our resource constraints will not only solve our problems today, it can help us develop useful new capabilities for the future.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Take the built environment sector for example, our drive for higher productivity in the construction sector requires bold moves, but the capabilities developed can enable us to find new opportunities overseas.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: And although the Singapore city is already held in high regard in terms of its infrastructure and quality of life, we can still do much better.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we can raise our green buildings standards even further; we can be a front runner in creating new economic infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: How about a food-self-sufficiency urban system, or creating more biodiversity even as we are building?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Private sector capabilities, capital and mindsets have much to offer.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The public sector has a key role in opening up the space for the private sector to participate and innovate.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Our future challenges are complex, in addressing them, more heads are better than one.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If more government departments adopt the same, we will encourage more collaboration and creativity around us, and create even more engines of growth in the process.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Private corporates, when called upon to act, need to step up and balance short-term pains with long-term gains.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Private corporates have to broaden the mindset of just serving their shareholders to serving their relevant stakeholders better.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To do so can in fact be good for business.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To emerge stronger, it will take many hands to work together and with a shared sense of purpose and ideals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It has also brought out the best of our Singaporeans in terms of teamwork, creativity and spirit of enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Within months, we came together to re-energise, re-organise our society and re-imagine our economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As we begin large-scale vaccination this week in Singapore, we can start planning for the post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We should also tap on this newfound teamwork that this generation has forged – especially between the Government and the private sector – for the betterment of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, I would like to speak about two ways to do so: one, accelerate government transformation by tapping on creativity and the capability of the private sector; two, accelerate the economy by beefing up our trade association and chambers in the matured parts of our economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond this, I will also speak about enhancing seniors’ livelihood through micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is an issue close to my heart and I spoke about this multiple times in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am delighted to see that over the years, the Government has taken on some of these suggestions, to inject private sector talent into the the Government and to tap on private sector insights to reduce business red-tape through the creation of the Pro-Enterprise Panel.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Pro-Enterprise Panel, which is helmed by the Head of Civil Service and distinguished business leaders, understands the complexity of governance, especially including inter-agencies coordination, or interaction between agencies and businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope that in future speeches, we can hear from the Deputy Prime Minister about more success stories created by the Open Innovation Platform, because process transformation by the Government can do much to spark growth and productivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Next, let me talk about strengthening the Government’s partnership with the businesses, especially mature businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At this point, let me declare my interest as Advisor to the Federation of Merchants Associations, which helps heartland enterprises transform and grow.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Since 2016, Singapore has achieved much through our Industry Transformation Maps, and have sharpened Singaporean’s competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This can be shown and seen through the anchoring of many impressive inward investments, and through the rapid restructuring of industries affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of these successful industries have enterprising leadership centered around their trade association and chambers or TACs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These TACs partnered with our economic agencies to imagine and implement their industry’s future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, there are still many parts of our economy which are only seeing limited transformation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: After much discussion with business leaders, I have concluded that the key to successful transformation is in the leadership, especially at the TAC level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The conventional wisdom is that TACs in certain industries are more likely to succeed, such as those with a small number of large and dynamic players, especially focused on manufacturing and exportable services; those in industries that Singapore is already competitive in, or those in new industries that the Government seeks to grow.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, we are beginning to see successful transformation in more matured part of the economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two prime examples are our food manufacturing industry, as well as our heartland enterprises.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And in both of these, there are common critical success factors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, they have a strong TAC with a capable secretariat comprising of seconded civil servants who have served in economic development agencies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, these TAC represents sub-industries rather than the broader business sector, and this gives the TACs focus and clarity in their mission.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, there is strong Government support, especially from Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, now that there is a clear formula, I think it is the right time for the Government to replicate this success in the other parts of the economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Unfortunately, the reality is that TACs are of uneven quality, because many of them have their roots in business networking.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A large number of them do not have effective secretariat capabilities, let alone the ability to partner with our economic agencies to forge new grounds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We already pour in so much resources to help individual companies transform and to build broad-base efforts such as SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, the relatively minor investments to beef up the sub-industry TAC leadership is a logical and wise next step.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Next, let me talk about improving seniors' employability through micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the next quarter, I hope the majority of our seniors will be vaccinated and this will allow us to shift more focus on improving their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When I speak to senior workers about their livelihoods, a number of them do not know how they fit into our future economy, or how they can overcome ageism.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is not due to a lack of effort by the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yet despite regulations, it is hard for us to fully remove ageism, especially towards seniors above the age of 67.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many companies, especially in the midst of COVID-19, are unwilling to take on the risk of hiring or even retaining senior workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This issue will get more serious as we continue to restructure, and as our workforce continues to age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I strongly believe the gig economy can help us combat ageism.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, two years ago, while doing PAP Senior Group’s engagement, I had the chance to be in the same dialogue as Nominated Member of Parliament Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I believe she shared that as seniors age, no matter how wonderful their resumes are, at some point many companies will have reservations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So rather than helping seniors polish their resumes for the next full-time job, we might want to consider identifying the portfolios of skills they have accumulated in their whole life, and these skills can be applied to part-time or micro-jobs within a variety of industries and not just the industries they serve the bulk of their careers in.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In particular, creating micro-jobs for our seniors makes a lot of sense to me.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On the one hand, a company may have reservations on the health and healthcare cost of the full-time worker.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But on the other hand, consumers who rely on seniors for micro-jobs do not face much risk because what is at stake is only that one single service experience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And customers can rely on customer feedback or reviews.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, customers using gig economy are less likely to discriminate against seniors compared to companies who are looking at seniors as full-time employees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us use the example of the delivery of home-based healthcare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, we sometimes send two nurses to visit patients, many of whom are bedridden or have mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are many seniors living in our midst who can qualify to do such micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Through this gig economy app that the Government creates, perhaps by working with existing gig-economy companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How do we prepare our seniors for these micro-jobs?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we equip our seniors to provide simple care-giving or respite care services to their neighbours?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If we do all that, how many purpose-built infant care, after school care centres, or respite care centres can we not build?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When I talk to civil service officers or social service agency leaders about these ideas, they get it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But they also confide with me that they cannot do it alone and that is why we need the Government to spearhead this, using social services as a start.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Perhaps we can tap on the Open Innovation Platform and customise existing platforms from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While preparing for this Budget debate speech, I took the chance to look through all my past Budget speeches in the last term of Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am pleasantly surprised that so many suggestions have been translated into actual plans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Now, of course, in making these policy improvements, the Government hears from people from all walks of life, including Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But this realisation convinced me that our present Government listens, consults and engages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And as we continue to recover from the pandemic, I am confident that this openness to ideas will serve Singapore well, in our journey ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in full support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can be attributed to the COVID-19 Resilience Package.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it stands, why $11 billion, and not, say, $22 billion is the prudent Budget deficit figure, can only be answered by a select few.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because the national reserves remain a national secret, we must take the Deputy Prime Minister's word for it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in the interest of the nation, especially during these tough economic times, I must raise the question again, as many others before me have done so, and ask if it is time to make our national reserves part of our national conversation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Elected President carries the responsibility of safeguarding our reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we still remember President Ong Teng Cheong's unsuccessful attempt to know the size of the reserve he was supposed to protect.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the current President aware of the exact size of our reserves when she made decisions on its drawdown?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I do not yet know the answer to that question, I do know that Members of Parliament are being asked to vote on a Budget that would require a drawdown on our reserves without knowing its size.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without knowing our nation's financial position, it would be difficult to make sound and prudent decisions, and certainly not informed ones.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, again, I ask that more transparency with regard to the national reserves be made, if not only that Singaporeans better understand the rationale for difficult decisions like the need to raise the GST to 9% in the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did Singapore get a bang for its buck?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To put the numbers in perspective, if we were to pay 155,000 people $4,000 per month, it would cost us $7.4 billion per year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One hundred billion dollars is sufficient for 13.4 years of payment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOF give a fuller accounting of the benefits of the Budget measures and an assessment of whether those resources have been used effectively and efficiently?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the Job Support Scheme, or JSS, payments either saved jobs, or were paid as additional wages, or stayed in the employers' bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The wages paid out either ended up in consumption, which would contribute to GDP, or stayed in the pockets of employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much of the JSS went to benefit companies that were unaffected by the COVID-19 problem, with the same or more profits?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the MOF report mentioned earlier, it was stated that the transfers did not result in such a high spend on consumption because of safe distancing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More benefits would come later when demand returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the forecast deferred impact from the transfers not spent on consumption or investment in 2020?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One hundred billion dollars is not a small amount.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We ask for a cost benefit analysis of each scheme put in place.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We recognise that it is not easy coming up with measures within a short timeframe to deal with a pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we ask not for a perfect solution, but an honest and transparent assessment and review.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With more business closures and unemployment expected to increase after March when many of the support measures start to taper off, more households will likely suffer financial stress.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will consider increasing its support for the many who are likely to need it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has a small domestic market so our SMEs need help to grow and develop into a size that will enable them to compete globally.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Budget has addressed the capital needs for Singapore businesses, the Government can do more.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1995, Israel approved the "Preference for Israeli Products" regulation that stipulated that a 15% price-differential preference be awarded to Israeli manufacturers for certain items and for products with 35% Israeli content and with a value not exceeding $500,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Israeli manufacturers in "National Priority Zones" even received an additional 5%-15% advantage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A "Mandatory Industrial Cooperation" regulation also required foreign suppliers that had won government or public tenders to engage in an offset procurement in Israel to the extent of 20%-50% of the contract value by local subcontracting, procurement of Israeli goods and services, cooperation in R&D and investment or assistance for an Israeli industrialist or exporter abroad.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have these regulations impacted Israel's competitiveness to a degree that it can no longer compete globally?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party or PSP urges the Government to consider similar preferential treatment for local businesses in Government procurements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his Budget Statement, Deputy Prime Minister stressed that the focus on growing the economy is to benefit the people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, PSP would like to suggest that the Government set a target for the wage component of our GDP to ensure that the fruits of economic development are enjoyed by its people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The operating surplus was 29% higher than wages.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their wage component was 45% higher than the operating surplus component.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the US and Switzerland, the numbers also compare favourably.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only with the focus on an equitable solution to the current crisis will Singapore emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as Parliament sits now, the recent Chinese New Year celebrations have been a rather quiet affair for many families and friends.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the on-going vaccination programme offers a sliver of hope that we might emerge from this pandemic sooner than later, the task of rebuilding for a new normal begins now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
