text: More than that, we must be cognisant that there has never been a more opportune time to take firm action, to reform our economy and social compact, with the hope that we might be able to come out of the woods stronger than ever.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the pandemic, we need to look at not just headline economic growth, but instead quality or inclusive growth; to sharpen our focus on how we can uplift our entire country and maximise the overall well-being of all Singaporeans in a sustainable manner, in the long run.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On this note, I would like to highlight three broad areas we should focus on in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first point I would like to make would be on the urgent need to restructure our economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And these were even before the effects of COVID-19 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With COVID-19 comes a crisis, but also an opportunity for us to use this time to restructure our economy, focusing our growth in areas where we might be able to develop and maintain a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To restructure our economy, efforts should be targeted at the building blocks of our economy, our local enterprises and local workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On local enterprises, I believe the initiatives announced by Deputy Prime Minister Heng to accelerate the growth of new digital capabilities are laudable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These include the emerging technology programme, CTO-as-a-service and digital leaders programme to help more businesses adopt increased digitalisation solutions, as part of their core competencies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are good solutions to support our local businesses, small or large.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should also, however, double down on efforts to better support SMEs to scale up and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this could involve Government agencies facilitating access to global markets, while providing technical and financial assistance, could we better incentivise large local GLCs or even MNCs, to partner with our local SMEs in their internationalisation efforts?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A vibrant SME eco-system is thus imperative for our future economy, with SMEs' success key to driving entrepreneurship and innovation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, while we look to support local SMEs' internationalisation efforts, our open economy and transparent business rules also mean that international MNCs can easily outbid local SMEs in domestic tenders, especially in price-based contracts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking around construction sites across Singapore, one cannot help but notice the large number of foreign conglomerates appointed as main contractor for building and infrastructure sites.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2017, it was revealed in Parliament that while 80% of Government contracts in number are awarded to SMEs, only half by contract value is awarded to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Could more be done to provide greater opportunities to local SMEs, to give them the chance to scale up and build up a requisite track record in our very own home market?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Supporting our local workers should also go hand-in-hand with supporting our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the shortening of business cycles and hastening of technological disruption, the threat of widespread job losses and rapid job irrelevance is only going to rise in future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During this crisis, the Jobs Support Scheme, or JSS, has been an important policy measure to provide direct wage support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the uneven economic recovery, in what is called a K-shaped recovery, it is important to ensure that the hardest hit sectors and workers are given a fair chance of survival.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there remains debate as to the tiering of sectors and the adequacy of continuing support, the extended JSS support to tier 1 and tier 2 sectors is nonetheless a welcome relief to companies in these selected sectors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The launch of the COVID-19 Recovery Grant to directly support lower to middle income workers, presently experiencing involuntary job losses or income loss is also a timely and important one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether or not COVID-19 is here to stay for the next few years, there will continue to be redundancies and job losses at any stage of the economic cycle.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As the schemes borne out of COVID-19 such as the COVID-19 Recovery Grant are already designed and implemented, could they remain a more permanent feature of our financial assistance schemes to workers?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, we may need to think of implementing automatic stabilisers instead of discretionary, ad hoc schemes to enhance the resilience of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An example would be unemployment insurance, which can provide workers with resources to alleviate near term anxieties associated with job losses, while reducing the incidence of under-employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, in a working paper published by the Institute of Policy Studies on 9 February this year, the researchers highlighted if the Government issues debt to finance a programme in unemployment insurance, inter-generational equality could be improved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The paper further stated, and I quote, "children of unemployed parents have a greater chance of social mobility if their parents are supported by a Government provisioned unemployment insurance programme".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second point I want to raise is a broader question on the appropriateness of our fiscal policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having recognised the challenging terrain that Singapore is in today, our Budget and financial policies should then be the key enabler rather than impediment, towards allowing us to chart our roadmap to success, and embark confidently on a journey towards truly emerging stronger from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In October last year, I spoke about the continued need for an accommodative fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite the hopes we pin on a successful vaccination programme, we are not out of the woods yet, and the economic recovery we are hopeful of, is a fragile one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should thus continue focusing on policies that aim to stimulate and boost domestic demand and keep our economy going, keep businesses and consumer confidence high, while minimising the long-term scarring caused by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we speak, the largest economy in the world, the US is looking to put through a $1.9 trillion stimulus package, equivalent to about 9% of GDP, on the back of a $3 trillion package in 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen has highlighted the case for increased fiscal spending to avoid a "longer, more painful recession".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She said and I quote, "the smartest thing we can do is act big.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the long run, I believe the benefits will far outweigh the costs, especially if we care about helping people who have been struggling for a very long time".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In order to reverse the pains from this recession, we must be willing to devote more resources to supporting our businesses and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that Budget 2021 is an expansionary one, similar to Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But this has to be seen against the context of Singapore’s unique budgetary policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be vastly different compared to the reported cumulative deficit of about minus $32 billion over the same period from 2011 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such a calculation, while simplistic would also be broadly in line with official data from the Department of Statistics, where the Government cash surplus from 2011 to 2019, the latest available data point, is a cumulative $261 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we run on a recurring basis an average of $29 billion of cash surplus a year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the official Budget is based on revenues that the Government of the day can spend under the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Not all Government revenues and receipts collected can be spent by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But when we say that we need to raise GST sometime during 2022 to 2025 and sooner rather than later, that “without the GST rate increase, we will not be able to meet our rising recurrent needs”, and that “it is not tenable for the Government to run persistent budget deficits outside periods of crisis”, then these statements ought to be framed in the context of the Government’s recurring cash surplus every year up to 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is the imposition of a broad based, regressive tax then truly justified?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even amidst the crisis of a generation, the NIRC alone is expected to rise by $1.4 billion in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With NIRC estimates supposed to be based off expected long-term real rates of return, and with a draw on the reserves amounting to a generation's worth of savings, what then has led to the increase, and is the growth in NIRC expected to continue accelerating?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line to me then is therefore that we must caution against being overzealous in strengthening our revenue position through multiple pathways, such as the impending GST hike, especially amidst the macroeconomic uncertainties of today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my third point, and that is on a countrywide level, while we talk about how much excess cash we truly have, and how much of our revenues are not revenues at all, on an individual level, Singaporeans are increasingly worried about their lack of a rainy-day fund, with many of our elderly residents suffering from retirement inadequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this month, I filed a Parliamentary Question on the number and percentage of active and inactive CPF members who are able to meet the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year, Deputy Prime Minister Heng shared that 435,000 Singaporeans aged 55 to 70 have not been able to set aside the prevailing Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This represents approximately 58% of Singaporeans in that age band in 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We can choose to think that outside of CPF balances, our elderly residents are likely to have other means of provision, which the CPF Board has no sight of.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We could also fall back on self-reliance through working beyond retirement, or family support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All this while the rising cost of living, increase in property prices continue to erode the disposable cashflow of households, and therefore the ability of the sandwiched generation to contribute more to their own and their parents' CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With rising life expectancy and an ageing population, how can we devote resources to ensure that Singaporeans who devoted their lives building the country, can retire with a decent living standard and live their lives in dignity?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, COVID-19 has undoubtedly brought about a crisis, but it has also brought about opportunities for change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is no doubt that we should take this opportunity to restructure the economy and encourage businesses to transform, so as to ensure that our economy can ride out the storm.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we should also bear in mind that in formulating policies, we should not just consider the economic aspects; we should give priority to the welfare of all Singaporeans and take care of the disadvantaged groups in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has said, the focus of our next phase of work should shift from tackling the pandemic to emerging stronger in the post-COVID era.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, while it is important to ensure the sustainability of our economy, the country’s sustainable development is also based on social sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is a continuous effort to strengthen and expand our social safety net.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Before I begin, I would like to thank the Finance Minister for a comprehensive and forward-thinking Budget, which I believe addresses a wide range of relevant issues and concerns that impact Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Twenty-twenty was a challenging year for many, including, the sports, fitness and wellness industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many businesses in this sector started to feel the effects of the pandemic as early as January 2020, when news of COVID-19 first emerged.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these gyms have developed and implemented digital strategies offering online classes and programmes; however, more thought needs to be put in on how these gyms and academies can successfully monetise these online programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Participation in sports and fitness in a broader sense can instil and develop physical resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Through the pandemic, we saw Singaporeans battle through several difficult situations, including social isolation and caring for their mental health.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Physical activity has a considerable potential to enhance our well-being.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: A short burst of a 10 minutes' brisk walk increases a person's mental alertness, energy and positive mood, as shown in a recent study in the Journal of Behavioural Medicine.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Participation in regular physical activity can boost self-esteem and can reduce stress and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: According to an article by the British Journal of Occupational Therapy, it also plays a role in preventing mental health problems and improving people's quality of life.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We experienced it when our athletes take to the pool, track, field, or court and bring glory to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We felt the high when Joseph Schooling had his "where were you when it happened" Olympic gold medal moment; we remember our Lion’s glory and the Kallang Roar.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In 2021, our Team Singapore athletes will have multiple opportunities to fly our flag high at the Olympics and Paralympics and Southeast Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that our athletes and support teams harness the opportunity whilst protecting themselves as they train and prepare for their competitions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I want to acknowledge and thank the MCCY and SportSG, to make the COVID-19 vaccination available for athletes who need to go abroad for training and competitions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask that we should not waste the opportunity to elevate these moments to inspire and unite our nation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, Mr Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to recognise our past athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They have done Singapore proud in times when resources were scarce and inspired generations after them to take on the mantle and fly Singapore’s flag high on the world stage: Neo Chwee Kok, Tang Pui Wah, Tan Howe Liang, Wong Peng Soon and many more.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These are some of the names I grew up hearing and inspired me to train and represent Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have no doubt these were household names for some of our fellow Members, too, and they perhaps inspired some of us to pick up a racket, stick, ball, or track shoes and compete.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that Singapore has the talent to produce world beaters if we provide the right environment for the enterprises and athletes to grow and develop.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These sports icons have shown us it is possible; however, we must recognise our past achievements and be proud of our sporting heritage.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our National Sports Associations (NSAs) form a key pillar in our local sports infrastructure locally.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The NSAs' developed their respective sports, whose programmes form great social significance by being the glue that binds communities together.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The challenge for our NSA programmes in times of the pandemic is access to facilities and the ability to pivot during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: International Olympic Committee President Thomas Bach urged International Federations, not once but twice in 2020, to consider their sport in electronic and virtual forms.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: An example of international sports federations pivoting to virtual platforms is the F1 Virtual Grand Prix.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I want to encourage the Government to work together with NSAs to develop their respective digital strategies.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Use technology as an enabler, keep our athletes in the sport where they may not be physically able to participate, and keep them engaged as it is vital piece of our pipeline for athletes to continue participating in their respective development programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Needless to say, while the pandemic has negatively affected the sports and fitness industry in general; however, there were those who were able to thrive and were able to find new avenues of business.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: E-sports and gaming, for example, were sectors that grew during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In a year where regular broadcast and scheduling of sports games have been affected, e-sports maintained most of its original programming.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Players and leagues moved to remote broadcasting and content was streamed from homes or other remote locations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is in an excellent position to develop this industry, leading to good jobs for Singaporeans in the fast-growing industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must also not forget the other parts of the sports industry and sports enterprises whom the pandemic has adversely impacted.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: More could be done to help the private sports enterprises survive and to allow them to recover and grow stronger.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The pandemic has presented a unique opportunity for Singapore to play a crucial role in international events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore should consider taking on these opportunities, as there are many benefits to hosting these industry events here.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They are reinforcing our role in the global sporting scene and add vibrancy to the local sporting environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sport is relatable to many of us – we have yet to realise the full potential in maximising the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sport is important to Singapore and Singapore can play an important role in global sports.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I sincerely hope that this year's, and indeed future Budgets, will reflect the critical role that sports and athletes and sports business can, and do, play in our country, both economically and socially.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the world continues to battle COVID-19, I am heartened that Singapore is positioned to plan for our future, thus with this Budget focusing on "Emerging Stronger Together".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Earlier, Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Louis Chua reminded the Government that while we rejuvenate the economy, we should not overlook the vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is why the Government has rolled out many schemes in a "kuih-lapis" style to support lobal businesses and the vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This follows up on the changes started five years ago with the Industry Transformation Maps.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To enable businesses to innovate, transform and scale up, the Government intends to co-fund businesses of all sizes at all stages of growth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the Government's decision to step up risk-sharing arrangements with capital providers through the extension and enhancement of the Enterprise Financing Scheme - Venture Debt programme.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This new measure broadens the existing scope of assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My concern is that many financial institutions may be so conservative that even bearing 30% of the loan risk is too much for them, resulting in smaller and newer firms not being able to get any loans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During this age of massive transformation, there will be new business models, products and services which are coming onstream.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these new projects can be very capital intensive and need expensive equipment, such as digital services and urban vertical farming equipment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): The senior executives responsible for approving loans at financial institutions will proceed with an abundance of caution because their objective – to preserve capital – is different from the perspective of our Government, which is to encourage innovation and new engines of growth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, they tend to rely more on track records, proven business models, tried-and-tested products and services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the more experienced they are in the financial services sector, the more likely they will have deeper in-built preconceptions and biases.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For this reason, venture capitalists fill the gap for funding start-ups.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But many newer and smaller firms will have difficulty attracting venture capitalists.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without Government intervention, our small start-ups will find it hard to assess the Venture Debt programme.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As long as a firm meets the criteria, it should be able to qualify for the programme.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to ask if the Local Enterprises Funding Platform could be opened to larger SMEs as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They may find this scheme useful as they do not qualify for grants nor are able to position themselves as regional or international companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another suggestion which I support is to require Large Local Enterprises (LLEs) selected for this scheme to make complementary local SMEs and start-ups part of their overseas expansion efforts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In other words, to hunt in a pack.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Local companies employ more than 60% of Singaporean workforce, therefore elevating SMEs' capabilities also improves social mobility.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And this brings me to talk about the support rendered towards the lower income families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For disadvantaged children, we must make every effort to assist them so that they will have the best chances of growing up healthy and living fulfilling lives.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am very glad that the Government will be boosting the provision of social services and holistic care for lower income families with children who are staying in HDB rental flats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I would like to suggest that we make better use of data technology to reduce the administrative work and processing time for assistance applications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As I had suggested before in my maiden speech, the Ministry may consider allowing Social Service Offices' records to be shared with schools so that needy children do not need to apply for the Financial Assistance Scheme and school pocket money fund separately.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, for vulnerable families, particularly those with adults who are unfit for work and thus unable to find employment, their medical records stored in the National Electronic Health Record can be shared with the Social Service Offices in a secured manner, with authorisation by the needy applicants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will enable the deserving cases to be assisted expediently.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of the applicants are frustrated as they have problems navigating the variety of programmes and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will save them from having to travel from their schools to another centre.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is safer for younger students as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At school-based Student Care Centres, we can help to ensure that needy children enjoy enrichment programmes and get nutritious lunches, even dinners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to request for more resources and the deployment of Allied Educators to assist this group of students with their homework.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such an arrangement will benefit children living in less conducive home environments where crowding and noise, and the lack of supervision, books and IT equipment, prevent them from learning well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the National Library Board install book dispensers at estates with rental blocks which house many young families, such as Brickland and Hong Kah North constituencies, so that the children can have easier access to books?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, I would like to request childcare for shift workers to help parents who work night shifts who have no family support and cannot afford a domestic helper or sitter to keep an eye on young children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to ensure their safety and well-being.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last but not least, I urge the Government to expedite and increase assistance for vulnerable families with children with issues or special needs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These can range from those with milder to severe conditions, whether these are learning or behavioural issues, such as ADHD or autism, or other disabilities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is there any shortage of vacancies and if so, how many more places will be made available in the coming years?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us send in more reinforcements and secure more victories.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.30 pm until 4.50 pm. ﻿Sitting resumed at 4.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Thus far, we have collectively fared well relative to other countries in our battle against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This has been largely due to the leadership of our Government and the trust and co-operation of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is critical that our Government continues to take leadership by investing in key areas to help us seize opportunities to maintain our competitive edge even in challenging times like this.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Not only does this Budget support Singaporean workers and businesses in need of assistance, it is also seeking to bolster Singapore’s position in the new post-pandemic world through capability building, along with strengthening safeguards.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is Deputy Prime Minister’s message about “Building a Stronger Singapore, Together” with the focus on "Ensuring equal opportunities for all and supporting the vulnerable segments of our society” that resonates with me.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support this Budget of pursuing a Stronger Singapore that is defined beyond the sole objective of economic vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The reason is that as we pursue transformation in 2021 and speak of a digital, innovation-driven economy, we need to keep focused that the key objective is meant to help our industries and our people to harness the power of data and technology, to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The end objective is to improve the quality of our lives as well as create better opportunities for ourselves, including those amongst us who are less digitally savvy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If we are to achieve this, then our Government must stay ahead of the curve by putting in safeguards to assist and protect the different segments of the digitally vulnerable groups as we jump onto the transformation train.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the transformation train moves fast, it is critical that we manage digitisation risks to better protect our public and maintain public confidence so that we can make this transformation together, safely.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There are specifically two areas that I would like to highlight.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They are: (a) redoubling our efforts to help citizens strengthen digital muscles to improve cyber safety; (b) addressing the escalating cases of scams As we push for greater digital adoption and innovation, our citizens will find themselves empowered to do a broader range of tasks and services conveniently.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we need to help them build more digital muscles as they will each face not just opportunities but also challenges – the digital life ahead is fraught with challenges.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: An Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) study released recently in December 2020 noted that the levels of digital literacy in Singapore is low.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: More than half who are deemed savvy information-wise did not spot signs that information was manipulated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What is concerning is that many felt that cybersecurity incidents will not happen to them and that less than half installed security applications even though a majority of them know the risks of not doing so.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that our Government has rolled out many digital literacy initiatives through the Media Literacy Council, National Crime Prevention Council or the National Digital Literacy Programme in schools, or CSA initiatives, such as the cybersecurity labelling on all smart home devices, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, perhaps some time is needed for these programmes to take effect and it could be worthwhile for a co-ordinating body to take stock holistically based on the learnings above.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is to shepherd our population towards greater digital discipline as well as build a deeper awareness, especially in areas that need attention, to strengthen digital muscles across our country.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: After all, in cybersecurity terms, it is often said that we are only as strong as the weakest link.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A more fundamental issue at hand is that more Singaporeans are falling prey to online scams, losing large sums of hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Of this, online scams made up 60%, of which, most were related to e-commerce and social media impersonation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: He had released his bank’s ID, password and authentication token to a scam.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The money, it seems, was transferred to Hong Kong and the Police had told him that he is unlikely to get his money back.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: My heart goes out to him and other citizens who are like him.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is tempting to say that “giving your ID, password and token is like giving away your house keys”.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At one level, we need to continue to emphasise the need for individual responsibility and education.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, social engineering can be sophisticated, which is why even savvy people can be duped.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that our citizens are faced with a full spectrum, from simple to sophisticated scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I often hear people say, “What are the Police doing about it or what is MAS or the Banks doing about it?” However, at the heart of the issue is that the problem cannot be approached by focusing on a single or a few parts of the digital eco-system.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We already know that it is impossible to secure an email or bank account if the mobile phone is not secure and it is also impossible to secure a transaction if the e-commerce website is also not secure and so on.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our solutions to scams – processes, actions, laws and regulations – need to reflect this holistic approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this point, I have five recommendations to further sharpen our approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, maintain our current stance on community education.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is an essential pillar for our multi-layered defence to strengthen awareness and accountability at the individual level.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, like cybersecurity, we must always assume that scams will succeed.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The economics are compelling enough – with the sizeable amount of monies lost through scams, we should allocate a proportionately higher expenditure to fight online scams head-on.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: MAS is very engaged with the banking sector, and perhaps we can do more with other sectors as well.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, let us make sure that our digital economy has a multi-layered defence against cyber threats that necessarily includes a multi-layered defence against scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Budget, aptly named "Emerging Stronger Together", balances the following considerations: immediate needs to overcome the pandemic; investing in business and developing people to emerge from this pandemic stronger; strengthening our social compact; building a sustainable future; and maintaining financial prudence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understandably, this year's Budget is in the deficit as we continue to assist our residents to overcome the pandemic while sending a strong signal on the need for transformation and supporting future growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond addressing the immediate needs, I will touch on three suggestions as we work towards an inclusive, rapid transformation to secure Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 is a catalyst for many workplace changes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past, there was no urgency to digitalise to bridge physical distances in a country like ours.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the pandemic made it necessary for organisations to explore digital solutions, such as the use of Zoom, e-payment and e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We now better understand how digitalisation can help make our operations more convenient and efficient.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next step is to move from pockets of digitalisation, or "pilots", to fully adopting real and sustainable digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will enable us to go beyond the superficial grafting of technology onto current processes and instead, leverage fully on digitalisation and create fundamental shifts to our business models.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can MCI, MTI and MOM work closer together to support companies in driving real sustained digital transformation by stringing together cohesive programmes across Ministries to enable companies to build a coherent, successful growth strategy possibly through a clear Operations and Technology Roadmap from MTI supported by skilled manpower through MCI's Digital Leaders Programme and SGUnited Jobs and Skills training guided by experienced practitioners using MCI's CTO-as-a-service while training organisational’s capability to use data better through MCI's Better Data Driven Business Programme?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coming from the industry, trying to navigate transformation is difficult as this is not merely improving productivity but this is fundamentally transforming business models.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many companies, especially SMEs, may need help to navigate the multitude of different schemes available.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To assist companies to fully leverage on the suite of support packages available, can the Ministries consider some form of over-arching business transformation support through a mentorship programme or hand-holding to help companies navigate the cross-Ministerial support for transformation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need a more concerted approach to business transformation to help companies gain traction and better navigate the diverse cross-Ministerial support provided.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of the many upgrading courses available, many are on digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These courses need to translate into real changes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we increase the efficacy of these trainings into driving real digital transformation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One suggestion is to move away from measuring success through course take-up rates to measuring transformation driven metrics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A tiered approach can be used, where applicable, to provide basic subsidy for attending the course and enhanced subsidy for achieving the improvement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has taught us that for 60% of PMETs in Singapore, our jobs are able to be done anywhere and at any part of the globe.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers are no longer confined to office cubicles and close physical proximity is no longer a prerequisite for collaborative work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers are trying to implement HR policies that strike a fair balance between work from home (WFH) and work from office (WFO).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: WFH and WFO represents both a boon and bane.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We find the lines between work and home get increasingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Considering new working norms, MOM must ensure that the rights of both employers and employees are protected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore must remain an attractive place to work and we must retain talent within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fair workplace practices and good work life balance will provide us a comparative advantage as we shift towards new working norms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: WFH has demonstrated clearly how jobs can be done anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we debate extensively on foreign workforce quotas, let it not distract us from the fundamental question: how do we keep our workforce competitive and relevant in the global market especially when workforce quotas are losing relevance in protecting jobs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we prepare and upskill our workforce such that we remain relevant in the global economy and not only do jobs in Singapore, but also do jobs for other countries remotely?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, our workforce must be able to compete locally, as well as globally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And we must continue to focus on driving best added value with the right skillset, mindset and attitudes needed to thrive in a remote working environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Remote working requires a different set of skills for both employer and employee.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Clear work targets must be set in order to manage the output of the team.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And targets based purely on clocking number of hours have become obsolete.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employees are expected to be more self-directed and not take advantage of the flexibility afforded to them due to remote working.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While it is important to upgrade our workforce in terms of hard digital skills, we must also adopt the soft skills and a more suitable work culture for remote working.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I do not think it is premature to consider how schools can better prepare our children for a future of remote working.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our industry transformation roadmap was designed pre-COVID-19 and remains relevant even in the face of this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We aspire to be a greener nation as expressed through our Green Plan and a successful transformation necessitates getting everyone on this journey.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is inevitable that certain industries, like petrol-based industries, face decline while others, such as cleantech, green financing and horticulture see an increase in demand.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Bridging between the contracting and emerging industries will be challenging and it would be erroneous to assume that everyone can make the transition smoothly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, we need to balance and manage this workforce transition, especially when most of the jobs that will be lost are those of the lower wage roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I applaud the cross-Ministry efforts for the Green Plan, we need to chart out our workforce requirement and our workforce transition plan.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One suggestion is to have our Industry Transformation Roadmap be updated to specifically include transition strategies for low-wage workers, seniors and persons with disability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Industry Transformation Roadmap should purposefully feature this group of workers so that the industries can proactively redesign jobs for them in the post-pandemic economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would ensure inclusivity even at the point of job design.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is notable is how COVID-19 has transformed our world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some industries will enjoy growth, although some will shrink.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our world continues to move towards digitalisation, industry 4.0, "electrification" and clean energy and we need to move in the same direction or we will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This rebate, together with the Family Support Package, to some extent reduces the impact of rising oil prices as we prepare for and weather through the challenges of a rapidly changing world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I hope that the Government can study which rebates and relief packages are sufficient or need to be re-evaluated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is no right time to raise taxes and we also cannot impose high taxes in the future in the hope that people will quickly switch to electric cars.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps this is an opportunity for us to start using vehicles with lower fuel consumption or hybrid vehicles first to enjoy cheaper road taxes and petrol usage while also starting to do our share to lower emission rates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to elaborate on the two things that need to be addressed as we move forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has, undoubtedly, shown that we need not necessarily have to be at the workplace to do our job effectively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we are debating extensively on the foreign manpower quota, we should not let this matter divert our focus from the basic question, which is, how we can maintain the competitiveness of our workforce in the global market, whereas the manpower quota is increasingly less effective in protecting our jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we prepare the workforce and expand their skills so that we can continue to play a role in the world economy, not only doing jobs in Singapore but also jobs in other countries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The first step in doing so is to change our mindset, because we can no longer sit still and try to protect our jobs with methods that are previously effective for that objective.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the other hand, we need to stand out and show the world how we give the best value to any organisation around the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we move towards a greener future together, we need to realise that some industries will enjoy growth, although some will shrink.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, we aspire to reduce dependence on petrol and engines that use fuel, namely the internal combustion engine (ICE), while promoting the use of public transport.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our future generations also need to make wise decisions to seize opportunities in an economy based on future trends and not just make decisions based on choices that are easy or readily available.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to place our community in a more strategic position so that we can seize new opportunities and transit more easily to a future workplace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: GST forms part of Singapore's overall tax and benefit system which is progressive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the beginning of its life, it had to face its own battle for survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Eggs are under constant threat by predators and harvested by people.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: After hatching, it would have to unbury itself and cross the open beach to reach the ocean, all without being eaten.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Even in the ocean, life is never easy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What then, counts as a good life for the Hawksbill turtle?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Perhaps to live pain-free, to escape plastic pollution and fishing nets?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To find enough food in our depleted waters?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Or perhaps to beat all odds to find a mate amongst the rare few that remains.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are in the Anthropocene Epoch, where human activities have a significant impact on the planet’s eco-system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Humans thrive in societies of interconnected individuals who work collectively.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And this collective culture that allowed us to progress far beyond other animals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: By teaching, learning and relying on one another for resources, it has given humans the ultimate edge.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But today, cities and countries around the world are facing a multitude of challenges.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: No one will spare us quarter, we have to fight for our lives and our future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This Budget will give us the strength to survive, pivot, and an edge to seize the opportunities of the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many have been severely affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must continue to support our workers, fight unemployment and embark on a massive scale of education, training and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must help our low-wage workers and fight for those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Job growth incentive is one of the best ways in providing support to our graduates and mid-career jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, more support is needed to quickly acquire skills that are relevant and deep in their new domains.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must keep our edge, sharpen the edge and ensure that we operate at the frontier with a trail-blazing spirit.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This competition and innovative edge, driven by the same ability to connect, learn, collaborate and execute, is most poignant for survival and leadership.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These attributes enabled the rise of global market leaders.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The largest and most valuable companies from the 1960s to 2010s were General Motors, Wal Mart, Exxon, Ford and General Electric.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, in the last 10 years, this list would have changed dramatically with Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Google and Facebook taking on leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Artificial intelligence has enabled the exponential ability to learn, connect, collaborate and execute.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is self learning, it does deep learning, ever enthusiastic, ever curious and hungry for more data, ever analysing and tweaking for optimum outcomes and executing with flawless precision.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In 2020, the total accumulated data in the world reached 44 Zettabytes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is 10 times more than it was in 2013.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: You can have data without information but you cannot have information without data.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The goal is to turn data into information and information into insight and with insight one will be able to have the ability to execute.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Information is the oil of the 21st century and artificial intelligence is its combustion engine.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Is Singapore ready for this? “Are we all going to be working for a smart machine, or will we have smart people around machine”.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This question was posed some 30 years ago but this 30-plus years old question has returned with a vengeance because of Big Data.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The Intelligent Age driven by Big Data has been accelerated by advances in emerging technologies and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In fact, we are living at a time where everything that you have seen, heard or experienced is fast becoming searchable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Machine Learning, a subset of the AI technology pillar, has been recognised as the engine of productivity and one that spurs economic growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When incorporated into an organisation, it provides a 360-degree, multi-dimensional view of important metrics of the company and significantly improves the decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The analysis of large volumes of data reveals trends and bolsters the innovation of new products and services and generating new revenue streams.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The granularity of data enables decision makers to drill-down to reveal insights into a variety of predictable behaviors and incidents.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To cite an industrial advantage would be the manufacturing industry as they stand to gain the most from the digital revolution.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Technology pillars such as the Internet-of-Things, 5G connectivity and Big Data Analytics are likely to transform the industry into a cyber-physical hub, capable of assimilating and leveraging on these technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The return-of-investments would be most evident in the long run, when AI would further cultivate automation, ensure robust quality control and possibly actualising a near-zero downtime manufacturing plant.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Future software development will be automated through data.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Deep learning will continue to develop future capabilities such as conversational computers, self-driving cars, and consumer apps such as Tik Tok.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Tik Tok uses deep learning to push video recommendations and its success has outstripped many other first movers in the market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In this Information Age, the distinction between market and society as a whole and market and individual has been substantially eroded.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is because human beings are fast becoming both the raw material and the customer.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The interesting development is that the raw material in the Information Age is the "human natural resource", is no longer scarce, but readily available and free.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our behavior is being captured, stored and processed instantaneously.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Services and products are being developed through us which has come to be known as personalisation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Essentially, this is a commoditisation of human behavior.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This situation will continue to influence and impact human nature, the future of societies and new business models as we ourselves are fast becoming "human natural resources".

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This requires new ways of thought leadership, Government policies and laws.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As Singapore hones itself digitally and in other areas, it can also aspire to be a leader in this space.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Andy Grove once said, "technology runs 3 times faster than normal businesses and the government runs 3 times slower than normal businesses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What are the existing models, regulation, assumptions, norms today, existed because of the industrial age?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Are they still relevant in the Age of Information?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A recent example is Facebook and Google in Australia.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: AI, Machine Learning, Blockchain and Crypto are paragons of how transformational this revolution will and can be.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Mrs Lim Hwee Hua’s latest book "Government in Business – Leading or Lagging", provides poignant examples in a landscape of disruptive technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At such a speed, will Singapore be displaced?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Like fire, the spoken language, pottery, electricity, steam and internal combustion engine, it will affect the entire economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And unlike its predecessors, this pervasive reach into the psychological, biological and natural world can and will alter societies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Imagine a world at the advent of electricity, to have a bulb and a plug ready.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Ready to plug in and light up the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Or remain plugged out like the Hawksbill turtle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The extension of Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) in sectors still facing headwinds and the Covid-19 Recovery Grant for severely impacted workers are welcomed by many of our sisters and brothers in the Labour Movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with the extension of the Wage Credit Scheme and the Capability Transfer Programme, these measures ensure that our workers have good jobs and job opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over the last one year, NTUC's key priority was on protecting our workers’ livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through our NTUC Job Security Council and the Fair Retrenchment Framework, our unions have worked with management to cut costs and save jobs, as well as train and redeploy workers to sectors of need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many of us in the House would know that the aviation sector has been severely impacted by the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: After Malaysia announced the Movement Control Order to control the spread of the COVID-19 virus in early March last year, many manufacturing companies had a manpower shortage as Malaysian workers who commute daily between Singapore and Malaysia were unable to come to Singapore for work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many of my brothers and sisters in manufacturing sector had to pull extra shifts and put in extra hours in over time, just to keep up with the manpower shortage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Both unions worked closely with the companies’ human resource team to coordinate virtual job interviews and continued to keep in touch with these cross-deployed crew members to support their adjustment in the new workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With many workers' jobs at-risk, our unions' actions helped to secure secondment, contract or part-time positions into other sectors of need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC was able to leverage on our strong labour-management relations and our network of partners to make a difference in a dire situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I salute our workers for their fortitude and resilience and their adaptability; and of course, our unions who have worked hard to support them in this time of distress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This year, as we prepare to vaccinate our population and emerge stronger from this pandemic crisis, NTUC will continue to pay close attention to vulnerable worker groups who are more severely impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and who may also face additional pressures in the new economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For today’s Budget Debate, NTUC's Labour Members of Parliament will be advocating for the various vulnerable worker groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is in the DNA of the unions and also, in the DNA of the PAP Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will also lay out NTUC's proposals to better protect and empower these workers in order to strengthen Singapore's social compact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Labour Member of Parliament brother Mohd Fahmi Aliman, Nominated Member brother Abdul Samad and myself, we will share more about NTUC's aspirations and ideas to expand Progressive Wages and Practices to uplift our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With an eye to our ageing and shrinking workforce, NTUC Deputy Secretary-General brother Heng Chee How will share about what “Emerging Stronger Together” really means for senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC Assistant Secretary-General brother Patrick Tay will advocate for boosting the employment and employability of PMEs, especially those in their 40s to 60s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And NTUC Assistant Secretary-General brother Desmond Choo will call to strengthen the structure of the gig economy and support for young workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Labour Member brother Seah Kian Peng will raise concerns on vulnerable citizens who fall through the cracks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A second key thrust of our speeches is on protecting jobs through this pandemic and beyond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will share our plans for more pervasive business transformation to ensure workers and businesses are future-ready via the Company Training Committees (CTCs) and the Operations and Technology Roadmapping (OTR) process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC Assistant Secretary-General brother Melvin Yong will offer insights on how we should respond to the Work-From-Anywhere and the Work-From-Home phenomena developing in our workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And brother Patrick Tay will also call to strengthen the Singaporean Core while Labour Member sister Yeo Wan Ling will advocate for better choices, potential and protection for women in the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will then talk about how the efforts of NTUC’s Training and Transformation Group in Training of our workforce and Transformation of businesses via the CTCs and OTR has been useful in our collective efforts to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Nurses and healthcare workers are not low-wage workers but they are perhaps the most visible and recognisable of all the frontline workers performing essential roles during the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singaporeans questioned the gap between their salaries and their contributions to society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and industry associations that the NTUC have engaged with, agree that lower wage workers should be paid a fair wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Consumers have also shared that they are willing to pay more, if lower wage workers can directly benefit though higher wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the height of the COVID-19 crisis in June 2020, a survey commissioned by The Sunday Times showed that eight in 10 Singaporeans are willing to pay up to 10% or 20% more for essential services, if the money goes to the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This mirrors two separate surveys commissioned by the NTUC in late 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While consumers are willing to pay more for Progressive Wage Model, or PWM wages, we too need to guard against companies profiteering from these efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To do so, I suggest that a tripartite committee similar to the Committee Against GST Profiteering be formed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This tripartite set-up could investigate allegations of profiteering and ensure that any price increases flow into the hands of our lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This reflects the desire of Singaporeans for a fairer and more inclusive society that cares about the dignity of those who are less privileged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Building an inclusive and compassionate society is also a key thrust of this year’s Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Indeed, Every worker matters and every bit of effort counts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ensuring that those in the lower wage rungs get a fair wage must be a manifestation of a more inclusive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There will always be a group at the lower end of the wage spectrum that we need to continually support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is something that we will always have to keep working on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But starting at the "right" wage level is only the first step.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If we just stop there, then we run the risk of wage and career stagnation over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We must ensure that there is wage progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to address the following four areas so that our sisters and brothers can start right and progress well in their careers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, narrow the wage difference between the 20th percentile or P20 earners and the median income or the 50th percentile or P50 earners; second, enhance Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) to provide an immediate uplift; third, expand sectoral PWM faster to cover more sectors; fourth, implement "vocational" PWM to cover remaining lower wage workers in job roles that are distributed across multiple sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, on the narrowing of the wage gap between the P20 and P50, via the PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Labour Movement first championed the PWM in 2012 to help all workers across different sectors achieve sustainable real wage increases in tandem with skills upgrading and increased productivity levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Building on the impact brought about by these three mandatory PWMs, I suggest three further enhancements that tripartite partners can consider.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Currently, the mandatory PWMs for these sectors apply only to outsourced workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our sisters and brothers working as in-house cleaners and in-house security officers are not included in the PWMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I propose that they should be included in the mandatory PWMs, so that those doing the same jobs should enjoy the same protection, progression and wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This should be implemented as soon as possible because the framework and mechanisms are already there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, the wage gap between the P20 and the P50 must be narrowed so that the wage and social stratification will not be too stark and lead to social fragmentation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I can appreciate the different social economic situations and structures in different OECD countries that could account for these observed differences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But regardless of the reasons, NTUC hopes to see a greater range of salary increases for our lower wage workers over the next five to 10 years, so that cumulatively, our lower wage workers can close the wage gap with those earning median salaries in these sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our sisters and brothers in the bottom 20%, should not become a social underclass.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope MOM and the tripartite workgroup will study this possibility and work on a mechanism to uplift their wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, repurpose the Wage Credit Scheme as transitional support for PWM implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Recognising that the current economic climate may be challenging for businesses and consumers to bear the costs of the faster rate of wage growth associated with PWM fully, NTUC calls on the Government to consider transitional support measures for companies coming on board the PWM to help with the increased wage costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many SME bosses I spoke to are concerned about the additional wage costs they must bear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Furthermore, it takes a longer time for outsourced sectors, like the Lift and Escalator maintenance to implement mandatory PWMs, because companies need time for current contracts to run out and renegotiate contract prices based on new wage costs with their clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This means that workers would have to wait a longer period to get their salaries uplifted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I thus urge the Government to provide transitional support to companies, especially to our SMEs, who commit to paying PWM wages, to allow such workers to benefit from PWMs earlier, rather than later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I suggest the Government further consider repurposing the Wage Credit Scheme as a form of transitional wage support to help companies in new sectors implementing mandatory PWMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Next, let me talk about enhancing Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While awaiting the wider implementation of the PWM, I hope that Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) scheme can also be expanded to provide an immediate uplift.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope the Government will consider removing the differentiation of the payout by age groups and base the WIS eligibility purely on income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, a worker aged 40, earning $1,500 a month gets an annual WIS payout of $1,704.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Another worker, 10 years older, aged 50, earning the same salary of $1,500 a month, gets an annual WIS payout of $2,496, an additional $792 more than the worker who is 10 years younger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The 40-year old worker is more likely to have younger dependants and would certainly benefit from a higher WIS payout to supplement his take home pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope that every worker, every low-wage worker with similar earnings gets an equal uplift regardless of their age, to further strengthen our social compact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition to the above recommendations, I call on the Government to shorten the income assessment period for WIS eligibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Currently, the recipients must fulfil the WIS income ceiling criteria in the preceding 12 months before qualifying.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This delays much needed support for lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Shortening the income assessment period for Workfare will ensure that we continue to support our low-wage workers in a timely manner, leaving no one behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Thirdly, let me talk about expanding the coverage of PWM to more sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: My fellow Labour Member of Parliament, brother Melvin Yong, has been leading this effort since 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I recall the story of brother Dickson Tong, my Union Leader in Metal Industries Workers' Union (MIWU).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Brother Dickson is a senior lift technician with Hitachi Elevator Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: He remembered being rather fearful after being stuck in a lift when he was just five years old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To his young mind, the lift technician who came to his rescue was like a superhero.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Imagine in a dark lift and the door opens, this lift technician has a halo of light around him, coming from the outside.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has inspired him to join the lift maintenance sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the past 20 years, as a lift technician, he kept up with the technological advances in his area of work, ensuring that he had the skills to stay relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Now, with the recommendations of the Sectoral Tripartite Committee for Lift and Escalator sector, brother Dickson and other lift technicians can look forward to two career progression pathways: supervisory or specialist tracks, where skills are the benchmark for career progression with corresponding salary increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The implementation of PWM in this sector will hopefully attract more new entrants for a more fulfilling career.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hopefully, we will have many more superheroes, amongst us, waiting to rescue anyone who may be stuck.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
