text: NTUC wants to speed up the implementation and expansion of PWM into six more sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Last year, NTUC mooted for PWM for the Waste Management sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since the formation of the Tripartite Workgroup for Lower-Wage Workers (TWG-LWW) in October 2020, the Tripartite Cluster for Waste Management has been formed in January this year, to develop and implement a PWM for this sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC has also been pushing for a PWM in the Food Services sector since 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In my recent engagement with business owners and members of the Restaurant Association of Singapore, many expressed support to raising the wages of the lower wage workers and are supportive of the PWM for this sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We certainly hope to make progress in this aspect over the next two to three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The tripartite partners also see the potential in the Retail Trade sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC hopes that the Tripartite Clusters for these two sectors – food services and retail trade sectors – will be set up soon, with recommendations released by this year and implemented within the next two to three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While most workers in this sector are technically not low-wage, a PWM for this sector can be an enabler for better progression and better work prospects for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is because their wages can remain quite stagnant due to the outsourcing nature of this industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This could potentially benefit more than 5,000 workers in the strata management sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC intends to submit our proposal to MOM by mid-2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Following the launch of the industry-led Career Development Plan (CDP) for the Solar Technology sector in December 2020, NTUC has also started discussions with the relevant associations to develop this CDP further into a PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Again, while this is technically not a low-wage sector, we believe a wage-skills ladder linked to productivity and career progression will be useful for this growing sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During my last Parliamentary speech on the topic of PWM in October 2020, I proposed that beyond a sectoral PWM approach, the tripartite partners should also look at a "vocational PWM" for lower wage occupations that cut across multiple sectors to improve their wage prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Expanding the PWM efforts beyond the confines of the sectoral boundaries will allow larger groups of workers such as clerks and logistics drivers to benefit from the PWM to uplift their wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The skills framework for these vocations that has already been developed by the Tripartite partners together with SSG can form the basis for a "Vocational PWM" to be developed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This approach should also form a key outcome of the TWG-LWW discussions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One key tenet of the PWM is sustainability, ensuring that the higher wages are coupled with higher skills and productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Training of workers and transformation of business is key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The NTUC Training and Transformation Group (T&T) set up in September 2019 aims to address this need by supporting the formation of Company Training Committees (CTCs) between companies and the unions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC partnered A*STAR in the utilisation of the Operations Technology Roadmap (OTR) which facilitates the companies' transformation process and develops mid- and long-term business strategies and workforce training plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Last year, with many more companies seeing the need to transform and respond to the challenges and restrictions imposed by COVID-19, NTUC T&T developed a virtual/hybrid OTR in collaboration with A*STAR, leveraging on digital technology to assist companies in their transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond engaging individual companies in CTC and OTR, NTUC T&T has embarked on Sector OTRs working in close collaboration with Trade Associations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: An example of a sector OTR is with Waste Management sector between NTUC, the Building Construction and Timber Industries Employees' Union (BATU), the Waste Management & Recycling Association of Singapore (WMRAS) and the National Environment Agency (NEA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Following the success of the sector OTR, NTUC T&T is engaging individual companies in WMRAS to form individual CTCs to develop their Company level OTR for customised action plans and deeper transformation of the companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We look forward to working closely with the respective TACs to advance our mutual interest of Training Workers and Transforming Businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In English): Sir, I will now conclude in English.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Upskilling and ensuring our workers have the skills relevant to industry needs is an important aspect of the PWM that ensures employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The PWM is minimum wage plus, because to the Labour Movement, the minimum is just not good enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We want to see progression of wages over time through upskilling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A progressive wage is about recognising the dignity of our workers through their work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is about paying a fair wage and ensuring that the wages of those in the bottom 20% keep pace with the rest of society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The PWM implementation must move faster and wider in line with the aspirations of Singaporeans to build a more just, compassionate and inclusive society where we leave no one behind – every worker matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with our Training and Transformation efforts via the CTC and OTR, NTUC wants to make "Every Worker a Better Worker", make "Every Job a Better Job" and to match every "Better Worker to the Better Job", so that we can make "Every Company a Better Company".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Only then, can we emerge stronger with a better economy and secure three wins all round for our tripartite partners and make Singapore a "Better Singapore for every Singaporean".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, I think the starting point is then, there are progressive elements in our tax system and regressive elements.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is especially poignant when the world is still dealing with the effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am encouraged by the "Emerging Stronger Together" Budget and I am certain that I speak for both myself as well as my colleagues in the Labour Movement in supporting the response of the Government in helping all sectors of society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As mentioned by our Deputy Secretary-General of NTUC Dr Koh Poh Koon, over the last one year, NTUC's key priority was on protecting our workers' livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Having said that, "Emerging Stronger Together" also means being aware of those with additional challenges, such as our lower wage essential workers and our foreign workers, and making sure they have the help they need so that we move together in unison.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: COVID-19 has undoubtedly changed how we live and work, and it has prompted us to question the norms that we have become used to.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One of these norms in question is the value our society have placed on the work of our brothers and sisters in essential services such as cleaning and security.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we adjusted to our new normal, these everyday heroes stepped up despite the risks to their health and took on extra duties such as the additional sanitisation of high-touched surfaces and temperature screening, so that we can safely continue with our lives.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The formation of the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower Wage Workers is a step in the right direction in acknowledging their contributions to our country.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Representatives from various stakeholder groups have come together in the tripartite workgroup in recognition of the importance of uplifting our lower wage workers, and NTUC will continue to contribute significantly to this conversation and champion our lower wage workers as it has always done.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement is sensitive to the concerns of these workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We are cognisant, for example, that workers, especially those who earn lower wages, are concerned about their cash in hand to meet their daily needs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC is also acutely aware from our interactions with essential service workers that many of them face barriers when it comes to training.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This could be due to factors such as time constraints, lack of support from employers and even language barriers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As part of the tripartite workgroup, NTUC is committed to finding ways for workers to overcome these barriers and look forward to working with our partners to ensure that any worker who wants to upgrade their skillsets to remain relevant will be able to do easily.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With it, workers have a clear sense of the skills needed to do their jobs and the skills they should attain to move up the career ladder.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Companies have also benefited from better trained and skilled workers while service buyers benefit from a more professional workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This move is to be commended and underlines the important work of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: On this note, I would like to call upon all the stakeholders involved in the PWM to take a hard look on the value of the jobs provided by our essential service workers and consequently increase PWM wages, so that all Singaporean workers are uplifted.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The reality is that in increasing the wages of our essential workers, consumers may have to pay more for their services.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is never an easy call to make but it is an important step towards a fairer and more enlightened society, where we ensure that all workers can live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To ease the initial transition, I would like to call on the Government to consider a form of transitional support to help service buyers in the interim as we adjust the wages of our essential workers to adequately acknowledge the value of their work to our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is also timely that we look into other sectors where the PWM could benefit our workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC is also constantly looking at other sectors to cover more workers under the PWM.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In 2019, it was announced that the pest management sector will be subsumed under the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map in the hopes of transforming and uplifting the sector to provide good and sustainable jobs to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This marked a step in the right direction in acknowledging the integral role pest management plays in safeguarding public health in providing essential services such as preventing the spread of dengue, rodent and pest infestations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite this, more needs to be done as the sector is faced with many of the same challenges as that of other outsourced sectors such as stagnating wages, lack of manpower and poor public perceptions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For the industry to meet the rising demand and expectation of service standards for services, there is a need to build a strong and skilled professional local workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In the Labour Movement’s interactions on the ground, we have also found that the workers in the Strata Management Sector take on the important and demanding task of managing estates and providing all with a conducive and safe environment for us to work and play, and their duties include the control, administration, maintenance and management of common property for the benefit of all.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The introduction of a PWM can uplift these sectors and their workers with a clear career progression pathway, coupled with the relevant skills, improved productivity and the commensurate wages.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC will continue to lobby for the expansion of the PWM into other sectors and will work with the relevant stakeholders to make this a reality for more workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One clear step is to procure and support companies that have progressive practices.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This admittedly may mean paying more, but we can and should be mindful of unethical companies who choose to undercut to win contracts at the expense of their workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Workers in these situations can suffer by having their wages reset or their benefits cut at the onset of their employer taking on a new contract.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Service buyers should also adopt outcome-based contracts or OBCs as a complement to PWM.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: OBCs prioritise the outcomes rather than simply warm bodies which allows service providers to use technology to make work safer and more efficient for workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Besides, OBCs should incorporate clauses to minimise wages and benefit resets and abide by the principle of proportionality where liquidated damages should be proportionate to non-delivery of services.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While we look at wages and work prospects, the welfare of our workers is equally as important.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Outsourced workers should have access to proper and reasonable rest areas for their well-being.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Services buyers will also benefit from well-rested workers who would be productive.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to call on the Government to issue a Gross Floor Area waiver for areas stipulated as rest areas to encourage more landlords to adopt the tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Another hard but necessary conversation that COVID-19 has sprung upon us is regarding our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I will not be the first to thank our migrant workers for their hard work and their contributions to our country, all while working in difficult conditions far from their homes and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In working towards a more progressive and moral society, we must not forget our vulnerable brothers and sisters who have come here to do hard work so that we can continue to move forward.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Via the Migrant Workers' Centre, NTUC mobilised together with our other stakeholders during the lockdowns at the dormitories to ensure that the migrant workers continued to have the necessities they needed and also reassured them that they had the full support of Singaporeans in tiding through the crisis.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One of the issues that the crisis brought to light was the immediate need to improve the living conditions of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While many changes have been made to make the dormitories safer and safe-distancing measures have been put in place, there remains a need for us at this time to review how foreign worker dormitories are regulated, and if these regulations should be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This move would ensure that more or all the foreign workers in Singapore will be housed in accommodations that are regulated and meet the minimal provisions for their health and safety.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: During the lockdown, it was also brought to NTUC’s attention that many foreign workers faced difficulties in remitting money to continue to support their families back home, many of whom were in more dire straits due to the global pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This was a distressing problem for our migrant brothers, despite the simple solution by ensuring that all migrant workers are paid electronically.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Extending this requirement to migrant workers would not only make it easier for these workers to manage their finances electronically, but also protect these workers from being exploited as all salary payments are recorded.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC has long looked after the welfare of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: An example is NTUC's MWC working with MOM’s ACE to materialise the Settling-in Programme at the various onboarding centres.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While this has been a challenging project, NTUC has stepped up and is ready and willing to work with MOM towards building a robust system for future new entries to protect the workers as well as the greater community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The MWC has also 5,000 ambassadors in the more than 1,000 dormitories in our volunteer network, and we are constantly looking for ways to scale up to support any new initiatives and programmes that can benefit our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This network has helped us reach out to our migrant workers and we will continue to work hard so that we can push on in fighting for their rights and welfare.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   In summary, I spoke today about how the Labour Movement has always championed our workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By providing adequate support to our workers, all of us will benefit from a more knowledgeable and professional workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I also said that mandatory electronic payments for migrant workers will not only make it easier for these workers to manage their finances electronically but also protect migrant workers from being exploited as all salary payments are recorded.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): In conclusion, we have come a long way since the first few cases of COVID-19 appeared on our shores.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: There is still a long way to go and, inevitably, there will be challenges along the way.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, as a country, we have weathered similar storms and emerged stronger.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Government and NTUC are committed to helping workers every step of the way and will continue our fight for a fairer and more progressive society for all because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Gerald Giam, you have a clarification of a Member who has spoken previously?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are questions that we are also working out in the tripartite workgroup because each and every sector will require a discussion with the relevant stakeholders, both on the employers' side and the other agencies, to determine which particular job roles we want to include in the PWM.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the numbers will not be something that we can tell offhand.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is a process to discuss, and also how, in the vocational type of PWM, we have yet to define what exactly are the vocations that we want to go into.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not something that you can just say that we want to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But we need to get more data, working with the relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will come back – I suppose at some point – to this House and, certainly, the tripartite workgroup will release a stronger recommendation with more details towards the end of the process.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will allow one more clarification, Mr Giam.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I understand that things are still in the works, but what is the kind of rough timeline?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Is it five years, 10 years or 20 years?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And for different sectors, some may be more ready to implement earlier, some may take a little bit more time because either the wage structure or the skills framework needs to be more tightly stitched together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One that is Focused, Forward Looking, For businesses and, most importantly, For workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I wish to make a special highlight for a segment of our workforce which the current downturn and the COVID-19 pandemic have impacted immensely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are the Professionals, Managers and Executives, PMEs in short, in Singapore, especially those in their 40s to 60s.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce, which was formed end 2020, has started to engage PMEs to better understand their concerns and priorities in the past three months.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We found that PMEs are particularly concerned with job security and employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The taskforce also conducted a series of Focus Group Discussions, which are still on-going, with various segments of PMEs from the young to the not-so-young, including our union leaders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The PMEs we met highlighted the concerns of unfair hiring practices, workplace discrimination, career progression, as well as health and mental wellness issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many also shared their personal anecdotes on difficulties in getting employed due to their age, inability to land a job despite undergoing training, as well as coping with disruption and the next normal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Despite that, it was encouraging to hear that many of our PMEs recognised and acknowledged the importance of continued upskilling, reskilling and multi-skilling to ride the wave of disruption and to stay relevant in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Against the current economic climate and the challenges that COVID-19 has brought about, I cannot help but emphasise the need to put Singaporeans at the heart of our policies and programmes that impact their employment and employability – in short, their lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For a start, more must be done to better protect vulnerable PMEs who are in their 40s to 60s.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need support from both Government and employers to ensure that they are not discriminated at workplaces, have fair access to PME roles, as well as training and progression opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is, therefore, timely to review, expand, extend and tighten related schemes, laws, policies and programmes which can better protect and support PMEs in the areas of employment and employability to ensure fairness and inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One, tougher measures to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While many of us recognise the contribution of foreign PMEs to Singapore’s economy and reasons why we need them, there remains a ground concern that the reliance on foreign PMEs has led to an unnecessary increase in competition in the job market and employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To safeguard the Singaporean Core and curb discriminatory hiring, we must ensure that Singaporean PMEs have access to a level-playing field for jobs while balancing companies’ manpower needs in the intermediate and longer term.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The qualifying salaries of both the Employment Pass and S Pass holders were recently raised in 2020.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But this needs to be regularly reviewed and raised in line with rising median wages of PMETs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The problem is that some PMETs view the increase in qualifying salaries as "raising" minimum wages for foreign talents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There are also ground concerns pointing to employers who raise the salaries or repackage the compensation and benefits of their foreign PMETs to comply with the rules, and not give similar pay hikes to the Singaporean PMETs who work alongside these foreign PMETs performing similar or even same jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We also hear that there are employers who "downgraded" their Employment Pass holders performing the same job functions to S-Pass to "comply" with the policy changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We therefore need to look at ways to further strengthen the S Pass criteria and conditions to prevent such a back-door approach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This also means we need continued stricter enforcement against errant companies with a weakening Singaporean Core, especially those who continue to be "triple weak" – companies with highly disproportionate number of foreign PMEs, weak commitment to nurture and strengthen the Singaporean Core, and weak relevance to Singapore's economy and society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Besides administrative and penal sanctions that are already in place and can be enhanced, I have lobbied before in this House and am highlighting again that enforcement can come in the form of revealing or publishing the "triple weak" watchlist which Ministry of Manpower and Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) maintain, so that the potential reputational loss would serve as a deterrence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We can also impose mandatory audits and penalties, such as removing preferential tax and other benefits, including curtailment of the award of public sector contracts on companies with discriminatory hiring practices and high proportion of grievance cases if no improvement is made within a stipulated time period.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I agree and support when Deputy Prime Minister highlighted the principle of "complementarity" when it comes to hiring of foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Often, employers bring in foreign PMEs to fill skills or knowledge gaps in their current workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As such, it is imperative that we monitor and ensure concerted, structured and institutionalised skills and knowledge transfer from these foreign PMEs to our local PMEs within a stipulated and agreed timeframe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Employers must also have clear development plans to grow the Singaporean Core and build a pipeline of locals to fill roles at all levels of the hierarchy including the top.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Anecdotally, some companies increase the hire of only the entry-level Singaporean PMEs to increase the workforce size to circumvent the issue of a disproportionate percentage or number of foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Besides employers and businesses, employment agents and agencies operating locally and also overseas, and hiring for PME roles in Singapore must also be closely scrutinised to ensure they keep within the boundaries of the law and eradicate unfair recruitment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token and in the spirit of strengthening the Singaporean Core and cases of preference for foreign PMEs, which is a form of nationality discrimination, we also continue to hear anecdotally of ageism, especially from the mature PMEs we speak to, as well as other forms of discrimination impacting workers, such as in relation to gender, disability and race and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Such a legislation could send a stronger signal than the current tripartite standards and guidelines, to send a clear deterrence, give TAFEP wider powers and eradicate all forms of discrimination and discriminatory practices at workplaces by employers as well as employment agents or agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, transitionary insurance, also known as unemployment insurance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we have seen in 2020 amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, many sectors and workers have been affected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I agree with Prof Hoon Hian Teck and I am cognisant that there is a need to do a deeper dive and examine the mechanics and the actuarial viability and sustainability of such a scheme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There are important considerations, such as the trigger event, premium amounts, duration and amount of payouts, whether it should be made compulsory to avoid self-selection, how we price the risk, the need for a critical mass or universality and whether it is to be implemented by any of our tripartite partners or all three partners together or by a private sector entity or a social enterprise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Notwithstanding, we have seen such a scheme work well in countries like Germany and in some of the Scandinavian countries without causing excessive burdens on governments, employers and employees alike.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There could also be a possibility to explore and seed fintech or an insurtech start-ups to come up with such a scheme but with strong support from tripartite partners especially the Government in the form of seed funding and support as well as co-funding.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, this year's budget is a targeted, forward-looking Budget, designed to help businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am most concerned about our mature PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: (In English): We recognise the growing need to ensure PMEs are adequately protected, have access to good jobs and are equipped with the relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we prepare for the next normal, it is important that we continue to entrench progressive and fair practices at workplaces and extend schemes to support local PMEs, especially the vulnerable workers because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement and our unions can support local PMEs by working closely with employers to put in place multi-faceted support and strategies to enhance one's job security and skills security through our Company Training Committees and Job Security Council.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, it continues to be crucial to level the playing field for our Singaporean PMEs, strengthen the Singaporean Core, eradicate all forms of discrimination through tougher measures and targeted legislation and support PMEs and workers in general, to transit effectively and less painfully between jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To put it simply, we need to prepare ourselves with new skills, pivot to new industries and jobs and persevere amidst the next normal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope we will upturn the downturn this year, build back better and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But while we continue to provide support to affected sectors, we need to also address new macro trends that are developing in our workforce and at our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will focus on two of them in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are the phenomena of Work-From-Anywhere and the Work-From-Home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In his speech, the Deputy Prime Minister spoke briefly about workplace trends and hinted how in the not-too-distant future, Singaporeans will be able to work from anywhere in the world, with just a laptop.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I cannot agree more with the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, I would argue that the Work-From-Anywhere trend is already happening today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This ability to work from anywhere is both an excellent opportunity, as well as a serious threat for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Competition for jobs will increase and this will no longer just be limited to talents located in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Instead, competition can come from literally anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What kind of jobs will be at risk?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With seamless connectivity, supported by 5G technology, every job is at risk.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But Singapore has never feared competition, even in the darkest of times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Instead, we learn, we adapt and we always strive to do better than the competition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To prepare Singapore for the eventuality of global competition, we will need to re-think our key manpower policies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Will our Work Pass and Employment Pass regime remain relevant when companies no longer need employees to be physically based in one location to perform the work?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How long will this conventional system of balancing our local-foreign workforce mix continue to serve us?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The ability to work from anywhere will bring the world closer to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A good example is James Kwa, a Business Development Manager at Asia Market Entry, a consultancy company that partners with the Economic Development Board to bring investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Prior to the pandemic, James had to travel up to three times a week to meet and attract technology companies to set up shop in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But his company had to innovate due to the global shutdown in air travel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: James now hosts overseas companies virtually through a suite of video content and video conferencing tools.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When the pandemic is over, James and his company intend to continue hosting clients virtually, as the time saved from travelling allows them to showcase Singapore to even more clients.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By 2035, technological advances will have a major impact on the social and economic foundations of society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, we are already seeing an increase in the popularity of online project management tools, such as Asana, which allows managers to remotely manage team members based anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As technologies like 5G and autonomous robotics begin to proliferate, governments will have to confront a major dilemma – how much of the country's key economic activities will be permitted to be run by companies and operated by a growing workforce domiciled elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our public officers will need adapt in the face of such major developments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But how many of our public officers today are ready to take on the challenges for tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are our public service schemes ready for the day where life expectancies in Singapore reach well over 90 years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will speak more about the pressing need for our Public Service to take the lead in remaining adaptable during the COS debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We also need to invest in the right public service infrastructure to seize the opportunities of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Contrast this to January 2017, just four years ago, when our first supercomputer, the Aspire 1, was then ranked 115th in the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Have we lost pace in the development of deep technology infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There is also an urgent need to re-look at SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Clearly, we have hit a point of marginal returns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to thoroughly review the SkillsFuture Credits programme and tweak the objectives of the programme to equip Singaporeans with future-ready skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my multiple visits to our Autonomous Vehicle (AV) trials locally, I met Ken Chia, a member of the National Transport Workers’ Union.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Ken is a bus captain who is now a certified AV operator.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When the AV is in operation, Ken’s responsibility is to ensure the safety of his passengers, and to take over manual control of the vehicle when needed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Instead of a conventional steering wheel, Ken uses a small hand-held console comprising two joysticks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: He jokingly said that it was easy for him, as he played plenty of video games during his teenage days.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But in reality, the initial training was anything but easy for Ken.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More comfortable with the Chinese language, he had a tough time understanding the original training content, as it was taught in English by a French instructor!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the company stepped in and the training materials were translated into Chinese for him.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The lessons were also adapted to provide more hands-on training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Working from home, however, has brought along its own set of challenges, relating to space and care-giving needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, being productive while you work from home requires sufficient space.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without a dedicated area to work, we are easily distracted with our children and by other things in the house that need our attention.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unfortunately, space is increasingly difficult to come by.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: HDB flats have shrunk in size, understandably, due to the reduction in our average household in size.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But with more working and learning from home, is it time for us to return to building bigger HDB flats once again?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: An extra 15 sqm can provide Singaporeans with a study room that can also double up as a home office.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, let us provide better support to care-givers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For many, working from home also means juggling work with care-giving needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These informal care-givers are often disadvantaged in their careers and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we have an opportunity to change this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a Straits Times survey, eight in 10 workers in Singapore prefer to work from home or have flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With this new normal of working from home, we need to encourage more employers to adopt flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will allow care-givers to concurrently work and care for their loved ones, without having to make the difficult decision to choose one over the other.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Radin Mas, we are building an eco-system to support our residents with care-giving needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Last year, we brought some of NTUC's most experienced career coaches to the community centre to help those who need career guidance and job placement services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This has been particularly helpful for care-givers who had left work for a period of time and were struggling to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Residents with care-giving needs often tell me that they cannot afford a long commute to work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With this initiative, we hope to plug this gap and help match our residents with nearby companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Most jobs on offer today are just a short bus ride away.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is an unprecedented move that befits the unprecedented crisis that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we tackle the twin challenges brought about by the pandemic and the macro global trends affecting our workplaces, I am confident that the resources set aside in this Budget will spur transformation among our workers and our businesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The extension and enhancements made to the Jobs Growth Incentive will help all segments of workers, including mature workers, persons with disabilities, as well as ex-offenders, to transit into jobs in growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement stands united with the Government in helping Singapore emerge stronger together from the shadows of the pandemic and tap on the opportunities that the future holds.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's only natural resource is our people, and safeguarding jobs for Singaporeans must continue to be our key focus.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged by the various measures in the past and current Budgets to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While we keep our economy open and have foreign workers to augment our local workforce, we must create more employment opportunities for our locals and continue to strengthen our Singaporean Core at both the sectoral and company levels.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The local and foreign talent complement has also resulted in high reliability standards that the sector is known for.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore Power (SP) Group, where I am working, there is a local workforce of more than 95%.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The employment practices in this sector to build the Singaporean Core can be a learning model for other companies to emulate.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to call on all employers to make the local workforce your employee of choice and ensure skills transfer to the local workers to moderate reliance on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, our Government can consider putting in place policies or incentives to recognise companies who build a stronger Singaporean Core and develop their local workforce across all levels, through positive differentiation among companies who do not.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There are many manpower policies that are at the disposal of MOM to achieve this intended outcome of developing a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: My next topic is about workforce transformation through training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Having a strong Singaporean Core includes ensuring that their skills remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my second point which is about the importance of training has shifted from equipping workers with today’s skills to preparing the workers for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions are committed to work with employers to help our workers build their capabilities, upgrade their skills and transform by setting up Company Training Committees.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, the Union of Power and Gas Employees where I have the privilege to be the General-Secretary, has collaborated with SP Group in their mission to develop future skills roadmap to enhance the employability of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Launched in 2018, Project Fusion, which stands for "Future Skills in Everyone", looks at how will current jobs change, what are the new jobs, what are the future skills, and how can our workers learn these future skills.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a holistic approach to future-proof the workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I urge employers to take the lead in the development of workers to meet the evolving needs of your industry by identifying relevant future skills and taking advantage of the economic downturn to train and transform your workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC can support by working with the companies to facilitate an Operation Technology Roadmap workshop to identify strategic technological changes and training needed to help the company transform.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Skills upgrading must go hand in hand with productivity improvement and career advancement to ensure sustainable wage increases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Workers who are performing higher value-added jobs should look forward to better wages, welfare and work prospects, in line with the productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This can be achieved through the PWM, which leads to my third topic for today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While it has thus far been implemented in low-wage outsourced sectors, including cleaning, security and landscape, the PWM is applicable to all sectors and PME jobs as well.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, many of the unionised companies in the Oil, Petrochemicals, Energy and Chemical industries have a structured career development plan for their employees that is mapped to skills and salary ladder.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is akin to the PWM's value proposition and has allowed many workers to achieve sustainable wage growth through upskilling and career progression.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe every responsible employer has a career development plan for their workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond having that career development plan reside in the individual company, I would like to echo NTUC’s aims to have PWM in more sectors and call for sectoral agencies to work with employers, unions and professional associations to implement the model, beyond the existing mandatory sectors.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The sectoral level PWM will allow workers to have the visibility of the career pathways and salary progression in tandem with the skill upgrading and productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Workers will have sight of the career and salaries that the sector has to offer them as well as the required skills and training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will provide a useful roadmap to attract fresh graduates, mid-career switchers, develop and retain locals in the sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: During downturns, the visibility of the sectoral PWM’s skills will facilitate cross-function, cross-company and cross-sector mobility for workers from restructuring companies to companies that are hiring.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With all the above effort and examples, I hope to see more sectors come onboard and implement the PWM!

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, they also hope that the Government constantly monitors this situation and continues to implement measures to reopen the sector with international partners, so that the industry can resume its activities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, the Labour Movement wished to express their appreciation to all companies that retain and support their workers through the Jobs Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As far as possible, please avoid any retrenchment because when a worker loses his job, it will impact the whole family's finances, and not just the worker's.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Make use this time instead to send your workers for training to upgrade their skills and to identify new skills that you will need, so that your workers are better equipped for any new job in the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Among the skills needed right now and in the future are the various technology-related skills such as digital skills, data analysis, artificial intelligence and so on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers need to identify the type of skills required from their employees when identifying the type of training required.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We always hear about workers having difficulty or refusing to undergo training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please do not blame the workers entirely on this issue of training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Actually, our hope is that such training will enhance our status as workers in order for us to have good careers, better welfare and a better working environment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we also hope that, after undergoing training, our salaries will increase in line with improvements in our productivity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Having a strong Singaporean core will encourage and motivate Singaporean core workers to upgrade their skills and compete hard to secure employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): I would like to close my speech by making two key points.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: First, NTUC will continue to help workers of all collars, ages and nationalities achieve gainful employment through better jobs and a better living through higher wages, so that they can live a better life.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We call on the Government to continue formulating and implementing labour policies that aim to develop a globally competitive workforce and a great workplace, for a cohesive society and a secure economic future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To our employers, who are tuning into this Budget debate, we hope that you will do your part to transform your business, enhance productivity and competitiveness and upskill your workers for future jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As a union leader and on behalf of all my fellow sisters and brothers in the Labour Movement, I would like to take this opportunity to express our utmost appreciation to all my fellow essential service workers, be it in healthcare, cleaning, security, transport, telecommunication, nearer to my heart – power and gas, even water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The impact of COVID-19 on the world and on Singapore has been tremendous.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While we in Singapore have kept fatalities to a minimum, the devastating effect of the pandemic on the economy and on our livelihoods is obvious.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it is not just the percentage points; that will convert into jobs loss, families impacted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, I think it is important for us to recognise what that massive action has helped stave off, in terms of suffering, for fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For 2021, whilst we must continue to look after our jobs and businesses, and contain the negative impact of the pandemic, we cannot just do that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must, at the same time, look at how to get back on track for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this is the theme of this year's Budget, "Emerging Stronger Together". "Emerging Stronger Together" is not a slogan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is not a nice-to-have, it is crucial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, why is it necessary to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We all know that we cannot count on an endless $100 billion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Never mind what size of our reserves but we would not have an endless $100 billion to keep on spending time after time to block pain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must also assume that there will be future downturns that will come our way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In what way, in what form, what triggers it, we do not know, but come they will, one day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, we have to find sustainable ways to replenish our national kitty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our reserves are like the airbag in our car.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If we used it, we have to refill it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Otherwise, the next accident, we may not survive so well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist for some time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Major economies will use fiscal and monetary policies to keep their economies going to avoid the recession, amid a tepid inflationary environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Now, what this means is that the returns we can expect from investments are likely to stay low.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As we all know, we already used a good proportion of our NIRC to fund Government expenditure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And if the outlook is so, then we cannot just plan on the basis that what we do not want to spend out of our reserves, should the need be that we will naturally get it from increased investment income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Third, whereas on the revenue and the money side, we have to more careful, but the need for the Government to spend more in upgrading our infrastructure, as so many Members have explained, in the different sectors is clear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And so is the crucial need to continue investing in our people and taking better care especially of our ageing local population and our workforce in an increasingly volatile environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is a reality that we cannot escape, be it structural.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To do that spending, we have to find the money somehow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These reasons and factors converge to make it imperative that we go back into maintaining a laser-sharp focus on transforming our economy and to get growth going again.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Otherwise, Singapore will be hard pressed to find or to create the resources that we need for that national journey ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As we seek ways to emerge stronger, we must also ensure that we do so together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And I can think of two reasons, at least.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, we must plan on not leaving any group behind as we emerge stronger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When we say in the Labour Movement "Every worker matters", that is Labour Movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is key to our national, social cohesion and stability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, we must enlist the contribution from every group, every segment and every individual toward emerging stronger and staying resilient and self-reliant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The more we can do so, the more we will strengthen national resource creation and moderate the rise in Government welfare expenditure or the need to bring forth more taxation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: How to emerge stronger together in the context of the senior worker – that will be the focus of my speech today, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: With regard to senior workforce, I would like to propose five measures in order for us to emerge stronger together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, continue to save jobs and create jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I name all these because sometimes they get lost as we look at the overall Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But I just want everybody to remember that all these schemes were rolled out purposefully in order to make a difference to the employment and employability of all our workers, senior workers included.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They have given much breathing room to firms in 2020 and have helped thousands of workers keep jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This has enabled the overall employment rate for our senior workers to remain stable last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I therefore fully support the fine-tuned extension of these schemes in this year's Budget to continue to save jobs and lighten the load on firms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It would not be easy for such displaced senior workers to find new work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I therefore urge more Government support in order to step up specific, industry-focused efforts to help senior workers in these distressed sectors to keep their jobs, or if not, then to proactively be retrained and placed into jobs in other sectors and industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Two, press on with agreed timetable to raise statutory retirement and re-employment ages and CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The tripartite partners have taken to legislation to ensure older workers have the opportunity to work longer by raising the retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: After all, being employed is the best safety net and companies need workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement called for tripartite discussions on this subject in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This schedule was first put in place by the tripartite partners to enhance the retirement and re-employment framework, strengthen older workers’ retirement adequacy, and to further promote progressive workplaces that value older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many companies and organisations have proven that this can be done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our social enterprises will do so from 1 July this year, also as earlier announced and this is a year ahead of the national timeline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Outside NTUC, outside the public sector, when we look within the unionised sector at the private sector employers, we have been encouraged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have seen more than 100 employers in the unionised sector who have voluntarily either upped the retirement age within the company or increased the re-employment age within the company, or both.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This number, compared to the number that we saw in 2019, it basically doubled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it covers companies across different sectors – we have companies who are in the attractions area, the hotels, food manufacturing, childcare and there are many other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To help workers enhance their retirement adequacy, we also called for sustainable increases in CPF contributions for older workers over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement deliberated hard but we supported that deferment because we understood that in the depth of that pandemic, in the depth of that disruption, the most important thing is employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We do not want our older workers to be put at unnecessary, greater risk of losing their jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Yet, Mr Deputy Speaker, while we do that, I want to remind this House and everyone out there, that we must be careful to keep pace with our original intent and purpose of helping older workers enhance their retirement adequacy, given our longer lifespans, on average.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This was the purpose for that workgroup, for my calling for it in 2018, for the consensus that was developed for that agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It was for a strategic purpose – in order to secure our national objectives and to make that as many of our older workers would have better retirement adequacy, which is a point that is shared by both sides of the House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, I also urge the Government to help employers defray the cost of their enhanced CPF contributions through the CPF Transition Offset, which was also within the plan prior to the deferment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In Budget 2019, I pointed out that if we can implement flexible work arrangements more systematically and pervasively, we will be able to retain significantly more local workers, and allow more middle-aged workers to undertake care-giving without having to quit work, and to return to work post-care-giving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I was very pleased that Mr Melvin Yong has made specific arrangements within his Radin Mas constituency in order to bring this forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it is important that we do so, because it would be a pity if our workers have to choose between work and family, just because companies do not offer enough flexible work options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It has forced the employers to re-assess how work can be conducted in non-traditional ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In other words, not necessarily at the workplace, not necessarily full-time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Certain roles can be done from home, at least a good part of the time or part-time work might be actually doable in combination, or to implement, for example, staggered starting times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the way in which you can maximise the use of your manpower and tap manpower sources can be a lot more flexible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: COVID-19 has opened the eyes of both employers as well as workers too to that possibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This can significantly improve employment outcomes for senior workers, for the middle-aged older workers who might otherwise have to leave work in order to look after older family members and then, cannot come back.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When COVID-19 struck, businesses started to pivot more to technology and individuals also had to quickly pick up new skills in order to be able to cope well within that new situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Nowadays, using our smart phones, laptops and tablets to order food, scan QR codes for services, to conduct meetings online and leverage e-commerce platforms have now become very normal, second nature to businesses and many individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Senior workers had to adapt and many did.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: What has that taught both employers and our senior workers?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That lifelong learning for lifelong employability is completely achievable, can be done, has been done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: COVID-19 forced us; a lot more amongst us have done so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, once again, just like my call on that flexible work arrangement insight not to go to waste, we must also not let the progress achieved through this painful adaptation during the pandemic with regard picking up new skills, using of new technology, we must not let that be wasted and must not allow old mindsets and prejudices and old practices to return that would only stymy us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Otherwise, with these fast-changing business models and technology, we can only expect even more and faster displacement of our senior workers and that would lead to all those negative scenarios we really dread and want to avoid – chief among which would be retirement inadequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To do so effectively, there must be specific mechanisms within industries and workplaces to operationalise the intent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It means that it is not only about policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is about who is supposed to get together with whom in the company to discuss what is needed, who is supposed to be sent for what and then, to execute that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They can then be our machinery to ensure that purposeful skills building takes place in the economy, and that workers of all ages – and here, I have a particular emphasis on senior workers, for reasons that are quite obvious to us all, that they are vulnerable to be left out and therefore, we must not let that happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: CTCs will be the machinery where we can better ensure that they are not forgotten but that they are included and they are part of this progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For many years now, workplace health has focused on wellness and chronic disease management – diabetes, high blood pressure and the like.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, COVID-19 has taught us something else, that we cannot say that we are not vulnerable to infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And depending on what we are talking about, these diseases can indeed pose a severe threat to individuals, corporates and even to our whole economy and society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Where such infectious diseases can be prevented or be better managed with vaccination, it must be to the advantage of workers, firms and the state to assess which are the most cost-effective, science-based ones, to vaccinate against.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will also help forestall potential discrimination against senior workers’ employment or employability on account of real or perceived higher risks of infection and the impact that might have on company operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to do our utmost to work with tripartite partners and senior workers to enhance their employment and employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must also ensure that the right HR practices are in place to tap the potential of senior workers and to recognise their contribution because every worker matters, our older workers matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is what emerging stronger together really means for senior workers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the coming Committee of Supply (COS), most of my cuts will be on social and family development issues, covering our social safety net, social service delivery, partnerships with community, building resilient families and also, how we can further make lives better for our women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I will not dwell on these here.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister’s Budget is a careful rendering of the bread and butter of our national life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It takes care of all the big moving parts – health, housing – and the big items – defence and education.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng said, and I quote him, "We averted the worst and prevented deep economic scarring and permanent impairment of our economic strengths." We saved jobs, spent on healthcare and now we are making sure all of us are protected.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the clear and visible, the immediate and vital policy goal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But there many things that are invisible and they take generations to grow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our sense of identity, what kinds of persons we are and how we relate to each other.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Increasingly, this is not just a matter of real life interaction, but also a matter of online culture – how we speak and write to each other when we cannot see each other face to face, when we think of the "other side", not as a human being with feelings, a sense of dignity and to whom we owe duties, but as faceless digits.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is then that we feel free to insult, to complain, to load with vulgarities, expletives and crass innuendos.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To live the good life there, we need to develop a good online culture.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A debate on the Budget may seem like an odd place to speak about this because I am speaking of things that money cannot buy – grace, civility, integrity and simple good manners.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These are things that we cannot tax into oblivion or incentivise into existence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But together, they form the culture of our public life and we can only cultivate these by mutual agreement and collective effort.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Increasingly, this means paying more attention to the way we live online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For many of us, using cash has become a rare occurrence, as we move more and more to tap our cards, or to scan with our phones.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But online payments require not just a smartphone but also reliable wifi or broadband – bare essentials to some, but expensive for others.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to do more to make these available to the lower income.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In an increasingly digital world, these must not be seen as luxuries but as basic transport into a life of dignity and ease.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Providing the basics of a digital life is as much a public duty as it is providing national defence and education.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In one of my cuts to MCI later on in COS, I will speak about the trend of rising online scams.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have already put in place a few piece of key legislation in terms of disinformation and falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One missing piece I think in our policy to protect Singaporeans against scams and to grow their digital literacy is to identify who among us is vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Government put together a simple online literacy assessment, or give guidance on a specific set of information that all of us should know so that we can see where our weak spots are?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
