text: This is a simple "scan", like the way we would scan our computers, so see where our weak spots are, or a health check-up so we can see if our cholesterol or blood pressure is too high.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think MCI would be best placed to see this through and provide different scans to different age groups.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: MOE is already providing the necessary hardware for all students to learn.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the pandemic that we are going through, the move to online learning and the use of technology has been very quick and much faster than originally planned.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, low-income families can already apply for subsidised computers and free broadband through the IMDA's NEU PC Plus programme.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to make sure that families have devices that are functioning at a high enough standard for good online learning.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More important, children from lower income homes are struck much harder.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I hope more can be done on this front by Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since 2014, the Home Access programme has provided many low-income households with subsidised broadband and cheaper devices.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, there are hundreds of families who have access to free broadband.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think this will be a great equaliser.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The above are some things that money can buy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Now, I want come to things that money cannot buy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, I call attention to the rising culture of negativity in the way we relate to each other online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have had, for many years, ambitions towards a kinder, a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While there has been good progress, there is much scope for further improvement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, first, I suggest we turn our good intentions into action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The is under the new Change for Charity Grant that he announced.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Corporations and public alike should give it full support to make it work and to bring cheer to the disadvantaged in our midst.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hopefully, this could become a regular feature and part of the Singapore way of life in future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Again, wearing my NTUC Enterprise hat, we are already doing some of this but I have asked my colleagues to see how we can participate and support this programme in a stronger way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we ourselves to be more considerate before we demand others to be so?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we cut everyone some "slack" especially when they get it right most of the time?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I had a resident staying in a nice $6 million house, that is my estimate of the worth of the house.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She complained and demanded to know why she was unable to get the SIRS payout.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another resident of mine who, without fail, will, on a regular basis, send me photographs of how a particular staircase in his block would be littered with tissue paper here and there.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Fortunately, for both him and me, this problem has been solved.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This culture is leading to a certain type of online persona, where cynicism, anti-establishment, is a shorthand for intellectualism and political sophistication.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this trend, general negativity towards all things Singaporean is taken as proxy for moral courage, especially when it includes a dose of disdain and disrespect for public institutions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a poor reflection on us, at a time where we have done so much that we can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, we need to recognise that being a nation of champion complainers is not all there is to being Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot help it, and taken in moderation, complaints are a vital part of public life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must notice mistakes, we must raise our voices and we must hold each other to the highest standards.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I do not want to be a Pollyanna about our political landscape.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I ask today for us to consider whether we have gone too far in the other direction, to feel every pin prick as a broken bone, to raise our voices and abuse our fellow countrymen, especially those in the public services and in the frontline, as if they are in our debt.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Building a culture of unity and a strong sense of identity has always been a challenge in Singapore, a country that is too small to count on its own domestic market, but an ambition too large to be denied, too diverse to take our nationhood for granted but united enough to agree, over 50 years, on things which have torn many other countries apart – race, religion, language, politics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Before I end, I want to highlight my strong support and thanks to Government for the continued enhancements and incentive schemes for organisations to build and to strengthen their local core and the strong support for mature workers, as what my colleague Senior Minister of State Mr Heng Chee How has just talked about.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Wearing my NTUC Enterprise hat, this is close to our hearts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, the more senior in age staff, they may be a tad slower, less physically agile but they make up for it with their patience, their dedication, their competence and their reliability.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must look out for each other and always make sure we bring people along in our transformation journeys and leave no one behind and most importantly, we must accord respect to all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These threats towards fragmentation and polarisation have become ever more important, as the reach of the digital empire grows.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To combat the dark sides of this empire, we must recall what we owe each other, an obligation and a duty to respect each other.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must recognise the role each of us play in our public life and join together in this journey with maturity and common purpose.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For my fellow Labour Members of Parliament and the many union leaders, like Nominated Member of Parliament Abdul Samad, and many other Industrial Relations Officers working hard on the ground, NTUC led by our Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng, will continue to walk the talk, will continue to push for workers' interests, always striving to do better with our actions amidst the complaints.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our sisterhood in the union is stronger than they have ever been, with our sisters being represented in leadership positions in every single union, and indeed, even in Parliament, the female voice is strong.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As I look upon the women in my life, whether it is my mother and sister who are always there for me, the ladies in the taxi unions who would make passionate points about the need for self-care; the young ladies at my Edusave Awards who would beam at me with such pride when I tell them to shine bright for other little girls; the women in my constituency who comes to me with tired eyes because of their relentless care-giving duties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I cannot help but think that there are miles to go before we sleep, that there are miles to go before we sleep.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, while we live in a contemporary society that promotes equal opportunities in school and proactively creates level playing fields at work for both men and women, the work must continue to hum along to allow women to: one, reimagine their career and livelihood pathways; two, protect women when their decisions impact their livelihoods; and three, to ignite women to fully achieve their potential as they reach for the stars and beyond.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even as we weather the storms of crisis, where households incomes have taken a hit, women have once again risen to the occasion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In World War II, as men were called to the frontlines, women held the fort by stepping up to the plate at home, in industry, in healthcare, to carry families and nations through, in times of great crisis.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our women warriors are gritting their teeth and putting on their battle gear as they enter, or re-enter the workforce, take on multiple jobs, or keep at it with their unwavering work ethic to maintain their family's livelihoods, while keeping the nation's economy vibrant and diverse.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 blew into existence, a strong and wicked storm that devastated many livelihoods and brought many to their knees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This same storm also brought with it, strong tailwinds that created the opportunity for reimagining the impossible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For decades, companies had struggled with the notions of flexible work arrangements vis-a-vis company productivity and bottom line.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With COVID-19, overnight, most companies had to deep dive into work from home arrangements and many companies are now considering making this the default in their new normal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the same forces which kept our women workers out of the workforce – long working hours, long work commutes – are now being resolved, and there is now a wonderful open opportunity for a different narrative on redesigning jobs for a more inclusive workplace, not only just for women, but also for workers who need flexible work arrangements such as PWDs, seniors and well, people who just prefer such progressive work cultures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, we must make use of this opportunity to continue to let women reimagine their many possible livelihood options.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women can be anything they choose or desire to be: a career in STEM, a professional crane operator, a plumber, a harbour pilot!

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our career choices are limited only by the imagination, and the union will work with our Labour Movement companies and associations to redesign and reimagine jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In turn too, I hope that the Government would be able to place more resources to encourage companies to have a relook into their work processes and to support companies through their job redesign strategies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every woman warrior needs to be equipped with armour so that they can go the distance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recently met with our female union leaders of our taxi driving sisterhood and they made a very passionate point about how the recent petrol duties hike would impact their livelihoods in adverse ways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This impacts the careful balance between their caregiving duties at home, self-care for their mental wellness and the time spent on their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, it might be worth noting that many of our female cabbies are single parents and thereby just makes the balance even more challenging.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: True to the protective gear that the union would provide for all our workers, our unions would take the feedback and work with our tripartite partners – LTA, the taxi, private hire platforms, taxi platform in coming up with further support to ease the transition into the higher duties and also other COVID-19 related difficulties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I met with a rather distraught constituent who was very stressed about managing her care-giving responsibilities at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She has three young ones and her youngest one has special needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After speaking with me at length about her issues, she actually heaved a sigh of relief and said that she would now go over to the nearby KFC.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She explained that once a week, she goes to KFC for 45 minutes for a coffee break.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She spends this time all by herself and she will watch a quick episode of a Korean drama, which, incidentally is also 45 minutes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I was intrigued and I spoke with my friend, who is a clinician about this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She smiled and brought up that, indeed, studies have shown that women need 40 to 45 minutes a week for themselves to recharge before going back to the marathon of life’s responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we see our pots boiling over on the stove, do we not remove the lid a little to remove the pressure?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An important figure in this whole eco-system to support the movement of Singaporean women returning to work are actually our foreign domestic workers (FDWs).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many women workers I know have shared with me that they see their helpers as an extension of their own families, and form close ties with these "aunties" who help look after the elderly and young in the family as if they were their own relatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although it is regretful that recent spotlights have been cast on negative practices between employers and their FDWs, I believe that the general undercurrent is optimistic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together with the NTUC’s Centre for Domestic Employees, my team over at the Women and Family Unit conducts a monthly advisory and legal clinic for employers and FDWs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I was delighted to observe that the vast majority of people who came to our clinics were here to ask for pro tips on how to best relate to the people who were living with under the same roof.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that with mutual respect, understanding and awareness of each other’s needs and boundaries, FDWs and their employers in Singapore, can be good model examples of exemplary employer-employee relations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we support women with their responsibilities at home and eagerly beckon them into the promised land of the workforce – work must be done to ensure that the land of opportunity does not turn into the land of the opportunistic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workplace harassment spares no gender, but women undoubtedly bear the disproportionate portion of such incidences.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Plenty of women go to work every day, looking forward to maintain a livelihood, support their families and fulfil their career aspirations – yet are forced by "necessity" and "conventional wisdom" to occasionally look over their shoulders in case of practices, actions or even speech that threaten to muddy the professionalism of their workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must enquire whether these narratives of "conventional wisdom" that suggest harassment is a mainstay to be expected, the default way of things, should still stand.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Surely, I do not think this is how things are meant to be.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coveted honours of being a "great place to work" must always play second fiddle to the bare necessities of a "safe place to work".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And this is the assurance our workforce needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, a safe place to work also extends to good fair hiring practices, good work-life harmony and progressive retention and employee development policies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Amidst the hustle and bustle in Singapore, is a 40-minute break considered long or short?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At a Meet-the-People Session, I met an angry middle-aged woman.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Honestly speaking, her aggressive and angry look was very intimidating indeed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We spoke for a while, gradually her anger subsided and turned into a stream of endless grievances and helplessness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To a woman in her 30s, troubled by endless family problems such as annoying children, no income, no food for the next meal and so on, a 40-minute break has unknowingly turned into a kind of luxury, a desire and an out-of-reach oasis.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must provide care-givers with respite service as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Respite service is a short-term service provided with the aim of alleviating the burden of care-givers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must raise people's awareness, build an inclusive and empathetic society together, and reduce the worries of care-givers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in English please.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world is still mired in COVID cases and lockdowns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are now seeing shoots of growth in key economies as vaccination efforts continue to expand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the worst of the pandemic has seemingly been averted, future recovery is far from certain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It must not be lost on us as we conduct the debate that we had narrowly averted a much deeper recession and that the next cliff can be just the next cluster away.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we need to deal with the current pandemic and recession, problems that come with it, it is equally important to plan for the nation’s future in a post-pandemic world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must tackle structural changes such as accelerated digitalisation, the new normal of remote working and reconfiguration of supply chains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First of all, we must continue to support Singaporeans through difficult times by enhancing and shoring up local hiring demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Protecting the Singaporean Core is a key priority for both the Government and the labour movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our labour market has shown a marked improvement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Resident employment has, in fact, returned to pre-pandemic level at end of 2020.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is the result of the Government’s initiatives in protecting the Singaporean Core, and the sacrifices of workers and companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While some companies have progressively started to hire, many are still hesitant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The JGI extension helps to bridge this hiring gap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also suggest that the Government can consider enhancing JGI for our workers above the age of 62 through added subsidies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These workers are more prone to cyclical and structural changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, they are likely not to be re-employed as companies reduce costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will help companies to hire older workers even during uncertain economic times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, the Job Support Scheme, or JSS, is one massive life jacket.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It kept businesses afloat and workers in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some industries have since stabilised, others have grown.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement supports the extension of the JSS to companies and workers in sectors that are still hard-hit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The unions and workers in the aviation, aerospace and hospitality sectors register their appreciation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the global border restrictions, these sectors will need longer recovery timelines as they reconfigure their business models.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These sectors need workers and companies to be ready to capture rebound opportunities when the world is eventually opened for business.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we need to provide additional assistance to our younger Singaporeans to adapt to the new economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pandemic has accelerated the growth and demise of many industries, jobs and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But many younger Singaporeans could now find themselves on the wrong side of the growth curve and are unable to take advantage of the new growth opportunities in fast-growing industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To do so, I have three suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some studies have suggested that students graduating in recession years earn less than their peers graduating in non-recession years, and the effects persist for a few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For some younger Singaporeans, they need to pivot to other sectors that are growing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I suggest that we can help to provide subsidies and loans for their second diplomas, or degrees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Not only would this improve the economy structurally, but this would also complement the lifelong learning attitude we wish to instil in all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This shows the importance of the programme in helping our graduates get skills and opportunities even during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry consider the provision of incentives to encourage and support host companies to convert these trainees to full-time hires?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will help companies hire these graduates ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, we must enhance the mental well-being support for our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The economic outlook has understandably caused much stress across the workforce, especially that of our younger Singaporeans still hunting for full-time jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To better support the mental well-being of our youths, could the Ministry consider training youth care ambassadors equipped with the requisite adjunct support skills to help fellow peers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The labour movement, especially that of the Young NTUC, will work towards extending our support for the Government's initiatives in providing peers with emotional and employment support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The key attraction of the gig economy is in its flexibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It gives workers the autonomy to choose when, where and how they want to work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As of 2019, there were about 200,000 residents who did freelance work as a regular form of employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the creation of new business models, this segment of the workforce is expected to grow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is already an important and permanent part of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And the measures must recognise that and support that growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pandemic has unearthed structural problems within the current state of protection for the platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SIRS was instrumental in supporting these workers during the crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Going forward, it is timely for us to review the regulatory framework to protect these workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the lack of protection for platform workers under the Employment Act and the Industrial Relations Act has provided significant power to platform companies relative to the workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has left platform workers on the shorter end of the stick without statutory recourse such as medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is understandable as the Employment Act and the Industrial Relations Act are premised on an employer-employee relationship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, most of these workers are lowly-skilled and wholly dependent upon the platform companies for their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The lopsided bargaining powers also means that companies can unilaterally change the terms of their service and incentive structures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Moreover, as workers are classified as independent contractors, they lack the ability to collectively bargain and negotiate wages or change working conditions with these companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement's recent formation of the National Delivery Champions Association is a positive step forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But their hands might be tied by legal restrictions on collective representation for service or employment terms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on the lack of social protection for platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The crisis and rapid growth of e-commerce have provided a livelihood for workers performing work for platform companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is seen in the food or goods delivery, especially during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, this can be a problem in the long run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a pressing need to review the social protection of these workers if we want this sector to thrive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ideally, platform companies should voluntarily commit to the protection of their workers' social security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, if there are such contributions, this might reduce the take-home pay for such workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The current nature of regulation towards these companies is rather light touch.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As with many other countries, many platform companies enjoy employer-type of powers without similar and few responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There can be more room for companies to commit to the protection of our workers, without curtailing the industry's viability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In this vein, can consider looking into subsidies and or disincentives to further encourage platform companies to commit to the longer-term social protection of our workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, because these workers are considered independent contractors, there are no incentives from companies to train them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, there are long term impact on Singapore's workforce productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To ensure that these workers can thrive as an essential part of the workforce, workers must work continually upskill for greater employment security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are difficult trade-offs in developing the gig economy, especially for the gig workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a big piece of work that the country has to work on and the Labour Movement stands ready to support the Government's initiatives to better protect gig workers to ensure the development of the gig economy as a permanent fixture of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have advocated for the greater protection and empowerment of vulnerable groups including lower wage Workers, Professionals, Managers and Executives, Self-Employed Persons, and mature workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We recognise that many of these challenges, the cyclical ones are still before us and we also deeply recognise that many of the challenges, the structural ones are existential threats to Singapore if we do not manage them carefully.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will take strong tripartism to tackle them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we must work even closer to re-tool, reskill and transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will and must continue to work with the Government as partners to support workers through job re-design, training and workplace support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our message is a simple one – "Protect Vulnerable Workers, Protect Jobs".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to work closely with the Government and employers to do right by our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We shaved 1.7% from the rise in unemployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I think that is putting workers at its core.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that similarly, this Budget reflects the People's Action Party's Government and NTUC's DNA that Every Worker Matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because tripartite partners have worked closely together and Singaporeans singularly united, did we avoid a deeper recession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So now, we must work together to emerge stronger from this crisis to ensure that workers continue to enjoy better wages, welfare, prospects in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Deputy Leader of the House, Mr Zaqy Mohmad.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This year, I received feedback from some Singaporeans about measures to restore our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead of the usual range of suggestions on spending, they are thinking of ways to add to our coffers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I find it most encouraging and comforting that despite the hardships, people are aware of how our predecessors’ savings have helped our generation through this crisis and want to do the same for future generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand and empathise with the predicament of residents who are cash-strapped but I am afraid I cannot support this kind of suggestion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education and healthcare, especially for our children, are too important to our future to be compromised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The defence of our little island is too critical for us to cut corners.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The world does not become a safer place during a global crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We just have to work harder and smarter to earn the funds we need.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, it is important that we continue to attract quality investments and see to the realisation of such investments to create quality jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a vibrant economy and job market, we will be able to rebuild our national savings slowly but surely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to upgrade ourselves to stay competitive and future-ready for many more years to come, as more jobs are at risk in the face of disruptive technology and the advancement of AI and big data.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are also potential new sources of tax revenues in the new economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we need to relook at our economic model.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: New technological developments are benefiting owners of capital and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need a harder push towards a more innovation-driven economy so that more Singaporeans are on the side of capital.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may be the only way to reap the benefits of technology developments and scale up to reach markets beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also timely to explore new economic sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The agri-food cluster is a good initiative to boost a new industry – one which we were not developing as much in the past due to concerns over land constraints.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, new tech enables vertical farming and new ways of fish farming.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are very much a people focused on property gains.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans dream of being a landlord with at least two properties – one to live in and one to rent out – or making capital gains from selling properties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I hope more Singaporeans will consider the other pathways to wealth creation – to create a new product or service, or a new type of business.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have already started on this journey and hence, more needs to be done to engage and help small enterprises and the self-employed, so that they can grow into bigger entities or continue their trades into their senior years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we have to ensure Singaporean’s love of properties will not drive up property prices beyond the reach of the majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us remember that residences are primarily meant to be lived in as homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, we have to be mindful not to be trapped by our properties, or some would say, be a property-slave, which is another way of describing an asset-rich, cash-poor property owner.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are in genuine difficulties due to sudden job losses or illnesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are willing to consider right-sizing their homes but need time for the sale of their properties to go through.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But there are others who request government assistance though there are alternatives available to assist them, such as right sizing, renting out rooms and signing on Lease Buyback Scheme which do not even require them to move out of their homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Government resources are finite, and financial support and assistance must be targeted at low-income groups who do not have the option of monetising assets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):    No matter how difficult our economic situation is, I hope that the Government will continue to support our elderly and senior workers through financial, healthcare and workplace support measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this most needy group, I hope that in addition to the Government, our entire society will continue to give them more care and love, and donate money or commit time to help them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): This Budget is commendable for the continuous support for the vulnerable groups through financial reliefs and various rebates and vouchers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More proactive measures to address the hardship cases of the unemployed would have been helpful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand from some residents they were unable to receive their financial assistance as quickly as they would like.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, I heard that a number of participants under the training programmes did not receive their monthly allowance on a timely basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During this period, every delay would have caused financial strain to the participants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to help middle-aged and senior workers who had lost their jobs to reskill and move on to new careers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would suggest the Government also look into incentivising companies with support to upskill their workers regularly, yearly, such as setting aside a minimum number of days of paid leave for the workers to upskill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To resume our economic activities, we need to get our people vaccinated quickly so that we can work with other countries to keep our air hub open to encourage business travellers and tourists to visit Singapore, with all public and safe health measures in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to ensure Changi Airport continues to remain the leading transport hub internationally.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has brought forth many changes, enabled by digitisation and high speed networks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, we need to help local enterprises to export and do online sale to overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is that it will be difficult to get more charging stations set up in existing carparks, including HDB carparks, private condos and office buildings.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many building owners are not keen to install them as the investment cost versus the demand for EV cars are still not well-matched.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Incentivising the continued investment to improve the technology are as important as incentivising car buyers to switch to EVs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if a young child falls sick, he is given at least five days' medical leave by the doctor due to COVID-19 conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At least one parent has to take leave to look after the child.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the same child falls sick again, the other parent will have to take leave.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Working parents with young children struggle to manage the demands of bringing up a kid with employment demands.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has thrown longer term trends into sharp relief, increasing inequality between industries and workers, with some industries basking in the sun even if sunset falls on other industries; some slowly, some more quickly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, fossil fuel-related industries will feel the long-term pressures from global decarbonisation, especially with the new US administration reinserting the world's largest economy back into the Paris Climate Change Agreement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, Sir, I shall speak about the changes going on in the world with industry transformation – a theme I have talked about in recent speeches in this House – and what are the strategies we should adopt to help our workers, firms and fiscal institutions adapt to these changes and use them to our advantage as a country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is my first Blackberry phone, which I obtained in the early 2000s and this is my second Blackberry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It took me a very long time to switch to a different device because I was comfortable with them, because they worked fine, because it meant I did not have to learn how to use a new device.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It was far more attractive to stay in the comfort zone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I only switched when things reached a point where I was concerned about being able to continue using the devices I had grown so attached to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I use this example because it tells us a lot about our relationship with technology, but also the economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When things are going well, we like to stay in the comfort zone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Even when you can see change on the horizon, even when you know you cannot go on in the same way forever, you say, "Well, why change today?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why not tomorrow?" But how do we nudge people out of the comfort zone to embrace change and face the future, even when things are, for now, going reasonably well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is also a national challenge for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many workers in delivery industries and doing driving work will see their jobs displaced by drones and autonomous vehicles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, for all these jobs, things are all right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To take another example – discouraged workers are workers who have given up looking for work because they feel their job search would not yield results, perhaps because of a lack of employable skills or confidence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will start with companies and as I do so, I declare my interest as the CEO of an international research consultancy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A look around the world shows that many companies and industry sectors, ironically, did well out of COVID-19 and grew financially as well as in terms of market position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Industries like FMCG, online retail, ICT and biomedical, on the whole, did fairly well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, has corporate Singapore, on the whole, fared as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, during this COVID-19 period, the Straits Times Index (STI) under-performed the broader MSCI Asia-Pacific Index, setting aside US markets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many, not all, but many of our larger firms are facing headwinds due to being in traditional sectors or not yet being able to innovate their way out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Even a number of homegrown companies have decided to go public on foreign exchanges rather than Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This calls in question why there are so few examples of local firms drawing on entrepreneurial talent rooted in Singapore, who have succeeded in becoming globally competitive?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is the environment conducive to start up and scale up?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Or is the talent and motivation not forthcoming?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In past speeches, I have talked about the role of education in fostering an entrepreneurial mindset.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Today, I would like to focus on the environment to start up and scale up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is an important national imperative to cultivate the core of locally based firms that have the DNA to be globally competitive to balance our dependence on MNCs, who may be fickle and buffeted by the winds of global economics and domestic politics in their home countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Have years of schemes, like the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) in the past, as well as host of other SME development schemes brought us closer to this goal?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would argue that we need regular published audits for our SME schemes to establish what causal effect such schemes have had on the long-term growth and competitiveness trajectory of local firms who use them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Only then would we understand the return on investment from such schemes and only then would we be able to design better schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, what is the evidence that the PIC scheme substantially catalysed productivity growth and innovation among the SMEs who were beneficiaries of the scheme?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A KPMG report from 2015 stated and I quote, "while take-up rates have gone up, the scheme's impact on productivity has been muted".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Major investments in schemes intended to generate economic outcomes – or in fact any outcomes – should be accompanied with regular measures of success.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not just numbers of companies helped, but how did the schemes move the needle in terms of productivity or other indicators?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And these measures should be published to support public scrutiny, accountability and debate, so that we can meaningfully speak of genuine participation in policy-making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave the subject of supporting the development of local firms, I would like to suggest one new approach that can be experimented with in incentive design.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We currently award incentives to MNCs and local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These incentives are tied to fulfilling certain conditions like meeting total business spending, headcount and/or fixed asset investment targets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can some of the incentives to MNCs be designed in such a way as to avoid a more generous degree of incentivisation if the MNC works with local partners to share know-how and gives the local firm a stake in the new investment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This approach is not novel and has been attempted in other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are risks associated with this as it might be seen as pursuing an nativist agenda of grooming local champions to compete with the MNCs, thus deterring MNC investment into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, those risks can be managed, by only awarding such a conditional incentive in fields where there are sufficient local firms who could make reasonably good partners to the MNC while not being involved in a domain that is substantially competitive with the MNC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is worth experimenting with such an approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Incentivising the development of MNCs and SMEs need not be a zero sum game.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, there are various schemes in place to encourage MNCs to work with local firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But this approach of building a local partnership conditional element into the incentive package to secure new MNC investments, is currently not being used, to the best of my knowledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like now to talk about how we can help our local workers better adapt to the winds of change that will blow from industry disruption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I shared earlier, it is never easy to rally the energy to change when things seem fine.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many of our workers are in jobs that are at-risk from industry disruption in five to 15 years' time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are a number of programmes in place that aim to address this like the Professional Conversion Programme, or PCP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, for workers in at-risk sectors, for example, drivers were at risk from autonomous vehicles in the next 10 years, can we do more to educate them about the need to consider reskilling and switching industries lest they become unemployed in their 40s and 50s?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, can MTI's economic agencies support and catalyse future-ready industry groups in fields like solar, urban farming and AI, for example, to form trade associations and chambers, or TACs; and then, can these TACs be nudged and supported by Government to run campaigns to encourage workers from sunset industries with relevant skills to reskill and consider joining their industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Government agencies can also use social media tools to target reskilling social media ad campaigns specifically at workers and such at-risk industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Existing programmes require workers to seek them out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need a national effort that is more proactive rather than reactive to nudge workers who are at risk to start thinking what their future career journey and how they can mitigate those risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This effort is needed even in industries that are cyclically doing well under COVID-19 but face longer term existential threats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, while some sectors of the retail sector have done very well during COVID-19, wholesale and retail has been identified as the sector most vulnerable to displacement in Singapore due to automation, according to a 2018 study.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to ask whether our education system is producing the skills the economy demands, and if not, what is being done to revisit our educational or economic planning?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2020, Polytechnic fresh graduates found it significantly harder to land good jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should carefully review our efforts to ramp up capacity in our education system for high demand skills and encourage students to consider these.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, sir, let me touch on internships and training attachments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a subject that is of current concern.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given the current state of the job market, many graduates of IHLs have taken on internships, traineeships and part-time work for their first jobs, partly, one assumes, because of the relative lack of attractive, full-time positions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Recent Government efforts have seen the creation of programmes such as the SGUnited Traineeship and SG Mid-Career Programme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Private firms like Google have also launched special trainee programmes during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have filed a Parliamentary Question on whether our IHLs can help our students gain sufficient access to internships in future-ready, disruptive industry sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But in this day and age, to work in a company, you need not report to work in a physical office.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: You can be an intern or trainee in a company by taking part in online meetings, undergoing online training, engaging with customers, suppliers and stakeholders virtually and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And there are companies abroad at the cutting edge of their industries who do not yet have a physical presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should select only the most promising companies for inclusion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The benefit to Singapore would be that Singaporeans would get the benefit of training, the skills, knowledge and culture that resides in these cutting edge firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another benefit is that the company, if it finds the quality of workers it engages as trainees and interns high, would consider locating a physical presence here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have received feedback from a number of older constituents who are keen to transfer their SkillsFuture credits to their children, nephews or nieces, to help them navigate the turbulent waters of the current job market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to speak about the localisation of jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There has been much discussion on striking a good balance between foreign workers and local Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We know that in many industries, such as construction, for example, we are more reliant on foreign manpower than other developed countries are.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a need to ensure a strong core of skilled, capable Singaporeans in key industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is also desirable to foster skills transfer from foreigners to locals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On localising jobs, I would like to speak about working conditions for lower wage workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government has said that the progressive wage model will be rolled out to more industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, in some jobs, even if we manage to raise wages through some policy device or other, we may find that Singaporeans may not want to take up those jobs because of the conditions of work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are workers in that role provided with adequate tools, protective gear and training?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are working hours and mandated break times sufficient?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are conditions of work made as physically comfortable and safe as they are in other countries?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is the culture in the workplace sufficiently respectful of the worker?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a lot at stake in this drive to raise pay and productivity in low-skilled jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Workers in such jobs are often one unfortunate accident away from destitution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One man I spoke to on my house visits did everything right, he and his wife saved up, worked hard, lived frugally, only for him to be injured at his job and be plunged into relative poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave the subject of workers, I would repeat the call I made earlier in relation to company incentives – for programmes that aim to address job market weakness, promote reskilling and so on, like Skillsfuture, SGUnited Traineeships and so on, let us undertake rigorous audits of outcomes that are made public, to ensure return on investment and facilitate course corrections or enhancements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to speak about our fiscal stance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Leader of the Opposition has shared some concerns about the petrol duty hike, with which I agree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a fiscal move would be progressive and would impact the capital gains made by sellers in the higher end of the property market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence the impact on the broader economy may be less than say a broad-based tax hike.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A tax on such a class of capital gains will not run the risk of unintended inflationary effects and will not damage work incentives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, such a move may not raise as much revenue as a broad-based tax hike such as hiking corporate tax or GST for example, but the former can be considered to reduce the need for and extent of a broad-based tax hike.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us always anticipate foreseeable change rather than react when change hits, even when things may be fine now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us nudge our stakeholders to recalibrate the balance in our economy towards local firms and Singaporean workers, but in ways that still embrace the role of MNCs and foreign workers where they add value.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us bear in mind that it is cultures and mindsets that are critical for change to happen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But at the same time, let us not treat cultures and mindsets as some rigid monolithic entity or a black box.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to score an "A" for outcomes, not only an "A" for effort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister shared that many persons who took part in the Emerging Stronger Conversations expressed their wish for a fair, equal and caring society, with more support for vulnerable groups, such as low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One particular group of vulnerable workers are outsourced workers like cleaners, security officers, landscape workers and maintenance staff, whom I will be speaking about today, and, in particular, with regard to their working conditions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Incidentally, Member Mr Leon Perera had addressed this as one of his points earlier and he has kind of stolen my thunder a little bit.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I am glad that this is an issue that has raised widespread concern about.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Before I go on, Sir, may I declare, my interest as the President of the Security Association Singapore and the Director of a security company.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Service buyers have control over at least four broad areas at their premises.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First is the actual work area of outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Workers should not be expected to work for extended periods of time in the sun, for example, or at places that are inherently dangerous without safeguards, like locations at height.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The provision of a proper work area concerns infrastructure and this is, in most cases, the sole preserve of service buyers who are the building owners.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Service buyers, therefore, need to do their part to ensure proper work areas in their buildings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even better, such provision should be made at the design stage of new buildings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second is the provision of proper rest areas and facilities, including washrooms.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The MCST had, instead, installed a portable toilet in a secluded area of the basement carpark for the workers to use.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I visited the site myself and I took some photos.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The area where the portable toilet was located was not well lighted and abutted a forested area.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even worse, there was no water pumped to the toilet on the weekends.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Workers had to scoop water from a dustbin outside the portable toilet to bring in with them, in order to flush the toilet and to wash their hands.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This arrangement arose because residents had complained that outsourced workers had dirtied the condominium toilets.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As we were in the process of engaging the managing agent and the MCST on this matter, the pandemic set in and the workers were then allowed to use the gym toilet during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The gym toilet was, in any event, closed during this period.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know what the situation is now.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamed launched the Tripartite Advisory on the Provision of Rest Areas, he did so while visiting Ikea, which provides excellent rest areas for all their workers, that outsourced workers could also avail.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Ikea is, unfortunately, also an outlier and the reality at most sites is somewhere in between.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, the norm is nearer to the portable toilet example than the Ikea exemplar.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The launch of the Tripartite Advisory on rest areas shows, however, that MOM and the tripartite partners are alive to the issue and have been quite gregarious and proactive to address it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We continue to see cleaners taking their breaks at basement carparks of shopping malls, and resting and eating their meals at bin centres at condominiums, or having no areas to rest at all, or even to place their belongings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine, Sir, that resting, and eating at bin centres or at cooler pump rooms would have an effect on our workers’ health and safety, not to mention their dignity.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy also said that the grant would be launched with a view to eventually legislating this requirement.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The third area is proper rest times and working hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The work that outsourced workers do can be strenuous, and break times should be planned for in their schedules, during which they should be undisturbed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In an article on outsourced workers by The New Paper in November 2018, an elderly cleaner was quoted as saying that people who saw her resting would complain to her superiors despite that she was resting in between her work slots.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the security association, we receive from time to time complaints about security officers sleeping – only to discover, after investigation, that they were doing so at their designated rest times.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And there should be no doubt, Sir, that if it so pleases workers to sleep during their designated break times, they are entitled to do so because it is their personal time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Related to my earlier point on the provision of rest areas, because most building owners do not provide a designated rest area, outsourced workers have to find some nook or cranny to rest, or have to do so at their actual workplace, like the guard rooms, in full view of the public.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards working hours, I would like to highlight, in particular, the working hours of security officers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The norm is for officers to work 12-hour shifts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Taking into consideration roughly two hours of travelling to and fro and eight hours of sleep, officers have around just two hours of personal time per working day with their families and for themselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If they need more personal time, they would have to cannibalise their sleeping hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, all these complaints of security officers sleeping on the job, of course, Sir, they are sleeping because they have not had enough sleep.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would wear the security officer’s uniform, like an undercover boss.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, my officers knew who I was – I was undercover not to check on them but to look at the working conditions on the ground.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are many things to do – from dealing with public enquiries to patrolling, to marshalling traffic and ensuring paperwork is up-to-date and, sometimes, these must be done concurrently.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And then there is dealing with difficult members of the public, which I personally encountered while I was on shift with my officers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is difficult, Sir, to remain focused and alert as a security officer for the entirety of a 12-hour shift.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will, of course, translate to higher costs for buyers as it necessitates an additional shift of workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, such long hours on a long-term basis would undoubtedly affect officers’ health – physical, mental and social.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, take a stand and do something about it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If they want security, they must be prepared to pay for it and our workers should not suffer to save their costs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, security service providers must also take responsibility for their own workers and insist on reasonable working hours and they must also ensure that higher prices that buyers pay translate to higher wages for their employers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The PWM for the security sector moving forward should incorporate this reduction of shift durations, to make sure that it does not lead to a concomitant drop in officers’ gross wages.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, the Government must take the lead and should move procurement of security manpower services towards eight to 10-shifts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, buyers should ensure that outsourced workers at their site are required to do only the tasks for which they were deployed and that they are trained for.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Often, buyers treat outsourced workers as general workers or odd-job labourers and call on them to carry out tasks that do not fall under their scope of work, for example, cleaners being asked to perform electrical works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The unfortunate incident in 2015 of a security officer falling into an elevator shaft while he was trying to prise the lift doors open is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This was not something the officer was trained to do, nor was it within his scope of work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He was asked to assist and he was being helpful.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, in order for us to deal with these longstanding issues, we need to introduce measures that mandate and encourage buyers to make provision for proper work conditions for outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I propose, for consideration by MOM and the tripartite partners, that a consolidated Tripartite Advisory be issued for buyers of outsourced services on the provisions they should make in the above four areas.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would incorporate and go beyond the existing advisory on the provision of rest areas.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have thus proposed three measures that build on existing mechanisms and/or positions already announced by the Government: legislation making the provision of rest areas for outsourced workers mandatory; the regularisation of security officer working hours in the security officers PWM; and the promulgation of a consolidated tripartite advisory for buyers of outsourced services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, I would like to thank our essential workers and our outsourced workers: our cleaners, security officers, waste collectors and maintenance staff, who continued to work to keep Singapore going during the circuit breaker and who continue to be on the frontlines.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It must become part of our workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When we have built this, Sir, we will no longer see people looking at a tired worker resting and think that this is something that they should complain about; we will not see rich residents demanding that outsourced workers not be allowed to use their luxurious facilities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, what we will see is them crying foul that workers are only allowed to use a portable toilet.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We will see building owners willing and happy to use up precious GFA so that workers can have proper breaks.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We will progress towards a fairer, a more equal and a more caring society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And, Sir, we will emerge stronger, together and we will do so at all levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It declared climate change a global emergency and recognised the role that multiple stakeholders will have to play to sustainably develop Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last week, we also heard about the Singapore Green Plan, with the Deputy Prime Minister highlighting the building of a sustainable home for all as one of the key thrusts of this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech, I will be talking on the need to protect our natural capital before talking about promoting green transport, as well as about the proposed petrol tax.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will then touch briefly on making progress in our manufacturing and construction sector and the support Singapore should give for climate change at the global and regional levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One aspect of the Plan is the one-million-tree movement which aims to plant a million trees by 2030.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I do welcome this measure, a glaring omission under the Singapore Green Plan is a lack of commitment to provide greater legal protection for our secondary forest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is important to note that even though NParks oversees the management of activities within nature parks and that activities which may damage trees within nature parks are regulated by a Subsidiary Legislation under the Parks and Trees Act, the mechanisms by which these activities are regulated, as well as the penalties for contravention, are much less robust than those applicable to areas designated as nature reserves in the same Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, the fate of other secondary forest spaces, which are not currently used as nature parks, hangs in the balance as they may be cleared for development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Workers' Party thus reiterates its call on the Government to commit to providing more secondary forests with greater legal protection, with some of these areas regulated as nature reserves, while simple recreation areas could be allowed in other areas, but with more stringent rules and penalties than is currently enforced in public parks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By legislating to this end, Parliament will send a clear signal to not only future generations, but to various actors, including contractors, Ministries and Statutory Boards, and the Government itself, that the destruction of forest areas will come at a cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The reason erroneous clearing of forested spaces in Kranji woodlands is a prime example, where the Jurong Town Corporation (JTC) said that it was caught unaware of the clearing of plots of land earmarked for future use and for which an environmental baseline study was reportedly being carried out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Thus far, the contractor has only gotten away with stern warnings despite clearing forests, while JTC has not faced any legal consequences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we await the Government to explain to the House its findings on the Kranji woodlands case, I hope that the Government will also commit to begin providing greater legal protection for our secondary forests and green spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In order to move towards a more sustainable future for Singaporeans, we should also take a critical look at how our people move.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Greening our transport infrastructure is an endeavour that, like other goals in sustainable development, must not only meet our need for environmental sustainability, but must also meet our social needs in an economically viable way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I move on to Electric Vehicles (EVs) and battery swaps.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my Budget debate speech last year when I commented on the then target of 28,000 charging points, I said that even assuming a 30% conversion from the current vehicle population to EVs, we would still only end up with one charging point for every 10 EVs by 2030.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is going to be a step-up from the over 1,900 charging points, 1,400 in public carparks, which we currently have as a January 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my Budget debate speech last year, I also urged the Government to consider the alternative of battery swap stations which have the advantage of speed, ensuring the load on our power grid can be managed well, while providing ready infrastructure for battery recycling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I said that this has really been tested in China and should be a key consideration here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Later on, in March 2020, in response to my colleague, the hon Member for Aljunied, Mr Leon Perera, the Government said that it was studying the potential of battery swapping as a complement to charging and that this consideration will influence the final design of our EV network.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government provide the House with an update on its findings on the potential use of battery swapping technology in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I now move on to EV chargers, charging points and carpark designs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While it is important to have a good number of charging points, we should also bear in mind that these numbers will be insufficient if we do not get the other details right.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For instance, will these points enable fast charging?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can we do in one hour as opposed to eight or 12 hours perhaps, which we can expect from the domestic charging rate?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But even at half an hour or one hour, will this be too slow and inconvenient for consumers who are used to spending five to 10 minutes in the petrol station.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And assuming that these charging points are all fast charging points, if we want an efficient system, we will still need to ensure EVs have correspondingly quick-charging capabilities as different EVs may have different capabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the charging technology improves over the coming years with the proliferation of EVs all over the world, we should also bear in mind the possibility of older EVs operating together with newer EVs may slow down the efficiency in the use of chargers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another factor to consider is the critical number of charging points required in all residential, commercial car parks and other public carparks, as well as the design of the carparks vis-à-vis the locations of the charging points.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Imagine a situation where you have 100, 200 cars coming back after work to an HDB carpark, with each taking, for the sake of discussion, say 20 minutes to charge their car.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the present design, will we have bottleneck issues to address?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, Singapore is not like the US or Australia where most people live in landed homes and have the luxury of charging their vehicles in their own garages overnight.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
