text: Fast charging is of course critical, but until we reach the stage where every or most of the carpark lots come with a charging unit, most of the present HDB, public and commercial carparks products are not adequately designed to prevent bottlenecks or congestion caused by more than a few cars waiting for the current few charging units available at each carpark.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The design of hundreds or more of our existing carparks will need to be evaluated to avoid the likely congestion scenario I have described.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to the Government's assurance that these concerns are being looked at and if so, to share details of any stepped-up plans to address them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I remember a conversation I had once with a driver in China waking up to queue for his car to be charged at 3.00 am to 4.00 am every morning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We cannot allow such scenario to happen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We cannot afford the loss of productivity this will entail.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the transformation of vehicle population internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to EVs and the resulting proliferation of large numbers of EV charging points in time to come, it may be timely to ask about its likely effect on our electricity generation infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While there may be an electricity supply glut now, the Government needs to plan for the additional electricity generation required for EVs in the years to come such that a step-up usage will be smooth and importantly, sustainable, and will at the same time not pose any strains on our power system at all times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And in answer to the House in January this year, Minister Tan See Leng alluded to how EVs were one of the drivers to increase electricity demand in the future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government will give an update to this House on its current plan to step up the electricity generation specifically for use by EVs in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I touch on the phasing out of ICE vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government therefore provide the periodic milestone it aims to reach in this regard in the run-up to 2040, including Malaysian ICE vehicles on our roads, which I brought up last year too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He gave the basis that, I quote, "usage-based tax has helped shape consumer behaviour towards a more efficient use of fuel or environmentally friendly alternatives".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, as I mentioned above our EV infrastructure is currently far from ready to allow large numbers of car owners to switch immediately to EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, aside from the Government wanting to raise tax revenue from this source, I think raising the petrol duty this abruptly on a basis of shaping consumer behaviour towards an environmentally friendly option, is in some sense putting the cart before the horse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Why was this hike not phased in with advance notice?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Just two years ago, in my Budget speech, I spoke against the diesel tax increase, highlighting that it would increase cost of doing business and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I think the increase of petrol duty may also increase cost of living which may be in these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As for rebates offered, unless the increase is only for a limited time like a year or two after which it will be adjusted downwards, such rebates are really short-term measures, and ultimately, owners, and even business owners, will have to face the full effect of the price increase later on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I move on to progressing in our manufacturing and construction sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In his Budget speech, the Deputy Prime Minister also reminded the House that the Government announced its Long-term Low-Emissions Development Strategy (LEDS) in 2020.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the decarbonisation of our electricity grid is but one way in which the manufacturing and construction sector will be able to reduce its emissions, what findings have the Government made so far in the study of emerging technologies under the LEDS which can help us decarbonise industrial processes in this sector to move us closer to our updated periscopes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I talk about providing support at the global and regional levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister also mentioned that Singapore will continue to play an active role at the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) negotiations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As a key node in our globalised world economy, we are well-positioned to work with other countries to reduce global emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The threats of climate change, which this House will be familiar with, require us to do more actively in a similar vein.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We also need to work more closely with our neighbours in ASEAN to curb regional emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the growth of emissions has slowed down for some of our neighbours, this has increased for others, and more work needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government thus provide the House with specific future plans to work at both global and regional levels to mitigate climate change?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Before I end, I want to touch on two other issues beyond climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He said he hoped that the vouchers would bring more business to our heartland shops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am glad that he thinks that our heartland shops could do with this help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I agree that more can be done to help our small businesses in our heartlands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is challenging times for many such businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, a resident who own a mini-mart in a heartland shared with me about his business challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Besides challenges from the supermarkets in the area, he also lamented on the challenges from Fairprice on Wheels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He wishes that the Government can consider how to give more space to SMEs, especially when it comes to competition from Government-linked businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I move on to the issue of commercial and industrial rents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have previously spoken about the concerns SMEs had with rentals during the debate on the Resilience and Solidarity Budgets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But this does not tell the whole story.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In a Straits Times article, it was quoted that many SMEs did not want to go through the process of confronting their landlords for fear of making things worse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As SMEs have comparatively less cash buffer compared to large enterprises, SMEs may find it hard to pay the rental on time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the medium term, the study of the commercial and industrial rental markets, as it stands, is necessary, with it studying offerings of low rent commercial and industrial spaces managed by HDB and JTC respectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we look at the threats of climate change today, when we look at how much further we must go to protect our natural capital, to promote green transport and manufacturing, to provide more support to our people as we sustainably develop Singapore, it is clear that we have much work to do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the debate on the climate change Motion earlier this month, Minister Grace Fu stressed that "sustainability has always been a part of Singapore's DNA because we have always pursue a balance between economic growth and protecting our environment since our early years".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But it merits mention that this pursuit while leaving us with good economic growth over the decades was also what left us with the limited green space today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our understanding of our environment today has become much more sophisticated than in the past, in part due to advances in our understanding of climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Likewise, our notion of sustainability must also advance with times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must do much more to address these threats we have never seen before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It can tear us apart or rally us together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Around the world, we observe social and political fractures, caused or exacerbated by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the UK, more than half of Britons surveyed by thinktank Demos resented lockdown rule breakers and people who do not wear masks, much more compared to only 33% of non-Brexiteers resenting the Brexiteers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the US, wearing a mask was so politicised at one point that it becomes a symbol of which political party one supports.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In big western cities, attacks were launched on Asians.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A Singaporean student was attacked in London last year at the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some elderly Asians also reportedly suffered violent attacks in California, a problem that was simmering since the pandemic began.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women in many countries were hit disproportionately compared to men.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors in some countries suffer greater income reduction or job losses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A consequence of this is poorer or loss of healthcare benefits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors in countries with government-funded medical benefits or insurance may still have access to basic services, but those in countries without would naturally suffer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We see how societies can fracture further and deeper along political, racial, gender and age lines when under pressure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is not spared from this same pressure brought upon by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thankfully, we have not observed the same fractures or of the same extent here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, we must do our best to prevent them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How we respond to this crisis of our generation is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Will Singapore emerge stronger and feel stronger as a people?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or will we look stronger but feel more apart instead?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I echo the importance of strengthening social compact, as highlighted in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this speech, I will talk about empowering our seniors and women in the workforce, so as to enhance overall well-being and strengthen our sense of togetherness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, we still encounter seniors who want to work but struggle to secure suitable and adequate employment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Most recently, while visiting the Geylang East Market and Food Centre in my constituency, I met an "auntie" who was in her late 60s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We greeted each other warmly before her tone took a turn and asked me, "MP, is there any Government rule or law that prohibits a person from working beyond a specific age?"  I told her of course not.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Curious, I asked her what prompted her question.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But my employer said that I am old and wanted me to be redeployed to a job with less scope and less pay.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And after I reach the end of the re-employment age, I will have no job.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I am still very fit, I can still do my original job.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I need the income too." "Auntie’s" predicament is not unique.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In serving our residents, we would have met other seniors who face similar challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are often the first to go and last to be hired.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite an ageing workforce, ageist mindsets can be found in many workplace settings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Negative stereotypes about older people – that they are slower, weaker, more rigid or less productive – can significantly hinder the deployment of precious human resource and discourage development even as we promote lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such perceived loss of opportunities affect morale and career prospects, and eventually impact self-esteem and the sense of togetherness with the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must proactively combat ageism in the workplace and recognise the value that senior workers can offer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, our ageing workforce means that employers have to accept the reality of an increasingly mature manpower supply.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, our default thinking should be to find ways to leverage senior workers’ strengths and not find ways to undermine or get rid of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To this end, I would suggest the following.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Push companies to review HR policies and encourage them to make it an SOP to hold conversations with senior workers on meaningful re-employment or re-deployment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be fair, there is a need for renewal so that younger workers have a chance to rise up and accumulate their own experiences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But where senior workers are still fit and keen to work, companies should discuss options that allow senior workers to preserve their work and compensation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two, the world is always changing and firms constantly have to change with corresponding strategies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, firms can adapt its working environment, job design and processes to be enabling for senior workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technology enablers are available, productivity does not have to suffer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, the jobs for senior workers of tomorrow will be increasingly intellectual and less backbreaking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, the earlier we get ready for an ageing workforce, the better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, for senior workers who have to leave or wish to give a shot in a different endeavour, have in place a centre that focuses on matching these seniors to new jobs or opportunities that allow them to contribute socially, for example, volunteerism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This can help redirect precious senior human resource to areas where there are unfulfilled needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And lastly, continue to encourage our seniors to stay positive and embrace learning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):    A crisis tests the mantle of any society and generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Around the world, we observe how societies can fracture deeper along political, racial, gender and age lines when under pressure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although Singapore has yet to experience similar or severe social fragmentation, we cannot afford to take it lightly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I agree with the importance of strengthening social compact highlighted in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Discord will lead to fragmentation whereas staying united will allow us to emerge stronger.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Here, I would like to talk about empowering the elderly in the workforce, improving their overall wellbeing and strengthening our sense of solidarity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is heartening to hear many examples of re-employment and the elderly staying in the workforce on media platforms from time to time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just now I shared the story of an 70-year-old auntie whom I met during a recent visit to Geylang East Market and Food Centre in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In serving our residents, we often encounter elderly people who faced difficulties in finding or staying in work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are often the "first to leave, the last to be hired" group.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite an ageing workforce and active government promotion, ageist mindsets can be found in many workplaces.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It can significantly hinder the deployment of precious human resource.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The employees feel that loss of opportunities can affect morale and career prospects, and eventually impact self-esteem and their sense of togetherness with the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must proactively combat ageism in the workplace and promote the idea of "active ageing".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should think hard on how we can leverage older workers’ strengths, rather than try to get rid of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have a few suggestions: First, push companies to review their HR policies, encourage them to make it a SOP to hold conversations with older workers on re-employment or job redeployment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If they are fit and keen to work, companies should discuss options that allow older workers to preserve their work and compensation, not automatically filter them out.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, companies can adjust their work environment, design and process to meet the needs of older workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Companies can make good use of technology to help them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, future jobs for older workers will be increasingly intellectual and less backbreaking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it will be much more effective to prepare for an ageing workforce early.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, for older workers who have to leave or wish to try other jobs, the Government could consider setting up a centre to help them match with new jobs or opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, with their years of experience, they can serve as a consultant to provide guidance or become a volunteer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will redirect valuable human resource of older workers to areas of need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Singapore is firmly set on our path towards a digital economy and Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must spare no effort to prevent inadvertently creating new gaps or exacerbating existing gaps as we transform.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need smart women for a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digitally empowering more women will also help to address the pressing digital talent shortage worldwide and generate greater economic growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, we can anticipate that the strive towards a future economy would mean that there are more job opportunities, better career prospects and wage growth in the tech and innovation sectors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we do not help women to capture these opportunities, they risk falling behind further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, while there is no significant change in the employment rate of women before and after pandemic at its peak – thanks to our very sound and supportive and progressive Government system and the workforce in Singapore – there remains a need for us to still step up in digitally empowering our girls and women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Though this percentage is higher than that of neighbouring Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines and Vietnam, it is lower than the overall women representation in Singapore’s workforce.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have hidden gems within our women population, waiting to be discovered or for the opportunity to shine.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A dear friend of mine, Nurul Sharafudin, is to me a great example who had an amazing journey as a young Singapore woman in tech.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nurul started out as an MOE Arts teacher – she was happy and well loved by her students.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But driven by her passion for learning and trying new things, she took a courageous move to switch career path.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She applied for an entry position in Oracle.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She stayed curious, acquired new digital skills, sought out her own mentor.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And today, in just a few years, she is responsible for Oracle’s Business Operations Organisational Strategy and Programmes in Japan APAC.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, Nurul is a confident woman, a regional leader in an American tech MNC, and a mother of two no less, making her mark in the tech sector and giving back by mentoring many others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nurul’s journey shows us how digital empowerment can make a positive big difference.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It opens new doors and offers many more opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When Singaporeans feel that they are progressing in tandem with the nation, there will be a stronger sense of togetherness, a stronger sense of pride and fulfilment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With a strong national psychological resilience, I am confident we will weather any crisis, come what may.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Budget, which allocates about 20% of our GDP, has provided continued support to fight the COVID-19 and the resources to accelerate our socio-economic transformation to a new and sustainable model.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is a need to help Singaporeans to survive and to do better, we think we should not hesitate to spend more, even up to the total NIR we earn every year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the foreseeable future, we do not see any shortage of fiscal revenues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Needless to say, we must ensure that the money spent will have a lasting effect on our people and give them the confidence to take ownership of and build their own futures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is in this regard that I think Budget 2021 has fallen short.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just like the Household Support Package, as an example.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have the GST Voucher Special, U-Save Special, Service and Conservancy Charges rebate, Edusave Top-ups, CDC Voucher and more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With such a confusing array of schemes, it is difficult for Singaporeans to find any lasting reassurance or peace of mind and create long-term plans for their futures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A true Resilience Package must contain long-term transparent and predictable schemes which Singaporeans will automatically qualify if they fall below a certain threshold.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, every Singaporean would know where they stand financially in every stage of their lives and how they can work towards a stable financial position.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is an urgent need to rebalance the local-foreign worker mix in our job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, foreign workers account for, on the average, 40% of our workforce at all levels, whether Work Permit, S Pass or EP holders and many of the foreign workers have even taken the helm of our local companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The growing numbers of displaced PMETs joining the ranks of the private hire drivers and gig workers is the best final evidence of the shortcomings of the current employment and immigration policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other urgent problem is the high cost of living and the heavy indirect tax burden of middle class Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Housing prices has continued to surge during COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other costs, like electricity, ERP and now, the petrol tax, are also increasing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Singaporeans above 50 years old, the worries over retirement and healthcare is worsening by the day.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seemingly, oblivious to all these pains of the middle class, the impending rise of the GST was brought up again during the Budget speech despite the Government agreeing that the GST is regressive in nature.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the top quintile income earners contribute more than 80% of personal income tax revenue but only 60% of the GST revenues, I hope the Government would also admit that a tax system relying more on GST revenue will burden the middle class most, namely, those who do not earn enough to hit the higher income tax brackets, but do not qualify for GST Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are also the people who have young families with children, spending most of their income on essentials.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Adding on social stress like the unnecessarily competitive Primary school education system and the yearly commitment of in-camp training for male Singaporeans, it is not difficult to understand how stressed middle class Singaporeans are.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, without the participation of the middle-class, the economic transformation is doomed because there will not be enough players to create healthy competition in the market if only the top quintile Singaporeans are innovating.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, it is because of an impoverished middle class that we need more foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, a good Budget must tackle the root cause of the problems with long-term, predictable policies and schemes, and it must aim to build a secure foundation of financial stability and social dignity for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With that objective in mind, we would like to make three major long-term policy recommendations to nudge the Budget in the correct direction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first recommendation is to introduce a living wage for the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Singapore Progress Party (PSP) strongly believes that a Singaporean who has put in a day's work should be compensated sufficiently to allow him to live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And we firmly believe that honouring our fellow Singaporeans must take priority over all other economic arguments and we should not wait for the Government to take another decade or two to slowly review the wages of the low-wage workers, sector-by-sector, through its Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2019, Asst Prof Ng Kok Hoe and his team from the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy had conducted a minimum income standards study on what older households need to meet their basic needs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The study postulated that single elderly households aged over 65 needed $1,379 per month and single households aged 55 to 64 needed $1,721 per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While not definitive, this provides a good benchmark to design a living wage policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The living wage will lift the wage share of the GDP, something that my colleague Ms Hazel Poa has recommended yesterday.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a consensus in this House that we should care for our essential workers who are also often low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We think the best way to achieve that is to have the living wage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Low-income Singaporeans will be able to have peace of mind with a living wage rather than those usual ad hoc, short-term and unpredictable schemes offered by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second recommendation is to level the playing field for our Singaporean talents in our very own job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is understandable that we need foreign workers to complement us, it puzzles me why the Government has allowed a wage disadvantage against the Singaporeans for the longest time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This wage disadvantage against our local workers has arisen from the fact that foreigners are not included in the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While this disadvantage has been slightly reduced in the case of the Work Permit holders and the S Pass holders through the levy system, it is not the case for the EP holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government needs more revenue, this is a good option to consider.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This levy will differentiate the true foreign talents, who are high salaried and less affected by the $1,200 levy, from the foreign talents who are simply cheap labour that compete unfairly with our Singaporeans and whom our economy has become overly dependent on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third and last recommendation is to strengthen the social security for Singaporeans by having the Government pay for all the MediShield and CareShield insurance premiums.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Base on our financial projections, most middle class Singaporeans cannot afford the MediShield and CareShield premiums in their old age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is not clearly explained to the people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The average Singaporean can accumulate about $1 million in savings in his CPF account, if he had contributed continuously from 25 to 65 years old.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the contributions compounded at the CPF interest rates of 2.5% and 4% per annum for the Ordinary, Special and MediSave account respectively.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ostensibly, all Singaporeans should have adequate retirement resources in their CPF account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the reason why our CPF system is rated as one of the best retirement schemes in the world.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But like the many other accolades that we have received, it only tells half the story.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because in addition to retirement use, the Government has designated two additional uses for the CPF monies, namely purchasing HDB flats and topping up the MediSave account.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The MediSave account is designed to pay for all the MediShield and CareShield premiums and out-of-pocket medical expenses of a Singaporean and his dependent family members, including his parents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, he or she is responsible for all his family members as far as medical expenses are concerned.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We estimated that the total premium paid by an average family of four, up to 65 years old for the parents, and 25 years old for the two children before they become independent, will cause a drain of $110, 000 from the parents' CPF resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Considering that those premiums, if not withdrawn from the CPF account, they could have earned a compounded annual return of 4% over the years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, if the family did not need to pay the MediShield and CareShield premiums, he would have an additional $110, 000 for retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, if the premium increases by 10% every five years, which is highly possible, given that MediShield premium is going to go up 35% this year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The drain on the CPF account will be from $110, 000 to $246,000.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The MediShield and CareShield schemes are thus a big drag on the retirement resources of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the current social security plans are highly unsatisfactory.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason why CPF rules have to be tweaked frequently, it is not because that the Government had lost the CPF money in bad investment, like some fake news have it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, it is because the Government knows that most Singaporeans do not have enough funds to cater for all the three uses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Managing healthcare cost is an on-going and complex matter, which requires many more policy and system changes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we believe our recommendation is a significant first step in the correct direction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe our recommendations will go a long way; helping to secure a foundation of financial stability and social dignity for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only with this secure foundation, can we really emerge as one people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, in his speech, suggested that foreigners are taking the helm of companies in Singapore at the expense of locals, and he suggested that there should be a levy on all EP holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We just did that last year as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We do that so that there is constant rebalancing of the foreign and local talent mix in Singapore, and the intent is to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I also recall that in his earlier speech during the debate on the Motion of Thanks to the President, he lamented that DBS was still without a Singaporean CEO, and even after hearing the clarification that the CEO of DBS is indeed Singaporean, even though not born in Singapore, he maintained his position.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I cannot help, but come to the conclusion that Mr Leong and PSP do not believe that Singapore should be an open city connected to the world, having locals and foreigners complementing each other.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And he wants Singapore to close up, for the top jobs to be given to Singaporeans only.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we must try to strike a balance between globalisation and building our own identity in Singapore, welcoming foreign talent and building our own talent at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And going by Mr Leong's logic, Singaporeans who are working overseas then, would not be given top jobs outside Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In my maiden speech in Parliament, I spoke about strengthening the Singaporean Core and being very proud of Singapore as an open and multi-cultural society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must do our best to equip our Singaporeans with the right skills and also the attributes to thrive in a vibrant and open economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Global companies with a presence in Singapore require a diverse team of foreign and local talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I also thank the Minister of State for the comments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP is in total agreement to the fact that we are an open global city state.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we are in favour of having foreign talents or foreigners to come in to compliment us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The fact is that taking over the top positions in our company is not the problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The problem is do we have enough policies to ensure that Singaporeans have a fair treatment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Today, I have pointed out again that for the longest time why the Government had allowed the wage disadvantage against the Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: With that, obviously, the employers would favour the foreigners over the Singaporeans a lot more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And during my maiden speech, I brought up the issue of the CEO of DBS Bank not because it was meant to be a personal attack, but I am trying to emphasise, why is there no succession planning, again, being done over the course of the 20 years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And recently, another of our local bank has employed another foreigner to be the CEO.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In my maiden speech, I have said that during my time in the 1980s and the 1990s, localisation is almost a must in our financial sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is what PSP and I are concerned about – the rebalancing and we have to do the rebalancing as soon as possible and as fast as possible.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And this is part and parcel of having diversity of views in the Chamber.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But I thought that I should just register that the Government has a different view, which is that, this is a difficult balancing act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are constantly working on it and that we will try our best to manage, do well to build a strong Singaporean Core in order to benefit Singaporeans for the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong and I had this exchange during the Motion of Thanks to the President's Address.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I gave a full speech, recorded in the Hansard, the efforts that MAS has taken all these years and decades, opening up Singapore, establishing ourselves as a financial hub, creating many jobs, allowing many of our young now to go to University, receive a good education and enter the financial sector; how Universities have now become a very good hunting ground for financial sectors to hire very good talent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And they know that Singaporeans are able to do the job.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And how Singaporeans – because we are now a regional and international hub – are now able to take up international roles overseas in other financial centres around the world, and then holding our own.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of course, we always wish there is a manual that says we get all the jobs, but yet no competition.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I am sorry, there is no such manual.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The manual is to open up, allow for more competition, but we build capabilities so that we can seize more opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All these, we have gone through during the Debate on the Motion on the President's Address.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I am a little bit disturbed when I hear Mr Leong grandstanding, saying that all these building up, growing our own timber, localisation, building our own talent is not in MAS' KPI.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think that is grossly unfair and ignores everything that we have discussed earlier.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe MAS does have the KPIs, but I think the KPIs are not showing enough results.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even the data that was quoted in Minister's clarification in September last year, I think I and a lot of Singaporeans still have doubts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: After all, retail banking is about our own domestic market, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Are we satisfied with a 60%, 70% percentage, for example?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Has the Government created a wage disadvantage by not having foreigners contribute to CPF in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I am as happy as a clam, to hear that Minister Heng has outlined in his Budget, a fiscal strategy that reflects the number of elements that I had previously raised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I just wish today, to develop a number of additional points in greater detail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, I will offer some further thoughts about borrowing when interest rates are low, then I would discuss some of the benefits of not prematurely removing Government expenditure support at the time of macroeconomic weakness, while spelling out some of the key signals to keep an eye on in deciding on the eventual withdrawal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And finally, I will close with suggestions on broadening the usage of funds financed by long-term debt issuance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Back in January, I shared about how, since governments are bound by very different time horizons and budget constraints, as compared with households and firms, as they have both the ability to finance expenditure through money creation, but also a fiduciary responsibility to evaluate the benefits of debt-financed fiscal policy, if macroeconomic conditions so warrant it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if this point may be a subtle one, the takeaway is remarkably straightforward: if real interest rates are low, as they are today, incurring additional debt, especially when directed toward investment, could give rise to higher growth and potentially improve national welfare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, if we accept this premise, how then should we execute such borrowing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOF has yet to detail the forms by which bonds issued via the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act, or SINGA, would take.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If I may, I now venture a few suggestions that may be helpful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we were to do so, we would hardly be alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other advanced economies, including Austria, Belgium and Ireland have already done.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even several emerging economies such as Brazil, Chile, Israel and South Korea and perhaps preposterously Argentina, have gone ahead and issued century bonds as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And corporations such as Coca Cola and Disney have likewise done the same.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Closer to home, Temasek has also issued half centuries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is evidence that when the growth rate of debt is too rapid, economic growth can suffer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The last thing we want for such voluntary debt insurance is for it to become a detriment to growth performance, a bane rather than the boom for our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And finally, we should be clear about when we may no longer wish to roll over this debt but instead choose to extinguish it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its face, this decision is a rudimentary, an accounting exercise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We will cease that issuance when the present value of expected returns from the investments toward which this debt is deployed, no longer exceeds the equivalent stream of interest repayments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All this is standard cost benefit analysis as any consultant worth their salt can easily attest to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is possible to simplify this argument even further to a set of key warning indicators, all supportable by theory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A second warning sign would be if long-term inflation expectations remain benign, but interest rates nevertheless face upward pressure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A third amber signal is when the short-term interest rate begins rising inexorably even as the economy has clearly exited recessionary conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Heng has also explained that SINGA Bonds would be directed toward investment in physical infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I am thoroughly supportive of this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, in my January speech, I explicitly indicated that investment in domestically-oriented infrastructure projects – such as sustaining MRT line expansion – represented examples of Government investment expenditure that would likely generate significant bang-for-the-buck.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The other suggested expenditure area, tidal walls, likewise represents a domestically-oriented infrastructure project that promises to yield significant, in this case existential benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, applaud the Government's decision to take this bold step of prudent, debt-financed investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will further concede that this approach is entirely consistent with this Government's general principle toward capital raising – that long-term sources of finance be directed toward long-term projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My remaining reservation here is directed toward our interpretation of "long-term infrastructure".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In our effort to boost productivity and growth, investments in human capital are low hanging fruit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only that, they are also consistent with our stated goal of re-invigorating our post-pandemic economy, and rebooting it into a knowledge-based, information-centric 21st century powerhouse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will develop this proposal in greater detail in my Committee of Supply (COS) cut directed at MTI, although I will just declare here that I work for a research-intensive educational institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another area where our human capital will benefit enormously with wise spending is in our Primary and Secondary schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will likewise elaborate on how we can channel more resources toward reducing class sizes in my COS cut for MOE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And finally, we should not forget the large mass of workers who will have to be reskilled and redeployed as we continue to transform our economic structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The existing Professional Conversion Programme and SkillsFuture programmes can be better weaved into an end-to-end jobs safety net that not only provides support following retrenchment, but proactively channels displaced workers into new jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will discuss this proposal in greater detail in my COS cut for MOM.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These are to reflect provisions for potential increases in R&D, educational expenditures for smaller classes and an initial redundancy insurance risk pool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All that said, I believe it is incumbent on us to also consider the deployment of at least some of these funds toward cyclical needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because of the material risks surrounding premature fiscal retrenchment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This uncertainty has, indeed, been recognised by others in this House, including Minister Heng himself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is generally impossible to define a precise set of conditions whereby we can be certain that the economy has returned to its long-run potential, it is also fair to recognise that we are likely to remain below our previous trend over the course of 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must bear in mind that, at the moment, the economy is very much like Swiss cheese.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By which, I mean that, while it may look solid, it is, in reality, still riddled with holes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we grow to attain the midpoint of the 2021 forecast by MTI of 5%, we will remain two-thirds of a percent below our pre-pandemic level of output.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even if we exceed expectations and grow by the upper bound of MTI's forecast, we will still remain more than 2% below the level that would have prevailed, had we grown at the 2019 growth rate through till 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also useful to remind ourselves of the relatively recent experience of a number of countries in Europe, which made the fateful decision in 2010 to embark on austerity programmes, as a means of shoring up their weakened fiscal positions, following the region's sovereign debt crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The end result of that episode was that many of those economies went into a double-dip recession, prolonging the economic pain just as households and firms were in the process of pulling themselves out of a massive hole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line, Mr Speaker, is that we should exercise an abundance of caution in any decision to taper the financial assistance that we have been offering to our families and companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, there are those who will argue the opposite, that if we take too long, we run the risk of over-stimulation, stoking the flames of inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I, for one, would err on the side of over-extending, rather than undershooting, short-term support for our beleaguered economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, with all due respect, this is not about calibrating a response that neatly threads the needle between two possibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is about how an error or premature austerity could translate into real economic pain for thousands of worker and businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, if we truly buy into the merits of controlled, short-term deficit financing, we should not allow traditional fiscal prudence metrics to preclude even greater support for our businesses, especially small and medium enterprises, that continue to struggle, and companies that will experience a more protracted recovery path, such as our national airline, even in the short run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, our key considerations should not be whether any given firm falls into Tier-1 or Tier-2 or elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, the metric for our evaluation should be whether the corporation would remain a going concern in the absence of the global pandemic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accounting and finance firms routinely gauge whether firms face temporary liquidity or more fundamental solvency issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our Government support programmes should do the same.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thankfully, our reserves buffer also means that we are comparatively less constrained in our use of the debt instrument as part of our overall fiscal strategy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that we can always cease our deficit financing exercise once conditions for doing so – a number of which I had earlier suggested – are no longer optimal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in the meantime, let us continue to support our struggling workers and businesses as much as we can.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I would, therefore, like to start by sharing the story of people, in particular, three women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The first person I want to talk about is Mdm Joey Lee.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Joey is one of the directors and owners of Bread Garden, a family-run bakery business which has an outlet at my constituency, Bukit Batok East.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Like many other businesses, Joey’s business took a hit as a result of COVID-19 and the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Events which were planned had to be cancelled.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She had several Malaysian employees who could not come back to Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Sales and revenue dropped and Joey and her team had to quickly pivot and learn ways to enhance their online business.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: All these happened amidst their plans to open another outlet.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The pandemic is not over and the challenges with regard to manpower and sustaining the business are still present.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Joey is, therefore, keenly interested in the extension of support to small and medium sized businesses like hers, as well as the plans on economic recovery.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The second story is that of Mdm Faraliza Zainal, a founder of MIJ Special Education Hub.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Fara has a son with special needs and she left her high-flying job at Dow Jones to set up the education centre with the hope of providing support to those in situations similar to hers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She is deeply committed to ensure that early and meaningful intervention is given to children with needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She would like to see society become more inclusive and embracing of people with different abilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She, therefore, welcomes the announcement made by Deputy Prime Minister Heng on the Inclusive Support Programme that will integrate the provision of early intervention and early childhood services to help children with special needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She also looks forward to the new Singapore Together Alliance for Action to support care-givers of persons with disabilities and hopes that, through this, more enhanced support can be considered for families with children with special needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The third individual I want to tell you about is Mdm Rajoo Meenachiammal, one of my volunteers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Meena is a dedicated volunteer who enjoys serving the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She lives with her 73-year-old mother and is the primary care-giver.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She works in the security industry and does the night shift so that she can spend time in the day to take care for her mother and bring her for her medical appointments.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Meena is grateful for the financial support she will be receiving like the S&CC and U-save rebates, and the CDC Food Vouchers as these help her alleviate her monthly expenses.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Joey, Faraliza and Meena are strong and resilient women who are passionate about what they do and care for the people around them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are many women out there like them and I want to take the opportunity in this debate to share and talk about the Budget from a woman’s perspective.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: COVID-19 cast a gloomy shadow over many women who struggle to overcome their challenging situations, but it also provided opportunities for them to show strength and become everyday heroes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is imperative for the Budget to help navigate the people through these difficult times.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our women, like their male counterparts, are very much involved and vested in our economic recovery and social development.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While we may not typically see the Budget presented in a gender-centric fashion, the reality is that, there are many aspects of this year’s Budget measures that benefit women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In fact, all the Budgets announced in the past years have had measures that impact women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This year’s Budget is building on past efforts to transform the economy and support Singaporeans through various changes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In this regard, I would like to share my thoughts on the top three things about this Budget that matter to women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are many women working in hard-hit sectors, like tourism and hospitality.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The extension of the Jobs Support Scheme and Jobs Growth Incentive, therefore, have had a significant impact on keeping many women employed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If these women were forced out of the workforce, like what we see happening in other countries, there would have been severe repercussions to their income, careers and even their retirement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of our healthcare workers are also women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They have made sacrifices working in high-risk environments during the COVID-19 pandemic while balancing their other roles as mothers, wives and daughters.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They have been working hard even before the pandemic, but showed true commitment in our battle against the virus.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To quote Deputy Prime Minister Heng, our healthcare workers have, over the years, been working hard to provide us with the highest quality of care.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The announcement that the Government will enhance the salaries of our nurses and other healthcare workers, such as support care staff, is, therefore, welcomed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At this juncture, I feel that we should also recognise women who have been at the leading edge of infectious diseases and public health, guiding our efforts in fighting COVID-19, such as Assoc Prof Lim Poh Lian, Director, High Level Isolation Unit, National Centre for Infectious Diseases and also Head, Travellers’ Health and Vaccination Clinic, TTSH.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Assoc Prof Lim is also a member of the Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2020, she was the fourth Singaporean to be recognised by the BBC in their annual 100 Women list.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I should also mention Assoc Prof Ong Biauw Chi, Chairperson of the SKGH Chief Medical Board, who worked tirelessly on the frontlines, managing the dormitories outbreak.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We, indeed, have a lot to be proud of, having our women at the forefront of this battle against the pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Household Support Package and the COVID-19 Recovery Grant, for example, matter to women and their families.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women are often contributing to the family finances or managing their families’ financial commitments.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In some families, the economic situation has led to some loss of income.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Financial support is necessary to help families tide over this challenging period.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Both men and women can be care-givers, and the Government’s support for care-givers is not specific to any gender.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Nevertheless, it is clear that, in many circumstances, women tend to take a disproportionate load of the care-giving role.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Various initiatives were rolled out under the CSAP, such as respite care pilots and the Home Caregiving Grant in 2019, to alleviate the community cost of care-giving.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH also worked with community partners to set up care-giver community outreach teams.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These teams support care-givers in self-care through health and wellness activities and also provide counselling services where needed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government remains committed to supporting care-givers and more plans will be shared at MOH's COS Debate.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are many other aspects of this Budget that would have a great impact on women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women care about the environment, too, and certainly look forward to further details of the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women care about their jobs and the economy and would be keen to see the roll-out of the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and the Jobs Growth Incentive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thirdly, the Budget builds on earlier Government policies and the work is not done.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have seen how policies and schemes have evolved over the years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2016, the Silver Support Scheme was introduced.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2019, we saw the Government announcing the Bicentennial Bonus CPF Top-Up.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Six in 10 of the citizens who benefited from the top-up are women in their 50s and 60s.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One-third of those eligible for MRSS are inactive CPF contributors, including full-time care-givers, with about 2.5 times as many women as men among them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There has been increasing awareness about women who have spent a large part of their lives not in formal employment but toiling to care for their families.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over time, there has also been conversations around the uneven distribution of the care-giving load and equal opportunities for women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, there are gaps that we need to work on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Gender bias and stereotypes and the disparity between men and women continue to exist.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: That is one of the reasons why the Conversations on Women’s Development was started – to encourage a whole-of-society discussion on this to nudge behaviours and call for changes that benefit not just women, but the whole community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The efforts are still on-going and there is still much to be done to meaningfully change mindsets and systems so that our boys and girls in the future have equal opportunities to pursue their full potential.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: My colleagues, in their speeches, will address some of the issues that continue to be of concern to women in Singapore and share their views on how we can build on our existing efforts to support and empower women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling spoke yesterday about challenges faced by female cabbies and also raised the possibility of introducing respite care to alleviate the burden on women workers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling spoke earlier about digital empowerment of women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Nadia Samdin will be talking about jobs, encouraging more women into certain sectors in the workforce and providing support for women to pursue their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan, Ms Joan Pereira, Ms Carrie Tan, Ms Hany Soh and Ms Ng Ling Ling will be covering various aspects of the women’s care-giving roles.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui will speak on assisted conception.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Their insights will show the broadness and depth of all the issues that matter to our women; reflecting how a Budget debate will always take into account the concerns of all women as our interests and development are intertwined with the development of this nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In Malay):    COVID-19 has brought many challenges to our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is important for this year’s Budget to ensure that there is steady support for the public and robust plans to improve our economy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women, just like the men, are impacted by COVID-19 and are very concerned about economic recovery and social issues that emerge in our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We seldom discuss Budgets through the lens of women, but if we think about it, there are many aspects of this Budget that benefits women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In Singapore, year after year, we see a lot of opportunities and support being given to women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These enable our women to progress at a better level than women in other countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we need to continue to increase support to help develop the potential of women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women in Singapore have made many sacrifices and contributions to their families, society and nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In some of my interactions with women comprising professionals, business owners, home-based business women and housewives, I have been very impressed with their resilience.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Although the COVID-19 pandemic has affected their lives, they remain positive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They also continue to play an important role in strengthening family institutions, becoming valuable assets in their organisations, improving the country's economy and becoming a role model for other countries to celebrate the achievements, progress and potential of women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Her achievements in the field of technology, which currently does not have many women from the minority groups, is something to be proud of.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of us may also know Ms Fatimah Mohsin, designer and founder of Fatimah Mohsin The Wedding Gallery.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Due to the spread of the COVID-19 virus, many functions and events had to be cancelled or postponed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This has affected her business, but she has not given up hope.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Fatimah has modified her company's strategy and has opened a new restaurant.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In fact, despite her busy schedule, she also managed to sew and distribute 600 face masks to frontline officers as a token of appreciation for their sacrifices.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Fatimah also rolled up her sleeves to help small businesses during the physical Ramadan Bazaar last year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She invited them to place their products in her shop.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Her never-say-die attitude, willingness to innovate and concern about the plight of other business owners are traits that we should emulate and admire.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, women have much potential to help Singapore emerge stronger from this pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I urge the whole community to have an open mind and provide unfettered opportunities for women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Do not underestimate the roles, responsibilities and contributions of women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As the saying goes, “the hand that rocks the cradle rules the world”.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the pandemic is far from over.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Its impact will be felt for years to come and there is a lot more to be done.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also need to remain committed to our long-term priorities and amongst other things, continue to look at areas where we can address gender bias and disparity between men and women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are not done building this nation and will have to carry on our efforts to build a fair and just society for all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And I have no doubt, the women in Singapore will stand tall alongside the men, doing their part for this country.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is apt that we are also Celebrating SG Women this year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There is indeed much to celebrate as we are celebrating the great leaders, the pillars of strength within the families, the everyday heroes, who inspire us to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Vaccines are giving us hope to get through the challenges soon, and as we brace ourselves through probably another year of an adjusted way of life, we must continue to look out for each other.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I spoke with residents in my constituency in Jalan Kayu after Deputy Prime Minister Heng had announced Budget 2021.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many felt that it is a balanced Budget that builds on the efforts to support Singaporeans and businesses to stay afloat, to ride the reviving of the economy and, more importantly, to ensure that the vulnerable amongst us are also well taken care of.
