speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The three groups are: one, persons with disabilities; two, women who are care-givers; and three, seniors living alone or with their spouse only.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, support for persons with disabilities or PWDs for short.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, children with disability can attend special education up to 18 years old and in some vocational track, up to 21 years old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Armed with knowledge and skills, young adults with disabilities and abilities can have almost five decades of work capable years ahead of them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng assured in his Budget speech that employment and training for PWDs will be supported by various initiatives such as those under SG Enable's Open Door programme and the Enabling Employment Credit.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that we can and must do more to push for a higher level of inclusion for PWDs in the workforce in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we should not merely offer employment to PWDs in quantity, but also in quality that will allow them to optimise their full potential.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, a young lady, resident of mine, shared with me that her job scope was limited because of her physical disability.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although she has a desire to interact directly with clients, her employer has assumed that a role in a backroom will be more suitable for her.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While she is thankful for the job, she was discouraged that the assumption of her limited ability will limit her career progression.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This example goes to show that as we have more employers willing to offer jobs to PWDs, we need to minimise stereotyping jobs roles and have in mind that they have abilities that can be stretched.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Government to work with the employers, Social Service Agencies and PWDs themselves to factor in the aspiration of the PWDs even as the number of jobs will be bolstered.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Complementing existing efforts under the Open Door programme, I recommend for the Government to consider the following suggestions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, add a develop-and-grow type of programme that will help employers identify, design and develop career growth path for PWDs within their organisations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will enable employers to build the confidence of the PWDs that their potential will be valued.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, develop a holistic outcome-based measurement framework for the employment of PWDs, covering end-to-end, from skills training, job placement to career development and growth.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a framework could integrate the tracking of training outcomes, employment placements, remuneration as well as progression data over multi years to provide a basis for the Government to continually adjust policy and programmes with employers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And three, incentivise and reward more employers to attain the Enabling Mark by SG Enable so that more workplaces can implement best practises for inclusive employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, the group that I would like to bring attention to are the care-givers, especially the women.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of the most common problems that women care-givers experience is a setback in their own health and career.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a report entitled "Explaining the gender gap in care-giving burden of partner care-givers" in the Journal of Gerontology published in February 2019, it shows that women care-givers also experienced greater burnout on healthcare due to multiple stressors such as relational, financial problems and problems integrating care-giving with social and work activities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Women care-givers also struggle with uncertainty over their future and financial adequacy in their older age as a result of their absence from the workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Holistic actions to support care-givers must address the social, health and employment needs to provide comprehensive and robust support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On this note, I would like to recommend expanding the partnership to include Agency of Integrated Care (AIC) and Workforce Development Agency (WDA) in the alliance for action.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mr Speaker, Sir, in the Budget, I hope that the Government can pay more attention to women care-givers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of the most common problems that women care-givers experience is setback in their own health and career.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The need for women care-givers’ re-integration, re-employment and retirement and their own health cannot be overstated.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to hear from Deputy Prime Minister Heng in the Budget Speech that the National Council of Social Service and SG Enable will form an Alliances for Action on support for care-givers of persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Alliance will emphasise more on women care-givers, who make up the majority, and also cover those caring for seniors with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recommend that Agency of Integrated Care and Workforce Development Agency be included in the Alliance so that we can look after women care-givers’ health and employment needs holistically.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): The third group I would like to speak about are the seniors who are living alone or only with their spouse.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These numbers show that we need to continue to improve the living environment of our seniors to help them age in place as far as possible, especially in mature estates where more seniors reside.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The BTO launch of the first Community Care Apartment Harmony Village @ Bukit Batok is an innovative and meaningful pilot for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However with the number of households with seniors living alone and senior couples living without children increasing so rapidly, it might not be possible for the supply of such Community Care Apartments to catch up fast enough with the demand.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MND can consider integrating some of the success factors of the Community Care Apartments into the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) programme where more seniors can apply too.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, in addition to incorporating technology for elderly monitoring and alert system, perhaps telecare, providing remote health monitoring devices supported by care providers could also be considered as part of EASE.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As of 2019, the EASE programme has benefited about 200,000 households.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MND shared in a 2018 Parliamentary Question response that HDB regularly reviews EASE by engaging healthcare sector stakeholders to develop and review the list of improvements that can be added to the programme.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MND can consider technology enhancements in the EASE programme, including telecare packages that can be delivered through technology by care providers to reap similar benefits like the Community Care apartments to more seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I rise today to speak about our efforts to support the vulnerable among us because as we recover as a nation, we must bring along everyone and leave no one behind.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our country moves towards the path of recovery, we must not forget those among us who are vulnerable and who can benefit from innovative ideas to continue improving their lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Supporting one another should continue to be part of our Singapore spirit.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On that note, I support the Emerging Stronger Together Budget 2021.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to thank the Minister for Finance for a Budget in which it is evident that the country tries to take care of the community as a whole for the present while at the same time is cognisant of the challenges we may face in the future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A Budget, to me, is like a blueprint for the future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With the Budget, people are able to see the priorities that a Government has for the country – its vision, its plan and its ideas.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: When I was part of the Singapore Youth Action Plan as a panel member, that was what we were trying to find out.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What do youths envision for Singapore in 2025.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Or more simply, what is the Singapore that they are striving for?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But what would our Singapore youths think of Budget 2021?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What do they think is really important for the future, especially with a pandemic happening in the background?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: According to the National Youth Council, youths are those aged between 15 and 35 years old.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I have worked with youths for a long time, with Mendaki Club and National Youth Council.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even in my daily work as an orthodontist, I see mostly youths as patients.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But with such a wide age range, it is evident that different issues may resonate with different age groups.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: An old youth, aged 33 like me, may have different priorities compared to someone who is 23.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But a common thread that runs between all youths is that they care.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They care about what is happening to the people around them, the spaces around them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They care about what is happening in Singapore and what is happening outside of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And they can be fiercely protective if they think an injustice has been done in some way.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Some may be a little more indifferent than others, but in such a highly plugged world like today, it is hard for the youths not to have an opinion on a variety of issues.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They wonder if they are able to remain nimble and adapt to the ever-changing economy.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Due to increasing digitalisation, they are worried about competition for jobs from within and beyond Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For low-income youths, the problem is infinitely worse.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A lot of these youths have lost their jobs and employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Adam, a community worker and lead for "Youth Want Work" for Beyond Social Services, was able to share more. "Youth Want Work" is a youth-led, youth employment initiative that aims to provide workshops and the necessary skills to prepare them for the workforce.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In his reflection, he shared about the uphill struggle low-income youths face in employment and the importance of understanding, inclusivity and sensitivity in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And I quote: “People often think that if an individual tries hard enough, they will get the necessary opportunities, but they don’t understand the struggles these youths face at home.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, there was a very smart youth who was offered a degree position, but she had to turn it down due to her care-giving responsibilities for her grandmother and younger brothers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We also met youths who decided to enter the workforce early because they don’t see the benefit of further education, especially since they always felt ostracised in school for their circumstances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There are also many youths who are engaged in delivery and ride-hailing jobs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Though it may also serve as a disincentive for these youths to continue in the unskilled gig economy, would a gradual introduction be less disruptive and give them more time to adapt?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I would urge the Government to closely monitor the effects of this.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Other than the low-income group, youths are also concerned about other vulnerable communities and want an inclusive society where no one gets left behind.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, we need to ensure that the national conversations we have are actually inclusive of all the different voices that make up Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a melting pot of races, cultures, religions and more.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How do we ensure that all the voices are brought forward, from the people with special needs to the person with disabilities?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to hearing more details about it in time to come.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The other issues facing the community and the wider world that youths are concerned about is sustainability and mental wellness.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: When it was made known that there would be a potential clearing of Dover Forest for potential BTOs, youths took to social media to create awareness.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: When Kranji woodlands was erroneously cleared, there was uproar on social media among youths about it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It shows that issues about the environment do strike a chord with them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I do appreciate that the Government is playing an active role to engage with environmental youth groups in a bid to combat climate change.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that there is a Green Plan for Singapore and I look forward to the upcoming debates.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I feel as though more can be done to encourage careers in sustainability among the youths.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This will be elaborated further in my Budget cut.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It has also caught my attention that there is no mention yet of any mental wellness initiatives in this current Budget.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A CNA article in February 2021 states that calls to mental health helplines have increased since the start of the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I also would like to speak about something that is close to my heart – the Malay/Muslim youths.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: According to the 2018 Future-ready Conversation Series report by Yayasan MENDAKI, our youths also reflect an altruistic notion of wanting to be of "service to society".

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They see themselves as members of the wider community and believe it is a privilege and responsibility on their part to contribute.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And there are ready examples in the community.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: One case in point, Mendaki Club, run by youths, is launching the Young Women in Leadership Dialogue Commemorative Book with support from the Singapore Muslim Women's Association.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Titled “Unprecedented – To the Beat of Her Own Drum”, it features 20 young Malay/Muslim women who overcame tough odds and achieved success in various forms throughout their lives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This book launch also serves as a fundraising effort for Casa Raudha, to support its shelter for women and and children who have been victims of domestic violence.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time reading those stories, I am overcome by a sense of awe by what these women have achieved for themselves while giving back to the community.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Take Nurhajah Haron who overcame difficult family circumstances which saw her family being homeless and having to sleep in void decks.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She nonetheless graduated from ITE as a valedictorian with a perfect GPA and as the top nursing graduate.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She is now giving back to the community as a nurse.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Or Azurah Khalid, a national silat representative and rugby player for the national team.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She is the owner of Lokalfeed a podcast and online platform for content featuring inspiring women, and Wilder Café, an eatery that practises sustainable cooking.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Being a woman may bring about its own set of challenges but the stories of these inspirational women gives me great hope for the future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More often than not, much of what they think and feel strongly about comes out on social media.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, after the Budget announcement, we see youths trying to create awareness about it, while others take to their accounts to comment and give their take on it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Admittedly, though, some are not interested at all.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, it also seems like many would like to see the Government take note of their views and opinions, acknowledge that they have listened and show how their participation has helped to shape future policies.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Are their recommendations too impractical to consider due to their lack of life experiences?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In my humble opinion, I beg to differ.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that that is the beauty of it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Because they have had fewer life experiences, they are unencumbered by them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More than a few times, in my role as a consultant for the Youth Action Challenge, a platform for youths to provide solutions that tackle community issues, I have been amazed by the ingenuity of the ideas proposed.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, I feel we should engage them further on the Budget.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Any ideas can be further developed by connecting them to experts and people on the ground.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With a richer understanding of what has been done before, what has worked and what has not, these synergies can result in workable solutions for the greater good.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As President Halimah said in her Opening Address of the 14th Parliament, “Singaporeans must come together, in partnership, to pursue the greater good, united by a belief in Singapore and a desire to turn our vision into reality.” Lastly, I have a personal message to the youths who are listening.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Each one of you holds the key to your own individual story.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And each individual story forms a unique thread in the tapestry of the Singapore Story.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And honestly, that is the Singapore we can all look forward to.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For it affects you and everyone around you.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The song talks about the value of the youth in the wider society, encouraging the youth to contribute to the country and the world.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And at the same time, do so with underlying love for all human beings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   To all the young people, Lend a helping hand To your motherland The new age is here Do not delay any longer Love humankind As much as you love yourself As how each individual beholds the community And as how the community beholds each individual (In English): Thank you.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But fortunately, with the availability of the vaccines, we are beginning to see some light at the end of the tunnel.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The signs of recovery are here and we will be, as Deputy Prime Minister Heng had said, "Emerging Stronger Together".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All of us contribute through our different roles in society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I would like to speak for the care-givers amongst us, particularly the women who form the majority of care-givers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How we can provide more support to our care-givers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some take on the role to provide more customised care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Others accept the task due to particular circumstances.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their needs are very complex, which also depend on whom they need to care for – children, elderly, differently-abled, or a combination.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Care may be multi-faceted and their time requirements may not be neatly parceled out.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As my resident who is a care-giver told me, "I am the housekeeper, cook, babysitter, nurse, accountant, concierge, courier and driver, and many many more." This work is onerous due to the wide range of responsibilities and the need to be constantly available, often on standby 24/7.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through the years, as we go through the feedback, the word "respite" has surfaced over and over again.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am proud to note that as a community, we are constantly improving in how we support our care-givers so that they can have their breaks, or even find the time to pursue interests and careers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For care-givers looking after children, affordable, accessible and good quality childcare services are increasingly available.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Support for care-givers of those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For care-givers of those with mental health conditions, they need better access to information and guidance with care navigation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With all these support services in place, what more can be done?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we need to raise public awareness about the availability of all these services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This can be done through public messaging through free-to-air TV channels and radio, social media platforms, and contact points such as clinics, hospitals, community centres, Residents' Committees and Neighbourhood Committees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have come across care-givers who are very worried about costs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must encourage them to start exploring these options and work through the financials with the relevant Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, the Government needs to continue monitoring the quality of care services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regular inspections and enforcement are necessary to uphold standards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such measures are already in place but vigilance is necessary to maintain confidence and trust in the system, so that care-givers can have peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, we must provide career counselling, guidance and training for care-givers who would like to start or return to work, including part-time and flexi-work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to self actualisation, work is important to one's sense of dignity and identity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Earned incomes contribute to household finances and retirement adequacies, and improve the quality of life for their families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last, I hope MOH will train and upgrade more mental healthcare professionals to support persons with mental wellbeing issues as well as to help maintain the care-givers' own mental health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like physical health, there are ways and strategies to keep our emotional, psychological and mental states in good condition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to raise the level of general knowledge and expertise in this field among our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):    Our country has many care facilities and services which can lighten the heavy responsibility of care-giving.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can raise public awareness of such services through the media, health institutions and grassroots organisations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government must ensure that the quality of services are good, so that care-givers can have peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must also provide career counselling, guidance and training for care-givers who would like to return to work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I hope the Ministry of Health will train and upgrade more mental health professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They will support persons with mental health issues and also to help maintain care-givers' own mental health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to raise the level of general knowledge and expertise in this field among our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):    I have been wondering why I want to be a Nominated Member of Parliament.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some friends criticised that Parliament already has so many doctors and does not need another.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some even commented at an online forum, “why choose a neh-neh* doctor?”   I was feeling angry and amused at the same time.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I told my children about this and they kept laughing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My mother is a housewife and my father a retired policeman.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I went to Woodsville Primary School and was fortunate to attend Raffles Girls' School later.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the first few weeks of Secondary school, the English teacher stayed behind after work to teach me the correct English pronunciation so that I would not sound like I was lagging behind the other students.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Another teacher noticed that I did not take part in some elective activities because of the additional fees and told my father how to apply for a bursary.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These stories illustrate the importance of equal access to education, resources and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: All these are not achieved through my personal efforts alone; instead I am able to do it with the support from my family, friends, colleagues and mentors.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I remember when I was a teenager, there was a Xinyao song called "xiao ren wu de xin sheng” (Voice of the Little People).

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: One sentence touched me particularly – “Perhaps I cannot achieve a great accomplishment by myself, but I contribute as much as I can, as best as I can”.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is what I hope to do now, to express my views from my multiple roles and represent the people around me.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Education is a strong foundation for personal growth.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am not just talking about formal education, but also education from parents, families and daily living experiences.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My children look up to me and emulate my words and behaviours.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For example, wearing a mask and returning dishes after a meal at hawker centres are good examples.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There are bad examples too, such as using vulgar language.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Education plays a huge role in healthcare as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: All doctors undergo compulsory Continuing Medical Education to keep up with the rapid advances in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In this era of shared decision making, the role of a doctor is as much a teacher as healer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In each consultation, I educate my patients on their conditions, so that they can make informed decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, it is a challenge when they are misinformed by what they read from the Internet.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As Dr Google becomes ever more popular, we need to help people be more discerning.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We need to learn how to fact find, how to distinguish myth from facts, and how to identify reliable websites.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Good health education is critical in empowering people to take charge of their own health.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For those of us who are middle aged now, we have to do our part in keeping healthy.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This includes health promotion efforts like eating right, exercising, to help in disease prevention, and screening for early detection of disease.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have immediate family members who need care for serious medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: One is a citizen and the other, a foreigner.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Interestingly, I have friends who are not quite sure how to navigate the healthcare system here and think that the process starts with going through polyclinics, or that they need to go to the Accident and Emergency department.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I will take a minute to summarise for everyone's benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Unless you actually needed to see a doctor, you might not quite realise how the whole system works.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Briefly, the restructured hospitals are team based, and patients get referred through a polyclinic, and will be seen by various doctors, nurses and allied health during the course of their treatment.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A patient may choose a particular doctor in a restructured hospital, but he/she will need to pay private rates.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, due to the sheer volume of patients, the waiting times for doctors, scans and operations will be subject to variable waiting times.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In a private hospital, most private doctors run their own practices and use the hospital facilities as needed.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Waiting times are usually much shorter and the patient would typically have their chosen doctor attending to them at all times.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There are pros and cons to each system.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have worked in both, and also been a patient under both systems.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: If you have the means and can afford a private insurance plan, it is good to have more options.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, in a Forum letter to The Straits Times, dated 19 February 2021, the writer asked many pertinent questions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For those of us who are parents, we also have the duty to teach our young on keeping healthy – both physically and mentally.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, having both parents working full-time means that the contact time with our children is often limited, and this is a challenge faced by many young families.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I always thank my kids' teachers for being their other parents, in imparting values and lifelong habits for learning.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Thanks to all teachers who have worked very hard in the past year.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: To switch to online learning during the circuit breaker and then to keep up a curriculum in the classroom, as well as being ready to resume virtual teaching should the need arise.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I also thank their efforts in keeping our children safe by reminding and enforcing the importance of masks, face shields and hand hygiene.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am in the generation who grew up before the Internet and came of age when the Internet became widely accessible.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I read with horror about cyberbullying and I am dismayed at how vicious online and often anonymous comments can be.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Minor incidents sometimes get blown out of proportion by thoughtless, insensitive comments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Cyberbullying, internet trolling is an ugly phenomenon in our modern world, for which many of us have no protection against.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My eldest child is starting to explore the world wide web.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As parents, we have done our part to restrict settings, and so on, but we cannot protect him forever.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We are learning so that we can equip him with knowledge on how to protect himself and not get hurt too badly.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I note that it is "reported incidents" and wonder how many unreported ones could there be?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While the Protection from Harrassment Act and the Protection From Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) exist, the average citizen may just fume, rage and cry helplessly, when reading horrible comments by commenters who are anonymous, and we have no resources to track down the offenders.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While it is best to ignore and not read these comments, we do have a younger generation of people who live and interact virtually and we have to think ahead on how to teach them to be responsible users and not weaponise digital shaming while being empowered to protect oneself.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge and agree with part of what another Member of Parliament said previously, "that civic education is the correct way for a society to recognise falsehoods".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let us teach resilience and learn to accept those who are different.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We classify people by race, religion, nationality, physical appearance, intellectual ability, mental illness, gender identity, sexual orientation.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We tend to identify with those whom we feel are "same", and feel that those who are different are just "not one of us".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I do not have a global solution – all I can do is to teach my kids to be kind, to think before they speak, and not to fear those who are different.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Every parent wants to teach their child the right values.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How can we, as a Government, best support this?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am hopeful that Singaporeans and those staying here will continue to care for each other in this COVID-19 recovery period.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, in the initial weeks of COVID-19, the healthcare community was very heartened by the generous support from many groups.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Arts is without boundary and can communicate to all people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Medical Association started an Instagram hashtag #sgartforhcw which allowed people to share their support for healthcare workers through artwork.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Many heartwarming reports surfaced on social media of neighbours helping each other and even random strangers showing kindness.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that we will all continue this spirit of caring and I urge the influencers on social media to use their power to keep this flame going strong.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let us all be decent, be kind, and do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While I recognise the need for the Budget to focus on jobs and re-building the economy, I hope that we do not neglect to nurture the softer aspects of our society, to unify and build social cohesion – only then, can Singapore "Emerge Stronger Together".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will deduct the minutes from the break later.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Through our nation's first ever circuit breaker and almost a year of job losses across many sectors, we have pulled through, thanks to the multiple Budgets and support provided by the Government.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We know from looking back on the 2008 Financial Crisis and what happened in the United States and other democracies around the world, that the most concerning effects of major economic downturns, are political and social.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Inequalities worsened by the financial crises led to fertile ground for populist movements and more pronounced political and social division.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We cannot be naive in thinking that Singapore can be spared.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: While it is critical that we innovate and invest in transforming our economy to keep Singapore relevant globally, the Government also has an imperative to help our people recover, psychologically and socially, from the impact of a large scale crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: What is the state of well-being of our people, amidst this historic disruption to lives and livelihoods?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We are lucky for Government that has cushioned us well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But, is it really sufficient for only a national care hotline to support our people through what is worldwide, the worst global recession since the Great Depression?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: At the same time that we ramp up investments and efforts to drive industry transformation, reskilling, career shifts and so on, we need to be mindful that not everyone can catch up so easily to this "turbo-charged" momentum.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Are those amongst us who are least resourced able to catch up?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Last week, an opinion piece in The Straits Times talked about "tightening class circles".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The writer Grace Ho discussed network diversity and the side effects of meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: While it was a necessary and effective foundation to build Singapore society on for the past decades, it is not perfect and we now need to address its side effects.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: A fault line that threatens our social cohesion and national unity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: This is likely to be made worse by the effects of the COVID-19 recession.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: And yet, we face the challenge of balancing support with prudence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: How do we lift up the most vulnerable, during and beyond the current crisis, while conserving our country's reserves?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: That is a critical question that our Budget needs to address.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I believe the answer lies in the word "optimising".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In other words, we need to, "spend less, yet achieve more".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I know, it sounds easier said than done.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Emeritus Senior Minister Goh spoke years ago about individual action, by those who have more, to reach back and help others behind us to climb the ladder and it is wisdom that is relevant today.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: When I was a child, I remembered being told by adults whenever I was given a treat or a snack, to share it with others.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: My mom or dad would always tell me to offer it to someone else first: "Jie Jie, Aunty, Uncle, would you like to share this with me?" And this reframe became a habit, even now, as an adult, for me.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The virtue of sharing that many of us learnt as children, needs to be "Turbo-charged" with the Government's will and support, so that there is a national strategy for sharing and optimisation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Because "Sharing is Caring", we can achieve better outcomes with less resources.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: My hon colleagues, Ms Tin Pei Ling, spoke about the potential of seniors, and Ms Ng Ling Ling spoke about the potential of persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We have an amazing public housing system to tap on to optimise social outcomes for the poorest families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Currently, rental flat residents face social stigma, poor living conditions and lack of care resources – barriers that prevent them from breaking out of poverty.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Yet, we have an opportunity that the aging society has given us, that is, an increasing number of isolated elderly in purchased flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling spoke about this earlier.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Such homes owned by the elderly living alone may be under-utilised, as some rooms go unused.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The elderly who live alone are more likely to be socially isolated and at increased risk of adverse health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Low-income families can then live in better environments, with care and support for the young, and elderly living alone, will no longer be alone and have social interaction on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Against the backdrop of falling birth rates, Singapore faces a workforce crisis in the coming decades.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Burnout and stress rank high amongst working age Singaporeans, making Singapore top the ranks in an international study for stressed-out Generation Z.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: A recent study showed that Gen Z makes up 24% of the workforce and millennials 50%.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Mental health struggles and declining local workforce due to low birth rate amongst these two generations is putting us in the path of a human capital crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I suggest we look into the Sharing of Care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Number one, to share the load of care through progressive workplace policies to relieve stress for sandwiched families; and two, to relief the burden of care, by sharing the cost savings from institutional healthcare, with low-wage stay-home care-givers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I will speak more about these Sharing of Care strategies during the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Such encouragement certainly goes a long way to increase the pool of financial resources being channelled to the most vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: However, beyond distributing cash support directly in the form of support schemes, I would like to encourage the Government to further develop our capacity for care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: What seems to be missing, is an investment in preparing and professionalising the work of care amongst the social services sector.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I have some suggestions to build a more effective social safety net and strengthen the trampoline for the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Beyond surviving, we need to set them up to thrive.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We need our social services sector to consist of experts who are skilled at discovering and building up the strengths and assets of our underserved communities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We need to share our resources towards care and to capacity build care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I will speak more about this again during the Committee of Supply Debates.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: At the same time, that forces beyond our control compel us to drive our people harder.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The tragic case of the foreign domestic worker Ms Phaing Ngaih Don suffering abuse that led to her death, it makes us questions ourselves – how might we have prevented it?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It shows that we have a long way to go, in paying attention to the people who work around us, who care for those around us.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Some of these people are in precariously vulnerable circumstances and how are they being cared for?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In our busyness and eagerness to keep Singapore relevant and competitive for survival, are we paying sufficient attention to the care and well-being of people?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But also those who enable us, the silent everyday heros and heroines including our foreign domestic workers and our migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Whilst the support packages in the Budget are helpful to reduce some day-to-day burdens of Singaporeans, we need to innovate and invest in transforming our social support structures, in order to achieve more with less, in the long run.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We must create Sharing policies in the system, sooner rather than later, to care better.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: More than ever, we need to put Sharing on steroids, with Budget allocated to build capacity into our system and to create for better long-term outcomes for the vulnerable and the under-served.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In doing so, we then have hope of bridging the gap.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Some of the ideas I suggested may seem daunting and fraught with challenges, and for this, we need courage, trust and collaboration.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Although some extent of inequality is inevitable in modern economies and societies, the least we can do and we certainly can, and we certainly must, minimise it.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our identity as a country, as Singaporeans, must go beyond being the strongest, the fittest and the fastest in economic terms.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The greatness of a nation can be judged by how it treats its weakest member.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Perhaps, by slowing down to take better care of the weakest and to enable them better, it can take us further.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our national unity, counts on it an our identity as Singaporeans, count on it, if we are indeed to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would first like to declare that I am a practising lawyer and the Co-Chairperson of the Law Society’s Community Legal Clinics’ Committee.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have previously shared with this House before about my G.E.L mission in Woodgrove – where "G" pertains to green living initiatives, "E" is about embracing parenthood and "L" is in relation to law awareness.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I intend to speak more about these three aspects today as I propose some suggestions on the Budget.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the recent debate on the Motion to Accelerate and Deepen Efforts against Climate Change, I spoke about the role of the 3Ps – the Government, corporations and our people – in promoting sustainability, as well as the initiatives that the Woodgrove community intends to implement and participate in.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am, therefore, heartened by the recent launch of the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As I had mentioned previously, Woodgrove intends to work closely with the 3Ps to embrace a greener living lifestyle for the better well-being of our future generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I welcome these initiatives as these new targets promise a natural infrastructure that not just cools the environment and improves air quality, but also provides more places for families to stay active and bond together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that said, I believe that there is a dire need for us to ensure that our parks and the facilities within them remain a safe environment of all users.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore suggest that we adopt a mindset of maintainability and sustainability as we attempt to preserve nature and undertake landscaping within our built-up environments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some suitable measures include: the selection of suitable trees and plants; siting the planting areas away from high human traffic areas; and the adoption of strict maintenance regimes to check the health of trees periodically.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, I would also hope that NParks will work closely with the grassroots committees to organise more awareness workshops, sharing tips on how to recognise potential hazards in parks and what to do when a park-related accident occurs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Together, we can work as a community to prevent any unfortunate accidents from happening.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I agree with Deputy Prime Minister that to strengthen our social compact, we must work together to address the challenges faced by the more vulnerable members of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I believe that another group that also requires more support and have not been mentioned in this year’s Budget are the first-time parents expecting or raising their new-born children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a mother of a two-year-old daughter, I can still remember the uncertainty and stress that I had experienced during my pregnancy and within the first few months of her birth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because I wanted to ensure that I was on the "right track" during my pregnancy, I devoted extra time outside of my busy work schedule to research and attending workshops.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Later on when my daughter was born, I encountered more unforeseen challenges in caring for her, which became another mental weight that I had to handle as well.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I eventually shared my experiences in more detail on several occasions, like the PAP Women’s Wing Dialogue session.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each time, fellow mothers would write to me afterwards to share their own personal stories of overcoming difficulties in parenting.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like myself, they had all faced tremendous stress and feelings of helplessness during pregnancy and after the birth of their child.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have since realised through their shared experiences that most of the care and concern afforded by society tends to surround the health of the child, but we may have neglected the well-being of the mother as a result.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In order to ensure a healthy, nurturing environment for the baby, I believe that it is important to take equal care of the mother as well.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I agree with the Deputy Prime Minister that children with special needs require more support from us.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from providing the necessary financial assistance, it is also important to seek more awareness and understanding from the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As members of society, each of us can and should play our part to make it as inclusive as possible by increasing awareness and empathy towards select groups in our communities, particularly for our youths with special needs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will not only allow them to achieve their fullest potential in life, but will also help us to foster a more tolerant environment for everyone.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During one of my coffeeshop walkabouts at Woodgrove, one resident shared with me that her daughter suffers from Selective Mutism, which is an anxiety disorder that prevents her child from speaking in specific social settings out of fear, such as in school or public areas.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: People who suffer from Selective Mutism may also exhibit other defensive behaviour such as disobeying instructions or shutting down entirely in stressful social situations, all of which can affect academic performance and social relationships with people outside of the home environment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On another occasion during one of my e-townhall chit-chat sessions with residents, the parents of a child with autism took the opportunity to apologise to their neighbours for one of their child’s outbursts during the middle of the night.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While they have consistently taken steps to minimise disruptions, such episodes can still happen occasionally.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In cases like these, some awareness and empathy from the public can go a long way towards mitigating the effects of such conditions, allowing the affected youth to not only focus on their studies and vocations, but also to integrate better within society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from providing financial support to vulnerable groups, we must also look into ensuring that the assets of these vulnerable groups are better managed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I share the same sentiment as my parliamentary colleague, Mr Derrick Goh, as what he had shared yesterday, that one of the prevailing concerns at the moment is the prevention of individuals from falling prey to scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, urge for continuous efforts and collaborations between the relevant Ministries, banks, Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), and the Law Society of Singapore, to conduct more outreach activities regarding consumer rights, in order to educate individuals – particularly our senior citizens – on how to identify possible scams such as fraudulent investments or purchasing dubious goods.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With more knowledge available to them, we will be able to safeguard more people from such practices.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another area that we should look at, is how to ensure that underprivileged households may continue to be well taken care of in the event that sole breadwinners are suddenly unable to provide for their families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A spouse may become mentally incapacitated one day due to a sudden severe stroke, or an only working child who is tasked to support the aged parents might have encountered an untimely death.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If feasible, the portal may also prove to be a suitable avenue to set out funeral arrangement plans, with the next of kin able to perform the necessary notifications and extract the necessary information required to jumpstart the administration of the estate upon the passing of an individual.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since the circuit breaker, the Law Society Pro Bono Services’ Community Legal Clinics have been offering preliminary legal advice service to residents in need via virtual platforms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):    Since last year, CPF members have been able to log into their CPF accounts using their SingPass and nominate their beneficiaries online.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many Singaporeans may not know that CPF nominations can bring many benefits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will allow the CPF Board to understand the wishes of its members and to communicate more quickly with the beneficiaries and disburse what is left by the CPF members after they die.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If you do not nominate a CPF beneficiary, your CPF savings will be transferred to the Public Trustee Office (PTO) who will distribute them to your family members under the Intestate Succession Act or the Muslim Administration Act after your death.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many beneficiaries from poor families, this procedure is cumbersome, time-consuming and costly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The PTO will also charge the beneficiaries a statutory administration fee, calculated based on the amount of CPF savings left behind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the pandemic, I encountered several cases where residents sought financial help from me because they could not pay for the funeral expenses of their deceased relatives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Speaker, notwithstanding the suggestions which I have put forward in my speech earlier, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Budget 2021, termed a Budget to "Emerge Stronger Together", does indeed try to achieve its objectives through continuing more targeted support for our ailing industries whilst providing large investments to transform the economy to ride on the wave of new opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While spending may appear more tapered when contrasted against 2020's historical spending over five Budgets, I am cheered and look forward to this new wave of growth.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While dipping into our reserves are justified to address the current problems, on a broader scale there have been repeated rallying calls for the Government to be more generous in social spending too.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am heartened that as a nation many are looking out for one another and calling for social changes through greater social support for the lower income, for the frontline workers and for the migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, have we envisaged and weighed the trade-offs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Often called a tiny red dot, we must never forget that we are still a small nation with limited resources and no natural resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I say this not to merely highlight the small size of our country and to think small but rather quite the opposite – to think big, to put this Budget into perspective and not perceive it as an annual ritual on what "goodies" or "penalties" it presents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I would ask that we think longer time – how would this Budget, the strategic investments, affect and impact our loved ones, our children and subsequent generations to come?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Would they benefit from these investments made or would they have to pay in terms of higher taxes in the future to fund our current expenditure?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Fifty-six years on since Independence, we survived not by chance but intentional efforts by our forefathers to ensure that we and future generations would benefit and lead better life than theirs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Against the backdrop of heightened international competition for investments, Government revenues are tightening as costs are escalating especially so when we have an ageing population and the new economic trends.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is important that we first try to think how to stretch our existing resources, our every dollar, instead of cultivating a mentality that we have reserves to dip into.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the concept of fiscal prudence in mind, I would like to touch on two areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, exploring alternatives in supplementing social policies to support specific groups.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As a nation, we try to level the playing field starting from pre-school, those with special needs are included to enable them to develop social skills and social inclusion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we look into the longer horizon when this community graduates from formal education and start the next stage of their life – work, how can we better ensure that they are prepared?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When circuit breaker happened last year with many businesses shut, many in the special-needs community struggled to find alternative roles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For this community, the larger impact they face goes beyond income as their routine was abruptly disrupted, with the mental state for many of them inevitably scarred.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With wider acceptance of remote working, this model of work shift can well be adapted to support the special needs and residents with specialised skills within the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Longer term, empowering the special needs community would benefit the society as well, with a reduction in reliance on social spending especially when their care-givers age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Another group that is often neglected is the women who provide care-giving for seniors, young children and those with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Care-giving is a service, a dedication that not many would embark on if they have another alternative.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It takes love, patience and commitment to provide for those that are dependent on others to get about their daily needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, as family units shrink and more are dual income families, there is a high reliance on day care centres, foreign domestic helpers and some family members had to give up their careers to care for the vulnerable at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This trend is likely on the rise in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But at the same time, the pandemic has changed the way we work and live.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the support of technology and identification of community-based resources, we should consider enabling platforms that augment the needs of families closer to home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Others who wish to volunteer and contribute through ground-up initiatives, can do so without unnecessarily being incumbered by regulatory frameworks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It not only highlights the value of kindness and giving, but also strengthens neighbourliness and instill the love for reading at a young age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such is the society we hope to build.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One that gives and one that cares by supporting one another within the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Another select group of individuals I wish to highlight that requires our help – the elderly who are "asset-rich", cash poor.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Traditional thinking conjures up the notion that these elderlies can easily liquidate their existing homes to unlock the cash for retirement needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Sociologists have also shared that getting the elderly to uproot and move to an unfamiliar environment can be a traumatising experience for some.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some of them live with their spouse, some singles and others living only with support of a domestic helper.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many have shared with me that some inherited the asset from their parents and others actually purchased them decades ago at a very low value.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: After retirement, they have minimal cash savings and are feeling the pinch from daily expenses and medical bills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is above and beyond the impending loom and anxieties on the uncertainties ahead on where they would live next.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Their property does not fetch much value with limited lease and downsizing to public property will also cost them almost just as much as the net sales proceeds if they are able to sell the asset now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With finite state resources and funds, the continuation of tax rebates to encourage charity donations is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Beyond these charity donations, could we explore the development of philanthropic activities in Singapore to plug these gaps, for those that fall through the cracks?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Perhaps more engagement with the wealthy naturalised Singaporeans alongside being involved with the community activities of Singapore could also help to ease and connect them to the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Make no mistake that Singaporeans are generous and many of the wealthy are already donating, with some even choosing to do so in their private capacity and keeping this private.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, what I am appealing for is a more consolidated effort in philanthropic activities, leveraging on National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre, to act as a better and more sustainable supplement to Government policies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And the second area: stretching our investment dollar.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my previous Budget speeches, I had expounded on the need in measuring investment outcomes beyond just monetary value and instead focus on building a social eco-system for more sustainable and long-lasting positive outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am heartened that in this Budget, with this industry transformation, more emphasis is being placed on connectivity and value creation – focusing on how local companies can grow and with the creation of partners to build new growing segments of future industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It will greatly help to bring about a value chain within the industry that can expand beyond our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the extension of SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, as well as other investments for business transformation and the pivot towards a green economy, how can we better ensure that these investments ultimately create positive spillovers for the economy beyond the basis that it is a wage subsidy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The Straits Times recently reported that, understandably so, fewer new graduates landed full-time jobs last year with MOM looking at ways to link up unemployed fresh graduates with opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Could the private sector be better tapped on for suitable matching of jobs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Beyond engaging the private sector through the engagement with the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP), could we have more engagement sessions with the private sector on a jobseeker level?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Additionally, as we make the pivot towards a more sustainable focused economy, what would the future green jobs be like?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I call that we work closer and define these in the new economy, and better harness the synergy between the public and the private sectors to reimagine how the future of job is like.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the push for businesses and workers to internationalise, the question is "how" for such emerging opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All in all, with greater geopolitical tensions and heightened competition for foreign investments, the perennial question would be how then do we allocate funds optimally given shrinking revenues and increasing costs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There would always be infinite needs and finite resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is time that we ask ourselves, how can we do better with this dollar being spent?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Solutions need not always to be monetary and grandiose in nature, simpler solutions like creating and enhancing the quality of local and community networks could just be what we need.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What is important is for all of us to come together with a "can-do attitude".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It focuses on a few key areas to prepare ourselves for life after COVID-19, especially to transform our economy and emerge stronger.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: That will certainly be a blessing to the families and a boon for our population.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I felt that the topic of assisted reproduction is neglected in this House, and today, I would like to focus on this topic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I applaud the Marriage and Parenthood Scheme, which offers a number of financing schemes to help Singaporeans with the costs of conception, maternity, delivery and newborn care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In particular, allowing the use of MediSave for assisted conception and co-funding for the assisted reproduction technology (ART) procedures in public hospitals, which has greatly reduced the financial burden for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On one occasion, a new mom told me, "Thanks to the Government, I got my baby." I was puzzled and she explained the ART co-funding scheme.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: You see, both her sons were from IVF treatments – the second was from her frozen embryo.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She also told me the experience with her second child at the same public hospital was better than the first.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said public fertility clinics have improved with shorter waits for procedures.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On another occasion, as I cradled a newborn, the new mum exclaimed, "Miss Cheng, she's asleep.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This determined new mom did three rounds of IUI and five rounds of IVF before her girl came along.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: All these chats with families made me more aware of the different experiences that couples go through to become parents, and I started to ask more and listen to their stories.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that by doing so, we can review how our assisted conception policies can be further enhanced to help couples fulfil their dream of becoming parents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In mid-2019, when the PAP Women's Wing wanted to do a paper, we put out a joint survey on flexi-work, pre-school considerations and special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I decided to put out another survey on my Facebook to understand people's views on social egg freezing and other related questions, such as donor eggs, single motherhood, raising the IVF age limit of 45 and if they have children, were they conceived naturally, through treatments or adoption.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also gave them space to write their views on every question.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What is egg freezing? "I did not know egg freezing is prohibited." "I spoke to my daughter in her 20s after I saw your survey.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She froze in USA before returning because she knows is prohibited here." "It was against my religious belief until I saw my daughter-in-law going through IVF.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Please allow it." "My cousins froze their eggs in JB." It seemed like quite a number of ladies go overseas for social egg freezing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, a woman who is about to undergo cancer treatment may freeze her eggs for future use.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is there room for a rethink on this long standing policy of not allowing healthy females to freeze their eggs?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One suggestion is to make counselling session mandatory for women who intend to embark on this procedure.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They should be fully informed of the procedure, financial costs, risks, the notion that it does not guarantee conception later on and most importantly, the emotional roller-coaster ride that they will be undergoing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Legislation can be put in place to prevent the abuse of voluntary egg freezing and they should include the following.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For egg thawing and fertilisation to take place in the laboratory, the couple must be legally married.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This means ladies of certain age or with poor eggs quality will have to source for donor eggs overseas or adopt.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A resident asked me what a donor egg was and I explained.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He told me that the option was never made known to him in public hospital.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: His wife's eggs could not be fertilised and after several extractions and failures, the emotional stress was too much and they gave up IVF.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If there was the option of the donor egg, his wife would have loved the chance to carry a child herself and fulfil her dream of motherhood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another couple came to my Meet-the-People session to tell me their story.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The wife wanted to explain the emotional stress to me personally so we could help others.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said she could not bring herself to return to the same clinic after each failed attempt or miscarriage.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Thus, each time, they had to change doctor and clinic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After years of ordeal, today, they have three lovely children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She wanted to donate the rest of her embryos and eggs but learnt from her gynecologist that there is no such option here.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For private fertility clinics, they can source for donor eggs overseas and they can have the procedures done here.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I know some of my residents who froze their eggs and/or conceived through IVF overseas.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
