text: A few couples have told me they felt that the cost of IVF here is higher.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The amount of money they pay for two IVF attempts here may be enough for three attempts overseas so they get more chances for the same investment.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Getai celebrity, Liu Ling Ling, also disclosed in the media that she had her son via IVF in JB when she was 50 years old.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Then, IVF procedure was not allowed for ladies above the age of 45.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do wonder what happened to couples who were seeking IVF treatments overseas before 2020.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For those who needed to access their frozen eggs or embryos in other countries, how did they bring them back for their IVF treatments last year?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the past, doctors used to tell me, "No worries, just courier back".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But with the current travel restrictions, I wonder whether these procedures can still occur.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I recall vividly this encounter when I was in a multi-storey carpark after one block visit and noticed a young couple with Police officers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As I approached, he ran over and thanked me.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He said his wife and him did the survey together.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: His wife had suffered a miscarriage before and they wrote about it in the survey.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He smiled and added that she was due the next month.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And when I enquired about the car, he said, "No, no, go do more important things.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We are happy you did this." Next, education and awareness.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is a lack of fertility awareness and on treatment and tests.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some hospitals gave out free fertility health checks in 2019 hoping to promote awareness but that stopped with the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to do more to promote understanding on the subject for couples.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of my Meet-the-People session cases was a lady who got married at age 40 in 2019.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She managed to extract two eggs, both successfully fertilised but did not result in pregnancy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, the Government can consider progressively reducing the co-funding amount with age but extend some help to healthy couples who just passed the age of 40.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My most recent appeal case was just in January 2021.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Lee and wife have been trying for a child for seven years and are both 37 years old now.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They have just completed two rounds of IVF but unfortunately, both resulted in miscarriage.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On CNA Insider in April 2019, it was mentioned that couples seek treatment just 10 minutes across the Causeway in the cluster of fertility clinics in JB because one, cost; and two, PGS is allowed there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This testing and screening for the correct number of chromosomes can improve the chances of success.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are many countries around the world where voluntary egg freezing is legal and have been allowed for many years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We will certainly be able to learn, adopt and adapt the best practices to suit our local environment.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Through all the families and women I have encountered who have shared with me their stories, I believe that women undergo voluntary egg freezing because they truly want to be a mother.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a beautiful and wonderful thought but unfortunately out of reach for some in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that as we continue to push on with our plans to re-open society and our economy in a safe and sustainable way, we will be able to relook at voluntary egg freezing and open our hearts and minds to support the hopes and dreams of many families here in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.25 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Singapore Government is fully committed to the advancement of all Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 1961, the Legislative Assembly of Singapore debated the Women’s Charter and subsequently institutionalised the rights and protection of women and girls via the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Women’s Charter celebrates its 60th anniversary this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have a longstanding commitment to building a society of equal opportunities where all Singaporeans, including women, can achieve their full potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we can always do more to further support and uplift the women in our midst.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 has brought challenges to women, from increasing the stress of care-giving for some, to increasing financial instability or risk of violence for others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will like to touch on how Budget 2021 builds on continuing efforts to support women and their families by: one, supporting women in care-giving; two, supporting vulnerable women; and three, supporting women in their career aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our women often play important roles as care-givers in our families, and we want to support them in caring for their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These efforts help women, by giving women real choices, as they give women peace of mind should they decide to go back to work when they have a young child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To ensure accessible, affordable and quality pre-schools, the Government has expanded pre-school capacity, and is on track to reach 200,000 pre-school places by 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Families are also now paying less for pre-schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have enhanced pre-school subsidies from January 2020, and appointed more pre-schools on the Partner Operator scheme with lowered fee caps for all Singaporean children from January 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Taken together, this means that a Singaporean child will receive about $50,000 in Government funding over five years when the child enrols in a full-day childcare programme with one of the Anchor Operators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Low- and middle income families can additionally receive up to $28,000 in means-tested childcare subsidies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Budget 2021 builds on these efforts and goes further.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We know that care-givers with young children with developmental needs may find it even more challenging to care for their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have thus announced that in Budget 2021, we are stepping up efforts to better support young children with developmental needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government currently provides Government-funded early intervention, or EI, services to about 5,600 children below age seven with developmental needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Of these, 1,900 children are served in the Development Support Learning Support, or DS-LS, and Development Support Plus, or DS-Plus, programmes delivered in pre-schools, while 3,700 children are served in the Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children, or EIPIC, delivered in EI centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Currently, about 75% of children, aged three to six years old, who attend EIPIC provided at EI centres, also attend pre-schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These "dual schoolers" shuttle between the pre-school and EI centre two to three times a week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I co-chair the Inclusive Pre-school Workgroup and the workgroup had engaged about 900 participants, including parents on their views regarding inclusion and support for children with developmental needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In an online survey, parents and care-givers, the majority being mothers, rated travelling time between pre-schools and EI centres as being among their top three concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will allow the children to meaningfully participate alongside their typically developing peers and reduce care-giver burden and stress, which arise when shuttling their children between the two centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Typically developing children and their families will also benefit from enhanced teacher training and development of stronger social skills from a young age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The InSP pilot will be launched at a few selected pre-schools and, if successful, we hope to expand the InSP to more pre-schools, and lighten the load for mothers who care for children with developmental needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For care-givers of Persons with Disabilities, or PWDs, the Enabling Masterplan 3 had highlighted the need to improve care-givers’ well-being and enhance their care-giving capabilities, including by creating more peer support and informal support networks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have thus introduced the SG Together Alliance for Action, or SG Together AfA, on Care-givers of Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through this, NCSS and SG Enable will work with the community to tackle the pressing issue of supporting care-givers of persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For a start, the SG Together AfA on Caregivers of Persons with Disabilities will focus on self-help and mutual support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: SG Enable will identify stakeholders who have common interests in peer mentorship and other informal forms of informal support, and shape and coordinate their efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If successful, a similar approach can be adopted to support other care-givers as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Next, I would like to touch on supporting women who may be more vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 has brought many challenges to families, with incomes and lifestyles impacted, all of which can lead to conflict within the family and in some serious cases, family violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Though not all enquiries are related to family violence, and they include repeat calls by the same individuals, or multiple callers reporting the same incidents, we have to keep a close watch on these trends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The NAVH operates 24/7, all year round to make it easier for victims of violence and abuse, members of the public and professionals to seek help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Task Force on Family Violence, that I co-chair with Minister of State Assoc Prof Mohammad Faishal, has also studied the landscape and possible causes of family violence and we will be putting up recommendations to the Minister of Home Affairs and Law, and the Minister of Social and Family Development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Conversations on Singapore Women’s Development was launched in September 2020 to take a comprehensive look at issues that impact women at home, workplaces, schools and the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Participants in the Conversations have raised the issue of what the approach to punishment should be for hurt and sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MHA and MinLaw have reviewed the sentencing framework for hurt and sexual offences, and a Ministerial Statement will be made at a later date.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are cognisant of the fact that regardless of the progress that Singapore women have made on many fronts, we must continue to guarantee the physical protection and well-being of our women and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 has also impacted the incomes of women, and we have introduced various forms of assistance, to help those who need help over this difficult period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 2020, we introduced the Temporary Relief Fund and the COVID-19 Support Grant, to tide Singaporeans through the financial impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Given COVID-19’s protracted economic impact, in January 2021, we launched the COVID-19 Recovery Grant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A Budget measure may thus not be explicitly targeted at women but it is no less impactful and meaningful for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And as announced by Deputy Prime Minister Heng in the Budget Statement, we will be introducing a Household Support Package, or HSP, in order to provide additional support for families, during this time of economic uncertainty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Lower to middle income families will receive more and this includes women who lack family support, such as elderly females who live alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even as we support our women for their needs and guarantee their protection and well-being, we also want to support them in achieving their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many women and men during the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development have shared feedback on how women can be supported in the workplace and their career aspirations, such as having more women in corporate leadership positions and putting in place formal and informal mentorship and networking platforms for women leaders to support and learn from each other.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Council for Board Diversity, or CBD, is one such platform, set up by the MSF, to look into having more women on boards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The CBD promotes sustained increases in the number of women on boards of SGX-listed companies, Statutory Boards and Institutions of a Public Character, or IPCs, by encouraging organisations to be more diverse and proactively identifying and grooming potential board-ready women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our women leaders play key roles in our IPCs, as leaders or board members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And our IPCs have stepped up their support during the COVID-19 period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government is strongly supporting such efforts through various Budget 2021 initiatives such as the extension of tax deductions for donations to IPCs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):    The Singapore Government is fully committed to the advancement of all Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 1961, the Legislative Assembly of Singapore debated the Women’s Charter and institutionalised the rights and protection of women and girls via the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Women’s Charter celebrates its 60th anniversary this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But each era brings about new challenges and we need to continue to work hard at ensuring progress for our women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Fundamental to this is our continuing commitment to guaranteeing the physical protection and well-being of our women and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 has brought significant stress to families and in some extreme cases, has led to family violence against women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have also noted the public’s concerns over hurt and sexual offences against women and the Ministry of Home Affairs and Law will be making a ministerial statement on their review of the sentencing framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are also concerned about COVID-19’s impact on women and their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In English): In closing, the 2021 Budget will continue to support our women in the roles they play, and provide support for those who need it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have dedicated 2021 as the Year of Celebrating SG Women and I hope you will join us in celebrating the different roles our women play, in our families, for our economy and in our society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The hon Member of Parliament Mr Pritam Singh asked about the CDC Vouchers Scheme and the role of CDCs and Mayors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am one of the Mayors and representing the Mayors now.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The CDC Vouchers Scheme was conceived for two purposes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, to help Singapore households defray the cost of living and, two, to support local businesses, especially those in the heartlands.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Supporting two target groups affected by the COVID-19 pandemic – residents and heartland businesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The scheme went beyond the "neighbourhood mom-and-pop shops" that were suggested by the Workers’ Party’s Mr Png Eng Huat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, the range of shops covered the smaller supermarkets, coffee shops, wet and dry market stalls, confectionaries, bakeries, medicine shops, hair salons and so on.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, Mr Singh should have found out that NTUC Fairprice, Sheng Siong and Giant were not included, right from the start.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The function of the CDCs in the Vouchers Scheme is clear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: From scratch, the teams organised the resources, communicated the scheme and got as many merchants as possible to sign up and to make full use of this well-intended help scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unlike what Mr Singh mentioned, local bodies like the grassroots Consultative Citizens’ Committees (CCCs) do not always have market and shop representatives sitting in their committees.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead, merchant and hawker associations are reached by tapping on a network that is organised by the CDCs that comprise CDC and CC staff, contract staff, grassroots volunteers and national bodies, such as the Singapore Federation of Merchants’ Associations and its subsidiary, the Heartlands Enterprise Singapore (HECS).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Grassroots CCCs are not set up to run schemes of this magnitude.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the last year, in fact, many grassroots volunteers were quietly helping in the massive distribution of free sanitizers, free meals, millions of face masks and the Trace Together Token.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even today, they are knocking on doors to encourage residents to go for their vaccinations to get the herd immunity that Singapore would need to keep us safe from COVDI-19.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In any case, the CCCs or the grassroots are not set up to organise schemes, such as the CDC Voucher Scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This third tranche is intended, of course, to help the residents and the heartland businesses as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is also intended by Deputy Prime Minister Heng and MOF to thank everyone for their support during the COVID-19 period and also to celebrate hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The CDCs are still working on the processes, cost and timeframe of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Details will be announced once they are ready.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that heartland merchants from all the constituencies of Members of Parliament of this House, including Hougang, Aljunied and SengKang GRCs, will join the CDC Voucher scheme so that both merchants and more residents will benefit from it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, I wish to speak on the role of CDCs and Mayors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The idea of the CDCs was first mooted by the then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong in 1996 as part of his vision of a "tightly-knit, compassionate and self-reliant community in Singapore, with the more able in society helping the less able".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unlike Government Ministries, which have very focused functions and missions, CDCs are geographic district-based entities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is another way to serve citizens who need help.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The key mission is to assist, bond and connect.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For many years, the CDCs focused primarily on "assisting" and are known mostly to the lower income households for administering, because they administer the Government’s financial assistance schemes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This administration has since been taken over by MSF’s Social Service Offices or SSOs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although the SSOs are now administering the financial assistance schemes, CDCs continue to assist in different ways.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the district level, CDCs perform duties that grassroots or Government Ministries are not quite set up to do – effectively, three functions – A, B and C: (a) Aggregating – finding out – aggregating the needs and distributing resources at the district level; (b) Building capability for our residents at the district level; and (c) Connecting all the players who are willing to help in the community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On the work of the CDCs, as I have said, the CDCs operate at the district level and continue to be called upon to support national initiatives, such as the CDC vouchers scheme I have mentioned.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We also do other things, support other national initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, many of us Mayors are very in support of the lifelong learning culture and SkillsFuture movement of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, a total of 4,819 free SkillsFuture Advice workshops run by the five CDCs had reached more than 127,000 participants in the last three years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: During COVID-19, the five CDCs quickly acquired online capabilities and aggregated resources from Government and non-Government agencies, such as MOE’s SkillsFuture Singapore (SFS) and MOM’s WSG, NTUC's e2i, the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and private training companies as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This network, assembled by the CDCs, helped residents navigate the SkillsFuture landscape for them to stay relevant and find jobs during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that is one of the examples where the CDCs support national initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: CDCs work at the district level, complementing the work of the grassroots and the Government Ministries, but, more importantly, they are active in the non-grassroots space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The CDCs keep in regular touch with non-grassroots players, such as the district’s business and corporate community, the social service agencies, schools and Institutes of Higher Learning, to name some.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A recent example is the CDC Student Meals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Within 10 days of the Circuit Breaker, the Mayors received ground feedback that vulnerable students who used to go to the school and received free school meals in school, might not be able to afford meals or might be deprived of free meals during the Circuit Breaker.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We sprung into action with a lot of help from the community, we garnered support from corporate partner Grab Singapore, raised funds from a philanthropist introduced by a friend and put in place an initiative to give out e-food vouchers to students in rental flats.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The agility and ability to garner resources are one of the CDCs’ uniqueness because we are not part of the big Ministry and we are on the ground with a small team but that is how we remain agile.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, the CDCs have also championed the culture of giving back to the society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have regular platforms to foster the spirit of giving by individual volunteers, individual donors, businesses and other partners, either for existing programmes or new ones co-created with our partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Donors, such as Far East Organisation, United Overseas Bank, StarHub, MayBank, Ngee Ann Kongsi and Kwang Ming San Temples, are but some of the donors that the CDCs were able to approach for our districts' residents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The value of the CDC structure, although within the People’s Association, is its relative agility and ability to respond and develop programmes in the district faster than a bigger Government Ministry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have developed programmes through innovative solutioning and collaborations with partners to better serve target residents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Speaker is always supporting as well, thank you so much!

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Purple Parade is Singapore’s largest movement to support inclusion and to celebrate the abilities of persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The disability cause has been supported by Central Singapore CDC since 2013 and is one of its signature initiatives – perhaps still unknown to some.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But many of the participants are not people with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are people who believe in the cause and they joined us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And we have just a small team to work on this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And how we did this was with so many partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic did not stop the Purple Parade and it went online for the first time last year and continued to receive very encouraging support – again, made possible by the strong network cultivated by the CDCs over the years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have been an active volunteer in the disability sector but I do not think I can pull off the Purple Parade without the support of the CDCs and my fellow Mayors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not even certain that there will be a Purple Parade, if not for the CDC.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is nothing to be ashamed about making sure one is always relevant and can add value, as times change especially.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans also ask what the role of the Leader of Opposition in our Parliament is, under the circumstances that all nine of the elected Opposition Members of Parliament, all one single Party.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nonetheless, I want to still thank Mr Pritam Singh for bringing up the subject of CDCs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the real work is in the work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How much publicity does one have to put out just to justify one's existence and to prove one's value-add?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Would Singapore society be worse or better off without the CDCs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I expected a robust response to my speech; and indeed, Ms Denise Phua's comments are not surprising.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When I called for a review of whether Mayors should be full-time, this was not a personal vendetta against the current Mayors or Mayors who have been full-time Mayors in the CDCs before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Neither was it an indictment against the programmes that are run by the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But having said that, it is helpful for us to take a look back at the evolution of the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think Ms Denise Phua tried to do that but I do not think she provided a complete picture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that is because the trajectory of the Government thinking at that time was Government programmes, ComCare assistance, KiFAS, things which are done by MOE today, for example, would go through the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Selection of where childcare offices or childcare centres also came through the CDCs and the budget of the CDCs was proportionately increased.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is helpful to look at the Hansard of that era, specifically Committee of Supply (COS) 2002.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, you find the evolution of the CDCs, I think, best encapsulated by what Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said when he was Minister, MCYS, I believe, in 2010 or thereabouts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said all Government schemes go through the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is what was said in Parliament, it is on the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many other functions are now not in the hands of the CDCs anymore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And concomitantly, the budget of the CDCs has reduced significantly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: That is because the Prime Minister feel that I am running the largest district here – 23 divisions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, I think that is the current situation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, I do not know whether you consider them full-time or part-time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But I am probably guilty of being the only full-time Mayor and I take it that that is why I do some national initiative projects as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And other Mayors, please feel free to speak up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, it will be helpful to hear from the other Mayors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think my question is certainly put out there already.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is for the Government now to determine the approach that they want to take in terms of whether Mayors should be a full-time or a part-time appointment given the comments I have made about the scope of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have made my point and it is now really in the Government's hands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would also like to make a point about this issue that the hon Member Denise Phua made about public mindshare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This has been a problem, in my view, for the longest time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is not just something recently that has cropped up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is again from the 2002 COS debates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Mayor Zainal Abidin Rasheed, the predecessor in my constituency of Eunos, was the Mayor of Northeast CDC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And these are his verbatim remarks at that debate: "Recently, Radio 93.8 started a series of programmes where they interviewed Mayors and staff of the CDCs to explain and to talk about the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To my surprise, most of those who were interviewed by Radio 93.8 claimed that they were not aware of what the CDC was all about and they do not even know who their Mayors were despite the fact that we have carried out quite a number of activities." And, of course, it goes on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the point here is nobody is questioning the projects that the CDC runs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The question is: is it ostensibly possible that these projects also could be carried out with charities, some of whom have a huge footprint not dissimilar to very worthy initiatives that the hon Member Ms Denise Phua herself helms, like the Purple Parade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think that there is a very valid question as to the roles and functions of the CDCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And beyond the points that I have made in my speech, I thank the hon Member Ms Denise Phua for her clarifications.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I would just like to share my inputs to address Mr Pritam Singh's last question about whether the work can be undertaken by charities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Coming from being the founder of charity, I think the capacity amongst the charity sector is limited.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: As far as I know from my experience, many charities want to focus their manpower and resourcing on the work of working, hand-holding, serving and supporting families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: And I think, at least from my experience, the value of the CDCs to the charity sector has been that it is able to carry out the work of consolidating, aggregating, reaching out to partners to pool more resources and support for the charities and the work that they do as well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, this is the part that I find, as a charity member in society, we do benefit greatly from the CDCs' amalgamation of resources from bigger corporations who are willing to give to the sector, but would like to be part of a bigger movement that then disseminates these resources out to the various charities who want to focus our resources on doing the work of supporting the communities directly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, I wish to address how we view and approach competition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Competition is a ubiquitous aspect of life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In school, our children compete for grades, awards and places in top schools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even in co-curricular activities, they compete for a spot on the school team to improve their chances of entering Secondary school via the Direct School Admission (DSA) scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We even grew a billion-dollar industry in the form of tuition centres, which have fuelled the competitive dynamic that is part of our education system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Employees compete with each other for raises and promotions or enterprises engage in the survival of the fittest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can draw out the best in each person and each firm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, when competition starts taking negative edge, we need to re-examine our priorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As we are told time and again, Singapore is a small and vulnerable country which needs to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, we must ensure that our competitive spirits are directed towards the right targets and adopt a more cooperative mindset with our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, Singaporeans at the workplace could orient themselves more towards looking out for each other and helping each other succeed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is how professionals and workers from other countries instinctively operate, even when they are working here.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should not see our fellow Singaporeans as competition for promotions but as partners we can cooperate with to improve the products and services of our company's, thereby improving our company's earnings and contributing to our bonuses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Government-linked companies or GLCs could look at more ways to collaborate with the SMEs in ventures overseas and form local consortiums with them, thus increasing Singapore's competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we must not forget the plight of the middle income who make up a growing proportion of our population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Middle income families often find themselves squeezed from both ends.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their incomes render them ineligible for many Government benefits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, they still have to cope with high costs like their home mortgage, children's education and aged parents' medical fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All this leaves them with little buffer against the vicissitudes of life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An unexpected shock, like a family medical emergency, can throw them into financial distress.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to provide more help to this group.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, I am not calling for universal handouts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such flexibility should be exercised at the first instance based on their merits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government agencies should not wait for these individuals to pluck up the courage to send in appeals before they can get the help they need.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has forced us all to re-examine what constitutes an essential job.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some supposedly higher skilled jobs have turned out to be less critical than their lower skilled counterparts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was amply demonstrated during the just concluded Australian Open Tennis tournament, which was held in Melbourne under the shadow of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To minimise the spread of viruses, all human line judges were replaced with Hawkeye, an electronic line judging system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Umpires are still featured, but their role seems to be relegated to calling the score, not adjudicating line disputes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It remains to be seen when they too will be made redundant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the bright side, ball kids face far brighter prospects since it is harder to build a robot which can run, retrieve and throw balls on cue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Naturally, to gear up my kids to be future-ready, I signed them up to be ball kids at the ATP 250 Singapore Tennis Open which is taking place this weekend in the Singapore Sports Hub.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Automation is by no means limited to the tennis court.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many other highly skilled jobs are either being taken over by machines or offshored to lower cost locations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Robo advisors are giving active fund managers a run for their money; X-rays can be read by radiologist in India; and mobile app development can be outsourced to developers in Vietnam and Romania.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The pandemic has showed us that many so-called "3D" jobs – dirty, dangerous or difficult – have turned out to be more essential than some white collar jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These everyday heroes, kept our country running when we were all locked down at home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that even here in Parliament House, workers were here until late last night to fix a broken toilet pipe.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But with the restrictions in the supply of foreign workers and the reluctance of many locals to take up 3D jobs, the demand for workers in these occupations often exceeds their supply.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on the law of supply and demand, these workers' wages should naturally rise to reach a higher equilibrium price.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In practice, however, many of their wages still remain painfully low.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is in part because of the structure of our industries and in part because our society does not esteem them highly enough.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The state needs to intervene to ensure that these workers' earnings increase to match the value they bring to society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTUC has announced plans to roll out the PWM to six more sectors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is yet unclear how and when all these 100,000 workers will be covered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said in his Budget Statement that the Government's aspiration is for every sector of the economy to have some form of progressive wages, echoing NTUC's call for a universal PWM.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam has termed the PWM a "minimum wage plus".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is not my objective today to debate the merits or demerits of the PWM vis-a-vis the national minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I think the parties have stated their position on this issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) has called for a national minimum wage, first set at $1,300 in take-home pay per month; and the Government and NTUC had explained why they have chosen the path of the PWM while pointing out that they are not ideologically opposed to the minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I accept that the Government is heavily invested in the PWM.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My goal today is to discuss how the PWM framework can be improved so that we can achieve our common goal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Whether Singapore adopts the PWM, a universal PWM, a national minimum wage or a minimum wage plus, I believe the common goal of everyone in this House is the same: to raise the wages of all our low-wage workers and ensure they earn a living wage that can support their families in what is one of the most expensive cities in the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to the MTI, the Average Household Expenditure for Basic Needs, or AHEBN, for a four-person household was estimated to be about $1,300 a month in 2017.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AHEBN is an estimate of the average that households spend on essential needs such as food, clothing and shelter every month.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is how the WP derived our figure for a national minimum wage, which will rise with the AHEBN.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the PWM's goals are not limited to setting a basic minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is something which the Government has emphasised as the very reason why it favours the PWM over a national minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The PWM also seeks to chart out skills ladders and career progression for workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These sectors include strata management and solar technology, both of which do not typically employ low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why are we venturing into PWM for these industries when there are still so many more low-wage workers who lack a basic wage floor to protect them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The basic principle of the PWM is that higher wages must be a result of improvements in productivity, not Government fiat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Higher productivity can be achieved by upgrading workers skills through training.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With a better skilled and more productive workforce, firms will be able to pay their workers better while still remaining profitable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This sounds great in theory, but is less straightforward in practice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the training element of the PWM may be well intentioned, but training can improve productivity only to a limit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In many low-wage occupations, there is a skill ceiling due to the manual nature of their work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many more HDB blocks can a conservancy worker sweep if we send him for more training?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After completing basic training, further training will reap diminishing returns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Worse, it could cost the firms money and lost work hours with marginal or no improvements in productivity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even as the Government subsidises much of the training and absentee payroll, it does not mean the training is free because it is still borne by taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, providing pathways for career progression for our low-wage workers is also a worthy goal to strive for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it has limited utility for many low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many elderly cleaners are striving to be promoted to supervisors, where they have to manage a team and churn out monthly reports for management?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For most of them, their priority is first and foremost to earn enough to provide for their families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And third, the PWM is designed to be rolled out to specific industries through licensing conditions set by the respective lead sector agencies: NEA for the cleaning sector, Police Licensing & Regulatory Department, or PLRD, for security agencies and NParks for the landscaping industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These lead sector agencies require that firms implement the PWM before they are issued operating licenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If an industry does not currently have any licensing conditions, the relevant lead sector agency will need to introduce a licensing requirement before implementing the PWM.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will be the case for the proposed roll-out of PWM to the retail sector, which currently has no licensing requirements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This two-step process will be cumbersome for both the Government agencies and the firms involved.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It would surely introduce more red tape and dent productivity, leading to more overheads to firms, which may cost them far more than just what a wage hike may cause them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It may cause them far more than just a wage hike to meet the basic minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to hear that the NTUC is looking at a vocational PWM and I look forward to more details of how this will be implemented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Someone on Reddit once remarked that the PWM is like a Rube Goldberg machine which tries to solve too many things at once, without solving anything well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This may be a rather harsh critique of the PWM and I know there are many officials who are working very hard to make the PWM work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe there needs to be a fundamental re-ordering of the PWM framework so that it can be rolled out faster, for the benefit of more of our low wage workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What is more, we have to-date only picked the low-hanging fruit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will be far harder to roll out the PWM, particularly in its current form, to the remaining industries and occupations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe it will be less bureaucratically complex and more efficient to first set a basic wage floor for specific industry sectors, and expand the list of sectors quickly so that we can eventually cover all our local workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The other aspects of PWM like training requirements and career progression ladders can still be brought in, but later.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that the pandemic period is not a good time to impose wage increases across a large swath of industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Dr Koh Poh Koon said yesterday that the Wage Credit Scheme (WCS) could be used for this same purpose.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can also have positive effects on our economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The lower income have a higher marginal propensity to spend because they need to meet their basic needs, so putting more cash in their hands will have a multiplier effect on our GDP growth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Higher wages for these occupations will encourage more people to enter the workforce and ease the labour crunch in many essential industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those already in the workforce will be more motivated at work, resulting in improved personal productivity and lower turnover and retraining costs for companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will be a win-win-win for workers, employers and our economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in order to emerge stronger together from this economic downturn, we need to jettison some legacies that have lost their relevance in today's world, and be willing to adopt new paradigms to bring our country forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to focus on two pillars of our nation – our seniors and the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Among those whose jobs are affected by the pandemic, our seniors are among the hardest hit group.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad to note that this Budget continues to recognise the importance of promoting senior employability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: All this is good news for older workers who wish to continue in employment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While technology and financial incentives go a long way to encourage companies to employ seniors, a change in mindset of both employees and employers is required to create truly senior-conducive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Research consistently indicates bias against older workers in Singapore, with impaired health and reduced cognitive abilities among top concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This negative labelling of seniors can impact their employability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Concerns about employing seniors can be overcome by redesigning jobs and the physical workplace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But this is something that companies find cumbersome to do.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One employer asked me, "Why review my workplace practices and design, when I can simply hire someone younger?" With this mindset, employers would miss out on the wealth of experience and problem-solving capacities of older workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Workplaces must adapt, or we will face a labour crunch soon.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors must at the same time continue to be willing to adapt and persevere despite the challenges that they may face at work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not uncommon for seniors who, despite trying their best, remain self-deprecating of their potential and mistakenly believe that technology is for the young.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fear of the uncertainty is part of human instincts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But senior workers too, must be optimistic and believe in themselves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must continue our efforts to push for greater digital adoption amongst our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because the withdrawal of the JSS will lead to increased unemployment in the near term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need more direct assistance and matching from the Government to help workers, especially senior workers, to stay in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another major way to help on the employability front is to facilitate the creation of more micro jobs for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Member Henry Kwek also spoke about this yesterday.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I want to emphasise that many of these jobs can be in the community, including carers for other older, more frail seniors, medical escorts to accompany other seniors from hospital to home and vice versa and handyman works for repairs around the estate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I see many senior residents at my MPS who have expressed interest to look for micro jobs near their homes because they have family commitments and cannot afford to travel far.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, Mrs Tan, a 63-year-old homemaker, has approached me to help her look for employment as she can spare a few hours when her grandchildren are in school.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government can play a role to promote such micro jobs by offering integrated search and listing platforms to match the demand and supply based on location.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government can also consider providing accreditation and training for persons who might want to take up micro jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an important sector that help to build our comfortable homes and world-class infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The past year has been difficult for the sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that this year's Budget did not mention additional support measures for the construction sector, beyond the JSS extension.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have we forgotten the people who toiled and sweat to build our infrastructure and for our beautiful HDB homes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their work has been badly affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have a good number of residents who work in construction, either as workers or employers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to do more to help this sector cope with the immediate fall-out in three areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we can do more on the manpower front.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Though industry players are receiving help from the Government, many short-term challenges have not been addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many firms with existing projects must cope with rising costs and labour shortage as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those who have recent travel histories to higher-risk countries must stay at a designated facility to undergo an additional seven days of testing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Employers would have to pay for their accommodation and the swab test costs, which can add up to a significant amount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to consider providing subsidies as all these amount to increased labour costs and cost of contracts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Housing the workers remains a challenge for some employers in construction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, some employers say that they are still struggling to obtain approval for building Construction Temporary Quarters or CTQ.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Time is tight and the TLQ should be extended while these approvals are being worked on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The foreign worker levy waiver and rebates were a lifeline for construction companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Due to safe distancing measures, productivity at worksites have dropped tremendously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During this difficult period, can the Government consider reducing workers levies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can reinstate levies when SMMs are removed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For projects that are eligible for cost-sharing relief with contractual parties, can the Government look into expediting early settlement and payment to the contractors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is supposed to help the contractors with their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we should consider giving some priority to our local construction companies for public projects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yesterday, Member Patrick Tay called for tougher measures to strengthen the Singaporean Core workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I would like to call for the Government agencies to build Singaporean Core companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 is not the first pandemic, nor will it be the last, that will impact our borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a stark reminder for us to improve our self-sufficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Local preference is relevant to our construction sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to give our local construction firms opportunities to develop their own expertise and grow such that Singapore will not stagnate even in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A potential critique of this practice is that it undermines competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And that the winning tender might not provide the best value.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The local construction companies would purchase from local supply chains and service providers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This in turn creates an "economic multiplier" effect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Investments that circulate locally boosts economic activity, employment and tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure that policies which favour local companies are transparent and fair, the Government can establish certification programmes and make public a database of companies that qualify for the preference.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Implementing specific definitions for local preference eligibility, establishing well-developed goals, clear tracking and reporting will help to ensure that the policies are effective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This ensures accountability and that projects are value for money.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Of course, in doing so, we should be mindful that there may be restrictions such as WTO or other international agreements of which we are a party to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But, if we put our minds together and work hard towards our goal, we should be able to find solutions to support our local contractors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly and lastly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, as we cast our minds towards a post-COVID world, we must review our infrastructure needs accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will in turn, create more employment, while ensuring that we are on track to adapt to post-COVID needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must not forget to review our support for those who are struggling to catch up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my speech, I focused on seniors and the construction industry as examples.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In times of difficulties, we must do what it takes to support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The hon Member Mr Gerald Giam made a few references to my two speeches; one from last year and one yesterday about the PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I thought I am obliged to clarify some issues that he has brought up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I have great sympathy for my brothers and sisters working in the strata management sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As I said yesterday my speech, this is an outsourced sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I think the nature of the industry behoves us to think about a PWM model where they can see career and wage progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The reason why we started with the lowest sector is because they are the ones that need the most help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They are our brothers and sisters who need the greatest uplift to catch up the rest of society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But beyond the lower wage sector, we want the concept and the idea of a PWM to be pervasive across all job roles so that everyone in the job can see progression in their career and no wage stagnation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Giam also talked about licensing requirement in diverse sectors at retail sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Giam also actually rehashed some of the points I already made yesterday about uplifting wages immediately using the Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And in fact, I am glad he agreed with my suggestion to consider the wage credit scheme as a form of transitional support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I hope that when we do so, we will get more support; and in that sense, if there were any wage increase that translates to consumer costs increase, I hope the Workers' Party Members can also help to convince consumers that they have to do their part as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: What I do not understand is that in advocating for a sectoral wage floor across different sectors, how different is it from what we are already proposing for sectorial PWM, which starts with a sectoral wage floor anyway?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And there is, in my mind, I thought there are some convergence there, in what he is suggesting and with what we are doing with the PWM sectorally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: What the Member has not said, however, is how does what he proposed, whether it is a pervasive minimum wage can prevent disemployment?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I have a great fear, that if we were to push pervasive minimum wage that is beyond what the industry can bear, my brothers and sisters will suffer from this employment and we will see more unemployment out there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I think this is something that we ought to bear in mind – the cure we are proposing cannot be worse than the disease itself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I will address some of the points that he responded to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: First, about strata management and solar technology sectors, and why he feels that it is important because of the wage stagnation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Why do we not work harder at that first, rather than venture into other things?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am not saying that career progression is not good and I am not saying that it is not good to have increases in salaries beyond the minimum wage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But I think we need to really double down and focus on the low-wage workers first, to ensure that they are protected before we go into other areas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I do not think we want to have a situation where perfect is the enemy of good.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: We want to make sure that we implement the good things first and then try and perfect it later.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The other point about the sectoral wage floor and the convergence he mentioned.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Yes, indeed, there is some convergence between our proposals because the minimum wage is the first component of the PWM and it should continue to be that way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, let us focus on that first component first before we go into career progression and other aspects.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: He also mentioned about the concerns about unemployment that will be brought about by increases in wages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Yes, it is true that if we increase wages by too much, there could be unemployment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But let us look at the actual real-world examples.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think the effects of this wage increases will be minimal on many other industries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think that is probably not quite accurate because actually that is already a PWM sector, which is why you do not see an increase in disemployment, because there is a wage ladder together with skills ladder.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And in his proposal now, he is talking about a sectorial wage floor, which in fact, is what sectoral PWM is all about.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Are you still advocating for your universal minimum wage that WP wants?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think you need to take the whole context of what we have in place.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Beyond the PWM, tThere is also the WIS component.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And we have been talking about augmenting this yesterday in my speech.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope the Member remembers my speech from yesterday.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Dr Koh is trying to understand whether or not we have changed our position on this minimum wage issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: That is the position that we are still pushing for, but two things: First is that we accept that we are not in Government, and the Government and the People's Action Party is in Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The People's Action Party has decided to proceed with this PWM model.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, we are trying, in the interest of protecting our low-wage workers, to find a way that we can propose how you can start off with this minimum wage, and then you can do those other things like career progression and wage increases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am not digging in, just to say that, "Oh, I want to stick with my position and my position is right, your position is wrong".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think we are all working together to find out what is the best way to benefit our low-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Indeed, Madam, this is what we have been trying to do in this House: to make sure that we take care of our most vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If the Member's position is that we should set the appropriate wage floor so that we do not create disincentive for employment, then surely it cannot be one single wage floor across all sectors, all job types that can be relevant and absorbed by all different types of services and service bias.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think this is why we propose that the advantage for PWM is that it is customised for a sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And that hopefully will address the larger swath of workers who are in the lower wage group.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: All right, Mr Gerald Giam, could you just clarify the point?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But it does not mean that we are saying that we should immediately start adjusting the different wages for the different sectors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: That can be done in the PWM but let us get the minimum done first so that we can progress onto the next step.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has not been an easy transition for her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In her first week, she entered school every morning in tears.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was difficult saying goodbye to her at the gate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it was comforting for us to know that the teachers were there.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was peeping through the fence, as we, parents, often do, and I saw the teachers holding Ella's hand, offering her a tissue to wipe her tears and showering her with love during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I saw how this was not just about teaching, but it was a labour of love.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every morning, the principal and teachers were at the gate cheerfully saying good morning to the students as they arrived.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We received phone calls from teachers updating us on Ella and we had Zoom calls with the teachers and other parents too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, Minister Indranee was asking me about this during our break earlier and she said that I now look like a mad dinosaur.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been called many things, but the first time, a mad dinosaur.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it has been a difficult Primary 1 journey for me too – waking up so early every morning to send Ella to school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, it feels like I have just fallen asleep and it is time to wake up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I guess I had a glimpse of what it is like being a teacher, waking up so early every morning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But a glimpse also because I am sure teachers wake up much earlier than me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been said before, but it is not said enough: teachers have a tough job; and I thank them again for their loving role in nurturing our next generation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have emerged stronger from this pandemic also because of our teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the pandemic and the circuit breaker, they work doubly hard, teaching physically in classrooms and virtually.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were out there while we kept ourselves safe at home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are things we can and should do to make their job a little better and this is what I would discuss today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, Madam, let me also start by thanking MOE for its reforms in recent years, which have made education a more nurturing experience.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have stopped reminding students of how they are ranked in both class and level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have stopped grouping them into classes based on academic abilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have stopped comparing students to their peers when grading the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The message to students has been clear: focus on your own learning; do not be distracted by how others are doing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As then Education Minister Ong Ye Kung put it, I quote, "Learning is not a competition, but a self-discipline you need to master for life." I agree.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And indeed, we have done a lot to help our students get rid of the distractions and focus on their own learning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I feel we have not done enough for our teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
