text: It seems contradictory to me that teachers tell their students that students are no longer ranked and compared relative to their peers while they themselves are ranked and compared relative to other teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had the privilege to hear some of their conversations and experiences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I left with a renewed appreciation for the genuine passion our teachers have for teaching.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The feedback that the teachers raised at these sessions were ultimately because they wanted to be better teachers for their students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will share four proposals to tweak and refine the appraisal system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These proposals reflect concerns on the ground, based on survey data by the union and personal anecdotes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not proposing to throw the baby out with the bath water.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am suggesting that we make the appraisal system more standardised, transparent, fair and formative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will better support our teachers to do their best work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My speech is about teachers because each of them influences tens and hundreds and thousands of young minds in their daily work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Starting from teachers, my hope is that the change in the appraisal system would flow through to the rest of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, teachers go through a two-step appraisal process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the RO takes this assessment to a Ranking Panel of senior staff members.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ranking Panel then decides on the rank and grades of teachers in the school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How do all these people decide on what a teacher really deserves?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As MOE has shared, it provides guidelines and conducts training to advise on best practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the stories shared by teachers reveal that current guidelines and training are not robust enough to ensure that the appraisal is standardised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the first stage of assessment by a RO, teachers report that subjective and irrelevant considerations are sometimes taken into account in the assessment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One teacher said that some ROs prefer yes-men, I quote, "If you are one who asks questions and give alternate suggestions, you are deemed to be uncooperative and calculating".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another teacher said that their RO favours staff who are his friends or used to work with him in other schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It should worry us that some teachers feel this way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have to fight for the teacher at the Ranking Panel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many ROs, themselves, feel frustrated by the Ranking Panel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They flag the roles of personalities and politics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One RO said that those on the panel tend to play up their own teachers while criticising others so that they themselves are ranked as being effective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another RO fretted about retaliation, saying that to speak up for unfairly ranked teachers means to risk, I quote, "suffering the same fate".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, we should be concerned that some ROs feel this way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our teachers are doing their best for the students and many do want to receive constructive feedback so that they can take steps to improve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the current process means that the outcome may not simply be a reflection of a teacher's performance and irrelevant considerations come into the picture.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the challenges of evaluating a teacher's work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also understand that MOE has frameworks in place, such as Key Result Areas for each job level describing key competencies and qualities to achieve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there is more that we can do to standardise the process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, MOE can provide greater clarity to its guidelines and provide more granularity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, Key Result Areas currently tell teachers what "good" looks like.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just like the detailed marking rubrics used for students, these Key Result Areas should be broken down by grade so that teachers know what specific standards are required to achieve an A, B, C and so on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clearer appraisal standards given to ROs and Ranking Panels make it harder for subjective and irrelevant considerations to enter into decision-making.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, MOE should formalise its guidelines on teacher appraisal as requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Good guidelines are not so useful if they can be ignored or circumvented.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers and ROs alike said that the appraisal process varies sharply from school to school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some schools have robust and objective processes in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other schools may have weaker processes which allow for more subjectivity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOE has said that its policy on teacher appraisal seeks to balance between consistency across schools and discretionary judgement by the schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The balance is currently tilted towards discretionary judgement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These stricter standards will move us towards consistency, limit biases and emphasise the performance of teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not just about what I think is right.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is what the vast majority of teachers think is right.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second proposal is that MOE enforces a clearer and more consistent feedback policy for performance appraisals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers do not know how to improve if they do not understand how and why they got their grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, the feedback policy that schools must follow when conducting their annual appraisal exercise are merely guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These guidelines may not have been successful in helping teachers understand the ranking process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we spoke to teachers to understand why they see the process as opaque, two main reasons cropped up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first reason is because information was not proactively offered to some of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One teacher said, I quote, "The grades were never explained to me for the years I joined service".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second reason is that even when some teachers asked about the process, they are given no explanation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One teacher sought to understand why they received that grade, but their RO said that there was no way to discuss the performance grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can anyone do better if they do not know what they are doing wrong?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think we can all empathise with how frustrating it must be to be in a situation like this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOE can implement a standard procedure for how schools respond when teachers request feedback and clarifications about their grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, this standard procedure needs to be enforced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the data shows, a large majority of teachers currently see the appraisal exercise as lacking in transparency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must make proper communication mandatory and enforce this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third and finally, we can work with the teachers to strengthen MOE's communication policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can implement a whistleblowing mechanism for teachers to use when their schools are failing to abide by MOE's communication policies on appraisal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, this mechanism must include measures to protect teachers from retaliation within their schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together, these measures will foster a more transparent system where our teachers will always know how to do better, and this means a better education system for our children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means a teacher's grade will no longer be affected by the limited number of As, Bs, Cs and Ds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can see how the quota system can distort incentives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the very top, each school can only give out a very small percentage of As and Bs every year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means it is not enough to be a terrific teacher; you have to be more terrific than everyone else.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The good quota rewards you for being a big fish in a small pond.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is a disincentive for being in a school where there are people better than you, whom you can learn from.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The quota also hurts those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that even if you are a good teacher in a school over-populated with super good teachers, the quota may still force you to receive a terrible grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, the system discourages you from surrounding yourself with the best of the best.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The quota system may also be applied in ways unrelated to a teacher’s performance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One teacher said that some department heads agreed to spread out the bad quota across departments by "pre-selecting" a few teachers from each department to get bad grades and then fulfilling the prophecy by assigning unimportant tasks to these teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The bad quota would not be so painful if the bad grades were, in fact, not that bad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong has said that schools have flexibility for assigning grades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, in practice, virtually all schools had teachers with C-, D or E grades, as Minister later shared.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be because of the additional paperwork, scrutiny and justifications needed to exercise that flexibility.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let schools assign grades based on a standardised process, as I proposed earlier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The risk of fiscal imprudence is limited, as each school is given a fixed quantum of monies for performance bonuses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Standardising the process as well as the existing practice of having a Cluster Superintendent advise each Ranking Panel are both powerful checks to guard against grade inflation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOE would not be alone in this shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some of the most successful companies in the world have dropped relative ranking and moved towards more flexible performance management systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amazon announced in 2016 that it would drop its stack ranking system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even General Electric, the American conglomerate where stack ranking was popularised in the 1980s, has dropped it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Its current CEO said he prefers "reviews that candidly tell an employee where they are not measuring up and what they need to do to improve, without rigidly adhering to certain percentages".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers who have struggled should not be denied the full resources to grow or the full prospect of being rewarded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three years with 0% chance of promotion is enough to make anyone lose interest in their profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why would we disincentivise hard work like that?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What I hope for is that our teachers spend more time improving their own performance and aspire to become better teachers, instead of spending time worrying about how they are compared to others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This has been a long fight by Member of Parliament Denise Phua and former Members of Parliament Zainal Sapari and Intan Mokhtar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Dr Intan said previously that our "appraisal system is quite summative" and spoke about the need for a more formative approach to the appraisal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Member of Parliament Denise spoke about the negative aspects of forced ranking, speaking of instances when employees get pushed up in terms of their ranking because of very vocal supervisors who were able to speak up for them at ranking sessions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the last few months, I have heard these exact concerns surfaced repeatedly by our teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Sapari, a veteran in the education service, first as a teacher, then a school principal, then a cluster superintendent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He asked for the forced ranking system to be abolished, and instead adopt a criteria-based approach for ranking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Sapari, Dr Intan and Ms Phua have been speaking about this since 2018.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a previous debate, Ms Phua said, "to run a race whereby only a few win the trophy might be a race that, I think, the Minister has been asking for us not to run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should run races where as many as possible can make it to the finish line, and as many as possible can meet a good or great performance standard”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all want what Ms Denise Phua is calling for but it is simply not possible under our current appraisal system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us make our appraisal system more standardised, transparent, fair and formative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The surveys show that majority of teachers support this call.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Madam, I know our performance management system of stack ranking is a sacred cow.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for once, I am not asking for a scared cow to be slaughtered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a vegetarian, I very much prefer that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am asking for us to look after this sacred cow better and for our appraisal system again to be more standardised, transparent, fair and formative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With a strong, engaged and empowered teaching workforce, we will continue to emerge stronger.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Twenty-twenty was a tough and disruptive year, with the pandemic adding complexity to our lives, our livelihoods and our norms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, I am grateful for the relief and assistance provided by the Government to cushion the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This year, while the fight against COVID-19 continues and we know it is far from over, we are in a better position to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I move for us to consider, or rather reconsider, some of the important lessons learnt.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 situation has surfaced one pertinent issue that has always been stigmatised – mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: After my Adjournment Motion last year, I received several emails.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some complained about working from home and the pressures that they face.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But coincidentally, it was during the annual ranking exercise and many shared the pressure that they faced and they have to perform.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The fast-paced and highly competitive nature of our meritocratic system produce the best results globally, but it also means our workers face immense stress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some highlighted the toxicity and the dog-eat-dog atmosphere.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Others felt the pressure to maintain a high grade whereas some are just trying to avoid a C-minus grade.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because a C-minus grade may mean limited developmental opportunities and, perhaps, the end of their career.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And in that way, we holistically support the emotional and mental well-being in workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instagram, TikTok, the latest app is Clubhouse, if you are not in that yet, and other social media platforms allow us to connect virtually, but it also means that nothing is private anymore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Name-calling, rumour-spreading, deliberate online falsehoods are pertinent and challenging aspects of social media.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have seen how both youths, as well as adults, are belittled online by their peers, and the damaging effects of cyberbullying.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a father myself, I am worried for our children, who might be vulnerable and having their mental well-being affected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Collectively, mental health issues become more apparent and intervention is much needed in times like this.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The strategies that I presented requires a whole-of-community effort.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not something that one has to go through alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There are ways for us to overcome these challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Early mitigation would certainly help, but we need to do it, together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We can only emerge stronger together as a united society, not only in terms of social and economic factors, but also in terms of our mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I had a chat with a resident who is about to finish his Diploma in Aerospace Engineering.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As the industry is deeply impacted by the pandemic, it is natural that he was feeling anxious.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He expressed that he felt that he made the "wrong decision" when choosing the course.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my maiden speech, I highlighted that early specialisation constrains skillsets and limits opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have taught many students from the Polytechnic Foundation Programme (PFP) and many have done very well – in fact, they do even better than the ones who come in through the "O" levels system or route and I felt that because they entered the Polytechnic slightly earlier than the rest, it allows them the time and space not only to settle down but to chart their education journey better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Without a doubt, our healthcare workers deserve all the accolades that come their way.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But we know it is not all about money.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Nursing is inherently a very demanding profession and entails long hours and overnight schedules.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Part of the job includes dealing with angry, mostly frustrated patients and family members.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to provide them with the best support possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: From ensuring work-life balance to enhancing their career pathways, to continually provide opportunities for them to develop and gain expertise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But above all, it is protecting them against the abuse and harassment that they face in conducting their daily duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I call for us to review the processes to enhance the support and protection of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):    I support the Budget that was presented last week.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As our economy recovers from the impact of COVID-19, other aspects of our lives will also begin to show signs of recovery.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, our battle against COVID-19 is not over yet.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we rise to combat this pandemic, I would like to highlight three important aspects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the importance of taking care of our mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, create access for those suffering from mental issues to seek immediate help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides mental health, I also touched on diversifying pathways in education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With the pandemic in our midst, many of our students are concerned about their future job prospects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It will make our graduates more competitive as well as provide better confidence and opportunities to obtain employment in the future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly is the support system for healthcare sector employees.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We are proud that our nurses understand their professional roles and continue to serve with excellence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, besides financial support, attention should also be given in terms of expanding career paths, enlarging spaces and providing opportunities to upskill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The final, and to me, the most important point is about giving them protection from the pressures and harassment that they may face when carrying out their duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my recent Facebook post about the launch of M3 at Jalan Besar, I quoted the Malay proverb uttered by the Prime Minister in 2018, "Tied up like a bunch of betel leaves, clustered like a bunch of lemongrass”  This year's Budget provides support to all segments of society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is only when we Stay United and help one another that we will be able to become a Community of Success and Emerge Stronger together.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It also takes a longer view of building a sustainable home for our future generations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While I applaud our bid to support businesses, workers and families in a more targeted fashion, I would like to sound the alarm on two issues.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, on our youth's state of mental well-being, particularly against the backdrop of COVID-19.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Second, on how we could take better care of a smaller but no less important segment of our society, that is, our differently abled youth.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Stigma could have driven them away from seeking help.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Overall, there is still a lack of understanding of mental health conditions, with one in three persons expressing the view that mental health conditions stem from a lack of self-discipline or will power.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Two in 10 felt that persons with mental health conditions should not be given any responsibility, while only a little over five in 10 were willing to work with a person with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I think these statistics paint a stark picture of our views on people with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is not enough for us just to have a conversation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We need to change the way we think about mental health if we have the well-being of our younger generations at heart, and more importantly, we need to act.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I recently met Courtney, a cheerful and confident 20-year-old lady; quite the high-achiever, or so it seems.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: She did well academically and landed a scholarship at a local institution.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Things turned southward when Courtney started struggling to turn up in school, had difficulty socialising with her peers and ran into trouble with some of her teachers over flagging attendance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Unknown to people around Courtney and even herself then, was the fact that this young life was, in fact, dealing with underlying mental health conditions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In fact, it did not even occur to her that it was why she had behaved differently from before.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And what she said to herself at that point in time was very revealing, and I quote her, "I had strong thoughts that I am a terrible person.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I don't deserve to feel like I am suffering.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How could I be someone who suffers?!" Things were soon bad enough and Courtney was dropped from her scholarship.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: She chose to leave Singapore in 2017 to pursue a vocational programme in New Zealand.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Courtney soldiered on in a foreign land, still not recognising her latent conditions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It all came crashing down again for her in November 2019, where medication she was on then exacerbated her severe mood swings.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: She regularly broke down, so much so that she could not carry on with public performances on several nights, which then, at that time, formed a big part of her assessment at vocational school.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: She was diagnosed with depression and the lesser known Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, or PMDD.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Looking back, Courtney's main regret was that no one around her and not even herself, had recognised that she had mental health issues.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The lack of awareness and stigma makes it hard for the community to identify such issues, much less to respond.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And it also makes it much harder for medical professionals to even get a chance to help.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Courtney is blessed as her parents have stood by her all this while, supporting her even in her darkest hours.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For Courtney, the key issue now is to help youngsters suffering silently from mental health issues to normalise help-seeking.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And this work is even more urgent now, given the backdrop of a global pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: COVID-19 reached our shores a year ago and has left the world grappling with the havoc it has wreaked on our lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For our youth, whether they are coping with home-based learning, or transitioning from student to working adult life, the pandemic has only made already stressful rites of passage even more daunting.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In fact, a National Youth Council survey found mental health a consistent challenge youths face during this pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We need to do more to help our young ones struggling with mental health issues and we need to do so sooner rather than later.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I would next talk about a group of youths that is also close to my heart but for different reasons – our differently-abled youths.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare that I am volunteering as a Board member with the Very Special Arts (VSA) Singapore, a charity that empowers youth with disabilities to pursue and realise their potential in the arts through continuing education.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After Deputy Prime Minister Heng's Budget speech last Tuesday, I reached out to a group of VSA parents.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: However, their consensus was also that not only can we do more to better serve youths with disability, we can do it quite differently, especially when they complete formal education at 18.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Raising a child is a lot of work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I know that from my own experience in the past eight months.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But I can only imagine the financial, emotional and logistical demands that parents of differently abled children face.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Roger, father of 19-year-old Floyd, a young man with autism, shared with me, and I quote, "Many fail to realise that it is more costly to raise a child with special needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Often, in such families, only one parent works, because the other parent remains at home to continue teaching life skills to the child, until they are independent and socially appropriate." Sally, mother to 19-year-old Amelia, a young woman with mild autism and dyslexia, shared with me that education for children with disabilities, can be expensive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As Amelia has mild dyslexia, Sally had to fork out an additional $400 a month for programmes at the Dyslexia Association of Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: All in all, $900 a month for Amelia's education.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, the gap between fees for an education in mainstream versus special education, or SPED schools has closed over the years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are financial assistance schemes available in both mainstream as well as SPED schools to ensure that no child is denied an education.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: However, could we do more to help, so these families are not unnecessarily burdened with financial strains, just because they have a differently abled child?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And could we also allow them to utilise their SkillsFuture credits to pursue: (a) Continuing Education, such as those offered at the VSA, or (b) for speech-, occupational- or psycho-therapy, services which many will need, well into adulthood?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I understand there is no one common international definition of disability but according to one UN report, 50%-70% of persons with disabilities of working age are unemployed, amongst industrialised countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This translates into an employment rate of about 30%- 50%.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While there are certainly differences in how disability is defined in the various contexts, we can do more as an inclusive society to improve employment prospects for this group of people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Parents I spoke to asked whether the Government can mandate a hiring quota for companies to recruit staff with disabilities, or to reward companies for inclusive hiring practices, just as how the Seoul Garden Group hired interns with disabilities through the SG Enable's school-to-work transition programme.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While there are schemes such as the enabling employment credits and the job growth incentive that encourages employers to hire inclusively, we need this to become the norm.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the workplace, we can do better by sensitising both employers and co-workers to be better equipped to work with differently abled individuals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We need to foster an inclusive mindset so mainstream employers and employees are mindful of both the sensibilities and sensitivities of working with their colleagues with disabilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I understand this is something that SG Enable is already doing through its Open Door programme, to equip workplaces with skillsets to interact with individuals with disabilities, but we need more companies to be on board, so collectively, we can make our workplaces truly more inclusive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many parents of children with disabilities worry endlessly about whether their children will be able to fend for themselves, long after they depart from this world.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This is also what Diana, mother of 25-year-old Aaron – a young man diagnosed with autism – related to me.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As many in the community work part-time, parents worry over whether their child will be able to afford a roof over their heads.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In December last year, HDB announced the launch of Singapore's first assisted living flats for seniors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Could we not consider a similar housing option for this community, in addition to existing options such as adult disability homes?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Not just on hard skills that will allow them to compete with their peers in the global marketplace, but also on softer skills of resilience, inner strength and overall well-being.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As we progress as a society in the grand course of history, let us all be kinder to one another, and not forget the vulnerable ones amongst us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Notwithstanding the points I had raised above, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we are in the recovery stage because Singaporeans have worked very hard collectively to keep us safe and make the best of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must push ahead with the momentum so we do not let these efforts go to waste.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my speech today, I will speak briefly about one key area to leverage on for further opportunities and change.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will share my concerns on immediate challenges pertaining to cost of living, particularly the petrol duty hike.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Manufacturing plays a key role in our post-COVID-19 economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also hires around 12% of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 has also propelled the demand for digital services and smart technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has led to an immense interest in smart manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The concept of digital twinning, in particular, has become increasingly valuable in transforming industrial operations, in an era where remote working is encouraged, and safe distancing required to limit the number of physically present workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The digital twin captures insights on key operations at the manufacturing plant, allowing employees to respond by remotely reconfiguring processes and mitigating problems in real time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also heightened demand for collaborative robots in healthcare and manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The goal is to pave the way for "qualitative transformation", with advanced manufacturing forming a larger portion of the sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But two key problems continue to plague the sector over the years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, how can we accelerate digitalisation in more of our manufacturing companies beyond the existing grants and programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Maybe we can help more of our companies embrace digital twinning technology, raise productivity in our current environment now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, retaining talent and speeding up capability transfer programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Companies also require talents to create, manage and maintain these technologies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to the Singapore Manufacturing Federation, companies have problems hiring talent like robotics engineers, software developers and programmers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Retaining local talent is yet another challenge, so companies express a preference for retaining their S pass holders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Undeniably, Singapore faces a labour crunch in the tech sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This skills gap will require some years to shore up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, the extension of the Capability Transfer Programme, or CTP, to 2024 to support foreign-to-local skills transfer is a viable support to grow the local pool of tech talents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my Adjournment Motion in 2019 on "Enhancing the role of the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices, or TAFEP, to tackle workplace and job discrimination", I spoke about localising jobs and legislation to address job discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had also proposed then, to leverage on the existing CTP and expand it to support the transfer of capabilities from foreign employees who are already in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I laud the efforts and the focus now on the CTP and hope we can increase the number of projects in manufacturing and include collaboration with MNCs, with the goal to facilitate more skills transfer and retention to build a core of highly skilled Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Separately, I was actually hoping to hear more plans from the Deputy Prime Minister in his speech, to expand the Professional Conversion Programme, or PCP, to potentially shore up supply of labour into the tech sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope MOM can share more in detail about the expanded PCP plans during the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is one area we need to focus on, the re-allocation of our young, middle-aged and senior workforce to sectors which are needed most and with speed, if possible, subject to existing constraints.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Domestic inflation will eventually go up, as the global and domestic economy recovers and following that, global easing by central banks will eventually be removed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is likely to be a global concern in the next few years if the COVID-19 situation improves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The inflation forecast for OECD countries is set to rise gradually to 1.8% by end of 2022.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Domestically, inflation was negative during the pandemic, but projected to climb up to around 1.5% in 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our economy is currently in the recovery stage, new jobs are created, Jobs Support Scheme continues for hard hit sectors, and there are real wage increases over time, especially with additional sectors identified for the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, Singaporeans need not be too worried about inflation for now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, it is undeniable that there are concerns about the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The petrol component makes up 1.9% of the CPI basket, and with the rise in oil and energy prices as well as the recent hikes, it will likely only add 0.1 to 0.2% points to the headline inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Prime Minister has stated that it is another important step towards cleaner transport and a car-lite society, and to discourage the use of vehicles with internal combustion engines.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, we can view this increase as part of a series of moves to restructure duties over several years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There was an increase in petrol duties in 2015 and a restructuring of diesel duties in 2017 and 2019.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree that the current hike is a smaller increase compared to 2015.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, for the man on the street, it is seen as another price increase or increase in cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those who drive or ride motorcycles for their livelihood, like the delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers, are the hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Apart from the petrol tax rebates for those who depend on their vehicles for their livelihood, if they are from the lower and middle income groups, they will be supported by various assistance schemes and social transfers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These support measures are partly funded by our taxes, which includes petrol duties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Apart from that, I am aware that this year’s Budget also provides the Budget 2021 Household Support Package consisting of GST vouchers, S&CC rebates, CDC vouchers and top-ups for school-going children, which will also go some way to ease the increase in cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To achieve long-term change and encourage motorists to go green, I urge the Government to help those affected like motorcycle owners to transit to electric or hybrid vehicles in the next five to 10 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The significantly higher cost of electric motorcycles compared to its petrol-powered equivalent is a deterrent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Electric motorcycles also have a long charging time of six to eight hours on average for a full charge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our push towards EV charging stations, I hope, will also involve seamless ability to charge motorcycles quickly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Government work with our local electric motorcycle retailers and manufacturers to secure affordably priced motorbikes for our delivery riders?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Government also work with electric vehicle rental companies to keep renting costs more affordable for users?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It currently costs more to rent an electric vehicle, compared to petrol-engine cars.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): I now move to my last point on fiscal strategy and plans during and beyond the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support Budget 2021 Plan to fund future infrastructure investments via the SINGA Bond and hope as part of our fiscal strategy in this current environment, we are not too constrained in speeding up our capital and fiscal investment commitments to put us in better state for the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, in the past Budgets, we had offered shares to citizens which are linked to GDP growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Singapore Savings Bond is also very well sought after.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, are there plans to issue more and smaller retail green bonds or notes to Singaporeans so as to have a stake in Singapore's sustainable future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I end, Mdm Speaker, with the multiple Budgets last year and the draw on our reserves, there is concern as to how we will fund things we need to do going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In that regard, some, including the hon Member Hazel Poa had called for a full extent of our reserves to be made known.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As someone who works in the financial markets and currency markets, I would like to share my frank thoughts from a professional viewpoint why we should strongly never reveal the data of our reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unlike most countries, Singapore utilises the exchange rate as the instrument of monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most other countries use the interest rate as a monetary policy tool.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This choice is made based on our economy’s unique circumstances and also the fact that exchange rate is relatively controllable through direct intervention in the foreign exchange markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, this makes us vulnerable to currency speculation and attacks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have seen such attacks during the Asian Financial Crisis in 1997/1998, impacting our economy and jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, I started looking for a job right smack in the aftermath of the speculative attacks on some currencies in the Asian region during the Asian Financial Crisis in 1998, right after school.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The impact then on sentiment, the economy and jobs in Asia and Singapore was bad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a financial centre, there is also the risk of capital flows if our currency is attacked for speculative reasons.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only that; other market participants may also join the bandwagon and ride the speculation and those are not just in billions of potential, it could be even higher.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our geo-political context is also vastly different from other countries that publicise details about their reserves, like Norway.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Norway’s monetary policy is that of an inflation-targeting regime to achieve lower and stable inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, with vastly different economic considerations, it is not wise to compare, and say that we too should disclose our reserves just because others do.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also remind that transparency is practised where it is safe and sensible to do so, and it is not true that our reserves are completely undisclosed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yes, hon Member Hazel Poa asked for the total reserves data from an economic, fiscal prudence angle.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, what is the amount and how it should used.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is understandable that people want to know.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But foreign actors, currency speculators and anyone who does not wish us well is also interested to know.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I mentioned, people may join the bandwagon.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The balance struck is that the Government discloses a lot already but not all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am glad it is done delicately and, so delicately, by our responsible Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be prudent that we do not make unnecessary moves to reveal our total reserves, though sincere in its intent for more information, that it can unwittingly lead to significant negative economic outcomes given our domestic context.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The results of decades of sound monetary and fiscal policies are evident in the resilience of our economy, which has weathered multiple storms over the decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, once again, I would like to explicitly state and indicate my concerns about any moves to be more transparent on our reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since we are on the topic of reserves, Mdm Speaker, I would also like to comment on the suggestion of hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai to use all the NIRC and not just 50%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would be seriously concerned if the Government were to do this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was to have fairness between the present and future generations even though it is not an exact science.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fifty percent for now this generation and 50% ploughed back for future generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we use all now, there is little, if anything left in terms of NIRC for the younger generation, the younger and future generations to come.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Importantly, by ploughing back 50% we continue to grow our reserves and that is important; while, at the same time, allowing the Government to tap on part of the investment income for current spending.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The principle of fairness, responsibility, prudent stewardship and having a thought for the future is important for the Government and permeates every Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I actually intended to ask Ms Hzal Poa to clarify on her unique suggestion to target wage component on GDP, as I assume she knows that the major reason why wages as a percent of GDP is lower than our operating surplus of corporates and other organisations of 66.2% of GDP, is because of heavy MNC presence and the structure of our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I was thinking whether she is suggesting to reduce our MNC presence in Singapore now, at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unfortunately, she is not here in the Chamber but that is something I was wanting to find out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am wondering if I could obtain a clarification from the Member on what he feels that the revelation of reserves would necessarily be destabilising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I will just point out a few reasons why I disagree.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first is that revealing a target as well as reserves certainly could encourage destabilising speculation but it could also encourage stabilising speculation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point I would like to point out is that actually, while it is convenient to argue that we have a distinct system in terms of exchange rate policy, by purchasing power parity, all exchange rate policy is in fact monetary policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, even though it is the case that we target explicitly the exchange rate, it will have implications for inflation and, hence, when other countries, as the Member has cited, such as Norway reveal that they have a certain amount of reserves and they are subscribers to an inflation targeting regime, it is not, in fact, distinct from our own exchange rate targeting regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The hon Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, if I can try to recall your first question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But I will probably take your second question first.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The second question is about, if I can recall again, Professor, you asked whether on the first one, there is stabilising and destabilising currency and speculative attacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am suggesting that speculation can both be destabilising as well stabilising.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I started off working in the MAS back in 1998/1999.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, what I saw in the Asian Financial Crisis, which was a perfect example of a speculative attack, led to economic ramifications that are not destabilising at all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That is from my own lived experience in 1998/1999; not theory.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the theoretical element that you shared from a theory perspective that there can be destabilising impact of currency adjustments or misalignments – yes, that it can be stabilising – in theory, does not make sense, unless you are talking about misalignments in the long run, that eventually correct themselves in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may clarify, I should point out that I am in fact old enough to have also lived through the Asian Financial Crisis and I am aware of the conditions surrounding it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, this is not just in theory, it was also my lived experience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: About Norway's policy and how is it different from the Singapore's policy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If I may put it in general terms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, I was pointing out that I did not think that they were distinct policies because all exchange rate policy is in fact monetary policy and I am wondering if you could clarify why you thought they were distinct.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Okay, okay, let me try to explain to you.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Saktiandi, can the two of you just speak to the Chair and just clarify the point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I mentioned in my speech about the different economic context of Norway where it is a petrol-driven economy and where Singapore is a very trade-driven economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the important issue here when you are talking about reserves in this situation for Singapore, when Singapore uses the exchange rate as its policy tool, there is a direct intervention in the markets – using currencies spot to have an direct impact on the Sing Dollar.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That is very specific because we target the exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, there is a very direct impact from a policy perspective; and thus, ramifications on our ability to have a direct rundown on reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In Norway's case, the policy target is totally different.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is using policy rates or interest rates.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it is also an opportunity to look back at the day and slowly remove paragraphs that other hon Members have already covered.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As you may well conclude from my written notes, I have thrown out my original and just gone for some key points.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The decision to vaccinate is not just personal to holder.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not just impact you as an individual.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a matter of life or death for loved ones, friends, fellow countrymen, especially those who, because of medical reasons, are unable to be vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we have invested significantly in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a bit like taking a cookie out of the cookie jar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is really tempting after that first delicious cookie to keep reaching in, cookie after cookie.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Soon, you end up a cookie monster, forever tempted when you see a cookie.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have been listening quite intently to many of the alternative suggestions that have been put forward in this House over the last two days.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I imagine that, for the Minister for Finance, it is a tremendously difficult task.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From the opposite bench, many of the suggestions seemed to indicate that everything can be easily funded because it is only X% of the GDP – very easy one, can be done.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But if we take all these suggestions together – X% here, Y% there, Z% somewhere else – it adds up significantly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That is a whole lot of cookies to be given out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, right now, while there is a lot of cookies that we are eating, there does not seem to be a whole lot of cookie-making.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our hon friends from the Workers' Party seem to say that eat, eat away, not everything, be careful, but here is a little chocolate chip and sprinkles while you at it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if we run low, instead of buying the ingredients, the Government should make more, yet not what is necessary to provide ingredients to make the cookies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our colleagues from the PSP, on the other hand, over the last two days, seemed to indicate we should take everything from the jar, everything, including the crumbs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, no one wants to say how much it would cost nor be the one to be buying the ingredients.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is, of course, up to the Member if he wants to give way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just wanted to ask whether Mr Alex Yam could identify which Workers' Party Members made the points that he is suggesting so that they can rebut him later on in the course of the debate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But no one wants to say how much it would cost nor be the one to buy the ingredients and bake those cookies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: That big elephant in the room, of course, is GST.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We cannot be constantly asking for more without being cogent of the cost.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Funding from recurrent tax ensures that all that we are doing is sustainable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: With these, we also give time for incomes to catch up so that we can deal with long-term cost of living.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The challenges that we face are many and varied, including an ageing society that will propel increases in many areas, including, most importantly, healthcare cost.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is not just us that are facing these challenges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Hong Kong and Singapore are very similar cities with very similar traits at the end of the day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: And they have just announced their Budget as well, just yesterday.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But despite the similarities, our Budgets have taken very different trajectories.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Some commentators point to a future deficit in the Hong Kong spending plan.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is certainly a scenario we will not be able to stomach locally.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Yes, there is always room to do more but raiding the cookie jar till it is empty does us no good, if we fail to top it up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: On the one hand, we may propose taxes, such as carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: On the other hand, by equal measure, we oppose petrol hike, both of which achieve similar goals.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: A government, however, needs to be cognisant of the fact that there are costs to everything that we do, both in terms of our revenue streams, what more we can do for our people and, more importantly, also our popularity and our standing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Populism and opportunism will, however, all but turn us into cookie monsters, always dipping into the cookie jar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I am sure the Minister for Finance is open to many other suggestions on how we can fund these programmes and yet remain sustainable as an economy and balance our fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: And if there is one that works as an alternative, I am certain it will take the biscuit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Much has been said over the last two days by both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Many new suggestions, all of which will cost us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The Minister for Finance has to decide which are for the long-term good of the country and which will take us to the next mile.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: All of us have the good of Singapore at heart.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We differ perhaps greatly on our ideas but, at the end of the day, we need to take responsible decisions to bring Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just a couple of clarifications on his cookie jar metaphor.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He mentioned that when we draw upon the reserves or when we suggest that the rules governing the use of the reserves should be changed, this is akin to sort of taking cookies from the cookie jar.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the Member is well aware that in 2008, I believe the Government itself, the PAP Government amended the rules governing the use of the reserves to create the NIR framework.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And in 2015, those rules were amended again to include Temasek into that framework.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is it the Member's position or argument that those were really raiding the cookie jar as well, in 2008 and 2015?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My third question would be really to ask, over time, over decades, as the absolute amount of reserves relative to GDP changes, does the Member not acknowledge that these rules should also evolve and change, and as society changes and the needs of society change and the opportunities to invest in our people, in the country change, should not those rules also be subject to change as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would just like to invite the hon Member Mr Alex Yam to agree with that general philosophical point.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I agree, because that is what I made as a closing point in my speech.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We all have the good of Singapore at heart.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We may disagree with the route to get there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But on the first point, yes, as we go along, we make adjustments, such as introducing the NIR.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But as was described earlier, we put in measures to ensure that we never empty out the cookie jar, that the cookie jar exists for moments of need, such as these.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: And even at the current moment, where we would benefit certainly from being extraordinarily generous, we have decided on what is prudent to ensure that there is always something left over and, not only that, that where we have the opportunity, to top it back up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: So, it is a quite different scenario from introducing changes to rob the cookie jar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We have always ensured that we are prudent about it, that we make returns to it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As things evolve, just as it has in the past, ideas can be considered and adjustments made.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But always with the view that we think about the future and not just about the now.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To this topic, my speech will focus on what we can do to further invest into the lives of our children from low-income families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I wish to propose two initiatives for our young friends for MSF’s consideration.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These initiatives may not be new to some of us, but I am convinced that when applied intentionally to our young, they will strengthen their access to a fuller range of positive life choices.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first initiative is a consistent long-term mentoring programme, and the second initiative is to facilitate personal saving habits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Please allow me to first share on the Consistent Long-Term Mentoring Programme.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While this bursary is important, and helps alleviate some financial burden, it struck me that the additional funds will not change the lives of our young.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Because of the complexity they face today in the ever-evolving environment, each child will require deeper interventions to access opportunities which are readily available to others.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over the past 19 years, I have had the joy of volunteering at Trybe, a social service agency that works with youths facing adversities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I believe that this intervention is not only effective for our youths at risk, but for all youths facing challenging home circumstances.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first benefit is a safe space to process pain.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Long-term mentorship provides our young an assurance that they are not alone in the challenges they face on a daily basis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Kai, a masked name, was raised in a violent home environment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He often fought in school and found himself expelled from both Secondary and tertiary schools as he could not rid himself of his aggression.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over the two years of mentoring, Kai was able to then reflect on the consequences of his aggression, subsequently shifting his focus to working out his life goals.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As Kai’s mentor created time and space for him to feel understood, Kai sought help for his anger issue and is now meaningfully engaged in work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: His friends have also noticed that he is experiencing better mental well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the midst of sometimes unpredictable or painful circumstances, the consistency of the mentor’s presence provides a safe environment and space for our young to process their feelings and thoughts for a more productive outcome in life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second benefit of a consistent and long-term mentorship is the ability to help our young recognise his or her innate value beyond circumstance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The strengths and passions of our children and youth can sometimes be overshadowed by family circumstance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Long-term mentorship provides an avenue to help them discover and more accurately identify what they are.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Abandoned by his parents when he was seven years old, Ken was raised by his grandfather.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Due to limited supervision, he lacked motivation to do well in school and eventually fell into bad company and vice.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Things started to turn around when he said yes to mentoring four years ago.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Ken grew to discover and appreciate his personal strengths and passion.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He is now looking to pursue a stable career in engineering while freelancing as a barber.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What is even more wonderful is that Ken has since reconciled with his family.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As our young friends discover their innate value as individuals through mentorship, they grow to become contributing members of their families, their community and the society at large.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The third benefit of long-term mentorship is the ability to break out of self-limiting habits and beliefs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A volunteer at a CDAC programme for low-income children once asked an 11-year-old which school she hoped to go to after PSLE.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This sweet girl then said, matter-of-factly, “Oh, can pass, can already.” The volunteer then asked “What do you want to do when you grow up?” Without missing a beat, she replied “Just help my father in his store, lor.” For this 11-year-old, her response came not from excitement to support and eventually take over her father’s business, but as her only perceived vocational option available to her, which eventually discouraged further efforts in her education.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One of the largest hindrances in the healthy development of our young people we note is learned disempowering beliefs about themselves and their future due to limited access to good counsel, financial and community resources.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mentors can show them a different way to live, and challenge them to remove self-limiting beliefs so that they not only have the best possibilities in life, but be motivated to choose wisely.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
