text: I will now move to the second initiative aligning to ComLink for our young friends, and this will be very brief, which is to facilitate personal saving habits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our youth must be empowered, not be afraid to hope, and be unhindered by socio-economic backgrounds.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Let us extend equitable access beyond finance and education to include the social and emotional support they need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: May we see every youth a success story as they author our Singapore Story for the generations to come.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, I would like to talk about how our social compact might look like as we emerge stronger, together from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, on Healthcare, which is a top concern for Singaporeans, especially as we get older.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I think this $5 billion is absolutely vital ammunition, for testing, tracing and vaccination.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It bears reminding that there are already 2.5 million confirmed COVID-19 deaths around the world to date, with many more unreported.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has done well in managing COVID-19 here so far, and the COVID-19 Package will give the Government the means to continue keeping all of us safe in 2021.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But beyond COVID-19, we might as well start getting used to healthcare being the highest expenditure item, and start getting used to numbers like $17 billion because, in due time, even with COVID-19 behind us, this would be our fiscal reality.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Within our social compact, the central question for the future of healthcare is this: How – and how much – would we, as a people, continue to care for one another, in sickness and infirmity?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One of my residents’ parent came to Singapore to visit before COVID-19 and could not go back home since last year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The parent declined in health, went in and out of hospital here, as a non-Singaporean and eventually passed on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The hospital bills came up to five digits, even in a C class ward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think his experience shows vividly the real cost of healthcare, and the real difference that Government subsidies for Singaporeans, at the outset of care, makes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, so, subsidies must continue to be a central feature of healthcare here, in order to keep it affordable for Singaporeans, but the challenge is how might we, as a society, keep these subsidies going, for the maximum benefit of all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, we have to try and contain cost per capita – in other words, the cost to care for each Singaporean, on average.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a difficult task, as ever more tests and therapies rapidly become standard in care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we need to continue making tough decisions on standard versus non-standard therapies and care modalities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, we all want the best care for ourselves, and our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But we need to also keep a firm eye on value and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this would only work, if all of us, as a society, embrace this basic principle.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Even so, I think it is inevitable that costs per capita will rise, and this is my second point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One reason is the need to duly recognise healthcare professionals for their noble and very hard work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, while I cheered at the plans to enhance salaries in public healthcare, we need to recognise that manpower is a key driver of healthcare costs and, ultimately, any salary enhancement must mean that subsidies and other financing tools must somehow keep up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If we can all intuitively understand and support this, it will be a good example of how we, as a society, can continue to evolve our consensus and do what is right and fair.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: All these, in turn, would mean that we need to raise more revenue.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But GST, fundamentally, relies on a robust consumption base.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is why I support the Budget’s laser-sharp focus on investing in our economy: investing in recovery from COVID-19; investing in industry transformation; and investing in our people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In his Budget Statement, the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned Xnergy, a local start-up in contactless charging.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, one of the co-founders of Xnergy is my resident, and I could sense the absolute energy as he talks about his team and his business.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For me, it is a glimpse into our economic possibilities, where Singapore is the place to create the future, for the world, yielding exciting roles for Singaporeans and, importantly, generating the means for us to better care for one another, as a society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, so, there is a direct link between our economic success and social objectives, and the economy must continue to be a basic parameter as we think and talk about our social compact going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify the basis for these projections amidst the severe economic contraction that we experienced last year?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My final point on healthcare subsidies is this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the aggregate, we must keep the growth in total subsidies to a sustainable pace because, ultimately, things do add up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This Budget draws on past reserves for a second year running.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as many Members have noted, eventually, we want to start replenishing our reserves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And some of us might get less subsidies, in order that those who need these the most can continue to get the right level of support.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we should review how subsidies could also be redistributed across various settings of care so that we can further channel care to each right setting and enhance care continuity across settings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I repeat the call I made in my maiden speech for the Government to invest more deeply in Intermediate and Long-Term Care (ILTC) so that we go beyond basic to dignified care for Singaporeans who need such care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our nursing homes ought to be more home than nursing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I believe that we, as a society, support such a basic direction.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But more subsidies for this sector may mean less subsidies for acute and specialist care in hospitals, for example.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, these are tough choices, but choices that we, as a maturing society, must continue to make.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In short, to secure the healthcare dimension in our future social compact, I think we need to flatten the cost curve, keep a lid on total subsidies and, within this, distribute subsidies judiciously across means and settings, and, number four, create better health and care outcomes for all Singaporeans, and, five, all these on the basis of a sound economy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need a refreshed consensus on how we can all lean in to make this happen.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have decided, fundamentally, that we will not impose a cap – a ceiling on our progress as a society – that the top, and the middle, will continue to grow as fast, and go as far, as they can.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our central task, therefore, must be to do our level best to help the bottom, especially children at the bottom, to level with their peers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For every tuition class, every sport, coding or other passion that their peers pursue because they can afford to, we have to help the young at the bottom level with their peers, as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we need to double down on holistic support for the entire family at the bottom, so that we help parents and care-givers to do well, and do better, even as they continue to do their best for their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Just yesterday, I spoke to a CEO about corporate giving.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I explained the gist of ComLink to him, and his first response was, "Oh, this is huge".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, his corporate instincts told him so immediately.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: ComLink has the potential to be the platform that transforms our social service sector, the galaxy that lifts all agencies and partners up to a higher plane and pulls everyone closer together, with its gravitational force.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as a society, I hope we can all help make ComLink succeed quickly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, our approach has always been Many Helping Hands.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, we need more helping hands, going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Many helping hands, one plan, because, ultimately, it is about one family, the same lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope this "social operating system" can become a core capability, at the whole-of-society level, for Singapore to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this way, I think every Singaporean can have his or her shot to become the fullest version of himself or herself in life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):    COVID-19 has allowed the world, Singapore and the individual to undergo a major change.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, we should capture the opportunity and transform.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: After all, salary cost is a key component of the healthcare industry.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It will be worth pondering over how the framework of Government subsidies can adjust to it, and how we can rebalance the allocation of subsidies within the framework.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In terms of supporting vulnerable families, I hope that ComLink will be upgraded to become a platform for future community service operations, integrating community services and resources in a holistic manner.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In English): Madam, in Singapore, we say the best welfare is a job.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this light, a key part of our compact must also be about how we, as a society, could enable and sustain good jobs, and good salaries, for our lowest wage workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And to frame this properly, I think it is not so much about reskilling and pivoting these workers to new industries, but about helping them to do better within their sectors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this way, we can emerge stronger, together, as a thriving democracy of deeds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One is the most important long-term threat the world faces; and the other, the most immediate threat that is on the minds of world leaders and people around the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The one thing they have in common is that both address concerns that can only be addressed by concerted effort on the global scale.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These problems must be addressed collectively and individual efforts are not going to be enough.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Climate change is getting more and more attention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is broad consensus that climate change is caused by carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As more carbon dioxide and greenhouse gasses are emitted, the faster global temperatures rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The drivers of carbon emission include the industrial development and agriculture, which are in turn driven by consumption.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other end of the equation, carbon sinks, which are largely forest and plants that absorb carbon dioxide and produce oxygen, are being increasingly destroyed as forests are cleared to make way for development.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The effects of climate change are going to be felt by everyone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As global temperatures rise, the arctic ice caps will start to melt and sea levels will rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has already started to make plans for dealing with this in the previous Budgets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, there will be increased desertification as temperatures rise, and more and more eco-systems and species face the risk of dying out as temperatures rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will be extremes of weather, droughts and floods.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While people may continue to make adjustments to survive, quality of life will definitely get more harsh and difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another casualty in this process is the natural world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I was very much moved by Sir David Attenborough’s documentary "A Life on Our Planet", which is really a sad reminder of what we have lost in the course of just one lifetime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are large numbers of species going extinct and the current age is being referred to as the Sixth Great Extinction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, our journey down this path has been paved with good intentions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People want better quality lives and development generally entails clearing land and development.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had a microcosm of this discussion just earlier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is also why the greatest carbon emitters are the biggest economies, namely the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The greatest carbon sinks are in the developing world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The developing world wants to develop and be more like the developed world, and this entails clearing land.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One area where this is being very publicly debated is the clearing of the Amazon rainforests in Brazil, where land is being cleared at one of its fastest rates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: President Jair Bolsanaro has publicly defended his country’s right to clear land for development, while the rest of the world insists it should not.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Brazil does not see why it has to forgo its own development for the benefit of the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the flipside, it views the developed world, where countries already benefited from deforestation, are not being fair in telling the developing countries not to develop.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Not only that, but the developed world still continues to have a significantly higher carbon footprint than the developing world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These ideas are not new; they have been developed in various international treaties like the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This way, countries will be incentivised to reduce emissions, in which case they pay less.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And countries that may be engaged in reforestation and absorb more carbon can get paid more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will hopefully create a virtual cycle where countries can be incentivised to reduce emissions and, if possible, even to engage in reforestation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In order for this to work, the countries emitting carbon have to acknowledge they have a problem.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We cannot really move the meter very much on the global scale.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our own emissions are probably a drop in the ocean.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think our Budget measures show a clear commitment to reduce our own carbon footprint and to maintain and manage our own development in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had a very long discussion earlier on on the clearing of land in Kranji.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The fact that land clearing gets so much attention in this House, to me, is a good sign of how seriously we take this commitment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We recognise the need for development but we also recognise the need to do so sustainably.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think what we also could do is to lend our voice and continue to do so on the international sphere, and to the extent we can aid in the assistance of working out global solutions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The two most important players in this space are the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While they are rivals on some fronts, hopefully, on this front, there is an opportunity for them to take the lead in unison.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both President Xi and President Biden have publicly voiced their commitments to reducing emissions, have taken measures, and the next step is to do so in the international scene.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we reduce emissions and ideally, incentivise and promote reforestation, the effects of climate change may be reversible, but we must work collectively to take effort.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second topic I will discuss is COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Just a little over a year ago, in the beginning of 2020, COVID-19 was a little known virus which had been spreading in China in the province of Wuhan, but had little footprint elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have had our ups and downs in dealing with this virus, the most difficult stretch being the two-month circuit breaker, the period when the virus was spreading rapidly in our foreign worker dormitories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many people played a part in this process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Frontline workers kept essential services like hospitals, food supplies and transport running, parents and teachers played their part in helping with home-schooling and later the opening of schools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, the situation is under control again, and our journey here was enabled because of collective effort and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All it takes is one or two clusters and it will spread again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most important next step in this battle is the vaccination.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: According to the BBC, vaccine efficacy based on data coming in is actually quite strong, with Pfizer, Modena, even Russia’s Sputnik V vaccine all having efficacy levels of above 90%, which is a measure of how much they reduce the risk of coming down with symptoms of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although no vaccine has 100% efficacy, even for those people who do come down with COVID-19 symptoms after taking the vaccine, it had generally not been fatal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what this means is there is close to 100% protection against serious effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The benefits are definitely there to the individual for taking the vaccine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But we have a slight problem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The slight problem we have is that our community spread rates are low and most people are less afraid of getting the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, a number of the people I have spoken to have suggested they would prefer to take a wait-and-see approach; there is no urgency to take it, so let other people take it first.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, if everyone does this, there will be a risk that our vaccination rates do not go up as quickly as we would like them to.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other Members in this House have spoken on how we should incentivise people to take vaccines, with Dr Lim Wee Kiak suggesting that vouchers be given out, and Mr Alex Yam suggesting it be made mandatory.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Workplaces may be allowed to operate at higher than 50% occupancy if everyone who is attending in the office has taken the vaccination.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, these are sort of gentle ways to, I think, nudge people into taking the vaccine, to give them very tangible, immediate benefits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is my hope that we will be able to get all people vaccinated as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Vaccines can remain optional but I think if benefits are linked to it, liberties are linked to it, people will take it up more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is my hope that all eligible people will take the vaccine soonest, as this will probably have the greatest impact in getting back to as close to normal as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Mr Speaker, the past year has been a difficult one for all of us because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of you or your loved ones may have been infected by the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many more would have experienced loss of income, loss of jobs and big changes in lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government provided significant support last year, providing companies with help like JSS, which provided support for up to 75% of Singaporean’s salaries which helped keep many people in jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Those who lost jobs or had significant loss of income were given financial support.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The self-employed were also supported, in particular, those in the affected transport sector like taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the lockdown period, many of us were wishing for a vaccine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This vaccine is now here and being rolled out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would thus strongly encourage everyone to take it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These vaccines have gone through extensive clinical testing and are generally safe to be taken.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those with serious medical conditions or concerns, you may check with your doctors to be sure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we are able to get a large part of our population vaccinated, then it will be harder for the virus to spread, protecting even those amongst us who are unable to take it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have put up with a lot of challenges in the last year – the next step, to take the vaccine, should be a lot easier and it is my hope that everyone who is able to will take it as soon as they can.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Fortunately, due to Singapore’s strong fiscal position and our reserves, we were able to turn the situation around.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The five Budgets announced by Finance Minister last year has helped many of our workers stay employed and helped many businesses stave off insolvency.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of my friends who are employers expressed their appreciation for the Jobs Support Scheme which has helped them to keep paying their staff.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also met many residents who were able to receive the Self-employed Income Relief Scheme or SIRS because this gave them much support for the leaner months due to the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There was also substantial support given by the Government for families to help build a caring and inclusive home and plans to transform and grow the economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Compared with many other countries, Singapore has done relatively well in managing the negative impact on the economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For that, I think it is appropriate to give credit to Deputy Prime Minister and his colleagues from the Finance Ministry as well as to thank the Multi-Ministry Task Force and the many frontline workers for their efforts in keeping Singapore strong economically and for keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has said that the Government will enhance the salaries of nurses and other healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Like several other Members of Parliament before me, I also urge the Government to consider enhancing the salaries of our other essential workers as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The COVID-19 crisis has shown us that during a health crisis of this nature, our essential workers, like our cleaners and those who clear our rubbish on a regular basis, they play an important role in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I submit that we must also give credit to Singaporeans who gave their full-hearted support for the efforts of the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singaporeans wore face masks when it was mandated, they used sanitisers regularly, stayed at home where necessary during the circuit breaker and coped with safe distancing measures.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our citizens did their part to help manage this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although the impact of the past five Budgets have made a great difference to many workers and businesses, the question is what next.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a country with no natural resources, we must always be mindful of digging into our reserves which is finite.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Members may also recall that during the National Day Rally in 2019, the Prime Minister said that it will cost $100 billion or more to protect Singapore against rising sea levels.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will we ever be able to put back the $100 billion withdrawn from our reserves for this COVID-19 support measures?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recall in 2011 that the Government returned the $4 billion which was withdrawn from the reserves for Jobs Credit Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How will we be able to pay for the huge expenditure required for future development projects?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the next week, during the Committee of Supply debate, we will hear many Members of Parliament asking the Government to do more and more for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And I hope that we will all exercise prudence and remember that the Government is but the trustee of all the taxes paid by all tax payers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Every additional tax relief or subsidy that Members ask for would mean that taxpayers would have to pay for those measures.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: No one likes to pay more taxes but yet, if we do not project for more tax revenue, we will not be able to fund those expenses which are necessary.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We may not be able to help those who truly need additional help from the Government's measures.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I agree with the general direction set by this Government to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think it is important for the Government to help our businesses transform so that they can create good jobs for our citizens and opportunities for all the businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We must be ready for a post-COVID future and build a stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our citizens must also be equipped and upskilled to take up jobs which may be different from the current jobs that they are used to.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We must never be complacent and think that our place in this world is guaranteed because Singapore had been successful in our earlier years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If our Singapore workers lose their desire to work hard, lose their hunger to be successful, other countries whose citizens are more hungry will step up to meet the challenge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year was described to be an unprecedented year in which Singapore suffered one of the worst recessions in our nation’s history.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, when I read the real estate statistics shared by URA in January this year, I was surprised to find that prices of private properties still managed to increase by 2.2% last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Despite so many unsold units, residential property prices remain high as developers did not reduce their prices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, agents tell me that some new developments which were launched recently in my constituency are priced at between $2,100 and $2,800 per square foot.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also urge Singaporeans to be mindful that we must all exercise financial prudence to prepare for uncertain times ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, we were like A&E, quickly reacting to where the blood flowed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We had an unprecedented four Budgets, where we swiftly came up with ways to help people and businesses cope with the loss of jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As we moved into our second year of the COVID-19, many of us learned to live in the new normal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Instead of only viewing COVID as a crisis, we are now better able to re-orientate ourselves to seek out the opportunities, to boost Singapore’s future health status.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As someone who is involved in the transport sector, I feel that COVID-19 gives us the chance to put in a place a more environmentally friendly and sustainable model of public transport which is also a better use of public resources.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The key reason for this is how working from home has taken hold around the world, and in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I must confess I was not a fan of working from home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I did not believe that people could be as productive when they are in the comfort of their home, and surrounded by distractions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But what I saw during the circuit breaker period made me a convert.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: More importantly, I observed that for the first time in my life, the roads were empty and public transport was not crowded during the usual morning and evening peak hours, which is what we call the devil horns of public transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The morning/evening peaks are the devil horns of public transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will working from home be a permanent feature of our working life?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even though cases in the community are low and we have started our mass vaccination exercise, MOM still advises companies to adopt working from home policies as a default option.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, Chinese newspaper Lianhe Zaobao reported that more than 40% of Singaporeans would like to continue working from home after the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To get a sense from actual businesses on the ground whether working from home is here to stay, I conducted a survey of over 30 of my fellow CEOs in the private sector, ranging from large companies to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: They include MNCs, law firms, architectural firms, financial institutions and manufacturing companies and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I asked them if working from home would be a permanent feature at their companies after the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One way we could go about this is for the Civil Service, which is the largest employer in Singapore, to weigh in and implement longer term working from home policies especially for the back-end and support staff.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I remember when all sorts of incentives, like free travel on certain peak hour periods, were introduced to try to change commuter travel patterns, it took months, if not years, to take effect.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: COVID-19 achieved that in a matter of days.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Without the devil horns, everybody has a more comfortable ride and it also benefits the environment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We should work to stop the horns from growing back.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Indeed a report from the International Energy Agency states: “Research has shown that disruptions can be a catalyst for shifts towards more sustainable transport behaviours but avoiding a return to pre-crisis behaviours requires governments to take decisive action.” In the same report, it notes that most people are shifting to cycling, in order to avoid potentially crowded buses and trains.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The same is happening in Singapore, though to a lesser extent, as sales of personal bicycles go up and bike-sharing companies report an increase in ridership.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: An example of the Government taking decisive action would be to invest in new and improved cycling networks to make sustainable transport more attractive and safer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On sustainability, I would like to move on to the topic of whether our bus services are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, there are many bus services running alongside and duplicating MRT routes, which are costing too much money, according to Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2020, only two bus services were profitable as bus ridership plunged during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I could not be sure how much subsidy was given out in 2020, but logically, it would be over $1 billion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we have made a huge investment into the MRT network.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Our current MRT network is about 230 km and MOT plans to increase the network to 360 km by 2030.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the last Budget, it was already announced that the Government would be spending more than $60 billion this decade to expand and renew the rail network.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After spending so much money, it is natural to encourage more people to use the MRT for longer distance travel, which are more comfortable and efficient, instead of taking buses running parallel to the MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The three longest bus routes in Singapore are service numbers 30, 51 and 61.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The above example shows that it is better for bus services to connect people to the train stations within a town, and that is for the first and last mile connection.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is more efficient to travel between towns using MRT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to propose a radical idea.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, many duplicate bus services ply through the Central Business District or CBD.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And yet, the CBD is well-served by the MRT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are many benefits associated with this proposal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We can even allow only electric buses to ply within CBD.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will help to reduce air pollution within the CBD and contribute to the Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The resources saved can be used to improve bus connectivity within each HDB town.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am sure many Members in this House have received feedback from their residents on the need to enhance bus connectivity within their respective divisions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The most common grouses among my Nanyang residents is the inconvenience of getting to the polyclinic and back home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is not uncommon that residents have to walk a total of 700 metres plus a bus ride or change bus services to reach the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When one is unwell, a 700-metre walk is not pleasant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Seoul has done it successfully, by re-organising its bus system to create safer, more comfortable and efficient rides.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am not advocating we reduce the $1 billion subsidies for the bus services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I think it is necessary to subsidise public transport just like we subsidise healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am advocating making bus services more efficient, complementing the train network and adjust to changes in transport behaviour, including the trend of working from home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The worst option is to raise public transport fares significantly to cover costs if ridership remains low.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has its perils but it has also provided us the golden opportunity to keep the devil horns away and create a more environmentally friendly and sustainable bus system that does not compete with the MRT, but is in synergy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When similar measures were announced last year, it electrified the debate.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This year, it has done the same trick again.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many car owners are wondering, why is the Government so eager to raise the petrol tax this year while the new incentive measures for electric vehicles will only be implemented next year?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Moreover, there are few charging points for electric vehicles today and they can barely satisfy the existing 1,000 or so electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is not enough to encourage Singaporeans to buy electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: URA and LTA have already put up tenders to invite operators to install charging points to cater for 600-odd electric vehicles at more than 200 public carparks island wide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Most of the charging points will only be installed next year, in other words, water from afar cannot put out fires nearby.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For taxi drivers and private hire drivers, the pandemic has significantly reduced their income.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The increase in petrol tax at this time is like adding frost to snow.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As the Government has said, taxi and private car hire car owners will enjoy a 15% road tax rebate of up to one year and an additional $360 in a four-month period.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The total rebate for these two types of rebates is about $513.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Fortunately, the Government has heard the taxi drivers' appeal and announced yesterday that full-time relief taxi drivers will also enjoy the additional $360 petrol tax rebate to further reduce the impact of the petrol tax hike.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As far as taxi drivers and private hire drivers are concerned, I would also like to mention that it is unlikely that their income will improve before the end of this year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is because it is unlikely that tourism will recover and nightclubs will reopen within this year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, notwithstanding the issues raised above, I support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Before this pandemic, many of us were guilty of not exploiting digital technologies in our everyday life in purposeful ways.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The pandemic has forced us to take an extraordinary digital leap in our daily practices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In a flash, an entire generation started to grasp digital tools in order to adjust to the new norm.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Despite social distancing and self-isolation, we are all finding ways to connect with one another.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Twenty-twenty was a year of disruptions and we had to disconnect to reconnect.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: COVID-19 is a game changer and has taught many of us about the importance of adapting and advancing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Just like a quote by Charles Darwin, "It is not the strongest species that survive, nor the most intelligent, but the ones who are most responsive to change." The pandemic has impacted different businesses and industries very unevenly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Inevitably, the pandemic will bring about new rising enterprises while traditional big wigs may be brought down to their knees.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government stands in solidarity with Singaporeans and will try to assist companies to adapt to the economic debacle that we are facing and there will be various assistance and grants.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, our workers and businesses must have the resilience to build their own muscles to innovate, have a creative mindset to reinvent themselves, be adaptable and be forward-thinking to compete against the best on the global stage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And we need to have the gumption and fortitude to succeed in spite of the risk of failure.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Last month, together with several fellow members of the GPC for MSE, we filed a Motion to accelerate and deepen efforts to combat climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And I am heartened to read about the Singapore Green Plan 2030 and the goals outlined by the five Ministries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will ensure that the access to capital for a large scale critical infrastructure is available to serve our next generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2021 is committed towards our long-term goals and sustainability and has given many Singaporeans renewed hopes after an uncertain 2020.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The world has been profoundly changed by this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has pushed us to re-assess our priorities and forced us to adapt to new ways of doing things.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, this crisis has accelerated digitalisation and flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The crisis also presents opportunities in certain sectors and provides the impetus for new approaches.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Budget has some bold initiatives, particularly green ones, which I am delighted will be implemented.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like water, food security is a critical national issue.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will be no mean feat, considering that we are at less than 10% today.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand the COVID-19 crisis has placed an enormous strain on our financial resources.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister share with us how much of the APF has been utilised to-date and provide a summary of the projects it supported, such as the type of farming projects and food production?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important that we continue to develop this sector and ensure its viability, as this industry is perceived to be less profitable than other industries, such as manufacturing and financial services.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of locally produced food.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are fortunate to have adequate national food reserves and have been able to work well with our regional and global partners to keep borders open for goods to flow between countries so far.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we should not take these arrangements for granted.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be prepared for other crises in the future and the more local food production sources we have, the less vulnerable we are to supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am heartened to note that we are exploring and tapping upon available technologies to overcome our land constraints for food production, whether these are for fruits, plants, livestock, or new types of production, such as lab-grown meat.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are capital intensive but necessary for food security.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To strengthen food security, besides sector-friendly Government policies and financial support, we need to develop a whole eco-system to make the agri-food sector a significant economic sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to nurture a new generation of local expertise, while consulting with leading agri-food practitioners and researchers locally and internationally.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need new faculties in our ITEs, Polytechnics and Universities to prepare our people for jobs and careers in this sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should continue to support small local household and community farming endeavors too.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The output from household and community farms may be small but every effort to contribute to our food security and resilience is important.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the saying goes, many little drops make an ocean.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned, we need a whole-of-society approach to succeed in realising our sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the efforts to support supply side factors continue to strengthen, it is also important to increase consumer awareness and confidence in local produce to build up demand from our local population.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I have raised in one of my previous speeches, we should encourage a "Buy Singapore" mentality where Singaporeans choose local brands and products in an informed manner. "Buy Singapore" will not only help ensure the sustainability of producing local food but also reduce our carbon footprint, as transportation and refrigeration required to move and store food over long distances are reduced.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, "Buy Singapore" can also be expanded to include goods and services beyond the agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are other local industries that may potentially have an advantage in serving our domestic market.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These should be supported and better funded to help them grow.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Three years ago, I had suggested that we designate a proportion of our borrowings for green projects to be in green bonds issuance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only will this support the Monetary Authority of Singapore's aim of growing the green bond market in Singapore, Government issues will help develop a green bond market of a significant size.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As ASEAN's largest green finance market, we account for about half of the cumulative ASEAN green bond and loan issuances.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can look forward to a more dynamic bond market with a greater variety of products to offer different investors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The bonds are expected to finance a wide range of green projects and I hope that the Government will include agri-food developments in these issues and its distribution can be sized such that even small investors can participate and do their part to support the growth of Singapore's agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many green and sustainability-linked projects will be pioneering initiatives and do not have track records.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To enable current and new enterprises in these endeavours, I hope the Government will consider more risk co-sharing with investors and banks so that green start-ups will have higher chances of bringing their visions to fruition.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The intention of the rate hikes is to encourage more green behaviour and reduce the purchase and use of vehicles using internal combustion engines.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, at this point in time, these users have no other alternatives but to use their current vehicles to earn a living.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of them deliver goods with the proliferation of online orders.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appeal to the Minister to consider providing more financial subsidies or rebates to help them tide over this difficult period or until they have time to switch over to electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, I would like to declare my interest as managing director and partner of a management consulting firm that does work in the area of sustainability and climate change consulting.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: COVID-19 has given us a unique opportunity – to "build back better".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Climate change is absolutely the biggest existential problem of the 21st century, for the world, for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am particularly proud that we are forging a brave new green economy, with new green jobs in green technology, including agri-tech, alternative fuels, the circular economy and also green financing and carbon markets and services.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am a consultant who works with businesses and Government.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I am also a lover of Nature and a global citizen who is deeply concerned about the world we leave behind for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I think, it is important to look at things from all sides so that we can carve the best pathway to fit our needs and our aspirations and bring everyone along.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In reducing emissions, we face constraints in our size and our geography.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A complete shift to renewables is probably not on the cards.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But it is not surprising; we are a hub economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our status as a manufacturing hub, a trade hub, is the envy of the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Oil and gas, petrochemicals, aviation and shipping – these are all hard-to-abate sectors where direct electrification or shift to renewables is technically not yet viable or too expensive, but they are also a significant share of our GDP.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For a hub like us, a better metric is emissions per GDP dollar, or emissions intensity, where we are in the best 20.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As a hub, we provide goods and services to the world, and as a hub, we are already doing this more cleanly than most.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: According to the International Energy Agency, 50% of global emissions reduction to reach net zero needs to come from technology that is still in the demo stage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, we cannot underestimate the progress of technology, nor the power of the people, especially young people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a gathering momentum on carbon reductions from the demand side, from businesses, investors and government.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I know because my clients are asking for advice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What if our trading partners introduce carbon border taxes – which Europe is already planning?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What if pressure on net zero shipping cripples long distance shipping?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Now, if that is not an existential crisis of epic proportions for Singapore, I do not know what is!

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In some sectors, a wait-and-see approach could be more risky than getting ahead of the curve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are unlikely to get to carbon negative by 2030 which is what it would take.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has the potential to lead the technological innovations, the business model innovation, the necessary eco-system collaborations in order to push the techno-commercial limits around decarbonisation, and then turn all of it into our new exports.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our economy will be more competitive, more resilient and we will be enabling, empowering the rest of the world to reach the two-degree goal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Surely, that is something to be proud of.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Pragmatic problem-solving, innovation, execution – that has always been the Singapore way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We aim for best in class, but we know that this will evolve over time, so our approach must be a humble, learning approach – learning from the past, learning from others – as we position ourselves to lead in policy, technology, collaboration and advocacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we build and learn, I call for the Government to stay open to revisit our commitments and put in more aggressive targets over time because a bigger ambition drives the pace of innovation, gives businesses and investors the confidence to invest, and gives us the licence to engage more broadly – to lead the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will focus on decarbonisation, leaving the also important restoration of our natural habitats and nature-based solutions to others.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, double down on the sectors for which Singapore can be the world's most sustainable hub; in doing so, increase our value-add and our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are sectors where because we are a hub, Singapore has an opportunity, and indeed, some might say, an obligation to define the 21st century vision for the sector.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are more than 100 petrochemical companies with major operations in Singapore, mostly on Jurong Island.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This manufacturing base and our position as a trade and logistics hub for petrochemicals make us uniquely positioned to incubate and scale technology, solutions and services to enable a green petrochemical supply chain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With best-in-class sustainable assets, and symbiotic relationships across the eco-system to unlock collective benefits and drive resilience in the face of externality pricing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is growing policy and social pressure to decarbonise shipping.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Maersk Mc-Kinney Moller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping is a coalition that has been established to drive the maturity of decarbonisation technologies in shipping, with seven founding partners.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore can set up or enable a similar coalition in Asia.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Thanks to our development history, we have a strong local core in areas like process engineering, energy management, control systems, from the vocational level to advanced engineering.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can be optimistic that this time, with some training, it is our Singaporean workforce who will benefit most from the transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My second proposal is to push forward on international and regional engagement, coordination and leadership, starting with ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Four of them are in the top 10 countries in the world most at risk from climate change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indonesia emissions from land use, land use change and forestry – or what we call LULUCF in the industry – are higher than their forest carbon sinks while Malaysia and the Philippines have net negative emissions from their carbon sinks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is scope for collaboration – things that can be done at scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), expensive in Singapore, but, with cross-border carbon sinks, we may be able to get the economics to work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore could tap on regional renewable energy grids while providing carbon offset markets and green financing to complement our neigbours’ green efforts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can lead the region down a collective 2-degree path; an ASEAN 2-degree path that plays to our individual strengths.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My third proposal is to be innovative in encouraging individual actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many of us in this House have made our green resolutions – from metal straws to collecting rainwater to planting trees.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the Budget, the Government will partner Singaporeans and support ground-up projects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope, I know, our wonderful youths will pick up the baton and push the boundaries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we cannot just preach to the converted.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For the ambivalent or the sceptical, it can be hard to make climate change relevant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It can be harder still to get Singaporeans and Singapore companies to pay more to go green.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We cannot simply tell people they must pay more, we cannot simply tell them to stop doing something.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we can provide a vision of a sustainable Singapore in a way that appeals to both reason and emotion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe that one way is through stories, poetry and literature.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, let us bring our creative arts community into this campaign.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then let us encourage all who have a stake in Singapore – individuals, families, communities, SMEs, corporates, to commit to climate change action.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We all hope for an inclusive transition, one where the disadvantaged are not further left behind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One that is free from the hypocrisy and power plays that, I hate to say, are often thinly veiled in their space.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: An inclusive transition means advocating to support developing countries to mitigate and adapt to climate change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Developing countries suffer the brunt of the impact of climate change, physically through flash floods, the destruction of flora and fauna, disease outbreaks and whole islands sinking, as well as economically through lower crop yields, for example.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, many emerging countries exhibit high emissions intensities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The developed nations are reducing their emissions, but it is a case of been there, done that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many developing countries, especially in Asia, are still industrialising – iron, steel, cement will be needed for years to come.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Developed countries have been able to mitigate their emissions partly because global manufacturing has migrated to emerging markets that have invested heavily in energy, in particular, coal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The average age of coal plants in Asia is only 12 years versus a useful life of 50 years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But many emerging markets will need help – aid, debt assistance, technical assistance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore can advocate for their voices to be heard, not to give them excuses, but to get them help from the advanced economies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We ourselves must be happy to help, happy to share our expertise and platforms in technical and financing aspects because that is leadership.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: An inclusive transition also means considering and mitigating the impact on the most vulnerable people, including lower income groups whose livelihoods depend on the carbon economy, for example, taxi and private car drivers and delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many of my colleagues have talked about them today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The petrol duty hike is an immediate hit to their pockets when many are already struggling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One resident told me that he needed to drive the equivalent of an extra day to make up for it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The rebates help but, may I ask, for how long will this be extended for this particular segment?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The duty hike comes when alternatives do not yet really exist, certainly not for this segment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is one alternative – e-bikes that many switched to after the PMD ban.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But Mr Speaker, it was with despair that I learnt that e-bikes are being financed in the market at exorbitant interest rates.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have got to stop these predatory behaviours.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Further, as technology continues to accelerate, driverless cars will become a reality.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   Climate change is going to affect all us, and more importantly, our children and our children’s children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a matter of life and death.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Technology will play a big role, but we also need to change how we produce, consume and dispose.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The government’s Green Plan articulates a compelling vision where taking care of the environment is no longer seen as at odds with economic growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many of these jobs will require a good foundation in Science, Technology and Engineering (STEM).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is already hurting us in the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us not miss the boat in the green economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Instead, let us identify the root causes, the key steps where Malays fall out – be it when they choose what to study in school, or when they choose their first job, and address those.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It means creating an environment that is attractive and conducive for Malay students to choose STEM courses and careers, for example, by ensuring that Malays are part of the faculty, providing better support systems and building confidence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have spoken to a Malay youth in Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Despite qualifying for Junior College, he decided to take the Polytechnic route.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I found out that he had shown promise in Science and Math, but ultimately chose to go into another field.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The reason was, the youth was uncomfortable, felt that he did not belong, there were few Malays.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He also believed that the STEM fields will be harder and yet the returns he might get or the levels he might get to will be commensurate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Malays in the workforce should have access to and take advantage of the training and reskilling required to support the transition to the new green economy and further their careers there, as part of a broad-based workforce transition or as part of a commitment to diversity and inclusion among our companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time our young Malays and their parents must be proactive to position themselves in the new green economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must hone their skills and learn, from Malays and non Malays, in the STEM fields.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: M3 must provide the platforms and the outreach.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must ensure that all in our community join in this climate change discussion – not just the fortunate few.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In English): We are all in this together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Green Plan outlines a whole-of-nation approach to climate change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is what it takes, the whole nation and our partners, to unite in this fight.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But good governance is only part of it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our success has been because our people trusted that we are doing our best to keep us safe during this crisis.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Devastating as the COVID-19 crisis has been, climate change is an even bigger crisis, with even higher stakes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope that, again, our people, our businesses, our partners will trust that we are doing our best, not only to keep us safe, but to keep the world safe; not only today but for future generations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that they will push together with us to lead the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we do this, Mr Speaker, I am sure Brian will feel proud that we are, indeed, doing our best.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am sure he will feel proud to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we have steadied the ship, this storm is far from over.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although the wind is still not behind our sails, we are making headway.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we face significant headwinds when, all around us, the pandemic is still raging.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Turbulent times still lay ahead on the horizon.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my maiden speech last year, I spoke about strengthening connections and the building blocks of our society in these uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I welcome this Budget which focuses on strengthening our people, our businesses and our reserves for the future as we emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I will be elaborating in the Committee of Supply debates but, for now, I will broadly outline three areas that we should strengthen: first, our relations with neighbouring countries; second, our social fabric as one united Singapore; and third, sustainability for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Council of Foreign Relations stated in April 2020: “Singapore, one of the world’s wealthiest and most trade-dependent countries, punches above its weight in regional and global affairs”.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This does not happen overnight or by chance, but by deliberate design, decisive actions and purposeful policies over the years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In times of crisis, however, some nations tend to look inwards, preferring protectionism over partnerships, sheer competition over collaborations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 has reinforced how important it is for Singapore to continue to play an active role internationally and deepen our interactions with key stakeholders and other countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think that maintaining and strengthening relations with our immediate neighbours will be more critical than ever to overcome the socio-economic impact of COVID-19, particularly in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This promotes not only more business travels and encourage more Singaporeans to take advantage of overseas opportunities, but it would also allow the flow of people and reconnection of families who have been kept apart in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, with Connect@Changi, quarantine-free business travel is made possible.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is hoped that aviation, tourism and retail businesses can benefit from it, thereby enabling gradual economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second part – strengthening our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have started living life more normally with less restrictions, at an earlier time compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And as we recover and adapt ourselves to a post-COVID-19 world, we have to engage and empower Singaporeans to play an even greater role in our Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should tap on our strengths as a multi-racial society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An SMU study had found that people living in more racially diverse neighbourhoods are more likely to lend a helping hand to others in need.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are some groups, however, that still require more targeted assistance than others.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, ex-offenders, upon prison release, face not only social stigma but real struggle to obtain and retain jobs in this already harsh economic climate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, our youths are now exposed to more radicalised views and deliberate efforts of disinformation around the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to actively engage them and have them invested in their stake here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And third, families, due to significant economic pressures, are more exposed to domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must do what we can to protect vulnerable groups, like children under the age of 12 or those with mental and physical disabilities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the greater resources for these vulnerable groups and those facing domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Rehabilitation and reintegration efforts for ex-offenders, especially those with drug offences, must be done in concert with their families and strategic social and business partners.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can also adopt technology to tackle recidivism.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, a US-based app called Pokket SM, facilitates information sharing and coordination among case workers, probation officers and ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through connecting justice agencies and human service providers, it encourages and sustains self-sufficiency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The third part of my speech is on sustainability for future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If COVID-19 is a crisis of a generation, then climate change is a crisis for all generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I applaud the Government’s Green Plan 2030, particularly on agri-food technology, green financing and electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that this will spur adoption of technology and make our food security more resilient.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, the plan to support green financing with up to $19 billion of public sector green projects is a good start.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The green bond market is a growing and innovative market, which has grown from US$1.5 billion in 2007 to surpassing US$100 billion in 2019.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green bonds attract a new base of investors and it can advance adoption of innovative new technologies and finance projects that provide green jobs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many thanks to Mayor Low Yen Ling for this.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green bonds in our region, also extend to non-conventional bonds, like Green Sukuk as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Other possible incentives can be to lower ERP rates for EVs and, with future technology, there can be a "progressive" road tax model that charges vehicles not only on time spent on the roads but also on actual carbon emission.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On adoption of EVs, I suggest the Public Service should lead the way by having more EVs and EV charging stations in its premises.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   This Budget aims to build on last year’s efforts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are not yet free from this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, without last year's budget and support schemes, our economic situation and employment rates this year would have been much worse, unlike the current situation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we are not only grateful for the effort, toil and sweat of our frontline workers, but we should also thank all segments of society who have come together to pool their energies and ideas with the Government, to face and combat this pandemic together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the focus areas of this Budget is to further strengthen the social compact of our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This cannot be achieved without the help of all communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here, I share a quatrain: This quatrain depicts a highly regarded Malay warrior who is seen as a beacon for those who are struggling to stay afloat or need support to survive.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, let us all help those in need to stay afloat and give them support.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in summary, we cannot let the difficulties faced by businesses to spiral downwards.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I am glad that there are targeted schemes to help them.
