text: Singaporeans can be assured that: they can always have a home to call their own; that they can expect their children are being well-nurtured in a world-class education system, which will prepare them well to take on good jobs and fulfil their potential; that we will provide assurance to our seniors over their retirement; and that the healthcare needs of their family will always be well taken care of.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, it is also natural for us to look out for "what is new" in every Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But it is important for all of us to appreciate what is already there, and to see the Budget in totality, over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Individual Budget measures are useful enhancements which sit on top of our already significant social spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the past decade, we have been gradually tilting the tax and transfer system in favour of lower and middle income groups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members of this House – Mr Darryl David and Mr Faisal Manap – have welcomed the salary increase for healthcare workers and have asked for salaries for other frontline workers and sectors to be enhanced.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I have said in the Budget Statement, there are good, meaningful jobs in healthcare for our locals, and it is important to pay them the salary that they deserve – commensurate with the work that they do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how we are able to attract and retain locals in the long-term, even as other markets compete for our Singaporean talents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out, Ms Hazel Poa’s conclusion that our workers are worse off due to lower wage share of GDP is wrong.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A capital-intensive economy open to investment and trade can have lower wage shares than labour-intensive economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, in the biomedical sector, the wage share of the sector’s output is less than 6% compared to over 60% in the accommodation and food services sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But workers in the biomedical sector earn more than twice that of the accommodation and food services sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, what will improve the lives of our workers are better wages and better prospects, not the aggregate share.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What matters more is that the wage growth of our workers is in line with productivity so that it is sustainable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members, including Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman, spoke about the need to continue boosting the incomes of lower wage workers, and the Progressive Wage Models.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Desmond Choo have also called for more help for our self-employed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have been studying for some time how best to boost protections and retirement adequacy for this group.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: MOM will continue working with the Labour Movement and our industry partners, through the tripartite mechanism, to uplift the incomes of all our lower wage workers and support those in the gig economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: MOM will share more on this at COS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Helping lower wage workers and self-employed persons is a work-in-progress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I hope that, if some of the new measures lead to a modest increase in costs, caring Singaporeans will agree that this is worth doing for solidarity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some members, like Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Yip Hon Weng, have highlighted another group of concern – our older workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng has shared, this is an example of a company which has fully utilised the reservoir of talent in its mature workforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To build on this momentum for all sectors, we are pushing ahead with our plans to raise the retirement and re-employment ages in 2022, with the Government and the Labour Movement taking the lead by effecting this in 2021.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: NUH is one of the organisations taking the initiative by redesigning jobs, offering flexible working arrangements and training opportunities for their senior workers in collaboration with the Healthcare Services Employees' Union.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Senior Staff Nurse Mdm Badthu Manne Doraisamy has been working with NUH for 31 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: She has benefited from NUH’s strong support for senior workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Agos Salim Sapuan is a security supervisor at NUH.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He shared how everything at his job is digitalised now, and he is no longer making manual entries in logbooks!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am sure he has benefited from NUH’s many training opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I hope that the Government’s Senior Worker Support Package will encourage more businesses to retain their mature workers and tap on their wealth of experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Mr Eric Chua have asked the Government to do more to encourage the hiring of persons with disabilities, or PwDs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Helping every Singaporean achieve their potential is a key priority for us in building an inclusive society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We agree that more can be done, and there are plans in the pipeline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The MSF will share more about this in the coming months.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Members have highlighted, there are specific groups of Singaporeans who have been deeply affected by COVID-19 and remain so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have seen this all over the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Dr Wan Rizal spoke on the issue of mental health.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Joan Pereira, on the support needed for care-givers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Rachel Ong and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin spoke on the employment and re-integration of ex-offenders and youth-at-risk, as well as Mr Don Wee on families with children with special needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Ms Carrie Tan spoke yesterday on how the CDCs are partnering Social Service Agencies, or SSAs, to multiply their reach for the vulnerable in the community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They have also asked to rally the community to help.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To support seniors with chronic disease management and to address issues of social isolation due to COVID-19, students from NUS and Yale University created a community space and monthly health subscription boxes to track seniors' health and keep them engaged.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For the pilot, the team received seed funding from MOH and sponsorship from the private sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the Government can only do so much alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Ms Carrie Tan said, we must look into the, I quote, "Sharing of Care".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will drive capability- and capacity-building efforts within the social services sector, to enhance SSAs' ability to serve the community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Like Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Derrick Goh have said, we must do more to "bridge the digital divide" and "grow our digital muscles", especially during COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We refreshed our plans to ensure that no one will be left behind in this digital age.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And who best to be our ambassadors of the digital world than our young people!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Under MCCY's and the National Youth Council's YouthTech Programme, youths will be deployed to businesses and organisations in diverse sectors, including the community and social sector organisations to support their digitalisation efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also need to boost the digital and technological transformation of the social sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Good ideas have come from the businesses who are partnering SSAs to do good and supplement the human touch with the human "click".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, Engineering Good, a non-profit organisation is working with community partners to provide digital access through refurbished laptops and Internet connectivity to low-income families, coupled with digital literacy and skills programmes as part of its Building Digitally Inclusive Communities project.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the spirit of Emerging Stronger Together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza said we need to embrace our multi-culturalism and diversity, and spoke about what it means to be a Singaporean, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And indeed, we are stronger together when we look after one another, and build a society that leaves no one behind.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the end of the day, our success is not measured in terms of GDP, but in the society and community we build together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides fostering a caring and inclusive community, we must ensure our clean living environment endures for future generations to enjoy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am glad that Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin, one of the youngest Members, if not the youngest Member of this House, also spoke in support of the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must not take our environment, whether green or blue, for granted – or for the matter, our reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What we have today is a testament to the foresight and hard work put in by many to distinguish Singapore as a City in Nature over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We made a big effort to improve our sanitation systems and clean up the Singapore River in the 1960s to 1980s.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We launched the Clean and Green Week in 1990 to encourage an environmentally conscious lifestyle.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To improve our air quality, we started encouraging the adoption of cleaner vehicle alternatives as far back as 2001.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Climate change and environmental sustainability did not become a priority overnight.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members like Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Dennis Tan have questioned why the Government is raising the petrol duty expecting many drivers can and will switch to Electric Vehicles, or EV, before the infrastructure is ready.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The petrol duty adjustments are to set price signals and change behaviour.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just like how we have made deliberate decisions to protect our environment, we want people to make conscious choices about how to drive, how much to drive, and whether to even drive at all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And EVs are not the only alternatives to driving.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Sharael Taha has reminded this House that hybrid vehicles are another alternative that are already widely available today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are also keeping public transport affordable and accessible through rail and bus subsidies and investing in public transport infrastructure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Dennis Tan asked if we are sufficiently prepared for an EV future, and on the cost-effectiveness of electric cars compared to petrol cars.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Ministry of Transport will elaborate on this at the Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There will never be a good time to raise petrol duty.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Members like Ms Mariam Jaafar and Mr Darryl David have pointed out that the petrol-duty increase would affect those who drive for work more, like our taxi and private hire car drivers, and delivery riders using motorcycles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I understand the pressure that they are facing, especially during this COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On top of the road tax rebates, more support will be provided to those who drive for work through additional Petrol Duty Rebates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taken together, the support will cover the increase in petrol duty for a year for motorcycles and taxis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taxi operators and Grab Rentals have agreed to pass on the road tax rebates to their drivers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Gojek will also be introducing additional incentive rebates for their drivers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With this, their drivers will receive rebates starting from next month.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Motorcycle owners will receive their additional Petrol Duty Rebates from May.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I hope these measures address Members like Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Ang Wei Neng's concerns over the impact on taxi and private hire car drivers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our broad-based rebates will not be able to cater to every unique circumstance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They may also not reach those in more informal work arrangements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are working with the Labour Movement to see how we can provide further help to self-employed delivery workers and limousine drivers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ultimately, protecting our environment must be our commitment to future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is just one of the many small but necessary steps in our whole-of-society, multi-generational effort to preserve our clean-living environment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Before I address individual issues, it is important that I reiterate this Government's fiscal principles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We abide by the same two core values of our forefathers: prudence and stewardship.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We spend on needs, not wants, and we seek to get the best value out of our spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must be prudent because these finite resources are entrusted to us by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the Unity Budget Round-Up in 2020, I said and I quote, "We have a duty not just to those who make their views known today, but also to the young and the future Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They are not here today to represent their views – because they are not born yet!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we have a responsibility to them, and we have to take decisions which are difficult for us, but which will safeguard their interests." In other words, we must be responsible stewards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During a time of high economic growth in the 1980s, our leaders managed our fiscal surpluses prudently.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead of finding ways to spend the surpluses and win popularity, they not only accumulated surpluses, but also took the bold step in 1991 to amend the Constitution, to require each term of Government to run a balanced budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is to ensure that future Governments do not make unrealistic promises, dip into our savings unnecessarily, and mortgage the future of our children.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They knew the temptation of squandering the easy inheritance would be too great for some to bear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore is in a new phase of development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We cannot expect the same kind of buoyant GDP growth as in the past, as our economy now matures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our expenditure needs will grow as new needs arise, and as our population ages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, we must continue to invest to build a better Singapore for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are once again confronted with hard choices.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must abide by our core values, and keep Singaporeans, now and generations to be born, at the heart of what we do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members spoke about building a fair and just society where no one is left behind.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is good, and I share this aspiration; but it is only one half of the conversation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Alex Yam, and Mr Lim Biow Chuan have reminded this House that just as importantly, we need to consider how to pay for these.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We do not have oil gushing out from our ground, and even Saudi Arabia, a country with huge oil reserves, is carefully planning ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It introduced a 5% value-added tax from 2018, which it increased to 15% from 1 July 2020.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members of this House must have the will and courage to make the same responsible choices as our forefathers did.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must be upfront – that if we want to spend more, we have to raise the revenue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, acknowledge that if we want more social safety nets, it comes with costs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Do not make irresponsible promises which burden future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If these are recurrent needs – which have to be financed year after year – we must find recurrent revenues – which we can collect year after year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Xie Yao Quan has rightly pointed out, we have already seen structural increases in our recurrent spending, especially in healthcare.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Seniors are four times as likely to be hospitalised compared to younger persons.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And each time our seniors are hospitalised, they stay for twice as long.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government heavily subsidises healthcare at our public healthcare institutions – up to 80%!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These structural trends are clear – we will have to spend more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, let me share some data and projections with this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This chart shows our spending, as a percentage of GDP, over the past 15 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How much is 1.5 percentage points of GDP?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is about two-thirds of the current GST revenue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Half of the increase in spending was for social support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We do not have a crystal ball but let us take a reasonable look at how our spending will change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our demographic trends will mean higher spending, outstripping GDP growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We estimate that healthcare spending will reach 3% of GDP by 2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If our healthcare spending grew like those of OECD countries with a similar demographic profile, it would be even higher, 3.5% of GDP by 2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This would be 50% more than in 2019.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, that is the chart that I just mentioned, over five-year periods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To see the impact of healthcare on Government spending, this chart made a simplifying assumption that non-healthcare spending will remain the same as a percentage of GDP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, we know this is a simplifying assumption and a very conservative one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, on security, threats have not diminished but are now coming in different forms – cybersecurity, hybrid, information wars, food security.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In Budget 2018, I mentioned that we could expect annual security spending by MINDEF and MHA to rise by 0.2 percentage points of GDP to meet rising threats.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, other social spending will continue to rise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are seeing higher spending on pre-school education and lifelong learning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, as I explained in my Budget Statements in this year and earlier, we will see a hump in infrastructural spending to enhance economic competitiveness, build our home, and improve connectivity across the island.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even with borrowing under the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act, or SINGA, we expect infrastructural spending to remain relatively stable as a percentage of GDP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked that we increase the scrutiny of expenditures, and to set up an independent parliamentary budget office to enhance such scrutiny.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am glad that Mr Singh agrees with the need to be prudent and accountable in our spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, it would be very helpful if each time Mr Singh or his colleagues ask the Government to spend more, to give us their estimates of how much it would cost and how they would fund it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as they call for more scrutiny on Government expenditure, we invite them to hold themselves to the same scrutiny.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I have outlined, prudence and stewardship are core values of this Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We hold ourselves to high standards and work hard to ensure that our spending is cost-effective, to deliver the best value for money for taxpayers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have achieved world-leading outcomes while running one of the leanest governments in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are always looking to achieve better outcomes with less, and we will say more about this during MOF’s COS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition to independent audits by the Auditor-General’s Office, we also have Parliamentary scrutiny of our spending through the Estimates and Public Accounts Committees.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, let us face the hard facts and be prepared to make difficult choices.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is meeting difficult trade-offs arising from our society’s growing spending needs, head on.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have shown that current taxes are insufficient to cover our spending needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since 2007, we have already increased various taxes to collect more from those with more means, which are then transferred to our lower income.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All this while, over the 14 years, the GST rate has remained unchanged at 7%.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We would be in a budget deficit if not for the contribution from reserves, in the form of Net Investment Returns Contribution or NIRC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Economic growth alone is not likely to raise enough revenues to meet our needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are not raising the GST rate now, as the economy is in the nascent stages of recovery.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we have been giving notice, since Budget 2018.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The fact is that some of the structural increase in expenditures will hit us sooner rather than later.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: MOH is already ramping up our public healthcare capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just two months ago, the Minister for Health announced that we will build a new integrated hospital in Bedok North by 2030, to serve the growing population in the east.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we defer this spending, we risk being unable to adequately care for our people when the need comes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some may ask if the projections are accurate, whether we really need to raise additional revenue within this timeline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We live in a complex world, filled with uncertainties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we must work with the information available.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, we could not have projected the biggest disruption of our generation, or that we would have to draw on our Past Reserves for two years in a row.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is a far cry from what Mr Pritam Singh said in February 2020, and I quote, "the current Government has had the privilege of far more budgetary elbow room, both political and fiscal, than any previous Government in Singapore's history." Unquote.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Unfortunately, instead of elbow room, COVID-19 has given governments around the world a very sharp elbow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ouch – it hurts, and will continue to hurt for some time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also do not know how Mr Leong Mun Wai could say with such confidence, and I quote, "for the foreseeable future, we do not see any shortage of fiscal revenues", unquote.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If Mr Leong could give me the basis of his projection, I will study it carefully.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But if it is his hunch, I hope that as a responsible Member of Parliament, he would agree that we cannot be advocating national policy on the basis of personal hunches.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: My caution to all is this: it will be foolhardy to underestimate the risks and uncertainties we are facing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us be honest, focus on the hard work that needs to be done and do not take the easy way out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That is the way to enable our people to make progress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members have expressed worries about the impact of the GST rate increase on Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I share your concern – as I said before, as Finance Minister, I do not have any joy in raising taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Assurance Package is on top of existing benefits and transfers such as the GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These keep our overall taxes and transfers system fair and progressive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we are concerned for the broad middle income.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members have asked that we consider other forms of taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I have said at my Round-up Speech at Budget 2018, we continually consider all options, so let me go through them again but it is a long list.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Members asked if we can do more on wealth taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Wealth taxes are not new in Singapore and we have in fact enhanced the progressivity of wealth-related taxes over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree there is scope to further review our wealth taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But first, let me address the elephant in the room.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Wealth taxes will not replace the need for the GST rate increase.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Already, the GST rate increase alone will not yield sufficient revenue to meet our growing healthcare and social spending needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I will share briefly our considerations for the suggestions raised.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har suggested a one-off wealth tax.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Argentina did this to fund higher spending for COVID-19 measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore entered COVID-19 with a strong fiscal position, and is fortunate to be able to tap on our Past Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The impact of the crisis has been uneven.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I believe Ms Foo’s intent is for those who came out on top of the crisis to do more for our community, and I share her sentiment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will indeed continue to review our wealth taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Leon Perera suggested raising Buyer’s Stamp Duty and Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty, or ABSD, for more expensive properties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, I am glad that he recognised that this move will not fully cover our higher resourcing needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The ABSD is a property market measure, not a revenue-raising one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We calibrate the ABSD carefully to maintain a stable and sustainable property market in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I agree that there is a role for property-related taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will continue to review this to ensure that it remains progressive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, we made property tax and stamp duty more progressive in Budget 2010, Budget 2013 and Budget 2018.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I trust that Mr Perera will give his strong support if and when we make such new moves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have also considered other options, including estate duty.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We abolished estate duty in 2008, because the middle and upper income groups were affected disproportionately compared to the wealthy, who were better able to avoid the estate duty through tax planning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We do tax wealth and we have been raising wealth taxes over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Rather, the practical question has always been how to design wealth taxes moves to ensure that they are effective.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, we must ensure that the tax cannot be easily avoided, especially by those with more means.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Otherwise, it will not achieve the social equity and fairness that we want.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, we must balance between progressivity and staying competitive to grow our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore must remain attractive to those who work hard and those who invest to create good jobs, because growing the economy is the most sustainable way to generate revenue and raise our standards of living.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, the move should add to our revenue resilience and adequacy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will continue to study wealth tax options and I look forward to your support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members have also said that we could rely on other sources of revenue, other than taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For instance, Mr Louis Chua cited the Government’s total estimated receipts and claimed that the Government has far more surpluses than we do for spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He must know that includes our capital receipts from land sales.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, he is really saying that we should spend our land sales proceeds directly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Louis Chua also cited the increase in NIRC in 2021 as one of the reasons we should not be, and I quote, "overzealous in strengthening our revenue position"; and Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested that we spend 100% of the NIRC instead of 50%.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First on using land sales proceeds directly in the Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We should treat our land as a scarce and finite asset.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Selling land does not give the Government more resources and should not directly support our expenditure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead, we sell the land that we need to sell for urban development and invest the proceeds.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This approach generates a sustainable stream of income over the long term, and has served us well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we had decided in the past to spend the proceeds from these land sales, we would not have built up our reserves today and would surely be worse off by now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Relying directly on land sales for fiscal revenue also has two risks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: You do not want Government revenues to fluctuate wildly with property cycles because it creates too much uncertainty for the Government to plan long term.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, even more serious, once a Government gets used to relying on land sales to fund spending, the Government has a vested interest to keep land prices high, or to sell more land.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can see the distortionary effects on the welfare of people, in places where local governments rely on land sales for revenue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The NIRC framework smooths the volatility arising from sharp fluctuations in the asset base due to market cycles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This avoids a boom-bust pattern in Government spending, driven by the volatilities of the market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: However, some variation is still to be expected for the NIRC as we update the net asset base and investment income figures over the course of the year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The global financial market remains volatile and uncertain.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How the post-COVID structural changes will affect long-term returns is still being played out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This did not happen by chance or merely because of good fortune.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is the result of years of fiscal discipline and prudence of our founding generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If they had succumbed to the temptation to spend more, we would not have built up our reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And without reserves, we would not have been able to generate this stable and recurrent source of revenue today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we adopt his suggestion, one day, even this mountain will be eaten up completely, like the saying in Chinese "坐吃山空".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Next, let me talk about the use of debt in our fiscal strategy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have expressed support for borrowing for long-term infrastructure, as part of our fiscal strategy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was happy to hear that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim was "happy as a clam" when he heard that our fiscal strategy reflected a number of elements that he had previously outlined.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I announced that we were studying borrowing in 2019, even before he entered Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I am glad he shares our views.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, perhaps if he reads more of our past Budget Statements, he would be even happier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Nevertheless, I must caution against the additional modifications that he has suggested to what is essentially a prudent and restrained use of borrowing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government's approach to borrowing is a carefully calibrated one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har said, there is good debt and there is bad debt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While we do borrow, the key difference is what we do with the debt proceeds.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is currently already borrowing, under the Government Securities Act and the Local Treasury Bills Act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But instead of spending the proceeds, we invest them for long-term returns, which is used to repay our debt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These investments will benefit and generate value over generations, but the upfront costs are hefty.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Borrowing is a fair and efficient approach to spread out the lumpy costs, to ensure that we better match the timing of the benefits with the timing of spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we do not, I will have to raise taxes significantly to fund these major expenditures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has asked if we can borrow more to fund "soft capital" like education.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have to refrain from the temptation to borrow for what are essentially recurrent expenditures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In many countries, there is a tendency to expand the scope of what constitutes "soft capital" beyond the original intentions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, the original intentions were good but it creeps.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, when used to fund increases to Government subsidies or social transfers, it is really more recurrent spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Borrowing continuously for them will just lead to ever higher debts which have to be repaid by future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When borrowing is not used productively, the result has often been high debt, low growth, rather than high growth, low debt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As debt level grows, interest payments can also increase, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim himself pointed out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This can lead to an unsustainable fiscal position and spiralling debt, affecting investor confidence, raising the costs of funding for businesses and ultimately, our long-term growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition, interest rates are low, in fact, ultra low for now, but this may change quickly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When it changes, existing debts would have to be refinanced and a higher rate could spiral the fiscal situation downward quickly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This usually happens in a crisis, when we can least afford it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Borrowing gives us cash for liquidity planning but it does not create free monies for spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today's debt is paid for by tomorrow's growth and tomorrow's generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I have explained earlier, our fiscal principle is that every Government must spend within its means and raise the revenue required to fund its initiatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members, such as Ms Foo Mee Har and Dr Lim Wee Kiak have noted, we must borrow prudently and sustainably.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will address Ms Foo's concern about rising interest rates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: More will be elaborated later when the Bill is presented in Parliament later this year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since the announcement of SINGA, credit rating agencies have also published articles affirming Singapore's strong credit standing, attributing it to Singapore's prudent and sustainable fiscal policy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked if we would consider one-off, special purpose borrowing for the economic investments under our emerging stronger strategies to help Singapore to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I have explained earlier, borrowing does not give us revenue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead, if the economic and fiscal outlook turn out worse than expected and we have to draw on Past Reserves for economic investments, borrowing would allow us to keep our reserves invested long term and earn good returns.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Borrowing from the market also means that we will have to have the discipline to repay amounts used for these economic investments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The key here is to use debt equitably and sustainably.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will borrow under the SINGA to spread out lumpy costs equitably across current and future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will study Mr Liang's suggestion of a one-off, special purpose borrowing to help us emerge stronger from this long drawn out crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Staying true to our core values of prudence and stewardship, we have built up significant reserves that are now our strategic assets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some commentators have questioned if we are dipping into the Past Reserves too readily.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And yet, there are others who downplay the use of reserves, saying that these are small amounts and we can afford to use more of our reserves by spending more through the NIRC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, they serve as an endowment fund, providing a key stream of revenue to supplement our annual Budget through the NIRC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, they provide a buffer against shocks and attacks on our financial system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, they serve as our bulwark against crises of an extraordinary nature.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Due to the strategic importance of our reserves, we have a two-key approach to managing and safeguarding reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Elected President serves as the custodian of our reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Constitution vests in the President discretionary powers to withhold her assent to budgets and expenditures proposed by the Government that may lead to a draw on Past Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On this note, I would like to address a question repeated by Ms Hazel Poa on whether the President knows the size of the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have just addressed this in June last year when I rounded up the debate for the Fortitude Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is public information that, under our Constitution, the President has access to information about the size of reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Under Article 22F of the Constitution, in the exercise of her functions under the Constitution, the President is entitled to any information regarding the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition, on the MOF website, it is already mentioned that the President has full information about the size of the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Hazel Poa also asked about the size of our reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Again, it is not in our national interest to disclose the size of the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat explained very well yesterday, Singapore is vulnerable to currency speculation and large capital outflows.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Revealing the size of the reserves is akin to laying bare our defence plan and will diminish the value of our reserves as a strategic defence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I was very alarmed when I heard Assoc Prof Jamus Lim citing theoretical literature that speculation could be stabilising.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I would also point out that there are other academics who recognise that currency markets can be marked by massive instability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is, in fact, well acknowledged by most economists today that market-driven short-term flows are and will continue to be fickle and extremely volatile.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The episode in 1992 when hedge fund manager George Soros took on the Bank of England by betting against the Sterling pound and dramatically destroyed the UK monetary system is one stark example.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To put it simply, foreign exchange speculations have been and will continue to be a threat to economies, especially small, open ones like ours.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As an international financial centre, portfolio and banking-related flows in Singapore amounted to S$294 billion last year, or 63% of our GDP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just last year, we saw extreme capital flow volatility in global financial markets due to the uncertainties and risk sentiments associated with the pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: MAS kept the Singapore dollar nominal exchange rate stable during this period backed by the full power of our reserves, giving banks and businesses certainty to make decisions under very trying circumstances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I personally saw this during the Asian Financial Crisis, when I was Principal Private Secretary (PPS) to Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee was invited by several countries in the region to share his views, as Singapore was relatively unscathed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It was very painful to see how speculation and the currency volatilities that these countries face was destroying businesses, big and small, and the lives of men and women in these places.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The exchange rate is far more important for a small open economy like ours compared to our neighbouring countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And if our neighbouring countries are so badly affected during the Asian Financial Crisis, you can imagine the impact on us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore is unique in operating in an exchange-rate centred monetary policy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: My team and I had to not just be alert to the domino effect of the failures of banks globally, but also the flights of capital and the risks of speculation on the Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we had been attacked, the businesses in Singapore, big or small, and the lives of our workers, would have been severely disrupted.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, as a Board member of MAS, I want to ensure that MAS is able to continue effectively using Singapore's exchange rate to deliver price stability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A very volatile Singapore dollar exchange rate, subject to market fads and bubbles, would not ensure low and stable prices for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In normal times, our nation’s reserves also underpin our triple A sovereign credit rating, thus underpinning confidence in our unique exchange rate monetary policy system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, as a practitioner at the frontline, who tries my best to understand the intricacies of the system, I must caution Assoc Prof Jamus Lim – let us not play with fire.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is about the lives of our people, not theoretical musings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I urge all Members of this House to focus the debate on the merits of the policies and programmes and how we can improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead of repeatedly focusing their attention on the size of reserves or other erroneous claims.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have inherited a strategic asset for the long-term survival and success of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the global outlook is highly uncertain, and we need to think ahead of how we can respond.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Prof Hoon Hian Teck articulated well the difficult balance Singapore needs to strike: stabilising the economy to avoid a sharp downturn, but also undertaking and investing in structural policies for transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The uncertainty over how quickly the global economy will recover makes this balancing act even more complicated.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we face a prolonged slump, it will be even more necessary for us to transform, but it will also be more challenging to find the required fiscal resources to both stabilise and restructure the economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taking the longer-term view, we have to press on with these economic investments, secure the next decade of growth and emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we hold back these investments, we will miss the opportunity to restructure, seize new opportunities and race ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we fail to change and our economic recovery is sluggish, it would have a long tail effect on our jobs and economic vibrancy, and affect Singaporeans adversely.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The President has expressed her understanding towards the Government’s approach and will consider the Government’s specific proposals, should there be a need to draw on Past Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But if we are to draw on Past Reserves for the economic investments to emerge stronger, we should do our best to make good on the draw.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These investments are expected to yield returns for the economy, which can give a boost to our tight fiscal situation and allow us to make good the amount drawn.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It will be a challenge to also make good this amount drawn given the magnitude of the crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the "crisis fund" function of the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Nonetheless, we should strive to remain fiscally prudent to build back our reserves gradually.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The fiscal situation ahead will be very challenging but I believe that Members agree on several issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is scope to do more to take better care of Singaporeans, especially the more vulnerable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With that, we will need to find the resources to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We need to consider all available options to raise revenues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to review additional options to complement a GST rate increase, but it is not realistic to hope for these to become alternatives to a GST rate increase, or to make the GST rate increase unnecessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each of the decisions we make or do not make today to tackle the challenges will determine the starting point we give our future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must have the courage to confront the hard issues now and not take the easy way out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are stewards and must keep faith with our future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are able to enjoy many opportunities and work towards our aspirations, because our pioneers were also good stewards with courage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have strong governance and trusted institutions today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have built a strong global Singapore brand.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We contribute to the world in our own way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: COVID-19 has taught the world that trust is a valuable currency, and there is a high premium for long-term planning, and reliability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, we plan long term and act in the best interest of Singapore and our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao rightly pointed out that we now have the luxury of choices in dealing with resource constraints, precisely because of the foresight of the generations before us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We do not shy away from difficult conversations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We explain the difficult decisions, as the well-being of Singaporeans are at the heart of what we do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, we honour our commitments and hold ourselves to high standards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Where we fall short, we learn and strive to do better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singaporeans know that they can trust us to lead the country.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We trust one another and advance as Singapore Together, as one united people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is crucial to our success, because Singapore is a small island nation in a big turbulent world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to work hard to deliver results to Singaporeans, and strengthen and grow our valuable reserve of trust and unity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The vaccine has brought hope for countries around the world in triumphing over the pandemic .

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the tremendous impact of the pandemic has also accelerated the structural changes which were already taking place.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: COVID-19 is a grave test for many countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also build trust and strengthen cooperation with other countries to overcome our common challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Drawing on Past Reserves is a difficult decision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When considering whether or not to draw on the Past Reserves, the Government has always adhered to the principle of fiscal prudence and long-term planning, as practiced by our forefathers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is to ensure the sustainability of our fiscal policy, that we act as stewards to safeguard the interests of future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today happens to be 元宵节 or the Lantern Festival.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The significance of the Lantern Festival lies in family reunion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When all of us are united as a nation , we have strength.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the past one year, Singaporeans have shown a spirit of solidarity and fortitude.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the new year, I hope that Singaporeans will uphold this spirit and work together to build a prosperous home with strong social cohesion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The future will change rapidly but I firmly believe that as long as we work together, we will be able to overcome the challenges ahead and emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In English): COVID-19 has tested the strength, unity and resolve of countries – socially, economically, and fiscally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our society came together as One Team Singapore to battle this invisible but deadly enemy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We looked out for one another, and we stood united.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We protected the livelihoods of Singaporeans amidst the immediate economic fallout.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, our economy is gradually, but steadily, recovering.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have been careful and prudent in the use of our reserves to protect the lives and livelihoods of our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we confront these unknowns together with confidence, knowing that we have built a deep reservoir of trust to meet the challenges head on.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have a narrow window of opportunity to transform our economy and forge ahead as One Team Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Whether we continue to do well cannot be left to chance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have laid out our strategy to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is committed to put in the investments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To succeed, every Singaporean must come together to build the Singapore that we want.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Businesses should continually innovate and support their workers through opportunities for training, growth and progression.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Workers should seize the opportunities to up-skill and re-skill.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And within our communities, I urge all Singaporeans to lend a hand to those who need more help.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But if we put our hearts, minds, hands together, I am confident that Singapore will continue to prosper and be a place we are proud to call home.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That is why I have given the name "Emerging Stronger Together" to this year’s Budget Statement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is as much about "Stronger Together" as it is about "Emerging Stronger".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We all need to each play our part.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have a clear view of where we are headed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Government, businesses, and the community must come together to overcome our shared challenges; and Singaporeans must care and look out for one another along the way; so that Singapore will emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I start, can I ask Deputy Prime Minister Heng where did he get the figure of $20 million for a Parliament Budget Office from?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Singh, I got it from your Member who mentioned it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that the information was shared with the Ministry in bullet points for my cut which has not been delivered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Committee of Supply debates have not begun.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe the MOF officials have asked Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Jamus Lim to deliver points for and it should not really be part of this debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But having said that, that was with regard to, I believe, a fiscal office and the cut has not been delivered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is a fairly new institution and, really, it is not to help the Opposition in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is to help all Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is constant with the separation of power schema.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I was a Member of the Estimates Committee some years ago, and I will never forget – and those Members of Parliament who were Members of the Estimates Committee will also remember – a senior civil servant said, "I cannot be smarter than my boss".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And so, a Parliament Budget Office or officer is there to provide independent analysis to confirm the nature of the Budget, to confirm that programmes are delivering the outcomes that are desired.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As was quite eloquently put by the Member for Aljunied, Mr Leon Perera, who said it is not just about getting an "A" for effort, it is about scoring and "A" for outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And to that end, as I acknowledged in my speech, and Deputy Prime Minister Heng also shared in his Round-up speech, the Budget is not about a one-year programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And in my speech, I asked Deputy Prime Minister Heng – for which I do not believe a clarification was forthcoming – about the headline $24 billion figure which is a multi-year initiative, questions about the accountability of this figure, how are we going to look back at this figure and say that money has been spent prudently?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point is with regard to the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
