text: I believe I had some questions about it and fundamentally again, the Minister committed until 2024, I believe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I had some questions about how many Singaporeans were trained?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And my query also sought information on how much money was spent on this initiative and whether these outcomes are outcomes that the Government is satisfied with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My third point is a carryover from the Unity Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister made the point about a remark I had made, elbow room, more fiscal elbow room than any other government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: More revenues, certainly, more expenditure, but certainly more revenues as well for the Government to spend and to consider how to lay out its plans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, there is nothing factually inaccurate about that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I would come to the point of the Driver Support Programme or the various programmes that the Government has laid out for private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the Unity Budget, I spoke about another community of individuals – private hire bus drivers – and many of them support the tourism sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think in this Budget with the JSS being extended to severely-hit sectors like aviation, I am sure the workers in that industry, the companies in that industry, appreciate the support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But this group of private hire bus drivers; there was support rendered in the subsequent Budgets from the Unity Budget.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I did not mean to go before the Deputy Prime Minister's response, but I just wanted to ask or seek a clarification from the Leader of the Opposition, because this may be helpful for either the Deputy Prime Minister's reply or perhaps for later.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When he refers to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and I think it was quite clear in his original speech and just now, that he indicated that the purpose of this Office is to assess outcomes of Government expenditure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Can I just clarify if that is the purpose?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Question number two, is this the same as the Independent Fiscal Council that the other Member of the Workers' Party, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, has filed a cut on?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Parliament Budget Office that I had shared in my speech in this debate about, actually mirrors the Canadian model, the Canadian Parliament Budget Office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Or under the Parliament of Canada Act, I believe it is called Parliament Budget Officer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the second question is then answered: no, it is not the same proposal that has not been delivered by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there are actually then two proposals: one, for a Parliamentary Budget Office, and the other for an Independent Fiscal Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think IMF refers to all these different agencies within Parliament as Fiscal Councils, but perhaps we should wait for Member Jamus Lim to deliver his cut.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Leader of the Opposition is well also the leader of the Workers' Party, so I assume he knows what he is talking about, and I assume he knows what his Member is going to to ask about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I am not asking in advance what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is going to say.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That, of course, he will do in the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I am just asking and I am sure the Leader of the Opposition must know this: is the office that he is asking to be set up the same thing as what his colleague is going to ask for, or are they both asking for two separate things?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But before I answer his specific questions, let me repeat what I said right at the beginning of this debate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said over the last few days, passionate debate went along a few threads.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members elevated the debate to help Singaporeans appreciate the changing landscape and the need to change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members highlighted importance of our reserves – the bold and decisive response mounted and what it achieved.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Unfortunately, some argue selectively without acknowledging the broader context, broader impact of COVID-19 and the outcomes of the Government's decisive interventions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, Mr Singh said earlier that we should set up such an office because it is important to examine outcomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He had an encounter with a Ministry of Finance official who say that, "I am not smarter than my boss".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Does the Workers' Party have any comment on that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because I sat through the debate, I read your transcripts, but no one no, one mentioned about outcome, no one raised a question about, "Could this have been done better, could that have been done better".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, what is the purpose of setting up an office when, with information that is publicly available is there for you to ask?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You have the Ministry of Finance, you have Political Office Holders who drive the agenda of that Ministry and you have a parliamentary platform where the proposed Parliament Budget Officer will sit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Those who are approving the Budget ought to have access to an independent analysis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is what the Parliament Budget Officer will give.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Singh himself, admitted that he has different names, different nomenclature.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I do want to prolong this debate but we have the Committee of Supply coming up on the Ministry of Finance and we can debate that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me just ask for the Workers' Party to be clear about what is it that you are proposing; and second, I am asking you a very simple question.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Have you or any of your Workers' Party Members scrutinised that interim report and have questions for us?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But instead, in talking about outcome, what you have asked us just now, you raised the issue about, what about the Capability Transfer Programme which MOM is going to do in 2024?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is going to be debated at the Committee of Supply for MOM.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, you asked what about the private hire car drivers and so on, and would it be extended?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This Budget debate is a serious debate about whether our broad direction is correct.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Do you have suggestions on how we can do it better?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I have to say, unfortunately, so far, I have heard none.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure another Member has capacity than to ask me about a matter I have not spoken about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, just as a point of order, I think we should make that clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I mean, the Standing Orders exist for a reason, I suppose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And insofar as the Minister's answers on Capability Transfer Programme, other issues being dealt with in the Committee of Supply, I can accept those answers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I can ask my questions during the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that the land sales revenue would form a key part of it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: So, in the spirit of accountability, just so all of us can better understand, where did the balance of $14 billion of cash surplus come from?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: And I understand the need for us to be prudent about the use of land sales and this is something which I understand, but I think it is not one where we are calling for the use of land sales revenue in its entirety.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: It is one whereby, if you look at the incentives to using land sales revenue, they already exist today, but probably in a different extent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: And I think it is also important, I guess, for me to share that — Sorry, so, what I mean is that the incentives for using land sales as a means to increase revenue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: I think that is something that is already done indirectly and so that is already in place although to a different extent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: But I think the broader point that I also would like to share, is in the context of Singapore, when it comes to land sales, it is something which I believe is a recurring source of revenue for the Government as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: The second is, there has been a lot of talk about our reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: Just now Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that is about 20 years of surplus.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: Yesterday, a different Member shared that we have blown about 10 years' worth of savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: And I think earlier today, a separate Member also asked how long do we need before we can replenish our reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: So, probably it will be helpful for Members of this House to understand, after accounting for the additional $11 billion of the draw at the end of FY2021, where would our reserves be?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: I mean, we do not need to know an absolute number, but where would our reserves be compared to 10 years ago, five years ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Aljunied)
text: That also helps us to understand the context, but without knowing the absolute amount of the reserves itself.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the second point about land sales, and that there is an incentive for the Government to use land sales because the revenues are already done indirectly, that is wrong.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said very clearly that when we do land sales, it is to meet the needs for our people, for our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You cannot plan land sales on the basis that we need the revenue, and therefore, I would have to do that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I totally reject your allegation that the Government has an incentive to sell more land in order to generate revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If the Government had an incentive, I would not have pointed out the problems in many countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have studied this in many countries where unfortunately, where the government, especially the local government, is so reliant on land sales that they have a vested interest to keep land prices high because they need the revenue, and, in turn, that creates a lot of hardship for the people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: URA has long-term plans – 50-year plans, 20-year plans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The land use planning has been a great strength of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think you should seriously look at what the agencies have been doing and do not make allegations like these.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because I think it will demoralise the many good officers that we have in our planning departments, in URA and the Ministry of National Development, who have over the years, allowed for so much development in so compact a land.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And by the way, one of the areas that I am hoping that we can do more in our research plan, is precisely on urban solutions and sustainability, something which Senior Minister Teo started when he was the Chairman of the National Research Foundation (NRF) and which we are continuing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because that is a constraint for Singapore and if we can overcome this constraint, we can do better.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not for us to sell land in order to do that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I would like you to take back your allegations that the Government has an incentive to sell land for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I would just like to share that I did not make the allegation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Basically, what I was trying to get at is that if you look at the context of Singapore, the land sales revenue, I think that is a recurrent source of revenue for the Government over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I am actually not belittling the work of our MND and the good officers of the URA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think that is something that they have done well in terms of the concept plan and the master plan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: What we are looking at is in terms of the level of cash surplus that the Government is generating, understanding where this comes from.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Because on the technical point as well, if the NIRC is something that is to be used, then that should not actually form part of the cash surplus if it has already been used.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Chua made the points in a very indirect way, to say that, "Well, the Government is doing it indirectly." I am glad that you are taking it back to say that you are not making that statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me repeat that the Government has no incentive to sell land for the purpose of generating revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves Protection Framework has safeguarded all the assets that we have.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You are just converting one asset to another form of asset and these are guarded.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a point of clarification for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier, in his wrap-up, the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned the point that I made about nurses and healthcare workers and how I was very supportive of the decision to enhance their salaries and to review their salaries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also made another point beyond that, which was to say that, I believe, it is not just about salaries; there are other factors that perhaps we could look at in terms of enhancing careers, mid-career conversions, perhaps in improving the work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I even suggested a bit of a radical idea, like paid holidays or mandatory leave that nurses and healthcare workers need to take to encourage them to step back from the frontline.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister did not quite address this in his speech and I wanted to ask if it is something that the Government can actually consider beyond the salaries and the financial aspects of a nursing career.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I myself am a big beneficiary of the care of our nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I believe that, not only myself but also the Workers' Party, agree with the principles of prudence and stewardship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And we also agree that we, of course, do not have oil gushing out of our ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, that said, I think we can potentially have ideas gushing out of our heads and that is precisely why I made the suggestion about soft infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I wonder why Minister Heng remains dismissive of soft capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key I think is ultimately that we invest what we end up borrowing and while I agree that we should not allow recurrent expenditures to be lumped into soft capital, it is easy to allow recurrent expenditures of all forms, like various HQ functions in hard capital projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key is that we always evaluate what how we define a given project as soft or hard capital; and its ultimate investment and repayment potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, I should also clarify another point on the exchange rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, the first one I was hoping for clarification on why he remained dismissive of soft capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am not suggesting a revision in our exchange rate regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am questioning whether there is a need to keep reserve information secret and whether that actually helps, or hinders, our effort to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What I heard Deputy Prime Minister Heng share was a lot of reasons why the exchange-rate-targeting regime is warranted for our country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I did not hear strong reasons why secrecy over our reserves actually helps in that case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Markets, I think, we both acknowledge, can be volatile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I think they tend toward the truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And indeed, speculation, as I conceded, can in fact be destabilising if our exchange rate is disconnected from the fundamentals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, it leaves me to wonder is if Minister Heng is suggesting that with our current situation, such secrecy can actually help us to maintain what is an otherwise untenable rate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because I know that the Ministry has routinely denied that we manipulate our exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the Member can keep the clarification short, please.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And the Ministry has routinely denied that we manipulate our exchange rate, only that we seek stability.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You said that I was dismissive of soft capital.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said that we have to be careful.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said, I sound a word of caution about soft capital.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Precisely because it is soft, it can morph into various shapes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I had mentioned how many good schemes started with very good intentions, with very good people, but precisely because it is soft, the shape changes, and over time, everything becomes capital investment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, I think there is a role for building all this soft capital.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you want to talk about whether my notion of partnership, working together, is soft capital, well, you can say that and say: should we invest a lot of money in that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been very careful to say how we can build our society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, if you want to use academic terminologies like these, there is a lot of soft capital in our neighbourhood because people are supporting one another, and we did see soft capital coming up.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have to be very careful with recurrent spending and the outcome focus, which was a point that Mr Pritam Singh mentioned right at the outset.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me share my experience as Education Minister.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said in my speech, and in fact, I have shown this slide many times.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Perhaps I should show it again and again until the message gets through.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have shown it many times how Singapore has been ranked so well in the international ranking of students.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have also shared that in 2018, when the IMF/World Bank meeting was held in Bali, President Jim Yong Kim of the World Bank invited the Prime Minister to talk about the Human Capital Index.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And when I was walking with President Jim Yong Kim to the venue site, I asked him: "Personally, I am not terribly comfortable talking about Singapore being ranked well because it is not our approach to talk about our ranking.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having been Education Minister for five years and visiting so many of our schools, I am convinced that our schools and our teachers have put in the greatest amount of effort, and the fact that we have parents who are so supportive of our kids' education is what allowed our students to do so well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You can have a number and say, "I would like to know whether it is 5% or 10% of GDP" and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have also said in this Budget debate and even in the previous round, about our healthcare outcome.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is the same – it is not what you spend; it is how you spend it and the dedication of the staff.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am extremely grateful to our frontline officers, to our teachers and our educators in their various roles in our schools, and which is why, as Education Minister, I talked about every school being a good school, because I am deeply convinced that that is the case.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not something that a Budget and a theoretical number can give you the result.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, President Jim Yong Kim told me, "I hope that Singapore is open to sharing this so that others can learn because there are countries who will need to raise this, and they are very concerned that they will not have the resources to educate their people better".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As an economics professor, I think he will fully understand that, that long-term sustainability for economic competitiveness must come from productivity growth and labour force growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And so we have to rely on productivity growth –which is why in the next phase of our transformation, we need to focus on technology and innovation-driven growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we do not manipulate our exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What is our exchange rate policy centred on?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not different from other central banks, which is maintain medium term price stability, so that economic agents, economic players can make decisions on the basis that these are the relative prices that they can make decisions on, that you do not have runaway inflations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even then, I will say that, right now, because of COVID-19, there is, again, new thinking about whether this inflation targeting is the right approach, and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But as far as Singapore is concerned, we have been maintaining price stability and that has allowed our economy to have the macro economic framework to stay competitive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, the question about our exchange rate regime, I am glad that the Member is not saying that we should reveal our exchange rate regime, that is good.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As to your question about why the secrecy, I do not wish to hold up this whole forum.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I devoted more than two pages of my reply to you on that, about the size of currency trading, about my experience in MAS during the Global Financial Crisis, about my experience when I was accompanying Mr Lee Kuan Yew to the countries which were so badly hit by the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, please, have a care that policy-making cannot be theoretical musings.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because I know he is very gung-ho on borrowing; he is entitled to his views.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I just want to add, in life, when you want to borrow, it does not automatically mean people want to lend to you.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because when the Government of the Republic of Singapore goes out to borrow, there is a premium.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The cost of debt is significantly lower than others.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I want to share a story with the House.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I had a conversation with our retired Member of Parliament Mr Chandra Das not too long ago.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not think he will mind me mentioning his name.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Das worked with Dr Goh Keng Swee in the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, I asked Mr Das, "During your time, did you go out to borrow?" And he said "Once"; only once but for a different reason.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And that was because Dr Goh saw a project, he was not entirely convinced that it was feasible and he gave instructions to the staff, "Go out to an external third party financial institution and get a second opinion and see whether they lend us".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, that is how careful we have been.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Okay, and that is why when we issue debt, the international financial world is willing to take it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are several reasons and the Member touched on two of them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, therefore, how do we spread out the borrowing?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, do we build or do we not build?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just because we do not have the resources to build it now, do we forego it?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must build it only if it gives you economic or social return.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The projects that we did for our MRT lines, for our airport, give us both the economic and social returns, and therefore we can justify why we are doing it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But at the same time, I mentioned that, in the coming years of, first of all, even if our fiscal situation was good, it may not even be enough for us to fund that lumpy investment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, lumpy investments need to be spread out over time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, the next question is how do I fund it?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One is, could you go and use the past reserve for that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not because the reserves are used for extraordinary and temporary situation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Well, I mentioned before that there are several reasons.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One, that it is fair for inter-generational equity, because you spread out the cost of borrowing, because various generations are going to benefit from that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, at this point, it is efficient because interest rates are very low and ultra-low.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And to your observation as to whether, therefore, we should not touch our reserves and liquidate our assets to borrow, you are a good investor.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Time is also not unlimited, so I will not borrow anymore time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Otherwise, we will not finish on time next week.
